Their anytime algorithm gives a real guarantee at every step, without the restart trick older methods used. Time varying Lyapunov functions, which track how badly limits are being broken, are the core device. The authors prove regret and total violation both grow only like the square root of time. Results also extend to targets that move over time.
arxiv-2510-22779:
A weak line quasar showed extreme X-ray swings in recent years. Its X-ray flux rose over twenty fold, then fell sharply. Ayushi Chhipa leads a team with eight co-authors. In 2025 they report radio follow up work. They used GMRT and VLA radio telescopes.

The source stays compact in radio views. Its spectrum slopes down with frequency. Radio flux shows no clear change over time. That holds despite the huge X-ray swings. So radio and X-ray output seem unlinked here. The pattern fits a thick disk plus outflow model. Survey sensitivity limits how firm the claim can be.
arxiv-2510-22979:
Rikiya Okazaki and Shantanu Desai test a proposed link between the energy and peak brightness of gamma-ray bursts. Using that link for cosmology faces a circle: distances are needed to prove the link, yet the link is used to get distances. The pair break the circle with distances from HII galaxies, which glow from young hot stars.

They use a neural network to fill in distances for 186 such galaxies and check two burst data sets below a redshift of about two point six. Best fits agreed within error, but spread was large at about twenty eight and thirty five percent. That spread, they argue, is too wide for precise cosmology.
arxiv-2510-23079:
Joel Honkamaa and Pekka Marttinen describe their entry to the LUMIR brain registration challenge, which tests whether image alignment holds up on new scan types. Deep registration methods often fail when contrast or modality differs from training data. The challenge for Learn2Reg 2025 grades methods on exactly those unseen kinds of brain scans.

Their fix is simple: convert images into MIND feature space before feeding them to the model. That change greatly improved robustness across contrasts. A special ensembling step added a small but steady gain. The entry shows a plain preprocessing idea can beat complex tweaks for medical image alignment.
arxiv-2510-23179:
Luigi Gisolfi leads a team of thirty two contributors presenting Tudat, an open-source toolbox for orbit estimation from TU Delft. The software began for simulating orbital dynamics and state estimation, combining optical and radiometric tracking from many sources. Recent work adds real tracking data analysis for planetary missions and space situational awareness.

Tudat now processes deep-space Doppler and range data among other types. High-fidelity estimation helps track natural and artificial bodies with care. As open source for research and education, the toolbox lets smaller teams do precise orbit work that once needed closed, costly systems.
arxiv-2510-23379:
Ashwin Srinivasan and five co-authors investigate Symbolic Neural Generators, hybrid models that pair symbolic learning with neural generation for drug lead discovery. A symbolic learner extracts logical specs of feasible data from a small set of instances, sometimes just one. Each spec constrains the input fed to a neural generator, which rejects any output that breaks the spec.

That design enforces formal correctness criteria on generated molecules. The hybrid exploits the complementary strengths of logic and neural nets. In drug design, generators that respect hard rules from the start could cut wasted synthesis of invalid candidates.
arxiv-2510-23479:
Xin Jin, Siyuan Li, Siyong Jian, Kai Yu, and Huan Wang propose MergeMix, a unified augmentation paradigm for visual and multimodal understanding. Post-training of multimodal language models relies on supervised fine-tuning, which is stable but needs human labels and generalizes weakly, or reinforcement learning, which learns from rewards but is costly and unstable.

MergeMix aims to balance scalability, efficiency, and alignment generalization between those poles. Better augmentation at the post-training stage could improve how vision-language models follow instructions across tasks. The authors present the paradigm as a middle path for aligning large multimodal systems.
arxiv-2510-23579:
Diego García, Sergio Arias, and Rosa López study a tiny quantum heat engine built as a ring that electrons travel around. In such Aharonov-Bohm rings, electron waves interfere depending on the magnetic flux through the ring's center. Earlier studies of these engines ignored spin effects, even though spin can change how heat and charge flow.

The authors add Rashba spin-orbit interaction, a coupling between an electron's motion and its spin, to the ring model. They find that this coupling raises the engine's figure of merit, the standard score for how well a device turns heat into useful work. The boost comes from steering spin-dependent interference inside the ring. Their results suggest that designing around spin effects could help make more efficient thermoelectric devices at the nanoscale.
arxiv-2510-23679:
Simone Colli and two co-authors present PanDelos-plus, a faster rebuild of a tool that finds matching gene families across many bacterial genomes. Finding families is a core task in pangenome work, but the standard method compares everything against everything, which grows brutal as genome sets swell. PanDelos skipped alignments and tuning knobs, comparing short k-mer profiles instead, and stayed fast and accurate.

The new version is built around genes and runs in parallel. Its heaviest steps are split across a pool of threads: finding each gene's best hit, then the pairs that hit each other back. Leaner data structures cut memory use. On tests, PanDelos-plus ran up to fourteen times faster and used up to ninety-six percent less memory, with accuracy intact. The authors argue that population-scale comparisons now fit on a normal multicore workstation, putting pangenome studies within everyday reach.
arxiv-2510-23779:
Jon Kristian Dahl and three co-authors trace the microscopic origin of the low-energy enhancement, an uptick in gamma-ray emission strength seen at low energies in the nucleus vanadium-50. The effect has puzzled nuclear physicists because standard models underproduce it. The team attacks it with shell-model calculations that treat electric and magnetic dipole transitions inside one framework.

Their valence space spans three major shells, handled with a modern interaction and the KSHELL code. The calculation juggles millions of basis states and produces nearly two million transitions. It reproduces the fourteen lowest known levels closely and matches the measured level density and gamma strength shape across the full energy range, enhancement included. The analysis shows the uptick is entirely magnetic in origin. Spin and orbital parts of the magnetic operator must both act and reinforce each other. One proton transition between f7/2 states drives the effect.
arxiv-2510-24079:
Ameir Shaa and five co-authors develop a fast method to predict wind flow in cities for use in urgent events. Knowing how particles spread in an emergency needs quick, accurate wind maps. Full fluid simulations are too slow to update in real time as weather shifts.

Their hybrid method blends tensor methods with neural networks to fill in wind fields between known cases. It breaks large fields for speed, pressure, and turbulence into parts, fills gaps over wind angle and space, then uses a network to fix errors. The result is a stand-in model that can refresh city wind maps on the time scale of weather changes.
arxiv-2510-24179:
Iván Martínez-Murillo and two co-authors study how outside knowledge affects the clarity and quality of text that a language model generates. They focus on a commonsense generation task, where a model must write a sensible sentence using a given set of concepts. The team built a new benchmark called KITGI from the CommonGen dataset.

KITGI pairs each concept set with semantic relations drawn from ConceptNet and includes hand checked outputs. Using a T5-Large model, they compare generation with full knowledge against generation where the most relevant relations were removed on purpose. Judges then rated the outputs for commonsense sense and concept coverage, showing how much the key knowledge matters.
arxiv-2510-24779:
Daiki Tanabe, Yuki Inoue, Vivek Kumar, Miftahul Ma'arif, and Ta-Chun Yu show how a planned cold gravity wave scope can mute noise from its own laser. The scope, CHRONOS, uses twist bars as test weights and a speed based read that keeps some quantum noise down. It aims to catch waves from mid size black hole pairs far off.

Laser light swings can push the bars by torque, a key noise source at low wave rates. The team shows the bar setup cancels that net push, and that a balanced read helps too. They give the first full math model of this noise for such a scope. That clears one path to the set goal sense level.
arxiv-2510-24879:
Lucas Z Brito, Ryan P Cabeen, and David H Laidlaw ask if broad traits of gray matter in the brain can foretell how well a person thinks. Diffusion scans have told much about white matter, the brain's long links, but gray matter has had less work. They use a scan form that maps fiber slant and density in each zone.

With scan and act data from a large young adult study, they boil zone reads down to a few broad traits. One trait, tied to the share of free water in the tissue, tracked read and word scores and fluid thought well. It held much of the spread between folks. The find backs broad gray traits as real signs.
arxiv-2510-25179:
Juan Ren, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem guard sight and word models from jail breaks with a team of agent guards. Past guards sit as a fixed skin on inputs or outputs and give a lone safe or not safe call. Their frame, Agentic Moderation, sets four named agents to work as one team.

Shield, Responder, Evaluator, and Reflector each play a set role in the guard loop. That team work makes the guard more sense of each case and more clear to read. On five sets and four large models, attack win rates fell by a clear share. Deny rates rose, while plain task keep held near still.
arxiv-2510-25379:
Adrien Weihs leads three co-authors on operator learning. Jingmin Sun, Zecheng Zhang, and Hayden Schaeffer join him. Their 2025 paper learns mappings between function spaces. Many machine learning problems use finite-dimensional mappings instead. They study learning collections of operators jointly. Both theory and test-based advances are given.

Two regimes are distinguished in their approach. One network handles operators parameterized by functions. Learning several distinct operators is the second regime. Each operator there is learned independently. For the multiple case, they present two architectures. They establish universal approximation results in three settings. Explicit scaling laws quantify needed network size. For several operators, hardness balancing guides subnetwork design. Their work unifies scalable neural operator learning foundations.
arxiv-2510-25579:
Vaibhav Tiwari infers binary black hole populations from gravitational waves. His 2025 paper analyzes one hundred fifty signals. The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaborations reported those signals recently. They appear in the fourth gravitational wave catalog. Population properties may reflect formation channel astrophysics. Most properties remain poorly constrained, he notes.

He uses the mixture-model framework called Vamana. One-dimensional mass and spin distributions are presented. Their correlations and redshift evolution are explored. A notable peak appears near ten solar masses. Chirp mass shows a peak near eight solar masses. Primary and secondary masses correlate in a unique way. Pronounced chirp peaks appear around fourteen and twenty-seven. Three peaks are roughly separated by factor two. A hierarchical merger scenario could explain peak placement. First peak arises from stellar origin mergers. Higher peaks arise from repeated mergers of lower ones. Most binaries lack expected high spins, though.
arxiv-2510-25679:
Federica Tonti and Ricardo Vinuesa navigate drones in urban flows. Their 2025 paper uses deep reinforcement learning for navigation. Urban flow is 3D and highly turbulent. Recirculation zones complicate flight through city canyons.

They develop an optimal navigation strategy using learning. A high-fidelity run represents the urban environment. Their method is flow-aware proximal policy tuning. A gated transformer architecture gives richer flow information. Results compare against several rival navigation methods. A memory-based variant and classic Zermelo method competed. Their flow-aware method increased success rate greatly. Crash rates fell compared with all rivals tested. Turbulence awareness helps drones exploit or avoid flows. Completely reimagined drone landscapes may follow from this. Urban delivery routes could become safer and quick.
arxiv-2510-25779:
Gagan Bansal led twenty-three co-authors on agentic marketplaces. Wenyue Hua, Zezhou Huang, and Adam Fourney helped. Amanda Swearngin, Will Epperson, and Tyler Payne joined. Their 2025 paper studies language agents mediating economic decisions.

Such uses promise benefits but raise accountability questions. Realistic market settings are needed to understand actions. Previous research tested agents in constrained settings. Single-task markets and pairs of agents dominated. Real markets require diverse economic activities coordination. Large dynamic ecosystems have multiple opaque agents. Open-ended dialogues occur between those agents. They develop Magentic-Marketplace, a simulated two-sided environment. Service agents represent competing businesses there. Key changes include utility, biases, and manipulation vulnerability. Search mechanisms shape market outcomes strongly. Frontier models method optimal welfare under ideal search. Results degrades sharply with scale.
arxiv-2510-26079:
Daniele Celoria, working alone, writes a short note linking two special functions from physics and pure mathematics. One side is the tetrahedral index, a building block of a three dimensional index introduced by Dimofte, Gaiotto, and Gukov for counting states in physical theories tied to geometric topology. The other side is the Hahn Exton q-Bessel function, a q analogue of the classic Bessel function, where q deforms the usual calculus.

Celoria spells out the correspondence between the two functions, which lets useful relations be translated from one setting to the other. The note also introduces the q-hypergeometric community to techniques, theory, and conjectures that arose from physical mathematics applied to geometric topology, with the aim of sparking new work on both sides.
arxiv-2510-26179:
Haruki Hoshino, Jungjin Park, Osamu Kaneko, and Kiminao Kogiso make a data driven control tuning method private by running it under encryption. Edge computing offloads heavy control calculations for cyber physical systems, such as robots and plants, to nearby servers, but attacks on those servers are a growing risk. Their target is FRIT, a fictitious reference iterative tuning method that tunes controller gains from data.

The key trick is to replace a matrix inversion step, which encryption handles poorly, with a vector summation form that homomorphic encryption can process. Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data without seeing it. Numerical examples under one hundred twenty eight bit security matched conventional performance, and the authors give guidance on choosing between encryption schemes for secure control.
arxiv-2510-26279:
Fuying Li, Yajun Wang, Zhuxian Lian, and Wen Chen design an efficient algorithm to maximize data rate in a wireless system aided by an intelligent reflecting surface. Such a surface is a panel of many elements that can shift the phase of reflected signals, reshaping the radio environment. In a MIMO system, with multiple antennas at both ends. The best transmit precoding and the best surface phases must be chosen jointly. That joint choice is a non convex problem that is hard to solve directly.

Their ADMM-APG method combines the alternating direction method of multipliers, which splits a hard problem into pieces, with an accelerated projected gradient method. Each subproblem has a closed form solution and low cost. Simulations show consistent gains in spectral efficiency and compute cost over benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-26379:
Shaojun Wu, Shan Jin, Abolfazl Bayat, and Xiaoting Wang work on a weak point of quantum algorithms. Variational quantum algorithms tune a quantum circuit to solve a task, but deep circuits pick up noise and stall, while shallow ones stay trainable yet weak. The team asks whether a better starting state can widen what a fixed circuit can reach.

Wu and his three co-authors build the starting state as a mix of simpler states, using a linear combination method. They prove this step always adds reach, for any circuit shape. Tests on three standard models, for Ising spins and for electrons in a lattice, gave more exact ground states for the same gate count. The idea pairs with circuit design rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2510-26479:
Emanuele Palumbo, with six co-authors, presents JCO, a software framework for designing superconducting circuits. These circuits use Josephson junctions, tiny weak links that make them strongly nonlinear, which is prized for quantum devices. Simulating them in time is slow, so JCO works in the frequency domain with harmonic balance, a method that assumes steady tones.

Palumbo and the team build JCO on a Julia library for such circuits, using a lumped-element view that treats each part as a single block. Bayesian optimization, guided by Gaussian processes and a device-specific score, searches for the best working point on its own. As a showcase, they tune a travelling-wave amplifier built from SNAIL elements, which boosts weak quantum signals near the noise limit. The framework suits circuits with many linked design choices.
arxiv-2510-26579:
Nathanael Nussbaumer, Markus Böck, and Jürgen Cito build a tool to debug Bayesian inference. Probabilistic programming lets users write Bayesian models as programs and automate the maths of inference. In practice, finding and fixing faults in that inference is slow and demands deep knowledge.

Nussbaumer and his two co-authors set out what a debugging framework for this task must do, then build a tool that meets those needs inside the development environment. Their approach is online and interactive, so users can probe a running inference rather than restart it blindly. In a study with eighteen experienced users, the tool cut both the time and the difficulty of debugging tasks by clear margins. The authors present it as a way to open Bayesian methods to more practitioners.
arxiv-2510-27079:
Jeffrey Kuan, Krutika Tawri, and Konstantina Trivisa study the long-run behavior of a noisy gas flow model. The system is the isentropic compressible Euler equations, which govern a compressible gas, with linear damping and white-in-time noise, meaning random kicks with no memory, on a one-dimensional ring. The question is whether the flow settles into a statistically stationary state whose statistics stop changing.

The authors prove such a state exists within a class of weak entropy solutions for every allowed gas constant above one. Their proof builds a multi-level approximation with a truncation and a small artificial viscosity, constructs an invariant measure there, then passes both parameters to their limits. New uniform entropy bounds make the limit work, advancing understanding of stochastic gas dynamics.
arxiv-2511-00679:
Alessandro De Gregorio and Roberto Garra find chance-based forms for solutions of abstract telegraph-type equations. These are written with operators, not coordinates, and they capture odd effects that depend on the past. One target is a time-fractional form of the telegraph equation, built on the Caputo derivative. The study limits itself to positive self-adjoint operators, so spectral theory can be used.

For the telegraph-diffusion case they give exact formulas and a stochastic solution, for a range of the fractional parameter. This extends older results, with the fractional Laplace and Bessel-Riesz cases worked out. A second target, the Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation, has a singular time coefficient. Its stochastic solution is tied to the abstract wave case, and also to the Erdelyi-Kober fractional integral.
arxiv-2511-00779:
Erfan Khordad, Peter Smith, and their co-authors study how tightly coupled antenna arrays can spot targets from echo signals. Such arrays place their elements close together, so the elements affect each other strongly. The team asks whether the wide range of frequencies these arrays can use helps detection.

Their setup assumes a sensing receiver that gathers time and frequency samples of echoes whose form is not known in advance. They handle echoes that stay steady, drift slowly, or change fast across frequency. A new detector is offered for the slow case, and likelihood based detectors cover the other cases. Tests show the new detector is more robust, and coupled arrays beat weakly coupled ones.
arxiv-2511-00879:
Hyeon Hwang and colleagues build an evaluation suite for checking whether a language model's step by step reasoning is truly grounded in knowledge. Models now reason in chains, but a fluent chain can still rest on missing or misused facts.

The suite has three parts: a large collection of atomic knowledge items that reasoning depends on, metrics that score how well a model recalls and applies that knowledge mid chain. A small evaluator model trained to compute those scores cheaply and reliably. The suite proves good at spotting missing or misapplied knowledge, exposing basic reasoning flaws. The authors also show the metrics can feed preference optimization, turning the evaluation into a training signal.
arxiv-2511-01279:
Sonali Gupta, Amit Kumar, Vikas Bhat, and Sushil Mujumdar locate single photon emitters more sharply than normal microscopy allows. Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond are prized quantum light sources, but a confocal microscope cannot resolve how many emitters sit inside one focal spot, and scanning by brightness is slow.

Their technique raster scans a map of photon antibunching, the telling signature that light comes from single emitters, across the field of view. An inversion algorithm then reconstructs how many emitters occupy each spot, on a grid finer than the spot itself, beating the diffraction limit. Simulations confirm robust reconstruction of nitrogen vacancy layouts. The authors offer the method as a fast check for fabricating nanophotonic devices.
arxiv-2511-01379:
Kun Hu and colleagues build a localization system for robots deep in coal mines, where GPS does not reach and the tunnels defeat ordinary mapping. Long, feature poor corridors starve LiDAR of landmarks, and uneven, slippery floors corrupt wheel odometry, so no single sensor can hold a position estimate.

Their framework fuses four sources: LiDAR, an inertial unit, ultra wideband radio positioning, and wheel odometry, all inside an iterated error state Kalman filter. Ultra wideband anchors the estimate globally where its range reaches; beyond it, tight wheel coupling with nonholonomic constraints and lever arm compensation takes over. An adaptive mechanism switches motion modes with the degradation level. Real underground experiments beat state of the art methods on accuracy and robustness, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2511-01579:
Diganta Das, Mihika Sanghi, and Sourav study a faint signal from the young universe. When the inflaton field decayed after inflation, some decays also shed a graviton. Those gravitons would form a background of gravitational waves that still fills space today.

The authors work out this emission for decays into pairs of heavy spin-3/2 particles. They take the inflaton's potential near its low point to act like a power of the field. Then they run the reheating stage on a computer and find the wave spectrum that results. The shape of that spectrum, they show, carries marks of the small-scale physics of inflation. A future catch of such waves could test ideas no telescope can reach.
arxiv-2511-01679:
A. N. Zhukov and dozens of collaborators report the first corona observations from ASPIICS, the coronagraph aboard the European Proba-3 mission. Proba-3 flies two spacecraft in precise formation about 144 meters apart. One carries the telescope. The other carries the disk that blocks the Sun's glare. Together they create artificial eclipse conditions for up to five and a half hours at a stretch.

The instrument watches structures such as coronal loops, streamers, and quiet prominences, plus eruptions, jets, and coronal mass ejections, getting as close to the solar limb as about 1.05 solar radii with very low stray light. Notably, it resolved weak but widespread small-scale outflows and inflows between 1.3 and 3 solar radii for the first time, extending the scales at which the slow solar wind is seen forming.
arxiv-2511-01879:
HM Shadman Tabib and six colleagues take epilepsy care where clinical brain-wave gear cannot go. Multi-channel EEG is scarce in many regions. So the team collected NEUROSKY-EPI. It is the first open dataset of single-channel, consumer-grade EEG for epilepsy. The recordings come from a South Asian clinic, with rich notes on each patient.

To show the data's worth, they built EmbedCluster. The pipeline borrows features from EEGNet models trained on clinical data. It adds features from a contextual autoencoder. Then it groups patients by their EEG patterns, with no labels. Even cheap one-channel signals sorted patients in meaningful ways. The authors stress human concerns too: use in poor settings, clarity for non-specialists, and guards for privacy and bias. The dataset and code are open.
arxiv-2511-01979:
Dorian Demars and sixteen colleagues watch a young giant planet eat. Delorme 1 (AB)b is a companion of about thirteen Jupiter masses, 30 to 45 million years old, still accreting from its surroundings. How accretion works at planetary masses, through magnetic funnels or shocks, is poorly constrained, yet it shapes planet formation and the disks around young planets.

With the UVES spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope, the team collected 31 epochs of high-resolution optical spectra spanning hours to years. Balmer hydrogen lines from H-alpha to H10 and an ultraviolet continuum excess both signal ongoing accretion, and everything varies. The lines split into two steady components that change only in brightness. The broader one tracks the ultraviolet excess. It matches magnetospheric funnel models, and dominates shape changes. The narrower one fits shock emission. It drives most flux variability. That variability stays low over hours, but reaches about 100 percent over weeks.
arxiv-2511-03379:
Samarth Toolhally, Joeri Roelofs, Siep Weiland, and Amritam Das build a digital twin for the drying unit inside drop-on-demand inkjet printers. Paper moisture makes or breaks print quality, and hot air in the fixation unit sets that moisture. Their twin tracks the drying process across space and time from only a few sensors.

Sections of the unit become nodes in a graph model, each with its own heat and flow behavior. Evaporation enters as a nonlinear edge effect tied into the nodes in a standard control form. Framed with an integral equation method, the twin supports stability checks, simulation, and robust design in one pass. Printers could use such a twin to watch drying live and correct drift before quality slips.
arxiv-2511-03479:
Mukesh Kumar, Pramod Sharma, Karabo Mosala, and Bruce Mellado map how future electron-positron colliders could confirm a hinted new particle near ninety-five gigaelectronvolts. Older and current collider data show faint excesses in several channels at that mass. The team studies making the particle alongside a Z boson, with clean muon and bottom-quark signatures.

A recoil-mass method plus deep neural sorting separates signal from background sharply. Under a modest mixing with the known Higgs boson, the signal would cross the discovery threshold at planned machine energies with a stated data volume. A confirmed light scalar would rewrite the Higgs sector, so a clear search plan matters well before those colliders run.
arxiv-2511-04179:
Oshando Johnson, Alexandra Fomina, Ranjith Krishnamurthy, Vaibhav Chaudhari, Rohith Kumar Shanmuganathan, and Eric Bodden present SAFE, an editor plugin. It uses a large language model to explain software vulnerabilities flagged by static analysis tools. Scanner warnings are notoriously generic, so developers misunderstand or overlook serious findings.

For each detection, the plugin explains causes, impacts, and mitigation strategies in readable terms. An expert user study found the explanations significantly helped beginner to intermediate developers understand and address vulnerabilities. Better explanation, the work suggests, can rescue value already present in scanners: the detection was there, but only a clear account turns a warning into a fix.
arxiv-2511-04279:
Xinyi Zhao, Pengjie Zhang, and Fuyu Dong use the decay rate of the cosmological gravitational potential to test gravity on cosmic scales. That decay is sensitive to gravity yet largely immune to astrophysical mess, offering a clean way to separate dark energy from modified gravity as the driver of cosmic acceleration.

A recent measurement across a wide redshift range, built from survey galaxies and microwave background maps, is applied to four one-parameter extensions of the standard cosmology. The growth index estimate sits close to the general relativity prediction within its uncertainty. Three effective-gravity parameters likewise land near their standard values. No deviation from Einstein gravity is required by this probe.
arxiv-2511-04479:
Surapon Nonesung leads eight authors presenting ThaiOCRBench, a benchmark for Thai text in images. Most tests for vision-language models favor rich-resource languages and plain text reading. Thai, with its own script and document layouts, has been left largely unmeasured.

The set holds two thousand eight hundred eight human-annotated samples across thirteen task types. The team tests leading commercial and open models without any task training. Commercial systems, led by Gemini 2.5 Pro, clearly beat open ones. Fine-grained text reading and handwriting remain hard spots, which gives Thai language technology a clear map of what to improve next.
arxiv-2511-04679:
Qingzhou Lu leads six authors with GentleHumanoid, a framework for compliant humanoid robots. Robots working near people must yield safely on contact, not just track motions rigidly. Most reinforcement learning policies push back against outside forces instead.

A unified spring-based model captures both resistive and guiding contacts in their design. Pressing a surface gives a restoring force, while pushes and pulls come from human motion data. Impedance control is woven into a whole-body tracking policy for the upper body. The result aims at robots that handle hugs, handovers, and bumps with natural softness.
arxiv-2511-05079:
Grigory Kovalev and co-authors add new Russian search test sets to the RusBEIR benchmark, built from the Did You Know part of Russian Wikipedia. The sets cover fact checks, search for use by chat models, and full-document search.

Facts and their linked articles are marked at sentence level with graded relevance, which gives a firm ground truth. The authors spell out how the sets were built so the resource can grow. Their tests compare a classic word-based search method with new neural designs, and place the sets in the wider RusBEIR suite.
arxiv-2511-05179:
Ragini Gupta and co-authors compare graph neural networks with foundation models for forecasting across space and time, using sensor data from the Internet of Things. Such data drive forecasts for the environment, but how often and where sensors sample shapes the scores.

The study varies sampling rate and spatial cover to see how each model family trades them off. More sensors can clean noise by adding context, yet they cost more to run. The results guide builders who must pick a model and a sensor plan together, not one at a time.
arxiv-2511-05379:
Eric Godden and co-authors present ETHOS, a robotic haptic display that lets a virtual reality user feel real touch in social acts like handovers, fist bumps, and high-fives. Static props cannot arrive on cue, so most VR touch stays out of sync with what is seen.

ETHOS uses a torque-controlled arm with swap-in props, such as silicone hands and a baton. A marker board aligns the real and virtual scenes, and a safety monitor gates motion by head and hand pose. Two control modes cover held contact and on-demand meetings.
arxiv-2511-05779:
Ahmed Saad Al-Karsani and Maryam Khanbaghi design a way for a network of microgrids to restart and resync itself after a blackout, with no central controller. Clean energy growth and inverter-based resources are creating such networks. In island mode they must black-start, synchronize, and regulate voltage and frequency on their own, jobs where instability can creep in.

Their scheme uses a distributed averaging control method at the secondary level, plus distributed logic for operating breakers. They modeled a modified standard 123-bus test system as seven linked microgrids and simulated it in detail. The results showed a smooth autonomous soft start, synchronization, connection, and steady regulation. The authors present it as a step toward self-restoring local grids.
arxiv-2511-05979:
Koushik Ray offers a simpler route to writing the conformal bootstrap equation in Mellin space. The bootstrap is a core method of conformal field theory, tying a theory's data together through consistency conditions. Its Mellin transform form is powerful but often messy to handle.

Ray relates conformal blocks to a system of equations due to Gelfand and Graev, built from conformal integrals. Those integrals, in turn, are generalized hypergeometric functions, a well-understood family. The resulting expression for the Mellin-space bootstrap is compact. He demonstrates its usefulness by deriving bounds on the spectrum of fields a theory may contain. The note is short and technical, aimed at theorists who compute bootstrap bounds.
arxiv-2511-06079:
Andrei Zlotchevski and Linan Chen study the Schrödinger bridge problem for a class of random processes not covered before. The bridge problem asks for the most likely path law that starts and ends with two given distributions while staying close to a reference process. Here the reference is a jump diffusion whose behavior also switches between regimes.

Regime switching means the process changes character as hidden environmental states come and go. The authors prove the bridge solution is itself the law of a regime-switching jump diffusion. They establish its properties through both stochastic calculus and analytic arguments, then apply the theory to an unbalanced bridge problem and gain new results there as well.
arxiv-2511-06179:
Joel Ward proposes MemoriesDB, a database design meant to hold long-term memory for computer agents. Each stored memory records when an event happened, what it means, and how it links to other events. The design aims to stop memory from drifting apart across time, meaning, and relation.

Built first on PostgreSQL with vector extensions, the system joins time-series storage, vector search, and graph links in one append-only schema. Memories sit as vertices stamped to the microsecond, with links that carry their own labels and notes. A working prototype shows fast recall and steady context using ordinary database tools.
arxiv-2511-06479:
Muhammad Shahnawaz and Adeel Safder pair Bayesian learning with inventory optimization to harden car supply chains. British automotive plants lean on just-in-time manufacturing, which cracks under supply disruptions and jumpy demand. Earlier work praised blending artificial intelligence with classic optimization in words, but a formal quantitative test was missing.

Their stochastic framework runs a two-level inventory system under random demand and supply failures. A static policy faces an adaptive one where Bayesian updates refresh the parameters feeding the optimizer. Across a simulated year, the adaptive policy cut costs in calm conditions and during disruptions, yet its cautious updating lagged when demand suddenly shocked, marking a clear boundary for the approach.
arxiv-2511-06779:
Anand Bhojan reflects on a teaching framework that joins design thinking, hands-on learning, and structured reflection for creative computing courses. The Holistic Cognitive Development approach follows a constructivist pedagogy built on autonomy, ownership, and scaffolding. Students in game design, virtual reality, and extended reality classes cycle through thinking, creating, criticizing, and reflecting on their own work.

AI tools now carry parts of that cycle at scale, through systems offering personalized feedback and knowledge-graph-enhanced comments from language models. Reported findings show deeper thought, better feedback quality, and learners left more in charge. Bhojan advocates supportive freedom in supervision: self-directed inquiry by students, steadied by guided reflection and feedback.
arxiv-2511-07079:
Masaki Gen and seven co-authors squeeze a magnetic crystal to see how its exotic magnetic patterns respond. EuAl4 is a square-lattice itinerant magnet where spin, lattice, and charge couple strongly, producing varied helimagnetic phases including rhombic and square skyrmion lattices. Combining resistivity and magnetization readings with neutron scattering, the team applied uniaxial compressive stress along one crystal direction.

Stresses of only several tens of megapascals strengthened the antiferromagnetic character and shortened the magnetic modulation period in the lowest-temperature spiral state, pushing the transition temperatures and fields of several phases upward. First-principles work shows the stress distorts the lattice and deforms the Fermi surface behind the magnetism. That response is strong evidence that Fermi-surface nesting is key to stabilizing the helical modulations.
arxiv-2511-07179:
J T Lunardi, S Salamanca, J Negro, and L M Nieto solve the planar Dirac equation for an electron confined by the most general contact potential supported on a circle. Contact forces, concentrated on the circumference, are singular, and radial symmetry reduces the problem to one radial dimension. The authors treat the singularity rigorously with a distributional method first developed for point contacts in one dimension, giving the coupling parameters a physical meaning.

The general coupling is described by four physical parameters: the strengths of a scalar term and the three parts of a singular Lorentz vector potential on the ring. For several parameter choices they compute bound and scattering solutions and analyze trapping, asking when the ring traps the particle. The work supplies a complete catalog of radial contact interactions for relativistic planar systems, each read in physical terms.
arxiv-2511-07279:
Yuvraj Singh, Chandan K Choudhury, and Rakesh S Singh model how salt changes the forces between polymer-coated silica nanoparticles in water. Such solvent-driven interactions decide how nanoparticles self-assemble into soft substances, yet no general system for tuning them exists. Using all-atom molecular dynamics, the team compares bare silica grains with grains grafted with polyethylene or polyethylene glycol across salt concentrations and thermodynamic conditions.

Bare grains barely reacted to salt, even at high concentration. Polyethylene-grafted particles developed strong salt-induced attractions, while the glycol-grafted ones changed only slowly, and these effects stayed largely unchanged across the heat and pressure ranges tried. Close analysis shows salt drains solvent from the gap between particles for both coatings, most strongly for the hydrophobic one, explaining the attraction and pointing to steady control of assembly.
arxiv-2511-07379:
Himanshu Pal and co-authors study how easily temporal graph neural networks can be fooled. Such networks track links that change over time and support finance, recommendations, and fraud detection. The team asks whether an attacker with few resources can quietly damage their accuracy.

Their method, called LoReTTA, works in two steps. First it removes edges that matter most, judged by sixteen ways of scoring importance over time. Then it adds misleading edges chosen to keep degree patterns hard to notice. Tests on four datasets and four leading models show average performance drops near thirty percent, without costly stand-in models.
arxiv-2511-07679:
Kohei Yamamoto, Hannah Tomio, and Charlotte Zehnder refine how space antennas cancel laser noise. Missions like LISA compare laser phases across vast arms, then use time-delay interferometry in processing to erase laser and clock noise. Adding an optical frequency comb can drop the onboard modulators and suppress jitter at once.

An alternative interferometry scheme built for comb systems is explored here. The goal is simpler hardware with noise removal intact across the observation band. Gravitational wave astronomy from space needs phase measurements of extreme purity. Cleaner metrology designs raise the chance that faint ripples from merging black holes survive processing.
arxiv-2511-07879:
Neelesh Kumar Shukla and Pranay Sanghvi forecast protests and rallies from tomorrow news written today. In democracies, unrest events are often announced early to draw crowds, and those announcements sit inside ordinary news articles. Officials who spot them in time can prepare rather than react.

Topic modeling and word embeddings first filter articles likely to mention planned gatherings. Named entity extraction then pulls out the who, where, and when behind each event. The pipeline turns scattered reporting into advance warning. Forecasting from public announcements respects that organizers want publicity; the system simply reads at a scale no office can match manually.
arxiv-2511-07979:
Wenhan Yu and colleagues introduce MSLR, a Chinese data set for multi-step legal reasoning by large language models. Earlier legal tests often mixed simple recall with real inference and broke reasoning into fragments. MSLR instead follows real judicial decisions and uses the Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion framework from legal practice.

A human and model pipeline together produced fine grained, step level annotations for the cases. Tests of several models show only moderate scores, so hard legal reasoning remains difficult. Prompts that let models start their own chain of thought improved coherence and beat prompts designed by humans.
arxiv-2511-08279:
Alan Magdaleno, Pietro Bonazzi, Tommaso Polonelli, and Michele Magno field test camera free eye tracking on smart glasses using electric charge change sensing. The method reads eye moves without skin contact pads, promising low power, low key gaze input. Earlier results came from managed labs, leaving open how the system copes with daily noise and differences between users.

Twenty nine users produced one hundred recordings in everyday settings such as working at a laptop. Classification accuracy ranged widely by user, averaging about seventy five percent, and nearby electronics degraded results notably. Contactless tracking still works under realistic settings, but user variability and interference must shape future wearable gaze designs.
arxiv-2511-08379:
Giorgio Piras and co-authors argue that refusal conduct in safety aligned language models lives along several axes in signals space, not just one. Earlier interpretability work packed refusal into a single axis, computed as the gap between average harmful and harmless prompt pictures. Evidence that concepts occupy low dimensional manifolds inside the model motivates a richer extraction method based on self organizing maps.

The team first proves self organizing maps generalize the older difference in means technique. Training maps on harmful prompt pictures yields multiple refusal axes after subtracting the harmless centroid. Ablating that whole set suppresses refusal more effectively than the single axis baseline and even specialized jailbreak algorithms.
arxiv-2511-08579:
Belinda Li and four co-authors ask whether a language model can faithfully describe its own inner workings. They fine-tune models to explain three things: what information single features encode, how activations cause later ones, and how much each input token sways the output.

Ground truth for training comes from existing interpretability tools, and only tens of thousands of example explanations are needed. The trained explainers generalize to new questions rather than memorizing answers. A model explaining itself also beats a different model explaining it, even when the outside model is much stronger. The authors suggest self-explanation could grow into a scalable partner for current interpretability methods.
arxiv-2511-08679:
Lorenzo Calibbi and two co-authors revisit a tidy idea about neutrino masses: in the minimal type II seesaw, perhaps two entries of the neutrino mass matrix are exactly zero. Such two-zero textures are restrictive, so each surviving pattern makes sharp predictions that experiments can test.

The sharpest tests come from charged lepton flavor violation, processes the Standard Model forbids but this framework can produce at visible rates. Using current oscillation data, the authors map the correlations each allowed texture predicts among these rare decays. Some patterns suppress muon-to-electron transitions yet leave a tau decay within reach of future experiments like Belle II. Running effects from high scales are included, and collider searches for doubly charged scalars add a complementary handle.
arxiv-2511-09279:
Tong Li, Kai Ma, and Man Yuan propose a search for light dark particles. It would smash intense laser pulses into muon or proton beams. The collision can produce dark photons or axion-like particles through nonlinear Compton scattering. Accelerator facilities already provide the high-quality beams such a search needs.

The authors compute the scattering cross sections for producing each candidate particle. They also analyze background processes where neutrinos carry away missing energy, which can mimic the signal. Their sensitivity estimates suggest the laser-based setup could compete with, and complement, existing searches. It suits invisible particles lighter than about one megaelectronvolt. That extends the hunt for dark-sector particles into a new experimental setting.
arxiv-2511-09579:
Junfeng Xu, Nabadwip Sarkar, and Sujoy Majumder study when a certain nonlinear partial differential equation in two complex variables has entire solutions. Entire solutions are defined on the whole complex plane. The equation mixes powers of the function's partial derivative and of the function itself. The right-hand side is a sum of exponentials of two arbitrary polynomials.

The authors attack existence using Nevanlinna's value distribution theory for meromorphic functions of several variables. That theory tracks how often a function takes values, giving tools to rule solutions in or out. The exponent in the equation is an integer of at least three, and the constants involved are all nonzero. Results of this kind delimit which exponential forcing terms an entire solution can possibly accommodate.
arxiv-2511-09979:
Saumya Shah, Zi-Yu Khoo, Abel Yang, and Stéphane Bressan use the AI Feynman symbolic regression method. With it they rediscover the lunar equation of the centre, a classic formula describing the Moon's uneven angular motion. Symbolic regression searches for formulas that fit data, and this physics-inspired variant adds structure to the search. The team fed it lunar position data drawn from ephemerides, along with deliberate physical biases.

With expert-chosen coordinates and a restricted search space, the method recovered the first-order analytic form of the equation. The authors stress that the manual setup is also the weakness: success leaned on human coordinate selection. They therefore propose an automated preprocessing step that finds the canonical coordinate system on its own, and discuss the wider challenge of embedding domain knowledge into symbolic regression.
arxiv-2511-10279:
Yanbei Jiang, Chao Lei, Yihao Ding, Krista Ehinger, and Jey Han Lau present PROPA, a training framework that grades vision-language models on their intermediate reasoning steps, not just final answers. In visual reasoning, early mistakes cascade, yet supervised training needs costly step annotations and outcome-only reinforcement gives sparse feedback. PROPA uses Monte Carlo tree search together with a group-relative reinforcement method to manufacture dense process-level rewards without human labels.

Training interleaves reinforcement updates with supervised fine-tuning on both successful and failed trajectories, curing the cold-start problem. A process reward model trained alongside then guides search at inference time. Across seven benchmarks and four model backbones, PROPA beat supervised and outcome-reward baselines, gaining up to about seventeen points in-domain and twenty-one out-of-domain.
arxiv-2511-10379:
Benjamin J. Chang and four co-authors study bandwidth, a measure of how fast a vibrating structure loses energy. Engineers use bandwidth in damping estimates, but the usual form assumes a single mode, light damping, and linear behavior. The paper extends a generalized root mean square bandwidth to larger systems with several degrees of freedom.

Their analytical version expresses the measure through a system's modal parameters and how energy is first spread among modes. They also give a data-only method for estimating that starting energy spread. Tests run from simple oscillators to a real experimental model aircraft, and the measure reliably captures how well each structure dissipates energy over time.
arxiv-2511-10879:
Dennis Wei and eight co-authors release ICX360, an open-source Python toolkit for explaining what language models produce, with the emphasis on the context users feed them. As these models move into higher-stakes work, from meeting summaries to medical questions, understanding which parts of a prompt drove an answer becomes a practical necessity.

The toolkit implements three recent explanation tools covering both black-box methods, which probe the model by perturbing inputs, and white-box methods, which use gradients. It ships with quick-start guidance and detailed tutorials spanning retrieval-augmented generation, natural language generation, and jailbreaking investigations. The authors position prompt-focused explanation as the natural counterpart for language models of the explanation toolkits built for earlier predictive systems.
arxiv-2511-10979:
Bowen Sun, Yujun Cai, and their colleagues present PAS, a fix for a timing flaw in models that watch video and answer in words. Small shifts in when frames are taken can flip which frames the model attends to, so answers become unstable. The team traces the flaw to how time codes ripple across nearby frames and distort attention.

PAS needs no new training. It adds small opposed phase shifts across the model's heads and then merges their outputs, which smooths the time ripple while keeping each head's signal intact. Tests on video tasks under matched budgets showed steady gains, which suggests a simple route to more stable video models.
arxiv-2511-11079:
Sejin Kim, Hayan Choi, and their colleagues present ARCTraj, a data set that records how people actually solve abstract visual puzzles step by step. Most puzzle data show only the start grid and the final grid, which hides the path a solver took. ARCTraj instead logs ordered, object-level actions as solvers turn inputs into outputs through a web interface.

The set holds about ten thousand solution paths across four hundred training tasks, each with task labels, time stamps, and success marks. A shared pipeline supports methods from reinforcement learning to sequence models. Studies of spatial picks, color choices, and strategy narrowing show the range of human reasoning in the set.
arxiv-2511-11279:
Petter Persson, Nils Henriksson, and Nicolò Maccaferri improve a generative method for inverse design of plasmonic nanostructures, tiny metal structures that steer light below the wavelength scale. Forward checks of a given design are easy, but inverse design cannot promise that a good design exists or is unique, and the design space is huge. A conditional generative adversarial network learns to propose designs from a target light spectrum.

Adding label projection and a new embedding network to that model cut errors sharply, by tenfold in the best case. Training also converged faster. The result makes data-driven inverse design of light-steering nanostructures more reliable.
arxiv-2511-11379:
Davi de Moura Esposti Moreira, Matheus Elias Pereira, and Alexandre Grezzi de Miranda Schmidt propose a molecule as a laboratory analogue for a particle moving in the gravitational field of a tachyon. Tachyons are hypothetical faster-than-light particles that have never been observed, so their gravity can only be studied on paper, here through an AII metric. The test particle's behavior is analyzed with the Klein-Gordon equation for a scalar field in that background.

The authors compute the system's quasi-normal modes and its Hawking radiation spectrum. With a carefully tuned external potential, both parts of the particle's wave function are matched by electron dynamics inside the hydrogen molecular ion, giving a molecular model of an extreme system.
arxiv-2511-11779:
Sabir Ahammed, Molla Basir Ahamed, and Ming-Sheng Liu extend the Bohr inequality. That classic bound limits power series. The new setting is slice regular functions. These are the quaternion-valued analogue of holomorphic functions. Bohr phenomena bound how large a series tail can be, relative to its leading term.

Bounds are proved first for slice starlike functions. Slice close-to-convex functions are covered next. The results are then generalized for functions on the unit ball. A refined version covers functions whose real part stays below one. Each result is shown to be sharp. The constants cannot be improved. Quaternionic analysis gains tools as precise as the complex theory's.
arxiv-2511-11879:
Yaghmorassene Hebib examines a mundane noise source that could quietly undermine tabletop tests of whether gravity can entangle two masses. Such experiments aim to prove gravity is quantum by creating entanglement through it alone, but classical timing noise shared by both interferometers can mimic the crucial phases.

Clock cross-spectra are mapped to an effective common-mode dephasing rate, and the resulting channel is shown to be local operations with classical communication, which by definition cannot create entanglement. Published clock and interferometer noise floors then give quantitative bounds on how large the shared noise can be relative to local dephasing in leading proposals. Visibility thresholds tell experimenters when a claimed signal could still be classical.
arxiv-2511-11979:
Md Ahsanul Haque and four co-authors present CITADEL, a malware detector designed for a world where Android threats mutate monthly and labels cannot keep up. Nearly three hundred thousand new samples appear each month, expert labeling does not scale, and detectors rot as both malicious and benign apps drift in behavior.

Semi-supervised active learning uses the vast unlabeled pool instead of ignoring it, while asking experts only where their labels pay. Earlier drift defenses stayed fully supervised and expensive, and generic semi-supervised methods assume smooth input transformations that high-dimensional binary app features violate. Long-term, real-world benchmarks are the test the framework sets for itself.
arxiv-2511-12179:
Ismaila A. Jallow and Samya Tajmouati examine what drives financial and digital inclusion in West and Central Africa, using World Bank Findex data from 2021. Access to accounts, credit, mobile money and digital payments varies widely across the region. Knowing which traits predict access can guide policy.

They fit binary models country by country, with cross-validation and model tests as robustness checks, for the full region and for each part separately. Gender, schooling, income and urban or rural residence matter in the full and West African samples. In Central Africa, gender does not, while age joins the key factors. Country contrasts, such as Ghana and Nigeria, are also detailed.
arxiv-2511-12479:
Navin Sriram Ravie, Keerthi Vasan M and Bijo Sebastian present ClutterNav, a system that decides which object to remove next so a robot can reach a target buried in dense clutter. Blindly pulling objects out can topple the stack and force many extra moves. Rule-based planners are slow and rigid, while end-to-end learning is hard to interpret and transfers poorly.

ClutterNav frames each removal as a step in a continuous reinforcement learning task, where the scene understanding updates after every move. A removability critic, trained from demonstrations, estimates the cost of removing each object from its geometry and position. That learned cost guides the search toward the target with minimal disturbance.
arxiv-2511-12779:
Zhenshuo Zhang, Minxuan Duan, Youran Ye, and Hongyang R. Zhang tackle a grouping problem in multi-objective reinforcement learning. When a learner must serve many objectives at once, one policy for everything gets worse as objectives multiply, a pattern seen in robotics, control, and preference tuning of language models. Their plan has two stages: first train one meta-policy across all objectives, then adapt it to random subsets of objectives and measure how well skills transfer between them.

Those transfer measurements form an affinity matrix, built cheaply because a first-order approximation predicts adapted performance within about two percent in their tests. Clustering objectives by affinity gives groups that train well together. On robotic control benchmarks, PolicyGradEx beat leading baselines by sixteen percent on average. Ablations support each design choice.
arxiv-2511-12879:
Ashish Kumar Perukari and Polina Khoroshevskaya coordinate resources for large fleets of autonomous vehicles and satellites. Fleets must share scarce things: energy, charger access, maintenance slots, time windows, and bandwidth, all under uncertainty about future consumption. Their approach gives each agent a risk model shaped by local side information, links the agents with chance constraints on failures. Lets them agree through a lightweight decentralized routine run over a sparse communication network, avoiding any single point of failure.

Tests used real urban road networks with autonomous vehicles and a representative satellite constellation, against greedy, uninformed, and all-knowing central baselines. The method cut failure rates by roughly a third to a half at the same cost. It scaled to thousands of agents with near-linear running time while keeping plans feasible with high probability. The work targets operators who need near-central quality without a fragile central controller.
arxiv-2511-13379:
Ettore Marmo, David Riley, and Thomas Weigel show how the Zassenhaus Lie algebra of a pro-p group can be presented through its Magnus Lie algebra. Both algebras encode group structure in Lie terms, but the Magnus side is often easier to reach. The bridge matters for groups where direct calculation is hard.

For groups whose lower central series terms carry no torsion, the Zassenhaus algebra can be computed explicitly from the Magnus algebra. The authors list broad families where the result applies, including surface groups, right-angled Artin groups, and pure braid groups. Fundamental groups of certain hyperplane and toric arrangements also fall under the same method.
arxiv-2511-13679:
Hyunwoo Oh and 7 co-authors present QUILL, an accelerator design that makes deformable attention hardware-friendly. Deformable transformers lead object detection accuracy, but their scattered memory access and low arithmetic density waste standard chips. QUILL reorders the work so data arrive in cache-friendly, single-pass order.

Queries are sorted by spatial closeness, and a look-ahead prefetches the needed regions into a spare buffer while compute proceeds. A fused engine runs interpolation, softmax, gathering, and projection in one pass without spilling data. Built as register-transfer hardware, it beat a flagship graphics card on throughput and energy by large multiples and stayed within a point of full-precision accuracy under mixed precision.
arxiv-2511-13879:
Hannah Kravitz presents a computing tool for studying irrational rotations, a classic topic in number theory. A certain running sum built from fractional parts tracks how evenly a rotation spreads points, but direct calculation is plagued by rounding error and missed jumps. Her algorithm instead defines the sum exactly through its discontinuities.

With that approach, values can be computed with errors near machine precision in fast linear time, and the full probability distribution follows soon after. Kravitz offers the method as a tool for experimental mathematics. Plots made with it reveal extreme behavior tied to how well the rotation number is approximated by fractions, including a spiked trapezoidal pattern that slowly degrades.
arxiv-2511-13979:
Harang Ju and Sinan Aral test whether the personalities of AI agents should be matched to the people using them. In a preregistered experiment, 1,258 participants were paired with agents prompted to show varying levels of the Big Five traits. The teams produced over seven thousand display ads for a real think tank.

Independent raters scored the ads, and a field experiment on X ran them before nearly five million impressions. Both human and AI traits shaped quality, and specific pairings mattered: some combinations, like extraverted people with conscientious agents, produced the weakest ads. Field results tied ad quality to click rates and costs, making personality pairing a practical design lever.
arxiv-2511-14179:
Yanshan Li, Ke Ma, Miaomiao Wei, and one co-author recognize actions from skeleton data using a game-theoretic contrastive method. Self-supervised approaches usually treat every body region alike and keep negative examples in a simple first-in-first-out queue, wasting motion information and picking weak negatives. Their network, DoGCLR, frames sample construction as a dominance game.

Positive and negative samples interact toward an equilibrium balancing meaning preservation against discriminative strength. A dual weighting scheme spotlights key motion regions for augmentation, while an entropy-driven rule keeps hard negatives in the memory bank and evicts weak ones. On the NTU RGB+D and PKU-MMD benchmarks the method posted strong accuracy across standard evaluation splits.
arxiv-2511-14479:
Kyle McKee studies optimal control of particles in a driven Stokes flow. The setting is a thin Hele-Shaw cell, a classic model for slow viscous flow. Electric and magnetic forces in a conducting fluid create tunable circulation. McKee asks which control paths move particles with least energy cost.

He shows those best paths are geodesics of a new metric that emerges from the flow itself. Under a power cap, the same paths are also time optimal. With random forcing at the boundary, particle spread follows the metric in an uneven way. The ideas extend past this cell to driven Stokes flows more broadly, including three dimensional cases.
arxiv-2511-14579:
Amanuel Anteneh and Olivier Pfister present gradient descent methods for quantum sensor tomography at larger scale. Tomography means learning the full measurement description of a sensor from probe data. For phase insensitive sensors, past fitting used constrained convex methods that can be slow. The authors instead optimize the measurement operators directly with gradients.

Numerical benchmarks show equal or higher reconstruction fidelity in much less time. The gain holds even with noise and few probe states. They also outline an extension to phase sensitive sensors. That extension parametrizes operators on a complex manifold so gradients stay valid. Faster tomography helps labs characterize real quantum sensors with limited resources.
arxiv-2511-15479:
Martin Slind Hagen, Emil Lundqvist, Alex Phu, Yenan Wang, Kim Strandberg, and Elad Michael Schiller formally check the security of a framework for updating car software. Modern vehicles run software for most functions and stay connected, so a flawed update can threaten safety. The Unified Software Update Framework was built to deliver secure updates that fit existing vehicle systems, but it had not been formally verified before.

The team models the framework and its assumptions to mirror real automotive setups. Using the ProVerif tool and symbolic execution, they check six required properties: privacy, integrity, authenticity, freshness, order, and liveness. All six prove satisfiable, supporting the claim that the framework meets its stated security guarantees.
arxiv-2511-15679:
Jianqiao Mao and Max A. Little widen the reach of the front-door method for identifying causal effects from data. The classic front-door setting gives a simple formula, but it is often seen as narrow. A general identification algorithm handles many more graphs, yet its answers are algebraically complex and hard to estimate or interpret.

Their notion of front-door reducibility is a graph condition that groups variables into three super-nodes matching the classic setting. They characterize the condition, prove it matches the existence of a matching adjustment, and give an exact algorithm with guarantees. Many graphs far outside the textbook setting qualify, yielding simple adjustments where general methods would be cumbersome.
arxiv-2511-15779:
Ian Pang and four co-authors ask how close modern jet taggers are to the fundamental statistical limit of jet classification. Better taggers improve collider searches, but unknown ceilings make progress hard to judge. Generative surrogate models with learned likelihoods offer a new route, if the surrogate captures the true distribution. Their SURF method validates such surrogates rigorously.

A tractable surrogate trained on real data becomes a reference for exact optimal tests. One flow based generative model passes as a valid reference for a standard jet data set. Against that reference, modern taggers already operate near the true limit. Autoregressive models, by contrast, exaggerate separation power unphysically. The result reframes tagging research toward the few gains still available.
arxiv-2511-15879:
Antonino Ficarra studies the gradient of a monomial ideal in algebra. A monomial ideal is generated by monomials, products of variables, in a polynomial ring. Its gradient ideal is built from all partial derivatives of its generators. Regularity measures how complex each ideal is to describe, and past work showed the two regularities are generally incomparable for hypersurface ideals.

Ficarra proves the two values stay apart even for monomial ideals with linear resolution, the simplest resolution type. That answers a question of J. Herzog. Constructions realize any set gap in either direction. He also defines ideals whose repeated gradients all keep linear resolution, and shows several known families have that property.
arxiv-2511-16079:
Mitsuo Higaki proves a quantitative Runge approximation result for the Stokes system. That system models slow viscous flow in a bounded region in three dimensions, over time. Runge approximation says solutions on a smaller part can be matched by solutions on the whole domain. A past qualitative result with Franck Sueur used a non-constructive argument. It gave no error estimates and covered only interior matching.

Higaki result gives explicit error estimates in the mean-square sense. It also extends the theory to the initial-boundary value problem, the case with start and boundary data that physics needs. The proof adapts a modern quantitative frame, mixing semigroup theory with a quantitative match for the linked resolvent problem.
arxiv-2511-16379:
Igor Lugo, Martha Alatriste-Contreras, and Brenda Coutiño-Vázquez model how empathy can propagate in schools to create inclusive patterns for students with special education needs. Their model adapts the classic Schelling segregation framework. Simple transition rules govern how students think of others as equals. Null models test whether apparent inclusion exceeds chance expectations.

Simulations show empathy patterns can emerge instead of the usual segregation outcome. Small changes in incentives around special needs status trigger inclusive patterns in some settings. Other conditions still produce segregation, as the classic model predicts. The complex systems approach maps which levers matter most. Findings suggest modest incentive design could shift school social dynamics toward inclusion.
arxiv-2511-16479:
Luca Sabatini surveys which group properties let finite groups produce expander graphs, networks that are sparse yet extremely well connected, through their Cayley or Schreier graphs. Expanders matter across computer science and mathematics, and the survey collects what a sequence of groups or group actions must satisfy for bounded-size generating sets to expand.

New results in the survey show that an infinite amenable group, and solvable groups of bounded derived length, never produce expander Schreier graphs. The proofs generalize classic Lubotzky-Weiss results for Cayley graphs with simpler arguments. A further moral is that poor expansion of a group action cannot in general be detected from its abelian sections or from the representations sitting above a point stabilizer.
arxiv-2511-16579:
Gaspard Ohlmann, Edwin Hamel-De le Court, and Francesco Belardinelli develop controller synthesis for probabilistic systems with richer safety rules than the usual avoid-this-state constraints. Safety here is expressed in Probabilistic Computation Tree Logic, a formalism that can state nuanced time-based requirements over random behavior.

The authors reduce global satisfaction of the rules to local constraints and isolate CPCTL, a fragment of the safe logic whose expressiveness they argue fits the synthesis problem well. On that foundation they build a value iteration algorithm that computes controllers meeting the stated rules, and they prove the method sound and complete. The work lets engineers state what safe means in a realistic time-based language and still get an automatic synthesis procedure with guarantees.
arxiv-2511-17279:
Stéphanie M. C. Abo and Ruth E. Baker build a framework for how cell populations spread, taking seriously a fact that classic models ignore: cells need time to mature before they can divide. Standard models treat division as having no memory and predict exponential waiting times, but lineage tracing shows peaked, gamma-like distributions with a clear maturation delay. The authors track time since last division directly, with age resetting at each division event.

Their moment-hierarchy approach produces explicit formulas for the steady-state age distribution, the cell-cycle-time distribution, and the invasion speed, and it recovers the classic Fisher-KPP model when rates ignore age. Three principles emerge: age structure lowers carrying capacity and shrinks the range where populations survive. Classical theory overestimates invasion speeds. And the survival condition exactly matches the condition for a positive invasion speed. The framework keeps these effects plain to see.
arxiv-2511-17379:
Lan Wen, Aaron L. Sarvet, and Jessica G. Young clarify a habit of thought in causal inference: treating the elimination of censoring as if it were a treatment. In survival studies, people leave observation early, and outcomes are often defined by imagining all such right-censoring removed. That framing has bred a belief that causal questions are ill-posed unless censoring is eliminated. The authors argue the belief is mistaken.

A well-defined causal estimand, they show, can be stated without indexing outcomes on censoring's elimination. The key is sorting censoring events more precisely than tradition has done, because different kinds of censoring carry different weight for identification. Their framework distinguishes those types and connects them to the definitions used in classical survival analysis. The paper gives clearer guidance for studies where follow-up ends unevenly.
arxiv-2511-17479:
Silvia Onofri, Andrey Shternshis, and Stefano Marmi ask how random stock market data really is, tick by tick. Efficient market theory says returns should be unpredictable, like outputs of a random number generator. Rather than relying on the usual correlation or entropy checks, the authors run financial tick sequences through comprehensive batteries of statistical randomness tests, the suites designed to certify random generators. These include the NIST suite and TestU01's Rabbit and Alphabit batteries.

Their main finding concerns aggregation: raw high-frequency trades are strongly correlated, but as trades are aggregated over longer transaction-time windows, the resulting return streams pass more and more randomness tests. The thorough testing also exposed surprises, like non-monotonic predictability patterns in certain assets. Beyond market theory, the model-free method can both audit financial series for randomness and harvest pseudo-random sequences from them.
arxiv-2511-17879:
Yusong Wu, Stephen Brade, Aleksandra Teng Ma, and six co-authors address a failure in training music generation models by reinforcement learning: the model games its coherence score and produces dull, repetitive output. In live jamming with a human player, that loss of variety is especially damaging.

Their adversarial post training adds a discriminator that learns to tell model output from real music data. Meanwhile the model tries to fool it as well as earn coherence rewards. Tests in simulation and a user study with expert musicians show better diversity, harmony, adaptation speed, and sense of control for the human partner.
arxiv-2511-18679:
Xiang Gao, Yuanpeng Liu, Xinmu Wang, and seven co-authors store and restore three dimensional meshes as neural geometry images. Turning an irregular mesh into a regular image grid lets powerful image methods process it. But building that image well is the hard part, since flat regions need few samples and detailed regions need many.

They use optimal transport to distribute samples evenly in the right sense and build a pyramid of image resolutions for continuous levels of detail. A single forward pass restores a high quality mesh from a low resolution stored image, with no decoder chain. Experiments show leading storage efficiency and restoration accuracy.
arxiv-2511-19279:
Victor Rambaud, Salvador Mascarenhas, and Yair Lakretz build MapFormers, transformer models that learn cognitive maps, the inner layouts animals use to relate places and things. A good map separates the structure of a space from its contents, which supports strong generalization to new cases. Standard AI systems still lack that skill.

MapFormers update their position encodings with input-dependent matrices built from learned symmetry generators. Two variants target episodic and working memory. On tasks covering gating, two-dimensional navigation, and nested hierarchies such as Dyck languages, the models far outperform current architectures. Their near-perfect scores on unseen cases suggest learned maps can support flexible reasoning.
arxiv-2511-19479:
Sangam Ghimire and eight co-authors present a federated learning framework built to run across a mix of supercomputers and cloud platforms. Federated learning trains models at many sites without moving raw data, which suits privacy-aware AI, while high-performance computing and cloud resources offer the power such training needs. The mix brings friction: unlike hardware, communication limits, and data that differ from site to site all complicate the job.

Their system tackles scheduling, communication overhead, and system diversity while guarding accuracy and privacy. Experiments on a hybrid testbed show strong scaling, fault tolerance, and convergence even when the data at each site follow unlike distributions. The work targets organisations that must train across facilities they cannot merge.
arxiv-2511-20079:
Levin calculates how often quarkonia emerge alongside crowds of other particles. His 2025 paper works in high-energy quantum chromodynamics. Quarkonia are bound states like the J/psi meson. Production rates may depend on event multiplicity. It counts how many hadrons join the event.

The approach rests on t-channel unitarity constraints. Dipole densities come from summing large Pomeron loops. Three-gluon fusion produces the quarkonium in this picture. Extra Pomeron ladders cancel out of inclusive rates. Earlier work had neglected that cancellation entirely. Levin derives count distributions with and without a J/psi. Their ratio grows with the square of multiplicity. That quadratic law matches earlier hopes in the field. Both distributions show KNO scaling behavior. The dipole counts trace back to the Balitsky-Kovchegov equation. Rare fluctuations in dipole scattering shape those counts. The framework avoids assuming how the saturation scale varies.
arxiv-2511-20379:
Damas, Hehn, Rojas-Sánchez, and Petit-Watelot track spin currents through a magnetic alloy's balance point. Their 2025 paper studies a GdFeCo ferrimagnet across its compensation temperature. Two magnetic sublattices inside point opposite ways. At one temperature their strengths cancel exactly. Spin currents generated there could power memory devices.

Resonance spectroscopy separated two torque mechanisms cleanly. The spin Hall effect makes one family of torques. The spin anomalous Hall effect makes the other. Both kept their sign through the compensation point. The anomalous torque points opposite to the Hall one. In the parallel setup it also dominates in size. Distinct electron groups explain the split behavior. Gadolinium 5d electrons carry the Hall part. Iron-cobalt 3d electrons carry the anomalous part. Neither flips because its source keeps its state. The Hall torque even grows near compensation. Earlier reported sign changes get re-explained. Ferrimagnetic spin sources look more predictable now.
arxiv-2511-20479:
Kalberla asks whether molecular hydrogen hides inside the same threads as cold atomic gas. His 2025 paper studies the cold neutral medium high above the Galactic plane. Atomic hydrogen lines reveal thin thread-like shapes in the sky. Most such threads, fifty-seven percent, also glow in FIR dust emission. They trace the direction of magnetic field lines.

The analysis used 241 molecule absorption lines toward stars. Far-ultraviolet data from the FUSE probe added 65 more sight lines. Nearly every sight line with molecular gas crossed an atomic thread.
