Second, a knowledge graph tracking links among catalysts, active sites, synthesis labels, mechanistic claims with evidence, and large-scale outcomes. Third, a query module for searching and viewing data across papers. Fourth, a test on about eight hundred peer-reviewed papers showing it works.
arxiv-2602-18579:
José Aldo Silva da Costa and seven co-authors watch novices read code. Their 2026 paper notes developers often extract methods to improve readability and understanding, while inlining keeps logic together. Prior static-metric work showed no clear differences, leaving comprehension and navigation underexplored.

The team studies Inline Method versus Extract Method refactorings with eye tracking, comparing visual effort, reading behavior, time, and attempts. A controlled experiment has thirty-two Java novices solve eight tasks across four programs in both versions, plus a survey of fifty-eight novices. Effects vary with task difficulty. In two tasks extraction improved performance and cut visual effort, with time falling seventy-eight point eight percent and regressions eighty-four point six percent. For simpler tasks extraction hurt, with time rising one hundred sixty-six point nine percent and regressions two hundred percent. Preferences favored extraction for readability yet did not always match performance.
arxiv-2602-18779:
When people form groups, some ties hold and others break. The rules for stable ties change when a tie can link more than two people at once. Rémi Castera, with two co-authors, extends network stability theory in 2026 to weighted hypergraphic networks. There, connections vary in strength and each person faces a budget on total connection intensity.

The work generalises pairwise stability, first set out for unweighted networks and later for weighted ones. That keeps it meaningful for multi-person relationships under budget limits. It then adds a stronger notion, full stability, in which agents may adjust several connections at once, borrowing insight from matching theory. Existence results, explicit solutions or algorithms, and counterexamples together give an almost complete theory. It bridges network formation and fractional matching.
arxiv-2602-19179:
Gaussian work on surfaces supports robots, but exact methods break down. Junghoon Seo, with two co-authors, studies tangent-linear Gaussian work in 2026 and derives direct non-asymptotic error bounds. Mapping sums and surface-measure tuning are both covered. Bounds separate local second-order geometric warp from nonlocal tail leakage.

For Gaussian inputs, closed-form diagnostics follow from mean, covariance, and curvature or reach surrogates. Circle and planar-pushing tests validate a predicted calibration transition. Normal-direction uncertainty dominates when locality breaks. Diagnostics thus trigger switching from single-chart linearisation to multi-chart or sample-based inference. Practical guidance replaces blind trust in linearised methods.
arxiv-2602-19379:
Microwave linear analog computers promise to run multiple-input multiple-output processing directly in the radio-frequency analog domain. Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx note that existing studies use idealized channel models and ignore antenna mutual coupling, yet coupling matters precisely because processing happens at radio frequency. It alters the operation the device implements, not just the channel it sees.

The authors develop a physics-compliant model using multiport network theory, covering devices at the transmitter, the receiver, or both. They formulate and solve a coupling-aware optimization problem, deriving a closed-form solution, globally optimal, that maximizes received signal power. Results show coupling helps on average, and that these devices can match digital architectures with matching networks while using fewer radio-frequency chains.
arxiv-2602-19479:
Rare kaon decays offer a sensitive probe for light bosons with vector and axial-vector couplings to non-conserved currents. Matheus Hostert and two co-authors study three- and four-body kaon decays. Searches for one neutral decay mode constrain light boson couplings to light quarks to about ten to the minus fifth power. Charged-pion modes give weaker limits near ten to the minus fourth power, but constrain complementary quark combinations.

Double emission of the boson in kaon decays adds further constraints, thanks to a double enhancement factor in the rate. For a 17 megaelectronvolt boson, these limits add to the tension between spin-1 boson interpretations of the ATOMKI experiment results and meson decay data. The paper also comments on negative pion capture, rounding out a systematic survey of kaon decay constraints.
arxiv-2602-19979:
Type IIB superstring amplitudes are organized by the number of external states and their charge under the theory's R-symmetry. A 2026 arXiv paper by Emiel Claasen and Mehregan Doroudiani analyzes the low-energy series of one-loop five-point amplitudes across all charge sectors.

The representative processes involve five gravitons, or four gravitons plus one dilaton. The authors compute one-loop contributions to moduli-dependent couplings in the effective action up to high-derivative interactions. Their results satisfy S-duality constraints in every charge sector. They display rich arithmetic structure. That structure includes single-valued multiple zeta values. It also includes logarithmic derivatives of the Riemann zeta function, evaluated at odd integers and combined in affine linear ways, plus a new constant whose nature is currently unknown. The paper thus maps five-point one-loop physics with unusual arithmetic depth.
arxiv-2602-20279:
Elias Furrer and Jan Manschot compute correlation functions in a twisted form of supersymmetric gauge theory. Their 2026 study treats SU(2) Yang-Mills theory with up to three massive matter fields, on a smooth, compact, oriented four-dimensional space with a stated topological condition. In that setting, the correlations reduce to a finite set of universal functions, whose mass dependence records intersection numbers of instanton moduli spaces.

The authors derive closed formulas for those functions by combining Seiberg-Witten geometry, the u-plane integral, and the blowup formula. When the space is a complex algebraic surface, the correlations match generating functions of Segre invariants for sheaf moduli spaces. The results agree with earlier formulas by Göttsche and Kool for those generating functions. The paper thus ties gauge-theory correlations, instanton geometry, and sheaf counting into one consistent picture.
arxiv-2602-20779:
Florian Lux and two co-authors tackle a flaw in 3D nano-printed lens scanners: the printed polymer creeps and drifts with heat, so open-loop moves lose accuracy over time. Their fix is closed-loop control, with a built-in sensor that tracks the lens position as it moves.

A tiny magnet around the microlens drives motion and also supplies the sensing signal, read by a commercial three-axis Hall sensor placed between a pair of drive coils. Subtracting the coil field recovers the magnet position. The loop holds mean accuracy to 0.86 micrometers and precision to 0.49 over a 150-micrometer range, wiping out creep and hysteresis.
arxiv-2602-20979:
AI agents now write code on their own, but the software world around them was built for humans. Mark Marron argues that world itself must change in this 2026 arXiv paper, sketching an Agentic Infused Software Ecosystem. The vision rests on three pillars: the agents, the languages and tools they use, and the runtime environment they operate in.

Agents have moved in the past five years from simple code completion toward independent development work, and that trend will continue. Languages and APIs increasingly serve as the shared medium through which humans and agents collaborate. The paper insists all three pillars must advance together, in ways that suit present agents, future agents, and the human developers beside them.
arxiv-2602-21079:
Thermal transpiration moves gas through a temperature gradient, a phenomenon Knudsen studied in 1909. Kai-Li Wang and I-Kun Chen demonstrate it mathematically in this 2026 arXiv paper for a bounded convex domain, using the stationary Boltzmann equation with a cutoff potential. The boundary is split into diffuse-reflection and incoming regions, and a solution is shown to exist in a weighted space.

For a domain with diffuse reflection in the middle and incoming conditions at the ends, Maxwellians at equal pressure but different temperatures drive total flux toward the hot end. Under a particular pressure-temperature relation, the flux becomes small, matching Knudsen's thermomolecular pressure difference. Readers get a rigorous footing for a classic rarefied-gas effect.
arxiv-2602-21179:
Graph-based medical splitting gives fixed landmarks and group matches, but training it usually needs hand-marked landmarks that rarely exist. Nicolas Gaggion, Maria Ledesma-Carbayo, Stergios Christodoulidis, Maria Vakalopoulou, and Enzo Ferrante remove that need in this 2026 arXiv paper with Mask-HybridGNet. The setup trains graph models straight from standard pixel-wise masks.

Chamfer guidance plus edge smoothing lines up varied-length edges with fixed-length landmark calls, refined by smooth raster work. Landmark spots then emerge steadily tied to body spots across patients, with no match guidance. That hidden atlas allows tracking, cross-slice rebuild, and group study, with rivaling hit rate across chest, cardiac, and fetal imaging.
arxiv-2602-21279:
Superfluid helium flows below one kelvin demand instruments that work in extreme cold and rotation. I. Skachko and six co-authors describe such an apparatus in this 2026 arXiv paper, built for optical observation down to a tenth of a kelvin. A wet cryostat with a dilution refrigerator sits on a vibrationally isolated platform capable of continuous rotation.

Laser light from a room-temperature table enters through an optical fiber, and images return through a bundle of one hundred thousand fibers at resolution around thirty micrometers. Piezoelectric positioners adjust illumination and focus remotely. The apparatus visualized excimer-molecule clouds and fluorescent particles in superfluid helium, with particle tracks filmed at nearly a thousand frames per second.
arxiv-2602-21379:
Daniel Tamayo and six co-authors introduce MrBERT, a family of encoders with 150 to 300 million parameters built on the ModernBERT design and pretrained on 35 languages plus code. The goal is a modern encoder that serves both local language needs and high-stakes specialist domains.

MrBERT sets state-of-the-art results on Catalan- and Spanish-specific tasks and holds up well in biomedical and legal domains. Matryoshka Representation Learning lets users shrink the vectors on demand, cutting inference and storage costs for production use. The whole model family is open-sourced on Huggingface, so researchers and builders can adapt it directly.
arxiv-2602-21479:
Beepul Bharti and two co-authors develop global sequential tests for auditing machine learning systems across many data streams. In risk-sensitive areas, systems must be checked continuously as new data arrive, to catch failures fast. The task is sequential hypothesis testing with k streams and a global null that the system works as designed on all streams.

The standard global test uses a Bonferroni correction, with expected stopping time growing like log k over alpha for large k. The authors build efficient tests by merging martingales through averaging and product rules. A balanced test matches the Bonferroni rate when only a few streams are non-null. Under dense alternatives with many non-null streams, it improves to log one over alpha divided by k. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data validate the theory.
arxiv-2602-21979:
Quantum systems open to their surroundings can sit in mixed states, which do not fit the neat phase labels used for closed, pure systems. Yuchen Guo and Shuo Yang build a framework that sorts out these mixed-state phases in one-dimensional systems with a doubled two-fold symmetry. They add a helper chain, called an ancilla, and use decorated domain-wall patterns to derive eight fixed-point models marked by three sign labels.

Dropping the helper chain recovers the full set of mixed phases, from plain symmetric states to broken-symmetry and protected topological kinds and their blends. Slides between the eight fixed points trace a cube-shaped phase map, whose edges mark basic transitions between phases. The framework gives physicists a clear, unified chart for phases that only exist once a system is open to its environment.
arxiv-2602-22079:
When one galaxy partly covers another from our view, the overlap lets astronomers measure dust in the foreground galaxy by the light it blocks. T. Butrum and thirteen co-authors expand the known set of such pairs with a new citizen-science catalog drawn from the DESI Legacy Survey. Volunteers classified candidate overlaps spotted in Galaxy Zoo DECaLS, working from survey images.

The resulting catalog holds roughly eight hundred occulting pairs, a large jump over the small sets used in past dust studies. A bigger catalog cuts pair-to-pair scatter and gives machine-learning methods enough examples to learn automatic identification. For galaxy researchers, it turns a rare curiosity into a statistical tool for mapping dust in detail.
arxiv-2602-22179:
Finding groups of patients or parts that live unusually long or short can guide treatment and maintenance, but standard subgroup methods lean on restrictive survival assumptions. Mhd Jawad Al Rahwanji and three co-authors propose Sysurv, a nonparametric, fully differentiable method that discovers readable rules selecting subgroups with exceptional survival. It needs no proportional-hazards assumption and no pre-binned features.

Unlike methods that compare group averages, Sysurv respects individual heterogeneity within subgroups. Tests across many datasets and settings, including a cancer case study, show it surfaces insightful, actionable subgroups and beats the state of the art. Clinicians and engineers gain rules they can read, trust, and act on, not just scores.
arxiv-2602-22579:
Pablo Valle and three co-authors tackle testing for vision-language-action robots, machines that turn spoken instructions and camera views into physical moves. Checking such robots is hard because a test oracle, a rule that judges correct behaviour, must be built per instruction. Existing oracles also track symbolic world states while missing how well a task is performed.

The team tests metamorphic testing as a workaround: change the input in a known way and check whether the robot's path changes as expected. Two relation patterns and five relations came out of the work. Trials with five robot models, two simulated robots, and four tasks showed the method catching varied failures, including unfinished tasks, without needing a test oracle at all.
arxiv-2602-22679:
Tiantian Sun and one co-author build a cleaner theory for Gaussian process regression errors and put it to work. Their framework rests on a function-space decomposition, splitting the problem into parts whose errors can be tracked separately. From it they derive a weighted Jacobi iteration that uses Gaussian process predictions for its parameters.

Convergence analysis comes with the method, and the conditions are shaped to play well with other error bounds, widening the analysis. In experiments, parameters predicted by Gaussian process regression sped up Jacobi convergence markedly. For numerical analysts, the paper pairs a general error theory with a faster solver built directly on it.
arxiv-2602-22779:
Chenhao Zheng and eight co-authors slim down video tokenization. Chopping video into patches spawns far too many redundant tokens, choking efficiency and scale. Trajectory-based tokenizers decouple token count from video length, but depend on slow, task-blind segmentation and tracking pipelines.

TrajTok instead learns tokens end to end with the video model, adapting token granularity to semantic complexity regardless of duration. One unified segmenter clusters pixels across space and time in a single forward pass, yielding object trajectories directly. Built into a video CLIP model trained from scratch, it tops accuracy at scale on classification and retrieval. It matches the best token-merging methods on efficiency, and it doubles as a probing head or vision-language connector.
arxiv-2602-22979:
S. Bellotti and five co-authors test whether GJ 504, a two-billion-year-old Sun-like star, was rejuvenated by swallowing a planet. The star spins once every three and a half days with intense magnetic activity, far livelier than expected at its age. One explanation is that stellar tides dragged a close-in, Jupiter-mass planet inward, spinning the star up and reviving its magnetic dynamo.

Spectropolarimetric observations with ESPaDOnS, mapped by Zeeman-Doppler imaging, reveal a large-scale, dipolar, non-axisymmetric field averaging about five gauss. Fed into a 3D wind simulation, the field constrains wind-driven angular momentum loss. Only the engulfment scenario matches the rotation, X-ray luminosity, and momentum loss, and HD 75332 emerges as a second candidate, so GJ 504 may not be unique.
arxiv-2602-23079:
Boyang Zhang and one co-author assess unmasking risks from style-metric-aided LLM agents. Large language models enable strong author-ID guessing, raising concerns about accidental unmasking in texts such as news pieces. The team offers an LLM agent that tests and curbs such risks through an ordered, readable chain.

Central to the setup is SALA, Stylometry-Assisted LLM Analysis, which joins counted style traits with LLM logic for sturdy, open author-ID tagging. Tests on large-scale news sets show high guessing accuracy in various settings, notably with a data store added. A steered rewrite plan then uses the agent's logic trace to write rewrite prompts, cutting author-ID visibility while keeping textual meaning. The findings show both the unmasking potential of LLM agents and the importance of readable, forward shields for guarding author privacy.
arxiv-2602-23179:
Gal Pomerants and five co-authors ask how protein language models spot repeating segments in protein sequences. Repeats matter for protein shape and function. Such models have been shown to find repeats when asked to fill in masked tokens, but the inner mechanism was unclear. That gap covers both exact copies and near-copies altered by mutations.

The team finds that the mechanism for near-copies functionally covers the exact-copy case as well. It works in two stages. First, the model builds feature pictures using general position-focused attention heads plus biology-tuned parts, such as neurons that encode amino-acid likeness. Then induction heads attend to aligned tokens across the repeated spans to favor the right answer. The picture joins language-style pattern matching with built-in biological knowledge, grounding future study of more complex evolutionary patterns.
arxiv-2602-23479:
Michael Frew and two co-authors introduce FHIRPath-QA, the first open dataset and benchmark for patient-specific question answering over real electronic health records. Patients increasingly access their records digitally, yet interfaces rarely give precise, trustworthy answers, and retrieval-based language model methods are costly, hallucination-prone, and hard to deploy.

Their text-to-FHIRPath paradigm shifts reasoning from free-text generation to query synthesis over the FHIR standard. For o4-mini, token use falls 391-fold versus retrieval-first prompting, from 629,829 to 1,609 tokens per question, and failure rates drop from 0.36 to 0.09 on clinician-phrased questions. Built on MIMIC-IV on FHIR Demo, the dataset pairs over 14,000 questions with validated queries and answers. Fine-tuning lifts query accuracy for 4o-mini from 27 to 79 percent, though overall accuracy tops out at 42 percent.
arxiv-2602-23679:
Emilio Barkett argues the two AGI firms, OpenAI and Anthropic, build socio-tech visions through a wordcraft plan, despite gaps in doing. Drawing on the Jasanoff frame, the paper reads two late-2024 essays: Sam Altman's 'The Intelligence Age' and Dario Amodei's 'Machines of Loving Grace.'

Side-by-side reading names four wordcraft moves. First, opt-out move denies prophet clout while using it. Second, fate-driven normalizing, placing AGI's arrival in history-fate tales. Third, hedged nod folds give-ins to risk into an upbeat frame. Fourth, must-have status, placing each firm central to the dreamed future without naming it a business actor. That two rival firms with other ways, views, and leaders of other styles converge on that shape suggests the vision reflects firm spot and firm-level plan. The paper extends the socio-tech visions frame from states to firms at the tech frontier.
arxiv-2602-23879:
Andrea Adriani and Alec Jacopo Almo Schiavoni-Piazza extend the theory of generalized locally Toeplitz sequences to unbounded domains of finite measure. The 2026 paper concerns matrix sequences that arise when partial and fractional differential equations are discretized, where spectral analysis guides solver design.

Existing GLT theory covers hypercubes and bounded domains, but many problems live on unbounded regions. The authors define a new class, unbounded GLT sequences, for any unbounded domain with finite measure, and study their spectral properties. The extension carries the GLT toolkit, which links matrix sequences to symbols that predict eigenvalue behavior, into a wider geometric setting. It supports analysis of discretizations on domains that stretch to infinity while keeping finite area or volume.
arxiv-2602-23979:
Wasyhun Asefa Gemechu and six co-authors report a simple experimental method for generating high-order Laguerre-Gaussian light modes, sending a Gaussian beam into a multimode fiber's cladding. The 2026 paper shows that the generated mode order stays fixed as input power, propagation distance, and pulse duration vary.

Measurements of spectrum and power confirm a mainly linear beam-shaping mechanism. Kerr nonlinearity, a power-dependent effect, mainly affects longitudinal phase matching and conversion efficiency, without changing the mode order. The result is a robust and scalable platform for tailored optical beams, useful wherever structured light with a stable, high-order pattern is needed. It serves uses from optical trapping to communications that encode information in beam shape.
arxiv-2603-00179: Condrey resolves the privacy-attestation paradox with ZK-PoP, a zero-knowledge construction. It lets a verifier confirm correct sequential work chains, human-range feature vectors, and content evolution consistent with incremental editing, without learning behavioural data, exact timing or intermediate content. Its Groth16 proofs use Pedersen commitments and Bulletproof range proofs, and it is computationally zero-knowledge and sound, and unlinkable across sessions. Proof generation takes under 30 seconds per hour of writing, with 192-byte proofs checked in 8.2 ms, at less than 5% accuracy loss in simulation.
arxiv-2603-00279: Cominelli, Pozzi, and Braghin present an automated design system for pentamode acoustic metamaterials. These materials act almost like fluids, with very low shear stiffness. Their system tunes the sound traits with care, using low-frequency averaging and an adjoint method to test changes fast. A virtual-temperature step keeps the built structures linked and fit to make. The team shows the system at work in a Lüneburg lens and an underwater cloak that hides objects from sound. Both pass acoustic-elastic tests.
arxiv-2603-00379: Oumer, Murali, and Zamani widen certificate based verification of dynamical systems against omega regular properties, where single ranking functions or closure certificates may fail for a fixed template. Their vector certificates bundle several functions that jointly overapproximate the needed invariants, generalising scalar barrier style arguments. Vector co-Büchi ranking functions extend scalar ranking functions. Vector closure certificates likewise extend scalar closure certificates. The richer template class offers a new route when a single function template fails.
arxiv-2603-00479: Shi and five colleagues improve radiology report writing for three dimensional scans. Current vision language models skip segmentation trained encoders and inject vision only at the language input, losing multi scale detail. U-VLM trains in stages from segmentation through classification to report writing, and routes U-Net encoder features into matching language layers. Each stage can use different data without shared labels. The small decoder beats far larger pretrained language models on CT-RATE and AbdomenAtlas scores, showing encoder pretraining matters more than model size.
arxiv-2603-00779: Jaszczak-Dyka and Płociniczak build one mathematical framework for blood and lymph flow in vessels, with a focus on lymph transport through lymphangions. From first principles they derive partial differential equations for fluid motion, coupled to two nonlinear non smooth ordinary equations for calcium and nitric oxide kinetics that govern valve opening and closing. A reduced two equation model yields parameter regimes with a stable limit cycle, matching observed lymphatic pumping rhythms. The framework offers a full description of lymph regulation and a base for studying disease and therapy.
arxiv-2603-00879: Mahapatra and four colleagues measure spin-orbit torques in bilayers pairing permalloy with the layered antiferromagnetic insulator FePS3. Joining the two sharply boosts the field-like torque over permalloy alone, while the damping-like part barely changes. Cooling flips the field-like torque's sign, tracking the antiferromagnet's ordering despite almost no current through the insulator layer, which points to interface control of torque.
arxiv-2603-00979: Tang and four colleagues close the realism gap in formula-driven pretraining for 3D medical segmentation, where generic shapes miss organ layout and relationships. They swap basic primitives for a shape bank built from label-only masks of five subjects, then place patches in anatomical order using spatial anchors and a graph of organ interactions. The result beats prior formula-driven and self-supervised methods on two benchmarks and keeps improving as synthetic data grows.
arxiv-2603-01079: Alekseev, Nasonov, and Panina give a new elementary proof that a sphere bundle carrying a smooth affine transverse foliation has vanishing Euler number when its base's fundamental group is amenable. As a bonus, they bound the Euler number in the general non-amenable case. The result links foliation geometry to group amenability with a short argument rather than heavy machinery.
arxiv-2603-01179: Li and six colleagues bind cryptocurrency payments to service execution for agentic commerce with A402, fixing the x402 standard's lack of end-to-end atomicity. Atomic Service Channels weave execution into payment channels for real-time micropayments. Trusted-hardware adaptor signatures finalize payment only when the service runs correctly and results arrive. A private liquidity vault aggregates settlements into one on-chain transaction, and tests on Bitcoin and Ethereum show orders-of-magnitude gains over x402.
arxiv-2603-01379: Chen and four colleagues design joint beamforming for a huge reconfigurable intelligent surface near-field sensing and communication system, where one base station serves users and senses targets in the surface's near field. They maximize the weighted sum rate of users under sensing beampattern gain, transmit power, and unit modulus phase constraints. A fractional programming block coordinate descent algorithm gives a locally optimal solution for the non-convex design. A customized graph neural network then generates base station beamforming and surface reflecting coefficients for high-dimensional near-field channels.
arxiv-2603-01879:
Chi-Ning Chou, Artem Kirsanov, Yao-Yuan Yang, and SueYeon Chung predict model failure from the shape of its internal representations. Their 2026 work borrows the biomarker idea from medicine: a system-level measure that flags future trouble. Reverse-engineering every circuit gives insight, but rarely a clear early warning for deployment.

The team designs network markers that probe how task-relevant object manifolds sit in representation space. Two geometric measures stand out: effective manifold dimensionality and a utility score for those manifolds. When both shrink on familiar data, performance on shifted data tends to fall soon after. The pattern holds across architectures, optimizers, and data sets in image classification. In transfer learning from a large pre-trained model, the same markers beat plain accuracy at forecasting shifted performance.
arxiv-2603-02179:
Jérémie Bettinelli and Dimitri Korkotashvili link two kinds of maps on surfaces in this 2026 mathematics paper. A map here is a graph drawn on a surface, split into faces. Some maps are bipartite, meaning their points split into two sets with links only across. The authors build a two-way match between general maps and bipartite ones.

Their method cuts along a chosen loop, slides one side by one notch, then sews it back. That small move flips the parity of loops that cross the cut. For doughnut-shaped maps with a single face, loops have a simple form. That makes the full link between the two map types clear. A paired swapping map on even-faced maps supports the argument.
arxiv-2603-02479:
Rituraj Sharma, Weiyuan Chen, and Noah Provenzano guide deep reasoning with step-level scores in this 2026 paper. DeepThink methods generate many candidate solutions, refine them, and merge the best. Without reliable correctness signals mid-search, deeper thought can amplify errors. Correct minority answers get drowned out, and extra compute yields little.

Their algorithm, PRISM, uses a process reward model that grades each reasoning step. Candidates act like particles in a landscape defined by those grades. Score-guided resampling and random refinement concentrate the population on strong reasoning while keeping diversity. On math and science benchmarks, PRISM matched or beat rival DeepThink methods. A mid-size model using it rivaled one six times larger. Analysis shows steady net correction during refinement, even from weak starting pools.
arxiv-2603-02879:
Fiona Spuler, Marlene Kretschmer, Magdalena Alonso Balmaseda, and colleagues separate the tangled influences of two oceans on East African rain. Their 2026 paper targets the short rains over the Greater Horn of Africa, which respond to both Pacific and Indian Ocean patterns. Untangling joint climate signals matters for seasonal forecasts, but model experiments carry model biases.

Their method, DAG-VAE, fuses deep learning with causal reasoning by planting a physics-based causal graph inside an autoencoder's hidden space. Trained on forecast archives, it recovered response patterns matching costly ocean-swap experiments. Trained on observations, it found a different Pacific influence, exposing possible model bias. It can also generate what-if versions of extreme rainy seasons for planning ahead.
arxiv-2603-03479:
Yacob Medhin, Tushar Sial, and Simone Servadio design a spacecraft and its flight path together instead of separately. Electric propulsion missions are usually planned with fixed thrust and efficiency, ignoring how power supply, propulsion, and trajectory pull on each other. Far from the Sun, where light is weak, those shortcuts can doom a design. Their 2026 framework optimizes all three at once as one coupled problem.

A detailed model of the SPT-140 Hall thruster ties thrust and efficiency to the moment-by-moment solar power available, including array degradation. The time-optimal trajectory problem runs on NASA's OpenMDAO and Dymos toolchains with efficient gradient methods. The demonstration case inserts a spacecraft into orbit around asteroid 16 Psyche, a regime where dim sunlight makes power-aware design critical. Results expose the key trade-offs realistic mission planning must respect.
arxiv-2603-03579:
Kunzhe Song, Maxime Zingraff, and Huacheng Zeng sense human movement with radio signals that already fill the air. Radio sensing sees through walls and darkness while preserving privacy, but the useful spectrum below ten gigahertz is scarce and contested. Their 2026 system, Ambient Radio Sensing, refuses to ask for new spectrum. It repurposes live 5G and Wi-Fi transmissions for sensing without disturbing their communication job.

A standalone device passively receives ambient signals, amplifies them to illuminate the surroundings, and captures reflections through a self-mixing radio design. That hardware extracts motion and angle features from ordinary communication waveforms. A cross-modal learning scheme lets a ready-made vision model supervise the radio model's training. The prototype, tested extensively on ambient 5G signals, estimates human skeletons accurately and segments body masks, proving the borrowed-spectrum approach.
arxiv-2603-03679:
Shunhao Ji and three colleagues report a burst of high-energy neutrinos from an exploding star, too powerful for the obvious explanation. The star, supernova 2017hcd, is a Type IIn, whose light comes from ejecta smashing into dense surrounding material. Analyzing public track-like data from the IceCube observatory, their 2026 paper finds a neutrino flare at nearly four-sigma significance. The flare lasted a month or two and was centered about two weeks before the supernova was even discovered optically.

The flare's total energy, spread evenly in all directions, comes out about a hundred times the energy of the explosion's ejecta. The ejecta-into-surroundings scenario cannot pay that bill. The authors instead point to a choked jet, a jet launched by the collapse but strangled inside the star's envelope, as the likely source of the flare.
arxiv-2603-03979: Juntao Lu and others derive a variance-based formula linking mean temperature to isothermal equilibrium temperature in heated radiative-conductive systems. Quartic radiation links make such systems nonlinear by nature under fixed total heating power. Working through the ruling equation and expanding to second order about the ambient temperature shows the mean drop scales with temperature variance.
arxiv-2603-04379: Yuan and colleagues present Helios, a 14B video model running in real time on one H100. It reaches 19.5 frames per second on minute long video at strong baseline quality. Helios avoids drift and acceleration tricks and trains without parallelism frameworks, fitting four 14B models in 80 GB. Unified inputs cover text, image, and video tasks, compressed context cuts costs near small models, and tests beat prior short and long video methods.
arxiv-2603-04479: Bonacorsi and Bordoni model Collatz stopping times with chance based machine learning. Stopping times are skewed, spread counts with strong number variety. A Bayesian NB2 regression predicts stopping time from log n and residue modulo 8, with Bayes doubt. A step generator shuffles odd block lengths via a Dirichlet-multinomial update. The regression beats the models on held out predictive fit. Grouping block lengths by residue modulo 8 lifts model fit a lot, showing modular structure drives variety.
arxiv-2603-05279: Chengdong Wu and team present a Vehicle-in-the-Loop and digital-twin test method for central car server software. Virtual runs miss real-world factors, so the method couples a test vehicle on a dynamometer bench with a virtual counterpart. It offers a safe, reproducible, cost-strong testbed for validating driving algorithms centrally, without separate ECU and rule tests. Unlike older methods, it runs full driving software on vehicle hardware after simulation, removing flashing and middle layers. Mixed testing reduces hardware joining needs, with case studies demonstrating effectiveness.
arxiv-2603-05979: Kleiner and colleagues consider Sobolev maps whose weak differential is invertible almost everywhere and preserves or swaps coordinate spaces. They show that for dimension at least 2, W^{1,2} maps split into component functions on each factor, possibly swapped. This conclusion fails for dimension 1, even for bi-Lipschitz and area preserving maps. These results complement prior work showing failure for dimension at least 2 with W^{1,p} below 2. The authors also discuss approximately split maps, whose differentials approach split linear maps, motivated by whether Sobolev maps on products of Carnot groups are split.
arxiv-2603-06079: Kuzmin, Lee, and Chng tackle a weakness of streaming speaker anonymization: systems that hide identity often flatten emotion. Codec language models trained to continue audio discard emotional cues and default to dominant acoustic patterns instead of paralinguistic detail. The team fine-tunes only, pairing neutral-emotion utterances from the same speaker with frame-level emotion distillation over acoustic token hidden states. On the VoicePrivacy 2024 protocol the method reaches 49.2% UAR for emotion preservation, a relative gain of 24% over the baseline, while intelligibility and privacy remain strong.
arxiv-2603-06179: Ballal and Halder study posets of subgroup classes in finite groups, grouping subgroups by shared sets of element orders. They show this poset forms a chain only for p-groups, and they characterize all finite groups where the poset is C2, the two element chain. The poset also forms a lattice for finite cyclic and dihedral groups, and the authors characterize when that lattice is distributive and modular.
arxiv-2603-06479: McGaugh and team combine far data to measure the relation between baryonic mass and dynamical mass read from kinematics or lensing. Their sample spans nine steps in mass, covering galaxies with motion or lensing data plus groups and clusters with lensing data. For rich clusters, the seen baryon fraction matches the cosmic value of 0.157, while at lower masses it drops steadily with mass. The shift follows a hyperbolic-tangent curve with a mass scale, similar to stellar links from abundance matching but with less scatter.
arxiv-2603-06579: Wright says Euler's quadratic polynomial, combined with nearest-integer rounding, finds exponents for Mersenne primes. For 43 known Mersenne prime powers, indices 10 through 52, leaving out small ones, the method gives seven exact matches and four near hits. Mean absolute error is about 614 over indices 30 to 52. A growth regression, by contrast, captures but gives zero exact matches and a mean error, while analysis shows precision under nearest-integer rounding. From prime values found among 560 unique tries, five cases are picked for GIMPS testing, cutting search space.
arxiv-2603-06679: Po and team address play limits of video world models: user control for editable runs, and shared inference where players influence a world. They bring an external memory, a lasting state free of the context window, updated by user actions and queried throughout roll-out. Unlike diffusion engines acting as next-frame guessers, their approach splits generation into Memory, Observation, and Dynamics modules. Users gain control over environment structure via memory shape, and the design extends to multi-user rollouts, keeping views coherent and cross-player interactions consistent.
arxiv-2603-06879: Friedman and colleagues treat robot looks as explanation, not decoration. Most robots wear sleek industrial styling. Hard glossy plastics hide motors and wiring, leaving a blank slate for users to dress up from stories they know. Fashion offers a better guide: color, texture, and material can signal how to touch a robot, what job it does, and what it can actually do. Done well, those cues build familiarity and legibility. Done poorly, they mislead users about capability.
arxiv-2603-07179: Yuan and colleagues rethink GraphRAG retrieval from a structural view, returning a small subgraph rather than loose graph pieces. Past subgraph methods lean on heuristics tied to one domain and fail in cold-start settings, giving contexts that are incomplete or bloated. Their GFM-Retriever repurposes a pretrained graph foundation model from entity ranking into a retriever that works across domains for multi-hop, path-aware reasoning. A label-free selector then trims the retrieved graph to a minimal, sufficient reasoning subgraph.
arxiv-2603-07679: Rohrmann reworks hydrogen photoionization in magnetized media with the rigid-wavefunction approach. Accurate opacity coefficients matter for stellar spectra, yet exact quantum data remain patchy, leaving the rigid-wave shortcut the practical option for magnetic white dwarfs. He gives a complete treatment of level-splitting with explicit transition odds versus field strength and polarization. High atomic states dissolve in strong fields, shifting absorption even below ten megagauss.
arxiv-2603-07879: Farhan builds a particle-physics model of interacting dark energy in which a stable dark-energy field exchanges only momentum, not energy, with weakly interacting dark-matter particles. The field arises as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson from a softly broken global symmetry. Dark matter sits in an inert doublet held by a discrete symmetry. Run through the CLASS Boltzmann code, the model caps how much clustering it can suppress, leaving a built-in limit on easing low-redshift tensions.
arxiv-2603-08179: Kuzmin and colleagues ask what always-on speech models reveal about speakers. User audio passes through a language model backbone, yet its hidden-state leaks had not been checked. With a lazy-informed attacker under VoicePrivacy 2024, SALM-Duplex and Moshi hidden states leak speaker identity at every transformer layer. SALM-Duplex leaks worst early, Moshi evenly, and linkability climbs fast in early turns. Two Stream-Voice-Anon fixes follow, Anon-W2W and Anon-W2F, the latter lifting the error rate over threefold, near the random-chance ceiling.
arxiv-2603-08279: Wysocki and colleagues propose OSCAR, an occupancy-based shape completion method that rebuilds complete 3D spine anatomy from partial sound views. Accurate 3D spine maps from ultrasound matter for guiding keyhole spine surgery, but sound shadows and view-dependent signal shifts make it hard. For surgery use, the method extracts the surface directly from the image, avoiding the need for labels during inference. It relies on a coupled latent space holding both image appearance and underlying shape.
arxiv-2603-08379: Boldrer and colleagues coordinate multiple robots without any communication, even in forests where dense canopy blocks GNSS. Each robot carries an onboard anisotropic 3D LiDAR sensor, used both for SLAM and for spotting obstacles and neighbours. Their perception-aware 3D navigation framework lets robots push safely toward a goal region despite a narrow sensor field-of-view. Long simulation campaigns across varied scenarios, plus real field experiments, show the approach scales, holds up under strain, and can be relied on.
arxiv-2603-08479: Li and colleagues simulate quasifission in chromium-54 plus americium-243, a route to element 119 that quasifission usually blocks. They use time-dependent Hartree-Fock with the Skyrme energy density functional. They scan many orientations of the nuclei and many energies from below to well above the Coulomb barrier. Side collisions are shell-dominated, end faster, and drive fragments toward spherical Z=82 and deformed N=52-56 closures, while tip collisions show less shell effect. The energy scan shows a shift from an octupole-stabilized regime near Z=88 to a spherical shell-driven regime.
arxiv-2603-08579: David Llamas and colleagues detail the geometry behind the grasshopper problem on a sphere. The puzzle asks for the best local hidden-variable stand-in for quantum singlet correlations at a fixed angle between axes. This companion paper lays out the framework behind earlier numerical answers, comparing three lawn variants and reading the best lawn shapes through spherical harmonics.
arxiv-2603-08679: Yang Cai and colleagues push the worst-case gap for the Random-Offerer trade mechanism wider. The Myerson-Satterthwaite result rules out a fully efficient, incentive-safe, budget-balanced trade rule, leaving the gap to first-best as the key question. An AI-guided evolution search over value distributions finds a case with a ratio of at least 2.0749, beating the prior example.
arxiv-2603-08879: Ibrahim Baroud and colleagues build a multilingual anonymization benchmark in ten tongues. Real patient data is scarce behind privacy rules, so they translate checked data by machine while keeping notes and fitting names to place. Medics confirm translation grade, and the benchmark's thousands of private notes support training, checks, and finding work.
arxiv-2603-08979: Sivaramakrishnan Ramani studies data-driven robust Markov decision processes on Borel spaces. With the disturbance unknown, he builds an empirical distribution and an ambiguity set from a distance function, proves robust and out-of-sample values converge to the true optimum as samples grow. For finite samples the robust value bounds the out-of-sample value with high probability, unlike empirical MDPs.
arxiv-2603-09379: Kirill Krinkin states an explicit bound on how much optimal circuit size can change when a truth table is perturbed. A one-point change alters the optimum by at most order n for any fixed finite complete basis with unit-cost gates. A telescoping argument extends the bound to general Hamming distance. Using exact sizes from SAT solvers for the AIG basis at n equal to 4, he confirms the bound is tight there.
arxiv-2603-09479: Durga Bhaktavatsala Rao Dasari and colleagues show how hybrid spin-photon interfaces can strengthen quantum tokens at all three stages of the protocol. Quantum tokens promise tokens that cannot be forged, secure beyond classical limits. The design uses Bell state measurements, strong tripartite spin-photon-spin entanglement, and coherent spin memories. A diamond version uses electron and nuclear spins, linked to photons by time bins.
arxiv-2603-09679: Will A. M. Smith and colleagues present a narrowband heralded single photon source built in fiber, for the telecom C-band. Photon pairs arise in photonic crystal fiber by spontaneous four-wave mixing, and the fiber's core holds a germanium-doped region for photosensitivity. A fiber Bragg grating written into the fiber reflects a sub-nanometre slice of the pair spectrum. Narrowband photons are then heralded at the near end by detections at the far end, with a coincidence-to-accidental ratio up to 70.
arxiv-2603-09879: Paolo Ventura and coauthors ask what sets the time by which most stars in a dwarf galaxy have formed. Their clue is the ratio of asymptotic giant branch to red giant branch stars in set colour bands. Using updated stellar models that include dust in the wind, they test which inputs move that ratio most. Mass lost by low mass stars on the red giant branch matters most.
arxiv-2603-10179: Ruan and coauthors present a halo streaming model for redshift space distortions in galaxy clustering. Extracting cosmology from surveys needs sound distortion models, yet nonlinear halo dynamics dominate the richest scales. Their frame joins the streaming model to a halo split of clustering into central, satellite, one halo and two halo parts. Emulators trained on simulations supply each core piece on its own, keeping the model open to check and easy to adapt to new tracers.
arxiv-2603-10379: Junzhuo Li and co-authors extend neural scaling laws to Mixture-of-Experts models, asking how compute should split between expert layers and attention layers. They define that split as a ratio of FLOPs per token and vary it with total budget and sparsity in GPT-style MoE Transformers. The optimal ratio follows a power law in total compute and shifts with sparsity, yielding an explicit formula. Folding this ratio into a generalized Chinchilla-style law gives designers a practical guide for building efficient MoE models under fixed budgets.
arxiv-2603-10579: Lachlan J Barnes and co-authors compare three automatic ways to find extended radio galaxies in the EMU survey. The field is GAMA 09, and extended sources are hard for automated detection. The team tried a DRAGN hunter working from component catalogues, a coarse-grained complexity metric, and a machine learning pipeline trained on the pilot survey. Together the three found nearly all extended sources, yet each found a largely distinct set, with only a few hundred shared by all. A complete census, they conclude, will need such methods combined.
arxiv-2603-10679: Tobias Geger and co-authors introduce a project-based education platform for AI-integrated agile software development. It runs as a shared research space between controlled studies and industry, with students and stakeholders on real projects. Agile practice changes fast, so research results arrive late or lack reuse conditions. The platform runs inquiry rapidly, through sprint rhythms and quality gates. Its framework sets out how each round is run and what gates AI-assisted work must pass, and early semesters show it generates practice-relevant evidence efficiently.
arxiv-2603-10979: Cenk Cetin, Shreyas Pouli, and Gabriella Pizzuto teach a robot arm to scrape samples from vial walls, a fiddly lab task. Materials range from granular and powdery to viscous. Their framework pairs a low-level impedance controller, which keeps contact stable and compliant, with a reinforcement learning agent. The agent adjusts the end-effector force using perception feedback about the material's location. Trained in simulation with per-particle dislodgement thresholds, the policy transfers to a real robot. It beats a fixed-force baseline across five material setups.
arxiv-2603-11079: Esteban Martínez-Vargas develops a general way to engineer fixed points into maps on quantum observables. He then uses it to bound how fast a quantum battery can charge. His formalism builds completely positive, unital maps. A chosen observable is the fixed point. So the map's output is constant by construction. A related quantity grows linearly in time. He applies this to battery charging. Multiple states are interchanged at each application of the map. The construction yields an upper bound on charging power.
arxiv-2603-11279: Yibai Li and coauthors apply psychometrics, the science of measuring minds, to large language models. They test the psychological reasoning of four leading systems under the technology acceptance model. They examine convergent, discriminant, predictive, and external validity, the standard checks that a test tests what it claims. All four models passed every validity check. The stronger models, GPT-4 and LLaMA-3, showed better validity than older models. This supports AI psychometrics as a way to judge opaque models.
arxiv-2603-11379: Maria Chudnovsky, Julien Codsi, Ajaykrishnan E S, and Daniel Lokshtanov study graphs excluding a complete bipartite graph and a grid as induced minors. A conjecture promises tree decompositions whose bags have only polylogarithmically growing independence numbers. They prove a weaker version, bounding instead a distance-based independence number, where vertices count as independent when no short path joins them. A second variant trades a larger distance for a different bound, marking progress toward the full statement.
arxiv-2603-11479: Wan and co-authors tackle event detection in multivariate time series, where events are defined by language. Dense labels cost too much to gather, so pure supervised learning struggles. Their Event Logic Tree turns text descriptions into structured temporal logic over signal parts. On that base, SELA, a neuro-symbolic vision-language agent, grounds the parts in signal plots. It returns both event spans and tree-shaped explanations that stay true to the logic. A new benchmark spans energy and climate data with expert notes.
arxiv-2603-11679: Demirel and co-authors use large language models to build the input features that supervised learning usually hand-crafts. Mixed data — time series, free text, records — often demand deep domain skill to encode. Their pipeline asks a model to read a small, varied example set and write a global rubric. That rubric then rewrites raw inputs into a standard form for downstream models. Across 15 clinical tasks, it beats count features, naive baselines, and a clinical foundation model.
arxiv-2603-11779: Pal and co-authors study dark energy falling onto a Schwarzschild black hole, using a Biswas-Roy-Biswas redshift form. They first pin the model's free parameters with differential age data. The fit shows a narrow peak over a wide plateau: the data pick one value yet allow a broad near-equal range. The log mass ratio has grown steadily since z=3, as expected if holes grow by accretion and mergers. The growth rate turns on the radiative efficiency, the accretion parameter, and the merger history.
arxiv-2603-11879: Dionne and Vergniory present a way to spot interacting topological phases from single-particle data alone. Most topology tests lean on non-interacting band pictures, which break down for strong correlations. Their framework starts from the single-particle Green's function. From the one-body density matrix they define an effective winding number and a quantum volume. Tested on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with Hatsugai-Kohmoto interactions, the tools separate three insulating phases, Mott states among them. Topology, they argue, can be read from how spectral weight spreads across excitations.
arxiv-2603-12479: Calamari and co-authors use brown dwarfs to check silicate cloud findings in four hot Jupiter atmospheres. JWST watched WASP-39 b, HD 189733 b, WASP-17 b, and WASP-107 b in this program. Chondritic meteorite evidence suggests giant planets take their star's magnesium-to-silicon value as they form. Current cloud species calls for all four planets match predictions from each host star's ratio, supporting the formation story from earlier work. Transit spectra for three planets also face brown dwarf spectra to trace absorption trends across mass and temperature.
arxiv-2603-12679: Yanna Jiang and co-authors show that neural structural obfuscation cannot kill white-box watermarks for good. Obfuscation edits inject dummy neurons and rescale parameters while keeping function intact, which breaks watermark checks. The team recasts the attack as a graph-consistency problem between producer and consumer nodes. Their Canon framework probes the model to find dummy channels, then rewrites all downstream consumers in step. Under strong combined attacks, Canon reached 100% recovery and restored watermark checks with task performance intact.
arxiv-2603-12979: Peter Benner and co-authors speed up fixed-point methods for multi-term Sylvester equations with reduced rank extrapolation. They give proofs of convergence and code for both small and large cases. Large cases run an inexact method that changes over time and uses low-rank matrix forms. That keeps storage and run time down. In tests, the added step often cut the needed rounds by a large share. Gains showed up across the scales they tried.
arxiv-2603-13079: Thomas Alazard and Ayman Rimah Said study long-time regularity loss in the two-dimensional incompressible Euler equation. For smooth starting data, solutions exist for all time in the classic sense. The authors show that a dense G-delta set of starting data loses regularity as time runs to infinity. That settles, for smooth data, a conjecture Yudovich posed long ago. Generic smooth flows thus grow small scales without bound in the long run.
arxiv-2603-14179: Dhar, Goswami, and Li give partition meanings to several identities on Slater's list of Rogers-Ramanujan type identities. The list holds 130 series-product identities, many with no counting story for their series sides. The authors build separable integer partition classes that fit those series. Each class yields a natural partition reading and wider, parameterized versions. Standard q-series moves then turn some of these series into infinite products. The work opens a steady route into a classic list.
arxiv-2603-14379: Jafarzade and Lebed analyze hidden-strangeness tetraquarks in the dynamical diquark model. They compute the fine structure and fall-apart decay patterns of states built from a quark-antiquark pair plus a strange pair. Established resonances like phi(2170), eta(2225), and eta(2370) are checked as candidates. Two isovector states seen by BESIII also fit the assignment. Predictions cover 28 states in all, some with exotic quantum numbers. Clear decay channels give experiments at GlueX and BESIII a sharp test.
arxiv-2603-14679: Kellay and Omari characterize complete interpolating sequences for Fock-type spaces with radial weights. Only some weight classes admit such sequences at all. Their test rests on logarithmic separation plus tame shifts of a reference sequence. The reference sequence meets an Avdonin-type condition. The result gives a geometric picture of the full sequence set. It extends Riesz basis results by Borichev, Lyubarskii, Baranov and Belov. Clear density tests for sampling and interpolating sequences follow from the criterion.
arxiv-2603-14979: Wang and co-authors read single radioactive decays from charge jumps on a levitated microsphere. A silica sphere floats optically while its net charge is tracked. Driven response to an oscillating field resolves charge steps below one electron unit. Lead-212 decays inside the sphere drive the jumps. A nearby scintillator catches the alpha and beta particles in coincidence. Matched timing ties each charge jump to one decay. Alpha and beta decays eject charge in distinct patterns. Single-decay study of low-energy particles opens up.
arxiv-2603-15279: Davtyan and co-authors present LOOM-CFM, a way to speed up flow-based generative models by improving data-noise coupling. Conditional flow matching trains continuous normalizing flows without simulation. Minibatch optimal transport can re-pair noise and data, but it forgets those pairings between batches. LOOM-CFM keeps and refines assignments across minibatches over training time. The speed-quality trade-off improved on several datasets. The method also strengthens distillation starts and supports high-resolution synthesis in latent space.
arxiv-2603-15579: Mustata studies a new invariant of hypersurface singularities built from the log canonical threshold. For a hypersurface and a point on it, the invariant uses the threshold of the point's ideal times the Jacobian ideal. He shows it shares most formal traits of the log canonical threshold of the function itself. Worked examples fill out the picture. A question from Dano Kim asks if it always bounds the minimal exponent from above. He answers a weaker form in the positive and raises a related question.
arxiv-2603-15779: Rosen shows how hidden companion stars quietly skew stellar mass counts. Surveys fit single-star models to samples that hold many unresolved binaries. The mix pushes the high-mass slope low by a fixed amount. Error bars shrink as samples grow, while the bias stays put. Past a crossover size, the true slope falls outside the stated interval. She calls that regime confidently wrong. Two simple operators bound the bias across four settings. A binary-aware mixture fit recovers the true slope in her tests.
arxiv-2603-15979: Palomino and co-authors read black hole hair from ringdown wave tones. Quasinormal modes ring at rates set by the hole's shape. An eikonal link ties those modes to unstable light orbits. Hair enters as an anisotropic fluid laid over vacuum holes. Perturbations shift the photon orbit rate and Lyapunov exponent. Set formulas turn those shifts into fluid equation-of-state terms. Schwarzschild and Kerr spectra serve as the clean baselines. The method covers a broad class of hairy holes directly.
arxiv-2603-16079: Li and co-authors map energy flow among modes in a Mach 6 boundary layer. Single-wave transition stories miss how unlike instabilities interact. Their frame splits the input-output system by mode family. Linear dynamics with nonlinear forcing drive the test case. Two primary wave types enter the layer at once. Rising wave size saturates the second mode first. The first mode then takes a secondary growth turn. Set triadic forcing terms birth each higher-order wave. Base-flow leverage decides which forcings reach the response.
arxiv-2603-16179: Tran and co-authors build 360Bench, a test set for how well AI models read 360-degree images. The images have 7K resolution and cover seven question-answering tasks. Human annotators curated the set. They test seven multimodal models and six boost methods, and find clear gaps. The team then offers Free360, a training-free fix. Free360 breaks reasoning into steps, reshapes the image for each step, and merges results into one scene graph.
arxiv-2603-16779: Beloshapka gives an account of a method that turns a CR-manifold and its holomorphic automorphisms into algebraic objects. This algebraization lets tools from algebra act on questions in CR-geometry. He works through examples that show how the method is applied. He then lists open questions that the method raises. He also discusses whether the same approach could extend to other parts of geometry and analysis.
arxiv-2603-16879: Ezeakunne and co-authors present PowerModelsGAT-AI, a graph attention network that solves power flow for many grid systems at once. Classic Newton solvers can be slow under stress, and most learned models train on one system only. Their model predicts bus voltages and generator output, with masking that respects bus types. A physics based loss penalizes power mismatch. Trained on 13 benchmark systems under double outage conditions, it reached a mean voltage error of 0.89 percent. Continual learning tests kept new system errors below 2 percent, where plain fine tuning forgot badly.
arxiv-2603-17179: Ionescu and co-authors test an agentic AI system that audits clinical models for fairness. Their case is early onset colorectal cancer detection, where demographic disparities are known. The system has two agents. A domain expert agent sums up the literature on disparities. A fairness consultant agent suggests sensitive attributes and fairness metrics. An ablation study tested three Ollama models in three setups: model only, agent without retrieval, and agent with retrieval. The agent with retrieval matched expert reference texts best, above all on disparity spotting.
arxiv-2603-17479: Körmann and co-authors study how hydrogen enters high-entropy alloys that contain aluminum. They mix lab tests at high pressure with two kinds of computer models. One alloy forms hydrides above 3 gigapascals at room temperature. The aluminum-rich B2 alloy forms none, even when heated to 50 gigapascals. Aluminum raises the cost for hydrogen to dissolve and weakens the sites it would sit in, they find. What the alloy is made of drives uptake most.
arxiv-2603-17779: Song and co-authors rebuild crowds of people in 3D from a single photo. Prior methods favor clear close-ups of one person and falter in groups. Occlusion, blur, and varied looks make crowd work far harder. CrowdGaussian outputs multi-person 3D Gaussian splatting scenes in one framework. A self-supervised step completes hidden body parts with plausible shape. Self-calibrated learning then sharpens coarse renders toward photo quality, they report.
arxiv-2603-17879: Chary and Ganapathy build a classifier for capsule endoscopy videos with rare disease classes. The Galar data skew hard toward common findings, which crushes rare labels. Their system fuses three frames at a time to stress brief pathological signals. An angular loss keeps class prototypes apart so rare ones do not collapse. A biological state machine then cleans anatomy event streams. Temporal scores rose about 46 percent over the prior entry, they report.
arxiv-2603-18079: Wang and Jiang present SLEA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that fetches fresh experience at each step. Past methods pull experience once from the first task text and hold it fixed. In multi-turn work, later observations drift away from that early pull. SLEA-RL clusters step observations, keeps a self-evolving library of wins and failures, and assigns credit per step. Tests on long multi-turn agent benchmarks beat standard reinforcement baselines.
arxiv-2603-18179: Sanders proves a bound in Rado's single equation theorem for integer colorings. For non-zero integers a and b, some N below an exponential bound in r has a key property. In any r-coloring of one through N, one color class holds x, y, and z with a x minus a y equal to b z. The result gives an explicit size cap for this classic partition regularity claim.
arxiv-2603-18379: Kennedy and co-authors infer how galaxies fill dark halos with a method that sets no fixed shape. Fixed-shape halo models limit what forms the galaxy-halo link can take. Their emulator learns links among galaxy pair counts, sample traits, and halo fill rates from mock lightcones. In a likelihood frame, it recovers TNG100-1 fill rates to within 0.2 dex. Its precision and accuracy match or beat fixed-shape tools on the same mock samples.
arxiv-2603-18579: Basu and Chakraborty ask whether model explanations stay faithful when the test method changes. Their ICE framework checks explanations against random baselines of the same size. It uses several intervention operators across seven models and four tasks. Switching operators flips the verdict in 18 percent of attention comparisons. Gaps reach 44 points. Random baselines expose explanations worse than chance in near one third of English deletion tests. The pattern holds across six other languages and two attribution methods.
arxiv-2603-18979: Han and co-authors train humanoid robots to walk rough ground with a natural gait. Their PRIOR system runs in a common simulator and needs no multi-stage setup. A gait maker supplies steady step paths drawn from motion capture. A memory-based estimator reads depth images and infers ground shape on its own. Step rewards push feet toward safe spots. Tests span stairs, boxes, and gaps. Each part adds clear gains. The full system clears every trial in their tests, they report.
arxiv-2603-19079: King and co-authors study slim invariant surfaces that persist as a system passes a Hopf bifurcation. Such surfaces help shrink big models to a few key motions. Near the shift point, resonances can limit how smooth the surfaces stay. The team shows that low order terms of the surface pass through the shift smoothly. They bound the range where a parametric model stays sound. A data driven case on cavity flow tracks the full shift to periodic motion.
arxiv-2603-19179: Bhatti and co-authors study thin films that mix two magnetic oxides on a strontium titanate base. They grow a single layer and stacked layers with one and five repeats. X-ray tests show sharp, clean borders between the layers. The five-repeat stack switches its magnetism in two clear steps, while the single stack does not. Resonance tests show wide lines, strong directional pull, and damping near 0.01. The team links these traits to exchange coupling at the borders.
arxiv-2603-19279: Fesaghandis and Maity survey how to spot hate speech and craft replies across many languages. English-only tools often miss hidden hate and local idioms in mixed-language posts. The guide walks through three phases: task design, data curation, and evaluation. It gathers current data sets, models, and scoring methods for each phase. Gaps include thin data for low-resource tongues and bias in how systems are built. The authors close with steps toward fair, context-aware tools for online safety.
arxiv-2603-19579: Hu and Luo present PA2D-MORL, a method for reinforcement learning with several conflicting objectives. It aims to approximate the full Pareto policy set well. Pareto ascent directions guide the choice of scalarization weights. A multi-objective gradient then improves all objectives jointly. Many policies are tuned under an evolutionary frame, each from a different direction. Adaptive fine-tuning adds density and spread along the Pareto front. On robot control tasks, it beats the prior best method in quality and stability.
arxiv-2603-19879: Kuijpers, Winter, and Dijkman present a way to find decision synchronization patterns in event logs. Such patterns delay one running case to favor another, so scarce resources go to the most valued cases. Most process discovery tools look at one case at a time and miss these patterns. The authors formalize four patterns, each a process construct plus a selection constraint. Their method recovers the constraint for each pattern. Tests on artificial models show all four patterns can be found, alone and combined.
arxiv-2603-20179: Moreno and co-authors report that AI agents can already run a full experimental particle physics analysis on their own. Given data, an execution framework, and past literature, their agent handled every stage. Event selection, background estimates, uncertainty work, inference, and paper drafting all ran with little expert input. Their Just Furnish Context frame adds literature retrieval and multi-agent review. They argue the field underrates what these systems can do today. Analyses on open data from ALEPH, DELPHI, and CMS covered electroweak, QCD, and Higgs measurements.
arxiv-2603-20679: Li and Zhao improve vision based robot policies through knowledge distillation. Small mobile robots face tight compute, sensor cost, and weak scene transfer. Their teacher policy uses omni view depth input, rich but heavy. The student sees one plain camera view. Training makes the student copy both teacher acts and teacher inner features. Tests show omni view depth boosts transfer and navigation skill. The distilled single view policy beat plain imitation, and real robot trials confirmed the gain.
arxiv-2603-20879: Araújo and co-authors make optimization iterations run in parallel across processors. Standard gradient methods can need tens of thousands of steps on ill conditioned problems. Those steps run one by one, which can slow large simulations. Their method adapts multigrid reduction in time, a parallel time stepping scheme, to iteration sequences. They test it on a convex quadratic problem and an elastic obstacle problem. Both tests show fast convergence. They also give theory that links convergence to the base optimizer, plus predicted speedups.
arxiv-2603-21279: Du and co-authors revisit the excess of bar-like structures in TNG50 early-type galaxies. A morphology agnostic census finds these features in about three quarters of dispersion dominated galaxies. They are not prolate rotators. Instead, they are real non-axisymmetric instabilities with coherent but slow pattern speeds. The structures are longer and slower than bars in late-type galaxies. Their histories show they began as fast bars in gas rich discs at higher redshift. Quenching and friction slowed and stretched them into fossil bars.
arxiv-2603-21379: Iannacito and co-authors give a mode-parallel implementation of the Tucker and H-Tucker tensor decompositions using randomization. Low rank tensor factorizations reveal hidden structure in multidimensional data, but they cost heavy energy and memory. Most methods parallelize within each mode while still visiting modes one by one. Their strategies work along all modes at once, using fiber sampling and randomized range finding. Tests show lower run time and storage, with good scaling on HPC systems.
arxiv-2603-21679: Shen and co-authors teach two robot arms to cooperate on objects that one arm cannot handle directly. A flat tablet must first be pushed to a table edge; a pen cap needs the body lifted first. Their framework starts from the final goal action and works backward. A visual affordance model envisions that end state, then guides one arm through preparatory moves that set up its partner. This anticipatory planning spans long horizons and varied object types. In simulation and real trials, success rates and generalization beat strong baselines.
arxiv-2603-21979: Bes and co-authors uncover a shortcut in how energy cascades through quantum turbulence at zero temperature. Classical turbulence passes energy scale by scale, but their theory and simulations show a direct route. Energy jumps from the largest scales straight to very small ones, leaving nonclassical spectra behind. The trick needs two ingredients. Superfluid helium flows span a vast range of scales, and quantum vortices line up with the large-scale velocity gradients. That alignment mirrors vortex stretching in classical flows. The mechanism looks universal, the authors argue.
arxiv-2603-22279: Zhen and co-authors teach language models to edit 3D layouts from text instructions. The input is a scene graph plus a plain language request. The model reasons over the graph and returns an updated graph. The update must meet the request and keep the layout coherent. The team tests the method on sorting, alignment, and room editing tasks. Against chain-of-thought fine-tuning and plain GRPO, it lifts IoU by about 15 percent on average. Center-distance error drops by about 25 percent.
arxiv-2603-22379: Zou tests whether a LoRA adapter's label tells the truth about what it improves. Zou runs one adapter across many tasks and compares name against fact. The test target is strict, machine-checkable instruction following on IFEval. Across seeds, base models, and settings, the label often fails to predict gains there. In one case, an instruction-tuned adapter sharply lifts a numeric benchmark. Its verifiable instruction following does not rise at all. Zou calls the pattern capability drift. The advice: test adapters across tasks before shipping them.
arxiv-2603-22479: Hongler and co-authors propose a way to grow general skills in language models on purpose. Building such a curriculum by hand is an open problem, so they define a family of tasks called cross-entropy games. The games are meant to be universal in a suitable sense. The authors argue that greedy skill discovery then forces one clear meta-objective, up to a few settings. They call the resulting loop cognitive training. With strong enough models playing and sampling, they claim it could drive skill growth.
arxiv-2603-22579: Carlucci and co-authors measure the exact logical strength of a family of Ramsey-style theorems. Each principle colors the exactly alpha-large subsets of an infinite set of natural numbers. It then claims an infinite set on which the coloring is uniform. Alpha-largeness is defined through fundamental sequences in the style of Ketonen and Solovay. The authors prove the family matches, level for level, systems built from transfinite Turing jumps. The result gives a fine scale of strength between two classic benchmark systems.
arxiv-2603-22679: Liang, Xu, and Yang study character sums in the Frobenius formula for three permutations. They look at three conjugacy classes of the symmetric groups and ask how the sum behaves for large n. When two classes have fixed points of a set scale and the rest are long cycles, the sum settles at a clean limit. That limit involves an exponential factor matching the birthday paradox collision chance. When short cycles are rare in all three classes, the sum tends to two instead.
arxiv-2603-22879: Tao and co-authors study confidence calibration when ground truth is ambiguous. Standard calibrators fit majority-vote labels and can look well calibrated. Yet they may miss the true spread of annotator views. The authors show this flaw is structural for temperature scaling. It biases toward understating annotator uncertainty. Their ambiguity-aware calibrators fit the full label spread with no retraining. The best variant cuts true-label calibration error by more than half versus temperature scaling. A variant using one label per item matches it on all benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-23279: Sodano and three co-authors map the social network of Moltbook, a platform run by language model agents. Their scrape covers 39,924 users, 235,572 posts, and over 1.5 million comments. They build a directed network where edges mark commenting between agents. Activity and link counts follow heavy tails, so a few agents dominate. A tiny core of 0.9% of nodes holds much of the connectivity. The network shrugs off random node loss but breaks fast under targeted attacks. The authors warn that agent societies can centralize and turn fragile.
arxiv-2603-23479: Carmona-Moreno and four co-authors study coupled cavities that host intercavity polaritons. These hybrids keep their light and matter parts in separate cavities. Driving the middle polariton branch in resonance brings a new regime. Coherent Rabi oscillations fade, and the system glides straight to its steady state. With interactions on, this regime hosts Bogoliubov modes with phonon-like spread at low momenta. The modes borrow their interactions from the exciton part. They still keep the split, intercavity character of the host particles.
arxiv-2603-23579: Gogus and Khan study matrix-valued cut-down Toeplitz maps of a lopsided type. Such maps, they note, are not in general complex symmetric. The pair define a new mirror map with traits of its own. They trace how that mirror map links to the lopsided maps. They also probe ties to Hankel maps with matrix symbols. The work binds two map families through the new mirror map.
arxiv-2603-23679: Syeda and three co-authors teach harvest robots to judge which fruit they can reach. Full motion planning per fruit wastes time in messy orchards. Their system reads depth images and learns reach as a yes-no call. Active learning picks the most telling cases for labeling, so few labels go far. Tests beat random sampling by six to eight points of accuracy. Entropy and margin picks shine when labels are scarce. All query styles level out as the labeled set grows.
arxiv-2603-24079: Leng and co-authors compare safety risks in multimodal language models and diffusion models for image generation. The newer models understand text far better, which may raise risk. Across unsafe content benchmarks, these models produce more unsafe images than diffusion models. Diffusion models often fail to parse abstract prompts, while the newer models grasp them and comply. Their images are also harder for fake-image detectors to spot. Longer, richer prompts can bypass even retrained detectors. The authors warn these risks are under-recognized.
arxiv-2603-24179: Magi and co-authors extend weak gravitational lensing theory to second order in relativity. The standard lensing map uses only the deflection angle, which is exact only at first order. With the Jacobi map formalism, they derive the rotation field, shear B-modes, and their spectra at second order. Careful transport of the Sachs basis breaks a known degeneracy between rotation and B-mode spectra. The change is about 5 percent on large scales for sources at redshift 0.5. Frame dragging dominates B-modes on the largest scales.
arxiv-2603-24279: Pousset and co-authors turn the Talbot self-imaging effect into quantum gates for time-frequency qubits. The Talbot effect makes a periodic wavefront re-form at set distances. Moved to time and frequency, it acts on entangled photon pairs encoded as GKP qubits. The authors show it implements Clifford operations on those qubits.
