It also gives the branching fraction for a lambda baryon decaying to a proton, muon, and antineutrino, plus form-factor parameters from a B-meson decay to a charm meson, muon, and neutrino. Together they test the Standard Model and possible new physics.
arxiv-2604-26979: Moureaux and two colleagues present a tool for N-ary in-memory crossbar architectures that retrieve matrix-vector results with minimal assumptions. Such computing performs matrix-vector products in memory arrays, promising energy gains. XOR and MNIST tasks run on an array of 4 by 4 magnetic tunnel junctions, with MNIST accuracy near 94 percent versus a higher software baseline. PCA reduction sharply cuts operations and lifts the baseline, for only a modest crossbar score cost. Weight quantization is the top error source, and cell noise proves less harmful than errors.
arxiv-2604-27179: Faust and Scheunemann propose EMSL, a simple and efficient reduced strain-space model order method. It targets hyperelastic sample blocks. The method groups the material domain into regions of similar behavior. It queries the material routine at one reference strain per region. Unlike the earlier E3C approach, it samples those strains only once per load increment. It uses typical values guessed from data. The stiffness at a reference point and strain measures then drive rapid online runs.
arxiv-2604-27679: Inoue and five colleagues demonstrate a parametrically driven iSWAP gate at zero flux bias between detuned transmon qubits coupled through a capacitively shunted double-transmon coupler. Using a simple flux-drive pulse without predistortion, they reach an average gate fidelity of 99.92 percent in 112 ns of total gate time. The high fidelity matches weak qubit-coupler hybridization plus weak effective ZZ coupling during the gate. Simulations reproduce the seen coupling rate and effective ZZ coupling, backing the theoretical model for both spectral and time-domain dynamics.
arxiv-2604-27779: F. Tolea and M. Tolea model solid-state phase change as nucleation and growth of plain plates. Squares, cubes, or lamellae grow alike until a random cap or a clash with earlier plates stops them. The reverse change drops smaller plates first while larger plates stay, so a later change yields a modified mix, a memory effect. Extending a flat model to cubes and lamellae, they introduce the size mass ratio as memory measure. Memory proves robust in all shapes but stronger in two dimensions than in three.
arxiv-2604-27979: Seoev and colleagues ask where arbitrage chances on blockchains actually come from, rather than how traders exploit them. They build four attribution methods and test them on over a million Polygon blocks, finding most atomic arbitrage traces to a single source transaction. Creation proves highly concentrated in a few protocols, a pattern useful to designers curbing leakage, validators ordering transactions and analysts gauging ecosystem health.
arxiv-2604-28179: Dunn Beltran's team removes the need for breath-hold protocols in bronchoscopic navigation, where breathing shifts the airway by millimetres and breaks CT alignment. Matching paired inhale-exhale CT scans reduces breathing motion to a single phase per frame, and a light reader reads that phase from scope video alone. Built into a mesh-based Gaussian splatting system, the method rebuilds the airway all through the breathing cycle. It pins targets down within clinical tolerances, far faster to train than unconstrained baselines.
arxiv-2605-00279:
Zawad Yalmie Sazid, Robert Abbas, and Sasa Maric compare machine learning models for spotting intrusions in intelligent transport systems. Connected vehicles, roadside units, and 5G links widen the surface attackers can reach, while roadside edge nodes have limited computing power. Protection therefore has to run close to the traffic itself.

The paper proposes a trust-aware federated hybrid detection framework. At each edge site, a random forest, a decision tree, and a linear support vector machine each learn their own view of the traffic. A central server then merges the local updates, weighting each site by trust. The design aims at proactive, low-latency defense that can work without constant human control.
arxiv-2605-00479:
Tom Kimpson, Mark B. Flegg, and Jennifer A. Flegg ask whether cheaper math can speed the stochastic simulation algorithm, the exact workhorse for random processes in biology. It crawls event by event, and large runs make it costly. Weather and climate work had already gained from working at fewer bits, which prompted the test.

Across five classic models from biology, their first approach, scoring reaction rates in 16-bit while keeping totals at 32-bit, matched the 64-bit standard closely. Doing it all in 16-bit brought in steady biases under plain rounding, sometimes badly. Rounding that uses chance, plus a scaling step, removed those biases and brought the match back across the board. The payoff is smaller memory footprints and a modest wall-clock speedup on current hardware, with larger gains likely on chips built for 16-bit math.
arxiv-2605-00579:
Kamila Szewczyk speeds up a small, crucial step inside data compression. Fast range coders and asymmetric numeral systems replace slow division with bit shifts, which works only when symbol frequencies are normalized to sum to a power of two. Normalization always distorts the distribution slightly, costing compression ratio, measured as added Kullback-Leibler divergence. Szewczyk shows the methods in current use are suboptimal twice over, in both running time and distortion.

The proposed method runs in time linear in the number of symbols and achieves the smallest divergence any normalization can reach. It rests on solving a separable concave optimization problem, which Szewczyk notes may interest readers beyond compression. The result is a drop-in improvement to a primitive that sits underneath widely used entropy coders: same interface, provably best fidelity to the original frequencies, and a faster algorithm to compute it.
arxiv-2605-00779:
Elsa Barrio-Torres and five co-authors test how well climate models reproduce summer air circulation over the Iberian Peninsula. They examine thirty-six historical CMIP6 model runs for 1979 to 2005 against ERA5 reanalysis, using the Lamb Weather Type scheme to classify daily circulation. Their framework also checks how types persist and change from one day to the next.

Daily frequencies alone kept sixteen runs, but adding persistence and transition checks narrowed the set to twelve. Models from the EC-Earth3 family performed best and most consistently, led by one aerchem run. Skill was stronger in the northwest and weaker in central and southern Mediterranean areas. The authors argue transition checks select models far better than daily counts alone.
arxiv-2605-00979:
Andreas Stergiou and Nicolas P. D. Sawaya prove that hardware-efficient quantum gates are universal for making states inside tight subspaces, such as those with fixed particle number or spin. Simulating physical systems on near-term quantum computers often requires staying inside such subspaces. Using Lie algebra methods, they pin down Pauli Z dressing as the key mechanism: commutators of overlapping gates produce projectors that split rotations into generators spanning the full algebra.

Adding separate complex phases extends the result from real to arbitrary complex state preparation. An efficient Jacobian criterion verifies whether a circuit can explore any direction from almost any parameter setting. Applications include Hubbard models and molecular structure, plus a completeness proof for a particle-number ansatz and symmetry-preserving circuits for a fuzzy sphere model.
arxiv-2605-01679:
Joydeb Kumar Sana detects falls among older people from wearable sensor data without leaking the private activity records behind the training. Falls demand fast response, yet the motion data that teach a detector are deeply personal, and standard privacy noise, spread evenly over all samples, dulls the model.

His framework sizes the noise to the class mix of each training batch instead. Batches rich in rare fall examples are treated differently from routine-activity batches. All this sits under a formal differential privacy guarantee that he proves and prices against utility. The detector itself pairs a 3D convolutional network with a bidirectional memory layer. On the SisFall, UP-Fall, and MobiAct benchmarks, scores rise over the uniform-noise model by clear margins on each set, and signed-rank tests confirm the edge is consistent. Formal privacy guarantees, the author notes, are what most earlier fall studies skipped.
arxiv-2605-01779:
Giuseppe A Orlando and four co-authors write CT scan reports by sending a language model out to gather proof before it speaks. Vision-language models that compress a whole volume into one embedding tend to invent findings and lose the anatomy, a dangerous habit in radiology.

MedScribe treats reporting as sequential decisions. The model forms hypotheses and calls pathology-specific tools that pull localized features from the volume, then queries a retrieval space where each pathology sits beside its textual evidence. Only after this quantitative evidence piles up does it synthesize the report. With no task-specific fine-tuning, the system beats leading 2D and 3D report models on two chest CT benchmarks in clinical accuracy, factual consistency, and interpretability. The authors present hypothesis-driven gathering, not bigger embeddings, as the route to reports a radiologist could trust.
arxiv-2605-01879:
Manuel Hernández and Eduardo Sánchez-Soto propose Sheaf-Theoretic Planning, a new base for planning by groups of autonomous agents. Older systems used logic tools such as event calculus and situation calculus to track action and change. Those tools work well in a closed world, but they struggle when agents act unseen, plans break, or beliefs drift from reality.

Sheaf theory, from category theory, offers a way to join local views into a global picture only when they agree. The report works through the maths, the prospects for building such a system, and its limits. The authors present it as a path toward agent teams that stay coherent under surprise and attack.
arxiv-2605-02379:
Andrea Forster and colleagues propose a design for fair personalisation by language model agents, when several stakeholders want different things. Such agents can talk with users and draw on outside knowledge. They can also negotiate with other agents, human or artificial. In a multi-stakeholder system, each agent may serve one party's goals. How those goals are set and joined decides whether outcomes stay fair.

The authors map open research challenges and propose a conceptual framework. It joins methods to align stakeholder goals with agent goals. It also covers ways to aggregate agent outputs, drawn in part from social choice theory. The aim is balanced personalisation that can be measured, not rule by one party.
arxiv-2605-02679:
Fabio Leoni and four co-authors review computational methods for making ultrastable glasses, solids frozen into exceptionally low-energy states. Such glasses are more stable in energy, motion, and strength than ordinary ones, and experiments have long prized them. Simulations can reach these states with unphysical moves that bypass slow cooling, opening a window on the glass transition itself.

The review lays out the key steps of the most effective algorithms in the field. For each, the authors discuss how well it works, where it falls short, and what it means physically. A comparative analysis then ranks the stability each method achieves. The aim is to give newcomers and experts alike a clear map of current methods and the chances they offer for designing robust glassy materials.
arxiv-2605-02779:
Erkinjon Karimov and Muzaffar Toshpulatov solve an inverse source problem for a mixed equation that blends wave and diffusion behavior, set inside a cylindrical domain. Inverse problems work backward from observed effects to the source that caused them. Here the governing equation carries a time-fractional derivative whose order varies with time, letting the model shift between wave-like and diffusive regimes as conditions change.

The solution is built as a Fourier-Bessel series, the natural expansion for a cylinder, using separation of variables and classic traits of Bessel functions. The authors analyze when the infinite series converges uniformly, a key step in trusting the formula. That analysis leads to a rigorous proof that a solution exists. The paper is a methods contribution to fractional mixed-type equations.
arxiv-2605-02979:
Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das propose a formal risk-cost model for adaptive login checks in finance, where a small rise in false acceptance can mean huge loss. Adaptive systems blend biometrics, behavior signals, and context risk scores. Current designs are fragmented, though, and often serve compliance first. Explicit modeling of economic and hostile risk is rare. That imbalance is the paper's target.

The model joins three parts. Cost-sensitive risk functions capture fraud loss, lost chance, and tail risk in one measure. Step-by-step decision rules adapt as hostile users probe and patterns drift. Privacy and rule limits sit inside the core optimization itself, not as an afterthought. Login checking becomes a dynamic risk-cost problem with hard limits: grounded in economics and aware of tail risk, rather than a static classifier.
arxiv-2605-03079:
Vamshi Nallaguntla, Shruti Kshirsagar, and Anderson R. Avila propose checking fake speech sound by sound, rather than treating each clip as one block. New voice tools can fake emotion as well as words, which makes detection harder and past methods hard to interpret.

Working with real and converted speech matched for emotion and transcript, they align phonemes and compare WavLM embeddings for each sound. Complex vowels and fricatives diverged most, while simple sounds stayed stable. Sounds with larger gaps were also easier to flag, across emotions and systems, making the approach both effective and readable.
arxiv-2605-03179:
Richard J. Young and Gregory D. Moody build a vetted prompt bank that separates requests for working malicious code from requests for harmful security knowledge. Safety benchmarks often mix the two, so a single refusal rate cannot show which pathway a model actually used.

Five judge models from four vendor families labeled over three thousand prompts from four public benchmarks under a majority rule. Agreement was near-perfect, and no prompts fell below the consensus threshold. The released bank holds over fifteen hundred code prompts plus a knowledge comparison set. Whether the split predicts model behavior is left to a companion study.
arxiv-2605-03379:
Yi Liu studies how much repeated language model sampling helps binary decisions under majority vote, and how to forecast those gains before spending the compute. Extra calls cost money, so sharp bounds on vote accuracy at each budget matter for test-time planning.

Just two independent answers per validation example, Liu shows, pin down a class of latent success distributions consistent with the paired outcomes. Optimizing over that class gives sharp accuracy and gain bounds at every finite budget, plus infinite-vote limits and curve forecasts. On two question datasets, the method separated settings with real voting gains from those with little headroom.
arxiv-2605-03779:
Nathan Findlay and Seshadri Nadathur present VERSUS, a fast, public algorithm for finding cosmic voids, the large spherical underdensities in the distribution of galaxies. The finder is inspired by excursion set theory, which predicts how many voids of each size should exist. It is designed for the Stage-IV survey era.

Checks use a synthetic particle distribution tracing a known void population, plus mock galaxy samples from a large AbacusSummit simulation with a realistic galaxy-halo link and survey-like systematic effects. In all cases VERSUS matched theoretical predictions for the void size function across the tested radius range, with no post-processing of the catalogue needed. Its speed and modular design support simulation-based models for upcoming surveys.
arxiv-2605-04279:
Ayan Pendharkar develops a theory of how tokens move and cluster inside multi-head self-attention, the core mechanism of transformer models. A single attention head can be viewed as a flow that pulls tokens together, but several heads interfere with each other in ways that break simple arguments.

Pendharkar defines a combined energy for the multi-head case and shows when it grows steadily along the flow. He identifies extra radial terms as the key obstacle, gives a condition that restores the steady behaviour, and checks that it survives when heads are only roughly separate. A simplified setting yields an exact threshold for clustering.
arxiv-2605-04379:
Andrey Kupavskii and Georgy Sokolov work on a classic problem in combinatorics about families of subsets that contain no large collection of pairwise disjoint sets. Erdős and Kleitman settled the maximum size of such families for certain set sizes in 1968, but many sizes stayed open for decades.

Later work tied the best examples to a famous matching conjecture for a range of parameters, and conjectured the tie holds more broadly. Kupavskii and Sokolov prove an approximate version of that conjecture for large enough parameters. Their result supports the view that the same extremal structures govern both problems.
arxiv-2605-04879:
Ray Ganardi studies catalysis in entanglement manipulation, where a helper quantum state enables a change that would otherwise be forbidden. The helper must be returned intact at the end, like a catalyst in chemistry. Most earlier work looked at single copies, while Ganardi focuses on preparing many copies of a target state at once.

He constructs an explicit catalytic protocol and shows it can significantly lower the exact entanglement cost of that preparation. The gain is not limited to entanglement alone. Ganardi notes the same idea extends to other resource theories, giving a general catalytic advantage in the task known as resource dilution.
arxiv-2605-04979:
Anvay Shah and three co-authors learn online in tree-shaped decision problems by treating each whole policy as one arm of a bandit problem. Tree decision problems model sequential games with perfect recall against steady opponents. The catch is that the number of possible policies grows exponentially with the number of states, far too many to track naively.

Their innovation is confidence bounds built from data shared across policies, letting known bandit algorithms run with polynomial memory and step cost. The resulting guarantees add a gap term per end state rather than per policy. In tests on hidden-information games, their algorithms consistently beat the available alternatives.
arxiv-2605-05079:
Maxim Shugaev and ten co-authors present a benchmark for fixing video filmed through rough air or water surfaces, where refraction warps each frame. Existing tests mostly cover mild air shimmer, leaving strong and broken-up warping unmeasured. Their benchmark spans from mild warping to extreme refractive bending, using both lab footage and computer-made clips built with physics-based bending.

Methods from simple baselines and classical matching to advanced learning approaches are scored with pixel, visual, and meaning measures. A proposed diffusion-based method is included for the hardest regimes. The authors frame the release as the first large-scale analysis of warping removal, and a foundation for fixing video from badly distorted optical settings.
arxiv-2605-05179:
Wilson Wu and six co-authors question a basic habit in machine learning: estimating a model's expected loss by sampling. Sampling means running many random inputs through a network and averaging the results. For a wide, freshly initialized multilayer network, they show there is a cheaper way.

Their method tracks how signal distributions change from layer to layer, using cumulants and Hermite expansions. It reaches a target accuracy with far fewer operations than sampling needs. The method is especially strong at estimating rare-event chances, and the authors also show it can be used during training itself.
arxiv-2605-05279:
Violeta Leoreanu-Fotea and three co-authors present quasi sdf-absorbing ideals, a new, broader form of a known ideal class in commutative ring theory. Ideals are special subsets of a ring, and absorbing traits describe how products of members are forced back inside them. The authors study when this quasi version of the property survives standard ring builds.

They check whether it lasts under localisation, surjective images, Nagata idealisations, and amalgamations of rings. Rules are set out for the radical of such an ideal to be prime, and a class of rings is named where the quasi property rises to a primary version. The study closes with a sorting of these ideals in the whole numbers, with cases that split them from nearby classes.
arxiv-2605-05479:
Talal Ahmed Chowdhury, Seokwon Choi, Kyoungchul Kong, and Kwangmin Yu simulate a model of interacting particles on real quantum hardware. Their target is the multi-flavor Gross-Neveu model, a one-dimensional theory used to test ideas about fermions. The simulations ran on superconducting processors with more than one hundred qubits.

A new approximation, called LDOA, cuts the cost of the four-particle interaction terms. Circuit depth then grows with the number of flavors rather than the system size. Results matched exact calculations and tensor-network checks across sizes, showing that careful circuit design can make field-theory simulation practical today.
arxiv-2605-05679:
Pulsar timing arrays listen for a background hum of gravitational waves from merging supermassive black holes. Shreyas Tiruvaskar and Chris Gordon use that hum to compare theories of how the binaries evolve. Ultralight dark matter, environmental effects, and pure gravitational-wave emission each predict different low-frequency power.

The authors apply Bayesian leave-one-out cross-validation to the five lowest frequency bins. Four models compete, including simplified and realistic dark matter versions. Earlier work had already used the friction effect to bound the dark matter particle's mass and its share of the total. The environmental-hardening model scored best on predictive accuracy, though its margin over the others was small compared with the uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-05779:
Bound states in the continuum trap light with, in theory, infinite lifetime; real fabrication always leaks. Nikolai A. Vlasov and six co-authors test how robust such states are in a metasurface of phase-change material bars. Lithography rarely cuts perfect rectangles, so they model bars as trapezoids and vary the imperfections.

Identical trapezoid shapes, despite keeping the required symmetry, lowered the quality factor in the amorphous phase through absorption changes. Random angle variations from bar to bar, by contrast, left the quality factor largely intact in both material phases. The study separates which imperfections matter from which can be tolerated.
arxiv-2605-06279:
Chengjie Wang and four co-authors measure a hidden risk in code written by language models: the library versions they specify. Generated Python code routinely imports third party libraries pinned to exact versions, and those choices can carry known flaws or break installation. No systematic study of version level risk existed before this large scale measurement on a benchmark of 1,000 programming tasks across ten models.

Models specified versions often, and between about a third and over half of tasks included at least one version with a known vulnerability. Most of those flaws were public before the model's knowledge cutoff, and models converged on the same small set of risky releases. Compatibility failures, mostly at installation, were also common. External version constraints cut both problems sharply.
arxiv-2605-06379:
Yu-Xuan Zhang and Jing-Ling Chen extract exact solutions of Yang-Mills theory with an algebraic tensor ring framework. The theory's nonlinear equations resist direct solution, yet exact classical solutions clarify its nonperturbative vacuum structure. Their method maps the nonlinear partial differential equations into differential algebraic systems that can be resolved systematically. It uses static pure gauge backgrounds as geometric templates. Their forms generate the cross terms that stabilize self interaction in the equations.

Three classes of exact solutions emerge. Relativistic color waves over an elliptic quotient ring split into decoupled and coupled branches, the latter generating a mass gap. Dynamic dyonic flux tubes branch into Coulomb, dyonic, and screening phases with Bessel type decay. A third family covers dynamic configurations of the larger gauge group, whose real branches hide a chaotic oscillator at their core.
arxiv-2605-06479:
Joshi and three colleagues keep deployed policies safe with little meddling. Predictive models often act through existing policies stakeholders will not change unless a risk rule forces one. Risk-controlled post-processing asks: given a fixed baseline policy, choose a new policy that agrees with the baseline as much as possible while meeting a chance constraint on a chosen loss. At the population level, the optimal policy follows a threshold rule. It sticks to the baseline except where switching to an oracle fallback cuts risk sharply.

With finite samples, a fitted fallback and score plus calibration data select the threshold. Expected excess risk then falls at a log-over-n rate under standard conditions. When an exact-safe fallback exists, the method achieves precise expected risk control under exchangeability. Tests on COVID-19 diagnosis, language-model routing, and synthetic decisions meet budgets while preserving far more baseline agreement than blind mixing.
arxiv-2605-06579:
Angus Mingare and Peter V. Coveney show how to load matrix product states onto quantum computers with shallow, log-depth circuits. Such states classically describe many quantum systems and could serve as reference states for algorithms like phase estimation. Loading them efficiently is essential for near-term hardware, where deep circuits decay quickly.

Their method uses a simple tree tensor network renormalization step, with an explicit knob that trades a little fidelity for large depth savings. Extended to operators, it also builds ancilla-free circuits for computing overlap quantities. Those circuits double as verifier circuits, with a use in calibrating quantum devices at the circuit level.
arxiv-2605-06879:
Zhongmou Chao and four co-authors predict protein function while correcting for survivorship bias in natural sequence data. Databases hold proteins only from organisms that lived, so working examples dominate and failed mutations stay unseen. Learning from positive cases alone is a known problem class, but generic methods ignore the process of evolution that decides which sequences ever get seen.

Their Evo-PU framework models nucleotide mutation in plain terms: a missing sequence one step from a common variant is suspect, while one mutation never arose is merely unseen. On flu, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 tasks it beats standard PU methods and one-class classifiers and protein language models, with caveats noted for messier multi-organism data.
arxiv-2605-07079:
Xinyu Zhang and five co-authors build world models that predict future visual features rather than raw video. Feature prediction can be faster and less prone to invented detail than image generation. Yet direct prediction often turns blurry or collapses during complex interactions.

The team found a new latent action signal hidden in differences between visual features, and showed it predicts how scenes progress. Their model generates that signal with flow matching, beating leading feature and video models while running far faster than video diffusion. Two robot methods built on it improve policy learning, including one trained entirely inside the learned world model.
arxiv-2605-07379:
Xin Chen and six co-authors teach visual object trackers to localize targets through reinforcement learning instead of handcrafted heatmaps. Conventional trackers rely on spatial priors that give only surrogate supervision, poorly aligned with the overlap and success measures used to judge tracking. RELO reframes localization as a decision process over positions.

A learned policy picks locations, rewarded by frame-level overlap and sequence-level success together. A token propagation method keeps meaning consistent across frames at negligible cost. Across benchmarks, RELO beat rivals and reached a strong success score on a hard text-guided dataset without template updates, confirming reward-driven localization as a real alternative.
arxiv-2605-07479:
Ziwei Ou, Xiaolong Yang, and Songpeng Pei report extended gamma-ray emission around the young star cluster Berkeley 59, using data from the Fermi space telescope. With updated catalogs and background models, they find significant emission spread over about a degree, well beyond a point source. The team then examines the surrounding molecular, neutral, and ionized gas.

The gamma-ray spectrum and the modest derived gas mass feed a relationship between cosmic ray acceleration efficiency and diffusion. Their results suggest the glow comes from cosmic rays accelerated by the cluster's winds striking nearby gas. The study links a single young cluster's outflows to high-energy emission visible across interstellar distances.
arxiv-2605-07579:
Yunho Choi and five co-authors improve reinforcement learning for reasoning models, where training needs a reliable baseline score to reduce noise. Group methods estimate that baseline from several tries at the same prompt, which crowds out prompt variety. Training a separate critic model avoids that trade-off but roughly doubles the cost.

Their algorithm, POISE, reads the baseline from the model's own internal states using a small probe trained alongside the policy. A cross-rollout trick keeps the gradient estimates unbiased. On two open model families and a six-domain reward corpus, POISE beat other baselines and trained more stably. The probe matched a full separate value model and stayed accurate as the policy grew.
arxiv-2605-07879:
Silvia Gasparotto works out gravitational-wave memory, the permanent low-frequency displacement left by passing waves, in a theory that modifies Einstein's gravity. Memory is a promising probe of strong-field gravity, but it had never been computed from full inspiral-merger-ringdown waveforms beyond general relativity. Gasparotto does so for scalar Gauss-Bonnet gravity.

The deviations from general relativity come out at the percent level, driven mainly by the changed merger dynamics, while the scalar field's own share of tensor memory is strongly damped. Including memory in the waveform greatly increases the mismatch between the modified theory and general relativity. That makes memory an extra observable for testing gravity with the next generation of detectors.
arxiv-2605-07979:
Santiago Cortes-Gomez and three co-authors study how to split a fixed aid budget between algorithm-led targeting and human screening. Machine learning hands out aid by predicted risk, cheaply and quickly, while physical checking sees true need directly but costs more. Even perfect risk scores cannot remove misallocation, because each person's vulnerability carries a chance that cannot be removed.

In their two-stage framework, a screening stage checks a chosen subset before final allocation. The optimal strategy screens the units at the margin of the algorithmic decision, those near the cutoff, while sending aid straight to the highest-risk units without screening. Screening and targeting act as complements or substitutes depending on conditions, and screening's gains grow as group uncertainty rises. Uses in Colombian social protection and humanitarian demining ground the theory.
arxiv-2605-08079:
Pavel Orlov, Rustem Sharipov, and Enej Ilievski refine the eigenstate thermalization picture. That picture explains how lone quantum systems settle down. The standard view ties matrix elements of local quantities to macrostate data. Those data are the densities of conserved charges.

The team shows the spreads can also hinge on the ensemble used to sample eigenstates. They swap fixed energy windows for ensembles with a tunable scale for charge spread. Their test bed is an integrable field theory. It allows fast sampling and clean scaling to large size. One class of states even allows closed-form work. The results reveal a multiscale pattern in thermalization data.
arxiv-2605-08379:
Jonathon Hirschi, Jan Mandel, and Adam Kochanski adapt a fuel moisture model across fuel types by warping time. Dead fuel moisture drives wildfire behavior models. Fuels are classed by their lag time. The classes run from one-hour twigs to thousand-hour logs. Sensors report the ten-hour class richly. The other classes are observed sparsely.

Their method rescales the learned dynamics of a recurrent network with an LSTM layer. It stretches or compresses time. A model trained on ten-hour fuels can then predict the slower and faster classes. Validation uses a landmark Oklahoma field study. That study calibrated the standard Nelson model. The test asks whether time warping is a sound bridge between fuel classes.
arxiv-2605-09079:
Astorga and two colleagues attack a stubborn weakness of large language models: causal reasoning, the ability to answer what if questions. Models beat humans at maths and coding, yet they stumble on causal questions, partly because causal systems are complex and true answers to causal queries are scarce. Their framework, CauSim, turns causal reasoning from a label starved problem into a scalable supervised one.

It builds increasingly complex causal simulators, runnable structural causal models assembled step by step by language models, which scale to globally complex systems while keeping answers verifiable. CauSim works across representations, formalising non executable causal knowledge into code for data augmentation, and informalising executable models back into natural language for supervision. The study shows generalisation across representations, steady gains from curriculum scaling and data volume, and self improvement through self generated simulators. It also shows data augmentation through formalisation of existing domain knowledge.
arxiv-2605-09279:
Yin and nine colleagues build CAGS, an adaptive volumetric video streaming system for 3D Gaussian splatting correcting colour distortion under fluctuating bandwidth. Volumetric video turns streaming into a live link to remote places, demanding photorealistic scenes, low latency, and robustness under varied networks. Density based detail levels suit Gaussian representations poorly, causing visible gaps and quality loss, while aggressive compression mainly distorts colour.

The team's Color-Adaptive scheme uses vector quantisation for levels of detail and corrects colour distortions with low resolution reference images. CAGS renders reference images on the server and restores colour on the client, compatible with diverse Gaussian representations. Prototype tests show CAGS beats adaptive streaming systems by 5 to 20 dB in PSNR under fluctuating bandwidth, runs far faster than scalable Gaussian compression, and generalises across Gaussian representations. The work targets telepresence, ecological surveillance, and robotic teleoperation, where video must stay vivid as bandwidth varies.
arxiv-2605-09479:
Ding and five colleagues study image quality from a machine-centred angle. Traditional assessment rests on signal fidelity or human agreement, yet many pipelines end with images consumed by downstream models like classifiers and detectors. A good measure should show how well a distorted image keeps task-relevant information across downstream models.

The authors frame machine-oriented quality as a hidden utility, gauged through pairwise predictive-consistency comparisons. They build a predictive consistency dataset, where PSNR-matched pairs carry soft labels from consistency votes of pretrained models. Their ML-CLIPSim metric, built on a frozen CLIP encoder, blends mid-level patch-token features and global embeddings, capturing local evidence loss and semantic consistency. It beats conventional fidelity and perceptual metrics on machine preference, staying competitive on human judgments. As a loss term for learned compression, it improves rate-task trade-offs across downstream tasks and codecs.
arxiv-2605-09679:
Chen and nine colleagues built a test that grades medical AI on three-dimensional CT scans of tumors, step by step instead of with one overall score. Their benchmark, DeepTumorVQA, follows the chain of evidence doctors use in tumor diagnosis, from spotting a tumor to measuring it and reasoning about what it means. It covers 42 clinical subtypes across more than 9,000 scan volumes.

The team created 476,000 questions and ran more than 30 model setups through them. Reliable measurement turned out to be the main weak point, and later reasoning steps grew harder still when measurement failed. Giving models outside tools, such as programs that outline tumors and measure them, eased the problem a great deal. Doctors and AI researchers can use the benchmark to find exactly where a medical system breaks down.
arxiv-2605-09779:
Ducimetière and Shelley model a thin suspension of rod-shaped particles that swim at steady speed through a slow, viscous flow. As the particles spread less by diffusion, a uniform soup of randomly pointed rods gives way to organised motion. It passes through one of two bifurcations, sharp changes of behaviour, chosen by swimming speed. A weakly nonlinear expansion shrinks the full system to a small set of equations for the amplitudes of the unstable patterns.

Past the onset, the particles settle into steady patterns or oscillating patterns of joint motion. In the oscillating case two stable cycles coexist, each a different dance of the swarm. Random forcing can flip the system between them, but only rarely. The authors compute very long mean waiting times and the unlikely paths between cycles, using both a probability equation and a rare-event sampling algorithm.
arxiv-2605-09979: Spin-1 dark matter coupling through the Higgs portal, with parity-violating interactions, could explain the galactic halo's mysterious gamma ray excess. This 2026 paper builds the case with care. It is particle astrophysics: dark matter with a handedness. It gives the gamma-ray excess a particle explanation.
arxiv-2605-10079:
Ouyang and four co-authors give video generators direct control over social interaction between people, a need in film production and social robotics. Current models offer no say over who does what, when, or toward whom, producing actor-action mix-ups, tangled social flow and wrong targets. Their training-free tool, SocialDirector, steers generation by tuning cross-attention maps.

Two modules share the work. Social Actor Masking restricts each person's visual tokens to their own text description through a space-time mask, blocking mismatches and disordered dynamics. Directional Reweighting boosts attention to pointing words like leftward or right, steering each action toward its target. An automated testing line built on open-source vision-language models shows SocialDirector clearly improving interaction fidelity, approaching the ceiling set by real videos.
arxiv-2605-10279:
Robin Manhaeve and six colleagues present DeepLog, a software framework that unites logic and deep learning inside ordinary PyTorch workflows. The field that joins neural learning with symbolic reasoning has splintered into many incompatible systems, an alphabet soup of paradigms and meanings. This 2026 paper offers one shared backend instead.

DeepLog treats diverse logic-based languages as high-level specs and compiles them by itself into optimized arithmetic circuits. Logic becomes a composable module for machine-learning users, while developers gain a common, fast base for prototyping. Unlike most rivals, it also runs symbolic parts on the GPU, avoiding slow transfers to the CPU. The code is public, and the framework can emulate many existing systems in the field.
arxiv-2605-10379:
Ivo Petrov and three colleagues argue that correctness alone is too low a bar for machine-generated math proofs. Proofs should also be clear, concise, insightful, and portable to other problems. Their 2026 paper introduces ProofRank, a benchmark curated from hard math contests, rating scalable proxies of proof quality beyond being right.

ProofRank rates five traits. Conciseness means avoiding needless steps. Computational ease means avoiding tedious calculations. Cognitive simplicity means using accessible techniques. Diversity means varying proofs for one problem. Adaptivity means following a specified proof technique. Across models, the authors find large quality gaps invisible to correctness-only benchmarks. They also observe strong trade-offs between quality metrics and being right, suggesting that future tests of math reasoning should measure how useful generated proofs actually are.
arxiv-2605-10579:
Yu-Hsiang Liu and two colleagues generate egocentric video to train assistant AI agents. Training agents to help humans daily, from household to safety cases, requires large visual data. Capturing such scenes in real life is often difficult, costly, or unsafe. Simulators lack the visual fidelity to transfer learned behaviors to real life. Their 2026 paper introduces VISTA.

VISTA is a video system producing vivid egocentric videos for training AI agents. It uses a script pipeline with reverse reasoning to create diverse intervention modes. Scenarios span two autonomy levels: reactive and proactive. In reactive modes, the user requests help from the agent. In proactive modes, the agent steps in unasked. Explicit types cover users who know help is needed but do not address the agent. Implicit types cover agents intervening before the user realizes help is needed. VISTA lets users customize video benchmarks for daily tasks.
arxiv-2605-11379: Shojiro Takeyama reviews megagauss physics, where destructive pulsed magnets create ultrastrong fields from 100 to 1,000 tesla. The review focuses on single-turn coil and electromagnetic flux compression methods. These best support precise measurement, including recent breakthroughs past 1,000 tesla. It describes miniaturized all-plastic cryostats and custom holders for magneto-optics, magnetization and magneto-transport. The review stresses the tools and care needed to get good data in such harsh, short-lived fields. Phenomena covered range from quantum phase transitions in frustrated magnets to semiconductor-to-metal transitions in correlated systems.
arxiv-2605-11479: Wang and three colleagues propose a new way to judge robot manipulation policies offline, based on discounted liveness. Manipulation rewards are often sparse, task progress is uneven as policies recover, and finite rollout length breaks long-run assumptions. Their liveness-based Bellman operator treats judging as task completion, giving a cautious fixed value that survives truncation. They prove it contracts and tracks task progress while cutting truncation bias. Tests on two simulated tasks and a cloth folding task beat TD-zero and Monte Carlo baselines.
arxiv-2605-12079: Alvar Haltia, Ville Hyvönen, and Samuel Kaski improve human-in-the-loop Bayesian optimization when expert knowledge is tacit and cannot be quantified directly. Instead of asking experts to pinpoint locations or state prior distributions, they elicit pairwise comparisons of designs, interpreted as noisy evidence about objective values. Their method combines direct observations with pairwise queries through a cost-aware value-of-information rule. When pairwise queries cost little it greatly lifts sample efficiency, and when costly or noisy it recovers standard Bayesian optimization performance.
arxiv-2605-12179: Xin Cheng and seven colleagues improve timing sync in video-audio generation with SyncDPO. Timing sync needs audio events to line up with visual triggers, yet mean squared error loss punishes small slips weakly. Preference optimization helps by adding misaligned examples, but standard pipelines pay heavily for sampling and ranking pairs. SyncDPO builds negative examples with timing-warp rules, needing no labels or sampling, and ramps difficulty from coarse slips to fine ones. Tests across four benchmarks show SyncDPO beats rivals on timing alignment and generalizes to new data.
arxiv-2605-12579: Postolak proposes a phase-resolved test for field travel in ekpyrotic, bouncing and cyclic cosmologies. Unlike inflation, these models lack a universal link between tensor amplitude and field excursion. Scalar and tensor ripples hinge on entropy change, bounce matching and the device that evades the null energy rule. His criterion bounds the total scalar field path along the actual path in a smoothing history. Those bounds give safe, cautious rules for small-field control, not model-free bans based on geodesic distance.
arxiv-2605-12679: Delong and Wüthrich study point predictors under mean losses given by Bregman gaps. They derive a new Murphy split of mean loss without the outcome itself, keeping only its predictors. They then relate bias and spread to Lorenz-curve fit gauges in wide use. Besides the usual area between concentration and Lorenz curves, ABC, they introduce ABC squared, which eases flaws of the first in spotting mean fit. Both rely on model-based weights, so they fail to align with mean scoring.
arxiv-2605-13079: Nguyen and five co-authors explain why Muon, which orthogonalises the momentum buffer before each update, tolerates far larger learning rates than other optimizers. The mechanism is spectral flattening: Muon's largest stable step scales with the average singular value of the gradient, not the largest, which bottlenecks standard gradient descent. Recast as a preconditioned gradient method, it improves the effective convergence factor under a Kronecker-factored curvature model. Tests confirm Muon stays stable where SGD diverges early and hits accuracy milestones epochs sooner.
arxiv-2605-13179: Wang, He, Gu and Heng ask whether the Engram memory module truly retrieves memories in autoregressive image generation. They adapt Engram to vision with 2D spatial n-gram hashing, injecting it into a generator trained on ImageNet. Across budget ratios, every Engram variant trails the pure autoregressive baseline in FID, saving compute without improving sample quality. Probes show disabling Engram is catastrophic, yet a tiny constant gate matches the learned gate. Engram thus acts as a gated side-pathway, not a content-addressed retriever.
arxiv-2605-13279: Fortz and colleagues study mutation testing for quantum programs under real hardware noise. Earlier work assumed noiseless runs, ignoring how noise blurs the gap between mutants and true faults. Across 41 programs on simulators mimicking three IBM devices, noise sharply shifts mutant behavior and makes equivalent mutants harder to spot. Density matrix measures discriminate best but are unavailable on real hardware, while output distribution measures reach about 73 percent accuracy.
arxiv-2605-13579: Jie Hu and four colleagues argue that assistive agents for blind and visually impaired users need accessibility alignment as a core design goal. From 778 assistance cases, they show current agentic AI stays failure-prone in assistive scenarios, mismatched to the checking, risk and interaction needs of blind and visually impaired users. Accessibility should be handled as an alignment problem rather than a side usability issue. The authors propose a design pipeline spanning research, design, deployment and later iteration, and say blind-centred tasks stress-test agentic AI.
arxiv-2605-13779: The Mind Lab team presents MinT, a managed infrastructure setup for Low-Rank Adaptation post-training and online serving of many language models. Instead of materialising every policy as one merged full checkpoint, while MinT keeps the base model resident. Scale Down moves only the exported adapter, under 1 percent of base-model size in rank-1 settings. Scale Out supports million-scale catalogs and thousand-adapter waves at cluster scale, with packed mixture-of-experts LoRA tensors improving live engine loading 8.5 to 8.7 times.
arxiv-2605-14079: Hathcock, Ravi and Sinha explain why splitting a fulfillment network into regions can speed up e-retail delivery. Common wisdom says one big global network wins through economies of scale, yet recent evidence shows smaller regions can deliver faster. The paper builds a simple abstract model of order fulfillment to explain the effect. It characterizes assignments that satisfy an equilibrium condition under greedy fulfillment, and quantifies how much delay regionalization cuts. Algorithmic results for low-delay assignments plus simulations support the equilibrium frame.
arxiv-2605-14179: Raj, Cao, Stuart and Bhattacharya offer a neural-network framework for learning history-dependent constitutive laws, plus an account of internal variable identifiability. Finding such laws is routine in engineering, whether fitting experiments to models or learning stand-ins to dodge the steep cost of multiscale simulations. Without a potential form, those models may break the second law of thermodynamics, material stability under extreme strain, or the theory guaranteeing solutions exist. The paper's causal and energetic form respects all three properties while learning laws that depend on history.
arxiv-2605-14279: Argüelles and four co-authors make the case for a long-baseline atom interferometer at the South Pole for gravitational wave detection. Atom interferometers offer a strong route to gravitational wave detection in the decihertz band, beside current light-based detectors. The South Pole brings very low seismic noise, built bases for large projects, and a spot that sharpens where wave sources lie through global triangulation. Such a device could expand the global detector network while enabling precision tests of basic physics.
arxiv-2605-14379: Lanier and colleagues propose Data-Augmented Game Starts, a way to speed learning in large imperfect-information games like StarCraft, where rewards are sparse. They sample intermediate states from skilled human play instead of always starting from the beginning, so agents reach strategically relevant subgames sooner. On Kuhn Poker, Goofspiel and a counterexample game, the method lowers exploitability under fixed budgets. Exploitability measures how far play sits from equilibrium. Biased start states can skew equilibria, they warn, so observation flags correct the bias.
arxiv-2605-14779: Kim and Oh propose Conservative Peng's Q(lambda), a model-free offline reinforcement learning algorithm with multiple steps. It adapts Peng's Q(lambda) operator for conservative value estimation instead of the Bellman operator. Its fixed point is claimed to sit closer to the behaviour policy's value function, giving implicit behaviour control. It is said to curb over-pessimistic values, match or beat the behaviour policy, and offer near-optimal bounds. On D4RL, it is claimed to beat existing offline single-step baselines.
arxiv-2605-15579: Xinmin Feng, Li Li, Dong Liu, and Feng Wu present TVRN, a full pipeline for video frame-rate rescaling that holds up under real lossy compression. A reversible build pairs a temporal wavelet transform with a high-frequency rebuild module. It guards detail lost when frame rates fall. A stand-in net mimics codec gradients in training, since codecs block direct gradients. An asymmetric add-on brings compression-aware traits learned by ranking. Tests under industrial compression show TVRN tops past methods on rebuild quality.
arxiv-2605-15679: Mattia Scomparin studies when two quadratic Lagrangians count as equivalent. Two such Lagrangians must yield the same Euler-Lagrange equations. That demand forces a compatibility rule between kinetic matrices and potential. For constant symmetric kinetic matrices, the rule becomes a commutation rule with the Hessian. The space then splits into orthogonal spectral parts. Motion splits into free subsystems, in blocks in general and fully when the spectrum is simple. Uses include the Sawada-Kotera system and a Hénon-Heiles extension, where classic integrable regimes return.
arxiv-2605-15779: Jianlin Ye and two colleagues build a real-time multi-drone vehicle tracking system for traffic monitoring. Drone use gives traffic views, yet deployment stalls on fragmentation, where identity is lost across drone views and tools act as isolated silos. Their system keeps global identity with a topology-based handover mechanism. A queue-based matcher uses overlaps and lane discretization to manage handover via FIFO queues. Tests on urban scenes show a handover success rate of 99.8 percent in flows, far above Re-ID baselines at 74.1 percent in the comparison tests.
arxiv-2605-15879: Jacob O. Wenegrat, Tomas Chor and Roy Barkan build a coarse-grained frame for the evolution of local available potential energy in fluids. A scale split valid for filters with horizontal and vertical support is recast as a series of band-passed energies. Evolution equations cover energy above and below the filtering scale, including the cross-scale flux term. Paired with coarse-grained kinetic energy frames, the results support an energy cycle spanning scales and reservoirs. A Kelvin-Helmholtz simulation gives scale-dependent budgets and maps of transfers and dissipation.
arxiv-2605-16179: Tiwary and seven colleagues present MAgSeg, a decoder-free method for segmenting smallholder farm landscapes in high-resolution satellite imagery. Fragmented plots, high within-class variation, and scarce labels make this hard in the Global South, and current multimodal models hit context-length limits. MAgSeg lets standard multimodal models segment without auxiliary vision decoders, using a new instruction-tuning format for scalable fine-tuning. Tests across three countries show it beats state-of-the-art multimodal baselines by a wide margin.
arxiv-2605-16379: Li, Sun, and Deng argue learning latches onto the most information-efficient signal, speeding training when intended and driving reward hacking when a simpler spurious pattern wins. Synthetic data help only when the generation-training loop stays open to outside signals. Verifiers or rubrics add task-relevant information the model lacks. Shut the loop to its outputs, and the data processing inequality says task-relevant information can only shrink, so collapse follows. Among open loops, binary correctness treats acceptable outputs alike, so its lesson travels across tasks and domains.
arxiv-2605-16579: Li, Shah, and Shang propose ARL2 in 2026, a hybrid attention module for autoregressive video diffusion. It avoids the quadratic cost and growing memory cache of softmax self-attention. It splits attention into an intra-frame softmax branch and an inter-frame recurrent linear branch. The recurrent branch keeps a fixed-size streaming state. It updates only after the denoised pass, so noisy states cannot corrupt memory. With 75% of layers replaced, it runs up to 2.26 times faster in their tests. It uses 54% less memory with better temporal consistency.
arxiv-2605-16679: Chen and colleagues introduce chi-Bench, a benchmark for agents automating long, policy-rich healthcare workflows end to end. Tasks span provider prior authorization, payer utilization management, and care management, inside a simulator of 20 healthcare apps reached through 87 tools and guided by a 1,290-document operations handbook. Across 30 agent configurations, the best resolves only 28.0% of tasks, and none clears 20% on strict triple-pass scoring. Running all tasks in one session drops performance to 3.8%.
arxiv-2605-17179: Wang and colleagues build iMiGUE-3K, the largest dataset yet for reading emotion from micro-gestures, small unconscious body movements. It draws on over 3,400 long clips from press interviews with 332 professional tennis players, covering 32 gesture classes across 37 million frames. The team also trains foundation models on it and sets five evaluation tasks, showing gesture cues sharpen emotion understanding.
arxiv-2605-17279: Zhang and colleagues present Rover, a system that resolves code-merge conflicts by pairing program analysis with large language models. A multi-layer code property graph captures dependencies across files, and graph clustering groups each conflict with its related changes into a context for the model. Tests show Rover beats standalone models, the MergeGen baseline and WizardMerge on similarity to true resolutions at character, word and meaning levels.
arxiv-2605-17579: Coquand scrutinizes thermal fluctuations in crystalline membranes. He focuses on two critical regimes of the renormalization-group diagram often skipped for their one-directional instability. Careful Goldstone-mode counting around each regime and analysis of large-scale fluctuation spectra identify fixed point P2 as a good candidate for membrane melting. Melted-membrane traits are compared with fluid membranes. As a byproduct, melting a two-dimensional crystal yields correlation functions free of the ghosts plaguing the usual Canham-Helfrich action under Monge parametrization.
arxiv-2605-17679: Zhiyuan Wang and seven colleagues built PULSE, a system that helps cancer survivors get emotional support even when they have not filled in a diary entry. Language-model agents pick from eight tools to read phone sensing data, compare behavior with personal baselines, and pull up similar past cases. In tests on 50 survivors, the agent-led approach reached balanced accuracy near 0.74 for spotting a desire for emotion regulation, beating fixed-summary methods.
arxiv-2605-17979: Thomas Renault, Antonin Bergeaud, and Clément Bosquet challenge claims researchers publish more after adopting large language models. Kusumegi and colleagues date adoption as the first month an abstract crosses an LLM-detection threshold. The trio show that rule is mechanically tied to output: months with more papers are more likely to contain a flagged paper. Event studies on detection can show post-event trends even with no adoption effect. Simulations with random productivity and no causal effect reproduce the pattern, as do placebo exercises, including a pre-ChatGPT window.
arxiv-2605-18479: Stephanie Lake and five co-authors show in a 2026 paper that patterned YIG funnels can locally make second harmonics from spin waves. Tuning wave dispersion by shape confinement makes intense magnons in set spots hundreds of micrometers from the source, strong enough for second harmonic buildup via magnon scattering. Frequency- and space-resolved tests confirm the effect is truly nonlinear, opening a path to low-power magnonic logic and readout.
arxiv-2605-18579: Yuhan Wang and eight co-authors present S2Aligner, a 2026 sparsity-aware LLM-as-Aligner system for pre-training on sparse text-attributed graphs. It treats meaning and structure separately, dividing representations into meaning and structure parts and adding topology cues to text vectors with consistency control. Cross-domain risk balancing tunes domain risks and downweights shaky sparse samples. Theory shows the goal narrows cross-domain generalization gaps, and tests across domains, sparsity levels, and tasks beat current baselines.
arxiv-2605-18779: Hamidou Tembine models Mali conflict over time with an intergenerational mean-field-type game. The model covers state forces, local hunters, militias, jihadists, criminal networks, civil groups, and outside proxies, with payoffs shaped by the whole group profile. Revenge-driven types such as trauma-shaped child soldiers keep violence cycling over time, while war dealers profit from unrest. Transfers that pay for proven peace work and fine attacks, he argues, can shift the balance toward lasting calm.
arxiv-2605-18879: Yujie Lin and four colleagues treat machine unlearning as careful remapping of knowledge, not retraining or harsh fine-tuning. Their ZeroUnlearn method maps sensitive inputs onto a neutral target and wipes their old forms. A closed-form update rule keeps the new forms apart, and a gradient-based variant handles many samples at once. Tests show it beats prior methods at removing chosen knowledge while keeping the model's broad skills intact.
arxiv-2605-18979: Qisai Liu and six colleagues replace the Q-network of deep Q-learning with a tabular foundation model that learns in context. TabQL represents Q-values through a sequence-to-sequence model over tabulated state-action-value triples, adapting rapidly from limited interaction. Zero- or few-shot inference comes from in-context updates, while warm-up with standard deep Q-learning bootstraps high-quality context. Theory shows the method interpolating between vanilla Q-learning and deep Q-learning, with Bellman updates amortized through in-context learning, and benchmarks confirm it.
arxiv-2605-19279: Yudan Ren and four colleagues propose FPED, a brain-decoding framework that rebuilds seen images from brain scans. Most methods flatten signals from visual cortex into flat vectors, breaking the brain's network layout and ignoring other regions that shape visual meaning. FPED instead treats each functional brain network as a specialist expert, routing signals between them to capture their joint contributions. With only 0.68 billion parameters it matches leading semantic reconstruction, and its routing patterns line up with known links between networks and kinds of meaning.
arxiv-2605-19579: Ribes, Dunlop and Mercado present TACK, a test of degradation activity on a new set of 3,514 PROTACs and 6,561 endpoints from three sources. Tests rank three learning methods on potency prediction, maximum-degradation scores and yes-no activity classification. Simple cell-context and protein traits rival complex protein codes, prizing feature work over fancy design. Potency proves far easier to predict than maximum degradation, classical methods beat a graph network in tests, and variance tracks error, giving ranked shortlists.
arxiv-2605-19779: Gao, Wang and Yu adapt conformal prediction to continuous evaluation of AI agents. This method gives coverage guarantees without assuming a data shape. Their intervals stay on target at a day-ahead horizon, widening after agent releases and then settling. Bounds for multi-agent pipelines and rules for holding back shaky rankings control false rankings. Across fifty agents scored hourly, coverage clusters near its target, and gaps between sentiment sources predict ranking wobble. A check that rules out circular use of benchmarks confirms signal beyond standard tests.
arxiv-2605-19879: Kouzinopoulos and colleagues present a hardware orchestrated power management architecture for battery sensor nodes in low light. Software sleep modes leak a persistent quiescent current that dominates energy use when harvested light is scarce. Their design power gates the microcontroller and all non essential peripherals completely, with wake up run by an ultra low power PMIC, real time clock and a novel latch circuit. The result is a minimal quiescent drain of four hundred fifty two nanoamps, far below software sleep modes, improving autonomy for solar powered sensor networks.
arxiv-2605-20479: Liao and two co-workers transfer oracle supervision for hyperparameter prediction in image denoisers. Each new denoiser setup normally needs its own oracle-labeled training set, built by grid search against clean truth. Their HyperDn predictor pools oracle labels across source setups to predict settings for new denoiser-noise pairs. With only 2 target labels it lands within 0.90 dB of oracle quality, beating a 64-label baseline trained from scratch.
arxiv-2605-20779: Siddhant Manna and Shantanu Desai model gamma-ray emission from the merging galaxy cluster SPT-CL J2012-5649, also known as Abell 3667, using the MINOT framework. The predicted hadronic flux from proton-proton interactions in the 1 to 300 GeV band is 2.82 times ten to the power of minus eleven per square centimetre per second within R_500, rising outward. About 76 percent of that flux comes from beyond R_500, broadly matching the Fermi-LAT reported value, while inverse Compton emission stays subdominant by a factor near twenty.
arxiv-2605-21079: Zhiyi Zhou and four colleagues present VDFP, video deflickering with flicker-banding priors. Filming digital screens with phones often induces severe banding due to hardware sync gaps. Old video restoration methods struggle with structured, periodic luminance swings, often leaving leftover marks or over-smoothed textures. The authors first build DeViD, a real-world dataset in mixed scenes to address the lack of available datasets. They then propose VDFP, a perception-guided generation design, introducing degradation field modeling based on the rolling shutter trick.
arxiv-2605-21179: Buqing Ou and Frederike Dümbgen improve sampling in Bayesian optimization, a method for tuning costly functions where each evaluation is expensive. Its usual two steps fit a model, then optimize an acquisition function treated as a generic black box. Their KSOS-BO framework instead frames acquisition optimization as a semidefinite program with kernel-induced representations, enabling structured global search. Across varied benchmark functions, it consistently beat derivative-free rivals.
arxiv-2605-21479: Basel Shbita, Pengyuan Li, and Anna Lisa Gentile introduce WikiVQABench, a knowledge-grounded visual question answering benchmark from Wikipedia and Wikidata. Most visual question answering benchmarks stress sight-based tasks solvable from visual content alone, yet many real cases require outside knowledge not seen in the image. The benchmark is human-curated, built by combining site images, article captions, and structured knowledge. Draft sets generated by language models are reviewed by human checks.
arxiv-2605-21779: Ze Sheng and co-authors present FuzzingBrain V2, a multi-agent system for vulnerability discovery and reproduction. Earlier approaches suffer high false positives without proof, miss bugs at coarse or fine grains, and struggle with cross-function dependencies. Built on Google's OSS-Fuzz, every report is fuzzer-reproducible. It localizes via control-flow abstraction Suspicious Point, with function analysis and dual-layer fuzzing. On the AIxCC final dataset it detects thirty-six of forty vulnerabilities. Real deployment found twenty-nine zero-days across twelve projects, all fixed.
arxiv-2605-21879: Komugi and co-authors hunt for a hidden active galactic nucleus in the Antennae galaxies, a merging pair with no prior sign of one. Using ALMA data at 100 GHz over two and a half months, they track two compact sources in the southern galaxy NGC 4039. One source, S3, could be a young star cluster or an active nucleus. The other, S4, flickers over about 13 days, which points to a region smaller than 0.01 parsecs and makes a heavily veiled active nucleus the likely cause.
arxiv-2605-22079: Ryo Kanazawa and co-authors present Ishigaki-IDS-Bench, a benchmark for generating Information Delivery Specification documents from building information requirements. Building Information Modeling projects use IDS to formalize requirements in machine-checkable XML, but authoring IDS conditions grounded in Industry Foundation Classes vocabulary demands expertise in concepts, validation tools, and property sets. The benchmark scores facet-level macro-F1 and content fidelity. Across 10 language models in zero-shot tests, GPT-5.5 reaches the highest Facet F1 at 65.6 percent, while Claude Opus 4.5 reaches the highest Content pass rate at only 33.1 percent.
arxiv-2605-22479: The LEGEND team describes energy calibration and detector work in LEGEND-200. The work supports the first unblinding in the search for neutrinoless double beta decay. The paper details signal processing, peak shapes and weekly thorium-228 calibration runs. Reconstruction reaches an average resolution of 2.47 keV at 2039 keV. Weekly peak spots vary by less than 0.05 keV up to 2614.5 keV, showing a stable energy scale across detectors. Corrections address residual nonlinearities and energy bias.
arxiv-2605-22579: Li and team show hyperfitting differs deeply from spread peaking, not simple heat scaling. It means tuning LLMs to near zero loss on small sets, lifting open text and cutting repeats in greedy reading. Controls show heat scaling fails to match range gains. The team kills static word re-ranking: it relies on live rank re-sort. Layer look finds a Terminal Expansion in the final block, where trait space growth lifts tail tokens. Late LoRA tweaks only the final 5 layers for robust text.
arxiv-2605-22679: Kubaty and others reveal the hidden compositional structure of vision language embeddings without expanding their dimension, unlike sparse autoencoders that distort geometry. Their CEDAR method learns an invertible transform with a top k sparsity bottleneck, concentrating meaning into axis aligned clean coordinates. In CLIP like models, single coordinates read as textual concepts, while in generative models such as BLIP they decode into plain language text. Tests show a competitive rebuild balance with readings closer to how people see them, which hints entanglement can dissolve under the right change of basis.
arxiv-2605-22779: Wang and others move log anomaly detection from session level flags to the message at fault, sparing operators from sifting lines per alert. Their FAME framework uses a language model once offline to label at most K lines per template and propose a partition of templates into failure domains, certified before training. A router plus domain experts then runs on premise, outputting anomaly calls and failure domain labels. On BGL data, FAME reaches an F1 near 98 while cutting annotation effort 76 fold, and on Thunderbird it reaches near 100 with recall.
arxiv-2605-22879: Alpay and Sarioglu introduce budgeted trace structures for keeping trace graphs and histories under a strict token or byte budget. The design mixes filtered reachability, cursor paging, capped recency logs, counted keys, delta overlays, and summary-plus-suffix compaction. A Rust prototype built graphs of tens of thousands of vertices in milliseconds. It shrank histories of millions of tokens to a few thousand.
arxiv-2605-22979: Ivey and Ryan construct a special class of ruled hypersurfaces within the nonflat complex space forms CP^n and CH^n. Starting from any smooth curve in a totally geodesic one-dimensional submanifold, they erect an orthogonal ruling over each point. In the two-dimensional case, they examine base curves of constant geodesic curvature. There the build yields exactly these real-analytic hypersurfaces of cohomogeneity one that meet a transversality condition.
arxiv-2605-23979: Fries studies reduced stochastic hedge ratios for Monte Carlo valuation, turning pathwise sensitivities to model inputs into hedge ratios against market instruments. Solving the relation on every path is costly and unstable, so he keeps only a few basis functions, far fewer than the number of paths. The sensitivity tensor stays in full, entering through averages over paths, while two coefficient rules are distinguished: one minimizing the full pathwise residual, the other a projected moment equation. The rules agree in special cases but differ when sensitivities vary by path.
arxiv-2605-24179: Kristoffersen and eight co-authors test whether 7 Tesla MRI plus deep-learning brain segmentation can separate Parkinson's motor subtypes: healthy controls, postural-instability-gait-difficulty cases, and tremor-dominant cases. With 21 controls and 24 patients, a U-Net reached a strong mean Dice score across regions. Using all features, classification stayed modest, but picking an optimal feature subset lifted results sharply. That approach reached perfect accuracy on the postural versus tremor task and strong scores elsewhere, supporting compact, readable imaging signatures for Parkinson's diagnosis, while larger multi-site studies are needed.
arxiv-2605-24379: Longyun Ding and Xu Wang study extensions of non-archimedean Polish groups, a class of groups with a compatible complete metric. They ask whether a group must sit at a certain complexity level when a closed normal subgroup and the group formed by collapsing it both sit at given levels. The answer is yes under an extra assumption, but counterexamples refute the original question from Allison and Panagiotopoulos. They also prove a general upper bound for the extended group.
arxiv-2605-24479: Jiarong Deng, Liu Chang, and Quanshun Yang study how adding one weighted chord to a ring network improves consensus speed and steady disagreement. A chord splits the ring into two resistance arcs, and that split governs both the connectivity gain and the coherence gain. Near-antipodal, resistance-balanced chords prove near-best for connectivity under bounded conductances. Since the best chord for speed and the best for coherence can differ, the authors frame design as a Pareto problem. Two screening rules keep only near-linear candidate sets.
arxiv-2605-24779: Rishabh Iyer introduces Complement Submodular Information for even data selection. Classical goals score only the selected subset, ignoring links to the rest. Yet train-test splitting, benchmark building, and robust picking depend on even structure across both sides. The framework quantifies shared structure between a subset and its complement, yielding Facility Location, Graph Cut, and LogDet variants. Under bounded curvature it shows near-monotonicity with near-optimal guarantees. Tests show wins on hidden-slice picks, preserving rare tail structure while suppressing noisy outliers.
arxiv-2605-24879: Enayat Ullah leads DP-SGD-RC, private training for large language models cutting memory and compute. Private training guards sensitive data, but fast gradient clipping carries heavy memory overhead that grows with model size and context length. DP-SGD-RC clips gradients randomly, using stochastic trace estimation to gauge per-sample gradient norms. A tight privacy analysis shows noise levels competitive with deterministic clipping. Fine-tuning a small Llama model on long-context classification, questions, and summaries matches baseline quality while sharply lowering memory and compute.
arxiv-2605-25579: Deng and Gao build a framework for time-harmonic Maxwell scattering with nonlinear boundary and interface effects. They treat three model classes: impedance, perfect-conductor, and transmission cases, all nonlinear. The usual tangential trace is too weak for those terms, so they work in refined spaces where the electric field admits a finite-energy trace. Under a small Lipschitz constant, they prove well-posedness by fixed-point arguments. They then show the fields vary smoothly with the interface shape and that the shape derivative has Hadamard structure.
arxiv-2605-25779: Nasyrov proves a 2020 conjecture on how the triangular ratio metric distorts under Möbius maps of the unit disk. The metric compares straight distance with the shortest detour through the disk boundary. The conjecture claims a sharp bound: after a Möbius automorphism, the metric grows by at most a factor tied to the map parameter. Nasyrov shows the inequality holds for every such map and every pair of points. The result settles the problem posed by Hariri, Klén and Vuorinen.
arxiv-2605-25979: An and twenty-nine colleagues present LLaVA-OneVision-2, the strongest model yet in the LLaVA-OneVision vision-language series. It builds on a native OneVision encoder with windowed attention for efficient local computation at full resolution. Its key advance treats compressed video as a stream of bit costs, letting cost dynamics choose temporal groups and motion cues pick salient spatial evidence. A shared three-dimensional rotary encoding then places video canvases, sampled frames and images in one coordinate system. Benchmark results lead the series across multimodal tasks.
arxiv-2605-26079: Wang and six colleagues audit AI benchmarks with an agentic system called Auto Benchmark Audit. Expert-written benchmark tasks often hide assumptions, incomplete environment specs and brittle grading that human review misses. ABA checks each task systematically for hidden dependencies, spec gaps and weak grading logic. Run over 168 benchmarks across nine domains, including frontier model benchmarks and prior NeurIPS papers, it flags critical issues in over 25.7 percent of tasks. Expert review backs the precision of these automated audits, the authors report.
arxiv-2605-26179: Penghui Yang and eight colleagues present AutoDFT (2026), a closed-loop team of language-model agents that runs density functional theory calculations from planning through repair. A strategic planner sketches step goals, while a step planner sets numbers just in time from prior results. A monitor-recover-reflect loop diagnoses failures and revises the plan when evidence warrants it. On a bench of thirty-four tasks across nine calculation types, AutoDFT succeeds on about ninety-four percent and gives reliable property predictions on established materials databases.
arxiv-2605-26279: Rafał Stachowiak and Tomasz Pawlak's 2026 MPMMine serves constraint acquisition, the field that discovers, checks, and betters mathematical programming models from domain knowledge. Existing benchmarks are loosely ordered, mix types and formats, target solvers rather than acquisition methods, and omit details for fair judging. MPMMine answers with a uniform structure, open formats, formulations per problem, tens of settings per model, and thousands of cases, valid and invalid, across discrete, continuous, and mixed domains. A Python package opens the data, and a leaderboard scores current methods under the same rules.
arxiv-2605-26379: David Klindt, Yann LeCun, and Randall Balestriero prove when LeJEPA, an alignment-plus-Gaussian learner, recovers a world's hidden variables from tangled observations. In worlds where latents move under steady, noisy steps, LeJEPA linearly recovers those latents. The Gaussian is the unique latent distribution where the guarantee holds. Alignment penalizes nonlinearity, crowning the linear map, while other alternatives fail the converse. Approximate recovery degrades gracefully, and linear recovery enables optimal planning. Tests span 2D cases, 1024-dimensional latents, and pixel-based robot control.
arxiv-2605-26779: In a 2026 study, Glittum and Syljuåsen settle a three-decade debate about the low-temperature fate of the classical kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Expanding in the number of spin components, they show the spin liquid ends in a weak first-order transition. It enters a root-three by root-three phase whose ordered moment saturates at zero temperature. Adding second-neighbor links extends the transition into a line ending at a critical point, while the pyrochlore antiferromagnet stays disordered at all temperatures.
arxiv-2605-27079: Dong and four co-authors tackle policy reinforcement learning for flows, where sampling destabilizes optimization.
