They build on Q Adjoint Matching, which recasts improvement as optimal control guided by a critic, and note small critic errors can amplify and cause collapse. Their Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching caps the path-space KL between fine-tuned and pretrained ones via dual descent, with a parameter weighting that KL in the objective. On 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM beats rivals offline and offline-to-online, reaching 68 percent offline success against a 46 percent baseline.
arxiv-2605-27579: Tenley Hutchinson-Smith, Angela Twum, and Enrico Ramirez-Ruiz run 3D fluid models of mildly evolved donors in luminous red novae. Donor central concentration governs the outcome: similar values give similar inspiral shapes and mass-loss histories despite different masses and radii. Modest concentrations plunge fast on local orbital energy, while dense-cored donors expand slowly as shocks spread energy and angular momentum.
arxiv-2605-27679: Julia Navarro and Mark Wilkinson build symmetry-aware neural networks for the order parameter of nematic liquid crystals in two dimensions. Seven architectures matching cyclic groups of increasing order satisfy the Q-tensor symmetry constraint to single-precision accuracy. Symmetry-aware models beat parameter-matched plain benchmarks with and without data augmentation, holding up better to unseen defects.
arxiv-2605-27779: Shixin Zheng, Yiwei Wang, and Haizhao Yang develop a geometric theory for how neural-network training converges under the minimizing movement scheme. Recasting each step as a minimization over increments, they show the flow follows a Riemannian gradient path and converges linearly to the subproblem's unique minimum. The analysis also bounds errors from inexact inner solves and network approximation.
arxiv-2605-27979: Ju Hyeon Lee, Beom Hyun Kim, and Bongjae Kim squeeze a manganite crystal in varied directions and get truly distinct phases. The shifts are not just strong or weak forms of one phase. With quantum models of a classic Jahn-Teller crystal, they show the squeeze direction picks the order. Each way favors its own mix of charge, orbital, and lattice orders.
arxiv-2605-28279: Jianzhu Huai shows that IMU preintegration and IMU propagation are one job in two coats. Preintegrated readings, bias slopes, and spreads can be wrapped from any propagation code, and a preintegration block can hand back shift matrices and spreads in turn. Checks against a standard toolkit agree closely on random runs.
arxiv-2605-28479: Dennis Uitenbroek, Jurriaan Langendorff, and Tjerk Oosterkamp cool a floating milligram gravity sensor with linear feedback to great stillness. A magnet floats in a superconducting trap, its motion read by a coil linked to a SQUID and damped through a piezo actuator. Two side-to-side modes reach below two picometers of motion and below ten millikelvin at once. The result moves quiet mounting and sensing toward future quantum ground-state cooling of levitated particles.
arxiv-2605-28579: Xiaoyu Dong and three colleagues introduce MUSE, a benchmark for text-to-CAD generation of multi-part assemblies. Existing benchmarks stress single parts and shape similarity, missing how parts fit together and join. MUSE pairs practical design cases with structured design specs and scores outputs on four fronts: runnable code, valid shapes, true part fits and joins, and consistent function. Tests show high execution success does not guarantee correct fits or joins, and a new check combines part graphs with direct boundary-representation analysis.
arxiv-2605-28779: Chinh Hoang and Mohammad Rashedul Hasan introduce CAGE, testing whether vision-language models reason causally or sound plausible. Their dual probes separate linguistic quality from faithful reasoning: a text-only probe scores language, while a chain-text probe requires chains first. The Abstraction Gap measures the normalized performance gap. Testing models on 49,500 questions across 5,500 images spanning Pearl's hierarchy, seven models show gaps above one half, with text scores 6 to 8 and chain scores below three. Fine-tuning on 45,000 chain examples fails to close the gap, though one model reaches zero.
arxiv-2605-28879: Ritvik Bhatnagar and three colleagues study whether mixed quantum learners give useful non-repeat information for network break-in detection. They test Quantum Support Vector Machines and Quantum Neural Networks, which learn and predict apart. To join them they propose the System-Level Meta-Quantum Ensemble, fusing QSVM and QNN outputs with a Random Forest meta-learner. That learner reads accord and discord patterns, improving guess balance and scores. On TON IoT and CICIDS2017 the ensemble beats several solo quantum learners on picked scores and trust metrics.
arxiv-2605-29379: Rohan Shravan presents BrahmicTokenizer-131K, a BPE tokenizer closing the Brahmic gap while preserving English, European-language, and code compression of o200k_base. It is built by a two-stage retrofit: a crop cutting 200,019 tokens to 131,072 by removing nine systems, and a retrofit of 2,372 dead slots across nine Brahmic blocks. Pre-tokenizer, decoder, and merge rules are unchanged, making it a drop-in replacement. On twenty-seven million documents, it produces about one quarter fewer tokens than Mistral-Nemo Tekken and Sarvam-m at the same budget.
arxiv-2605-29479: Taesoo Song and three colleagues apply the Remler formalism at SPS and FAIR energies to charmonium made in heavy-ion collisions. It probes how baryon-rich matter creates and destroys charm-anticharm bound states. They validate the method in proton-proton collisions, then extract the nuclear absorption cross section from proton-nucleus collisions. Fed into simulations with an in-medium heavy-quark potential, the approach matches SPS results when the J/psi meson dissolves near the critical temperature. The same setup yields figures for lower SPS and FAIR energies.
arxiv-2605-29579: Shizhe Zhou and six colleagues present ReactBench, a benchmark that tests why multimodal models hallucinate, not just whether they do. Most tests score wrong answers, while ReactBench builds adversarial images and trick queries in an exam-style format. Four tasks target distinct failure roots: erased relations, counterfactual traits, traced changes, and dense counts. Chain-of-thought reasoning then traces sub-causes within each task, exposing co-occurrence bias, language habits, weak cross-image comparison, and fine perception limits. Tests show current models stay open to cause-specific triggers.
arxiv-2605-29979: Anna Wimbauer, Jonas Möller, Erik Imgrund, and Konrad Rieck show model-running machinery leaves a trace in a language model's words. Engines, attention back ends, and hardware bend numbers, so the same model answers a shade differently per setup. Those quirks reach visible text, open to any querier. Their fingerprint method reads prompt-response behavior and names engine, attention back end, and hardware platform even at non-zero temperature. Blocking such tracing looks fundamentally hard, since it would need identical numbers across all stacks, so partial defenses are offered.
arxiv-2605-30179: Yang Song and seven co-authors introduce iLoRA, a Bayesian graph-conditioned low-rank adaptation framework. It exposes latent interactions driving labels, which standard LoRA hides with a static low-rank update. iLoRA builds a latent interaction graph out of the input and makes input-conditioned updates, learning prediction and interaction structure jointly. For microbiome diagnosis, where disease depends on species levels and microbe cross-talk, it beats LoRA and Bayesian baselines. Across question answering and multi-cohort bowel disease diagnosis, it recovers human-aligned graphs with calibrated uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-30279: Siqing Zhang shows that, whenever a smooth variety has a non-closed global one-form, a certain Azumaya algebra fails to split on a degree one cover. Crystalline differential operators on a smooth variety yield a non-split Azumaya algebra over the cotangent bundle of the Frobenius twist. In some cases this algebra splits when restricted to finite covers. Zhang proves that a non-closed global one-form forces a degree one cover on which the algebra stays unsplit, settling a question of Sasha Petrov.
arxiv-2605-30379: Leonidas Kordalis and Samis Trevezas give algebraic and FFT methods for discrete matrix convolutions, with uses in Markov models. They invert a sequence in a series algebra, mixing formulas with FFT and Gauss-Jordan elimination. They prove exact finite-horizon inversion, shift identities, and left and right residual bounds. Error bounds hold, with fixed-horizon limits, second-order for smooth kernels. The same framework yields entry odds and uptime. The fast methods keep the odds work while cutting the cost of inversion.
arxiv-2605-30479: Hanneke and Wang study online classification where the learner sees all the unlabeled examples in advance but must predict labels one by one. They ask which concept classes can be learned with mistakes growing only slowly as predictions accumulate, even when the label set is unbounded. Their answer admits just two optimal mistake rates: bounded, or growing logarithmically. A new combinatorial object, the level-constrained Littlestone tree, together with an indifference property, characterizes exactly which classes are learnable, with extensions to noisy and stochastic settings.
arxiv-2605-30679: Chabert raises the upper bound on the L2 to L4 norm of the spectral projector for the Euclidean disk. Bandwidth here is much smaller than target frequency. Splitting on the joint eigenbasis of the square-root Laplacian and the angular derivative, given in terms of Bessel eigenfunctions, she reduces the analysis to precise estimates of shifting phase oscillatory integrals. She uses a convexity effect both for these estimates and for summing eigenfunction contributions. The method extends to other circle-symmetric surfaces meeting similar rules.
arxiv-2605-30879: Kolotilin and Wolitzky model markets where many people join one firm, school or neighbourhood and peers affect value. When prices move freely, they show, competition reaches an efficient outcome, though workforces split into alternating bands of sorting by skill and mixing. Fixed prices flip the gain: peer value flows to schools, not pupils, and sorting can run too far. Their framework also covers assignment models and Bayesian persuasion.
arxiv-2606-00279:
Cankaya shows that AI work can be checked bit for bit with no speed loss. Fair checks on AI runs are key to trust in AI rules. GPU math looks loose, so checks most often take near matches as good. That slack can hide swapped code or secret extra work.

Cankaya reads how top run tools make firm, if not fixed, outputs. With the right run facts at hand, a run can be traced bit for bit. No slow strict flags are needed, if no clash-prone calls sit in the back end. A soft-only mimic replays big model runs across chip types. Round-off drift then acts as a print of the rig and code used. That print turns a weak spot into proof a check can use.
arxiv-2606-00479:
Chen and He study heat-time shape traits in a class of layered insulators. Such solids hold their odd traits at edges and corners, not the bulk. Warmth can blur those traits as heat climbs. The Uhlmann phase gives a gauge for shape at set heat.

They build the test on the BBH model, a stock case in the class. Its parts rest on a set of linked square-root style mats. That frame pins the Uhlmann phase to one of two marks. Sharp jumps in the phase thus flag the odd state at set heat. When jumps fade, the team read off the flip heat. For a choice case, both phase and flip heat come out in closed form.
arxiv-2606-00579:
Chen and co-authors show that boxed code agents can solve sight-and-sound tasks with no ear of their own. Such agents see text and stills, and call tools in a safe box. Stock tales held that sound tasks need born omni-modal models. Their tests break that take in more than one field.

The agents write code and run tools to pull proof from tapes. Text logs, stills, and side marks give them what they need. Whole sound streams need not be fed in at once. That turns sound tasks to hunt and sort tasks in their hands. Trace reads show where the route fails and why. Skill packs, by hand or self-taught, lift scores by much. A train plan and a new bench for real omni work close the work.
arxiv-2606-00879:
Bejan and Meriç extend a class of geometric structures in this 2026 maths paper. Almost contact structures pair a manifold with fields that mimic how a surface meets its surroundings. A B-metric, also called a Norden metric, adds a special way to measure lengths and angles. Weak versions of these structures were defined not long ago by Rovenski and Wolak.

The pair define weak almost contact structures with B-metric. Their class widens the classical almost contact structures with Norden metric. They then work out several geometric traits of the new class. Special subclasses get a closer look, one by one. Examples run through the whole work, built to show each concept in concrete form. The paper is a reference for differential geometers who study contact-style structures with unusual metrics. It maps fresh ground rather than closing a known gap, and its stock of examples anchors the new definitions.
arxiv-2606-01179:
Sahoo and Patra build one neural frame for entropy across unlike systems in this 2026 paper. Entropy production rules irreversibility in physics and uncertainty in information systems. Physics informed networks solve differential equations well, but each build is domain bound. Whether entropy features can be shared across unlike laws was unexplored. Their frame enforces equation residuals and information bounds in a single architecture.

Two case studies carry the proof. A stirred tank reactor model solves its thermodynamic equations, with a Softplus constraint that enforces the second law by construction. A finance model solves an inverse Fokker-Planck equation to infer hidden drift and diffusion, with positivity guarded the same way. The shared encoder model holds zero second law violations, they report. It retains over 90 percent predictive accuracy using merely 30 percent of the training data in its tests. A geometric post check on the learned entropy surface flags phase instabilities.
arxiv-2606-01279:
Zhao and co-authors give AI agents a skill for building training data. Agents now help automate AI research itself. Post-training turns base models into aligned assistants. That step rests on high-quality data above all. Web hunts for data are long and noisy. They can swamp an agent's limited context. Dataset quality then falls, and training suffers too.

Andes reframes data generation as a plug-and-play skill. A self-evolving World Tree routes the synthesis work. Diagnostic reports let trainer agents steer the loop. Agents guide the process through a closed feedback cycle. Under tight compute limits, weaker agents gain a lot. Andes tops PostTrainBench and generalizes across tasks.
arxiv-2606-01379:
Tiwari and Ji let later tasks improve earlier ones in continual learning. Prompt-based methods fight forgetting by isolating task prompts. That isolation blocks backward transfer to old tasks. SABER enables controlled backward refinement without replay. It is built for prompt-based continual learning setups. Two criteria decide when refinement should help. One reads prompt-gradient geometry between tasks. The other compares loss-distribution similarity.

Refinement stays safe by construction in their design. Updates move only along non-interfering directions in prompt space. Tests span many benchmarks and diverse backbones. T5-Large, LLaMA, and Qwen models all take part. SABER achieves positive backward transfer consistently. Strong overall average performance holds at the same time. Code is public.
arxiv-2606-01679:
Kumar and co-authors explain why models verify claims worse from charts than tables. Multimodal models increasingly assist scientific peer review. Verifying claims against evidence is a core need there. Models do far better when evidence is a table than a chart of the same data. The question: do they fail to extract chart data, or fail to use it? Layer-wise probing and attention analysis test three open-weight models. Table and chart versions carry the same underlying data in the tests.

Chart information is encoded in intermediate representations, they find. It just does not reach the prediction position. That gap is absent for tables and holds across conditions. Attention analysis shows two distinct forms of the disconnect across model families. The gap is a routing failure, not an encoding failure.
arxiv-2606-01779:
Chen and co-authors build a way for AI agent systems to adapt as wholes. Agent tasks vary a lot in how they must be run. Fixed agent setups fit such mixed work poorly. Past work tuned the outer harness or the inner model. But the fit between those two parts was left loose.

Their HarnessForge method treats the pair as one unit. It splits build structure from thought behavior. Fault clues then shape the harness to each task. The inner model is tuned to match that harness. Tests span five benchmarks from varied fields. The authors report gains on two Qwen3 model sizes. Gains reach up to 12 percent over the best rival.
arxiv-2606-02279:
Jooken and Zamfirescu count Hamiltonian paths between two fixed vertices in graphs. A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once. The graphs here are traceable and ban a fixed induced subgraph F. At least one Hamiltonian path joins the two endpoints. The question is how many such paths must exist.

The count is studied as a function of graph order. A sharp dichotomy is the main result. If F is not an induced subgraph of a certain path family, counterexamples exist. Infinite families then have a unique Hamiltonian path between the endpoints. If F is such an induced subgraph, a lower bound holds. Every F-free traceable graph then has many Hamiltonian paths. The dividing line is exact in the theorem.
arxiv-2606-02379:
Xiangli and co-authors tackle a scale flaw in depth estimates made from a single image. Strong models still shrink far landmarks and wide landscapes. The team blames the training data. Most metric-scale sets come from car-mounted LiDAR or short-range indoor scans. Synthetic sets lack the mess of the real world.

Their fix is a new dataset called MetricScenes. It draws on internet photo sets and stereo images. Camera poses and first depth maps come from standard tools. True scale comes from geo-tags and known stereo baselines. A two-stage Poisson method then cleans the depth maps. Fine-tuned on this data, MoGe-2 shows far less scale collapse. It also keeps top scores on standard benchmarks. The gain holds in open, unconstrained scenes.
arxiv-2606-02579:
Boukhtouchen and co-authors turn an everyday mineral into a dark matter detector. Muscovite mica is a layered silicate with clean cleavage. It has low radiogenic background. It keeps particle tracks over geological timescales. Exposures run to gigayears. Those traits suit searches for rare particles. The team targets heavy composite dark matter.

Melt track formation is modeled with a Sedov-Taylor thermal spike formalism. SRIM and TRIM simulations validate the sub-micron regime. They also calibrate how recoil energy deposits locally. A new readout uses rapid X-ray fluorescence mapping. A copper backing contrast trick spots micron-scale damage over large scan areas. Laser-ablated defects calibrate the smallest visible track. Projected sensitivities cover opaque and diffuse composite dark matter. A sub-melt hole-channel mode extends reach to large composites. Old exclusions from etched mica searches are revisited and found shaky.
arxiv-2606-02779:
Wu revisits spectral sequence theory through a newer categorical frame. Filtered spectra form an infinity-category. The cofiber-of-tau formalism of Burklund, Isaksen, Pstragowski, Wang, and Xu structures it. Within that frame, Wu defines hidden extensions along arbitrary maps of filtered spectra. Computational principles follow. They extend the generalized Leibniz rule and the generalized Mahowald trick of Lin, Wang, and Xu.

Burklund's Leibniz rule for total differentials is also extended. The formulation uses a layered notion of extension. It slightly sharpens the statements even for the Adams spectral sequence. An application studies equivariant slice spectral sequences. New families of exotic transfer differentials appear. They live in the C4-slice sequences for the Hill-Hopkins-Ravenel theories, for every level m at least 1. The work widens tools that stable homotopy theorists use daily.
arxiv-2606-02979:
Natan and Miura present a compact model for autonomous driving perception. The model handles several perception tasks in one forward pass. It covers multiple views of semantic segmentation, depth estimation, LiDAR segmentation, and bird's-eye-view projection. It needs no separate helper models.

An adaptive loss weighting algorithm balances learning across the many tasks. Data preprocessing and intermediate fusion combine inputs from RGB cameras, dynamic vision sensors, and LiDAR units placed around the vehicle. Tests span three CARLA simulation datasets and one real-world nuScenes dataset. The proposed variant beat the combination of recent rival models while using far fewer parameters. It thus runs faster and uses less GPU memory. The authors share code and files publicly. The work targets perception systems that must be both capable and light enough for real vehicles.
arxiv-2606-03179:
Chan and co-authors tackle a drift problem in editing the knowledge of language models. Edits must keep facts fresh over time. Real facts are often n-ary: they link more than two things at once. When edits are forced into triples, the event's unity breaks. The team names this n-ary structural drift.

Their framework, HyperPatch, treats a run of edits as a stability problem on hypergraph shapes. It keeps each event whole in three phases. A hypergraph network first builds a topology-aware embedding space. Edits then proceed with fast conflict checks and a light adapter that tracks drift without retraining the base model. A last phase reasons from fused text and structure evidence. On two multi-hop benchmarks, gains over the best baseline were large. A plain graph variant's scores collapsed under streams of updates, while HyperPatch held up.
arxiv-2606-03479:
Ramlal and Zelek keep moving objects alive in 4D scenes while no camera can see them. Dynamic Gaussian Splatting rebuilds scenes from synced multi-camera video. Once an object hides from every training camera, its signal vanishes. Its Gaussians then get no updates and decay. Past fixes lean on learned priors that favor looks over physical truth.

PersistGS couples a differentiable rigid body simulator with Gaussian Splatting instead. The scene splits into per-object Gaussians and collision meshes. Friction and velocity are fit from the path seen before the object hid. The simulator then rolls that path through the hidden stretch. Bounces, friction slowdowns, and turns come out right, unlike straight-line guesses. A centroid silhouette loss cuts trajectory error by 40 percent versus photometric loss. On synthetic scenes, PersistGS beats constant velocity by 2.46 dB PSNR. It lands within 0.19 dB of a ground-truth path bound.
arxiv-2606-03879:
Ding and co-authors measure what each vision encoder really adds inside multi-encoder language models. Fusing varied visual streams is a growing design trend. How encoders interact under joint training was poorly understood. Rankings from masking a fixed checkpoint may mislead. The team retrains all 31 non-empty subsets of five common encoders on the Cambrian-1 suite. The effort totals about 20,000 GPU hours.

Retraining reshuffles encoder rankings, including which encoder leads overall. Each encoder's role splits into Capacity and Necessity. Capacity is its solo score; Necessity is the drop when it leaves the full pool. The two axes do not swap for each other. The best pair joins a high-Capacity anchor with an adaptive complement, matching all five encoders. Extra encoders add little beyond that pair. Pre-projector rank explains the leftover score spread at fixed size. Designers get concrete primitives for leaner multi-encoder builds.
arxiv-2606-03979:
Behrouz and co-authors propose that language models need a sleep stage. Current models predict fast and learn in context. Yet they fail to turn short-term context into lasting parameter knowledge. Human learning, with replay and consolidation, guides their design. Sleep lets a model keep learning and improve itself over time.

Two stages make up the scheme. Knowledge Seeding distils a smaller self into a larger network, adding capacity while keeping knowledge. Their proof of concept mixes on-policy distillation with RL-based imitation. Dreaming then lets the model build its own practice data by RL. Tests on long-horizon and continual tasks support the sleep stage. Few-shot transfer tasks also back its value, they report.
arxiv-2606-04079:
Atom Computing and collaborators report in 2026 a demonstration of repeated quantum error correction using the toric code on their neutral-atom platform, where individual atoms held by laser tweezers serve as qubits. Error correction is the missing step between today's noisy devices and reliable quantum computers.

The team ran many rounds of syndrome extraction, the checks that reveal errors, while measuring qubits mid-circuit and replacing atoms that were lost from a stored reservoir. Logical information survived through repeated reloading of that reservoir. They tracked the logical error rate across up to ninety correction cycles. Comparing two sizes of the code over eight rounds, the larger code showed the lower error rate, as theory predicts for a working correction scheme.
arxiv-2606-04379:
Richard Cloete and Abraham Loeb report in 2026 a candidate interstellar meteor. It crossed over the South Atlantic in April 2026 on a near-polar path. If its speed truly exceeds the Sun's escape velocity at Earth's distance, it came from outside the solar system.

Starting from the satellite-reported velocity, they removed Earth's gravity with a two-body model. Then they added Earth's orbital motion. The resulting heliocentric speed cleared the escape threshold comfortably. The polar component alone exceeded local escape speed. A million Monte Carlo trials perturbed the measurements with a calibrated error model. Not one produced a bound orbit. That puts the interstellar confidence above ninety-nine point nine nine percent.
arxiv-2606-04479:
Hong and Zhou test whether image generators that write text inside pictures are really reasoning, or only copying patterns, in a 2026 arXiv study. Such text serves documents and slides. The open question is whether the models preserve reasoning. This matters when a full solution must appear as rendered text. The authors probe this reasoning fidelity across four areas. They test long text rendering, factual knowledge questions, context understanding, and multi-step reasoning.

They find that current models often produce semantic errors. They also produce logical inconsistencies and wrong intermediate steps. This happens even when the rendered text looks clear. Text-only models handle the same tasks well. So the failures are not about question difficulty. Hong and Zhou conclude that a substantial gap separates visual text generation from procedural reasoning. They motivate work on making image-based text more reliable. A polished page can hide broken logic.
arxiv-2606-04579:
Zhao and colleagues build a reward model that grades each step of a scientific solution, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Process reward models score intermediate reasoning. They work well in mathematics. Science adds factual consistency and precise tool use, where models hallucinate. The authors first build SCIPRM70K. This dataset holds Chain-of-Tool trajectories. They interleave reasoning with executions of scientific tools in biology, chemistry, and physics.

Trained on it, Sci-PRM gives fine-grained supervision in one inference pass. It covers tool selection, execution accuracy, and result interpretation. The model helps in two ways. At test time, Best-of-N selection picks better solutions. Inside reinforcement learning, it supplies a dense reward signal. This mitigates advantage disappearance, the failure where all sampled solutions score alike and learning stalls. The authors report that this lets models break through existing performance ceilings. They release Sci-PRM publicly.
arxiv-2606-04979:
McKevitt, Ugarte-Urra, and Young watch the Sun's corona change across a full solar cycle the way stellar astronomers must watch other stars, in a 2026 arXiv solar physics paper. They compile eighteen scans from the Hinode satellite's EIS instrument spanning 2013 to 2024.

Disk-integrated coronal intensity correlates strongly with the solar cycle, consistent with stellar observations. No clear cycle variation appears in the Doppler or non-thermal velocity distributions, and active region intensity per unit area correlates moderately. Sun-as-a-star intensity variability is driven mainly by the changing fraction of the disk covered by active regions, not by changing plasma properties within them. The known link between upflows and line broadening persists all cycle, implying active region kinematics ignore the global field configuration.
arxiv-2606-05179:
Sungmook Woo, Hyunku Kang, and Chanwoo Kim restore punctuation in streaming speech recognition with a weighted lookahead scoring method in this 2026 arXiv paper. Punctuation makes transcripts readable, but a streaming recognizer must decide online, with little future context. Generation-based fixes, where a model rewrites the sentence, are prone to latency and can break alignment with the fixed transcript. Their method scores without generating: it preserves the input transcript and decides at each word boundary.

It compares punctuation insertion hypotheses against a no-insertion baseline under a lookahead of K subword tokens, calibrated on a validation set, with no parameter updates at inference time. On the IWSLT 2017 benchmark it reached a four-class F1 of 0.893 with no fine-tuning, and 0.937 after fine-tuning, beating a prompt baseline at 0.566 and a fine-tuned ELECTRA baseline at 0.913 under the same budget. Ablations map the accuracy-delay tradeoff of the lookahead budget.
arxiv-2606-05679:
Summers and Wu move data safety rules into the database itself in a 2026 arXiv paper. AI agents now write queries and run pipelines for users. A query can be correct yet still break privacy law or business policy by joining data wrongly. Checking by prompt or after the fact is fragile. Their framework, Data Flow Control, states safety rules over how each row's data may flow and combine.

Rules are written as conditions over provenance, the record of where each value came from. A rewriting layer called Passant enforces them inside the query, with no provenance tables built. The layer runs on five database engines, from DuckDB to SQL Server. Measured overhead came out near zero. It also beat rival enforcers by orders of magnitude. The authors pitch the work as the first step from prompt-level promises to infrastructure-level guarantees for agent data use.
arxiv-2606-05779:
Van Le, Tran, and Tan Le test tiny onboard models for spacecraft cyber defense in a 2026 arXiv paper. Satellites must spot radio and cyber attacks fast, with little computing power to spare. The SPARTA framework catalogs the attack styles, from uplink jamming to command injection. The team compares four small classical models on speed against accuracy. Theory on complexity and scaling sits beside bench tests on corrupted radio spectrograms.

Logistic regression, the plainest model, answered in microseconds. It gave up only about one percent accuracy against random forest, the strongest rival. That trade makes it a strong baseline for onboard autonomy. Support vector machines and small neural nets filled out the comparison. Attack fakes came in three corruption styles, including band erasure and noise bursts. The authors point to richer signal features and multi-timescale learning as next steps. Lightweight math, they argue, already guards a satellite well.
arxiv-2606-06179:
Naïl Khelifa, Richard Turner, and Ramji Venkataramanan argue that diffusion models are being graded with the wrong ruler in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate images by reversing a gradual noising process, guided by a learned score that points toward more likely data. Training minimizes the L2 score matching error, and theory uses it to bound how far generated samples drift from the target distribution.

The authors split the score error into two geometric parts: a gradient part and a swirling solenoidal part. Only the gradient part feeds the dynamics that shape the final sample distribution, so the other part is invisible to sample quality. They prove no monotone function of the full error can lower-bound distribution mismatch, then bound the Kullback-Leibler divergence using the gradient part alone. On CIFAR-10, that part correlated with sample quality near ninety-six hundredths, well above the full error.
arxiv-2606-06479:
Akarsh Kumar and Phillip Isola rethink how recurrent networks learn memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recurrent neural networks process sequences step by step, but training them by backpropagation through time is sequential, slow, and plagued by gradients that vanish or explode over long spans. Their Supervised Memory Training avoids unrolling the network entirely. A Transformer encoder first learns what is worth remembering: a compact state that keeps only the past information needed to predict the future.

Those learned states become labels. The recurrent network is then trained by supervised learning to make one step transitions between states, a task that parallelizes across time and keeps gradients stable. Across language modeling and pixel sequence tasks, the method beat backpropagation through time, and the models captured longer range dependencies. Decoupling what to remember from how to update, the authors suggest, could finally let recurrent models scale.
arxiv-2606-06579:
Christopher Yang and co-authors let a material generate its own laser like drive in this 2026 arXiv paper on quantum materials. Floquet engineering reshapes a material's electronic bands with a periodic drive, usually an external laser: power hungry and hard to integrate. Their alternative embeds a semiconductor layer in an optical cavity wired to leads and a phonon bath. Direct current pumping builds a coherent field inside the cavity through light matter coupling, until the system self organizes.

Above threshold, the system settles into a stable time periodic limit cycle. Its strength is set by the cavity's quality factor and dissipation. That home grown field dresses the electronic bands just as a laser would. In a material with broken time reversal symmetry, the dressed bands' geometry changes the anomalous Hall response, measurable through ordinary in plane transport. Electrically controlled quantum phases, with no external light at all, come into reach.
arxiv-2606-06779:
A food delivery app knows what you order for dinner, but not what groceries you might want. Sinha, Saboo, Wang, and Das attack that cold start problem at DoorDash in this 2026 arXiv paper. Newer shopping areas like grocery and retail have thin user histories, while the restaurant side holds years of rich behavior that could hint at wider tastes.

Their framework uses a large language model as a bridge between the two worlds. A retrieval pipeline digs through each user's restaurant orders and searches, then generates features describing long term tastes and short term intent at several levels of detail. Those features feed the production ranking model that decides what each shopper sees. Offline and live tests showed clear gains in personalization and engagement for the newer verticals, strongest for users with no history there.
arxiv-2606-06879:
Scam texts that unfold over many messages are hard to catch, and real examples are scarce. Lochstampfor and Roy expand a synthetic data set for that fight in this 2026 arXiv paper. The crime is smishing, fraud by text message. Their collection, COVA-X, holds almost eleven thousand invented conversations. The scams target older people in eight categories.

The new corpus fixes flaws found in its smaller parent. Generation glitches, mismatched labels, and leaked stage directions were cleaned out. Label corrections fell sharply as the pipeline improved. All classifiers were then retrained on the bigger set. A transformer model called Longformer now beats the older gradient boosting champion. It reached about eighty percent accuracy on the tests. That confirms the team's earlier guess: transformers need larger conversation data before their context skills pay off. Artifact rates in the trickiest scam type also dropped.
arxiv-2606-06979:
Ordinary particles pair quarks with antiquarks, but theory allows stranger bundles of four. Yuheng Wu and co-authors hunt for fully heavy tetraquarks in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tetraquark packs four quarks into one particle. Here all four are heavy: charm or bottom quarks and their antimatter twins.

The team works inside a chiral quark model. They test two internal arrangements for the bundle. Bound state calculations found no truly bound state in either system. A real scaling method, though, revealed resonance states. Resonances are short lived humps rather than stable particles. The charm system showed two, near seven thousand and seventy two hundred million electron volts. Those match candidates for the observed X(6900) and X(7200) structures. The bottom system showed one resonance near nineteen thousand seven hundred. The authors urge experiments to search the double Upsilon spectrum for it.
arxiv-2606-07079:
Diffusion image models usually dirty the whole picture with one noise level at a time. Papa and co-authors let each region follow its own schedule in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their AsyncPatch Diffusion assigns distinct noise levels to different pixels or latent tokens. One patch can be nearly clean while its neighbor is still pure static.

The team proves the asynchronous process is a valid generative model, with the first correct evidence lower bound for it. Training needs care: random per region noise over samples chaotic mixes. A controlled sampler balances average corruption against spatial variety. One pretrained model then generates, fills missing regions, and extends images without retraining. Clean patches can guide the generation of unknown ones, improving local consistency. Quality matched standard diffusion on ImageNet and LSUN benchmarks. Bonus strategies include speeding up easy regions and generating autoregressively, piece by piece.
arxiv-2606-07179:
Streaming a detailed 3D scene to a headset means sending coarse versions first and refining on demand. Yuang Shi and co-authors rebuild that refinement as a family tree in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is 3D Gaussian Splatting, which renders scenes from millions of soft colored blobs. Earlier progressive schemes stacked independent layers of blobs, one per quality level.

Independence wasted bytes and let errors accumulate between layers. EvoGS instead grows an Evolution Tree. Each parent splat refines into children that can correct the ancestors' mistakes, wavelet style. Redundant splats fell from over sixty five percent to under twenty five percent. Transmission payload shrank by up to about two point four times. Graphics memory needs dropped by up to five point five times. Quality also changed smoothly rather than in jumps. The sparse differences between layers compress well for streaming. Immersive scenes on weak connections are the target use.
arxiv-2606-07479:
Karakaş and Şimşek test whether language models can tell idiomatic Turkish expressions from literal ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Light verb constructions pair a noun with a verb like make or do; the same surface form can be an idiom or a literal phrase, which makes classification tricky. Their test set holds 150 sentences with matched negative examples, including literal controls designed to look like idioms. A supervised Turkish encoder model serves as the baseline against 3 prompted language models.

With no examples, the language models handled negatives well but missed most idioms, showing low recall on the positive class. A single demonstration sharply improved idiom detection but brought model-specific biases toward over- or under-predicting. Richer few-shot prompts restored calibration, and 2 models matched or beat the supervised baseline on idioms with careful demonstrations. The authors release code, prompts, and materials, stressing how prompt-sensitive metalinguistic classification remains.
arxiv-2606-07579:
Rucker and Erickson measure how imposing boundary conditions changes accuracy in physics-informed neural networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These networks solve mechanics equations by training against the physics and boundary data. Soft enforcement penalizes violations in the loss, while hard enforcement builds them into the answer's form. Where boundaries are described implicitly, by a level-set function rather than a mesh, the authors interpolate boundary data. They construct the hard version for traction conditions on shapes.

The testbed is elastodynamic plane strain, the deformation of a slice of material, in first-order and second-order formulations. Networks achieved higher accuracy on the first-order formulation. A trade-off emerged: all-soft gave accuracy at longer training times, while all-hard trained faster with worse error, with mixes in between. The result matters for inverse problems, where model reliability caps downstream.
arxiv-2606-07679:
Trevor and colleagues describe upgrades to PyCBC Live, the search program that flags gravitational waves from merging compact objects in near real time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The upgrades served the fourth observing run of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detector network, which ran from May 2023 to November 2025. Faster, cleaner alerts let telescopes on the ground chase the light that some mergers produce.

Changes include background noise models that update daily, cheaper recovery of signal strength, and a way to use Virgo for sky maps even when its data cannot confirm a detection. A new early-warning search spots neutron-star mergers before they collide, sending alerts a few seconds after the data arrive and up to a minute before merger. In mock-data tests the new setup found about seventy-nine percent of injected two-detector signals, up from roughly half under the older configuration.
arxiv-2606-07779:
Tanoglidis and colleagues test whether vision-language models spot faint dwarf galaxies as reliably as people do, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are among the hardest objects to find in survey images, and astronomers have used volunteers to flag candidates in multi-panel diagnostic plots. A general-purpose model that matched human judgement could scale that hunt enormously.

The team compared zero-shot model predictions, made with no task-specific training, against annotations from a large citizen campaign. On average the models closely reproduced the crowd's overall calibration, and they performed well on clear-cut cases. Agreement broke down on individual examples, where predictions varied a lot. Worse, neither self-reported confidence nor repeating the query produced uncertainty estimates an astronomer could use. The authors conclude the models are promising assistants for large-scale discovery, but not yet reliable judges on the ambiguous cases that matter most.
arxiv-2606-07879:
Osaro and co-authors automate one of quantum chemistry's most judgement-heavy choices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multireference calculations, needed when electrons correlate strongly, begin by selecting an active space: the orbitals treated exactly while the rest are approximated. Experts pick it by intuition and costly trial and error, and a bad pick ruins the calculation.

Their engine, RLEASE, has a neural network score each orbital from cheap Hartree-Fock descriptors, while a learned threshold splits orbitals into active and inactive. The threshold policy is trained by reinforcement learning, rewarded by how closely energies from the chosen space match costly reference calculations. Trained on a small set of molecules and geometries, the selector transfers to diverse test systems, producing compact active spaces and energy surfaces competitive with entropy-based selectors. Deployment needs only cheap descriptors and a network evaluation, suiting high-throughput work where expert time is the bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-08379:
Zaznov and colleagues apply reinforcement learning to the problem of selling a large block of stock, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optimal execution means unwinding a big position without moving the price against oneself more than necessary. Their algorithm, TT-DAC-PS, is a deterministic actor-critic architecture, where an actor proposes trades and critics judge them. It combines twin critic targets with a pessimistic minimum backup, target policy smoothing noise, delayed actor updates, and conservative regularization that curbs overestimates.

Exploration uses correlated noise with a hybrid schedule: a deterministic decay across episodes, adjustment guided by recent reward dispersion, and a learned temperature that maps onto the noise scale. The trading setup combines a classical Almgren-Chriss model of market impact with real limit order book data and caps on per-step participation. The authors apply the algorithm to order book data for ten United States stocks.
arxiv-2606-08779:
Liu and colleagues address a hidden cause of failure in training large language models with reinforcement learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning here means improving a model by rewarding its better answers. The problem is a mismatch. The engine that generates answers during training differs slightly from the one serving users, so the model learns from subtly wrong numbers.

They reformulate training as a constrained problem that pursues reward while keeping the mismatch under a limit. Experiments reveal a tolerance region where the gap does little harm, and forcing it smaller hurts learning by narrowing exploration. Outside that region, shrinking the gap steadies training and raises final quality. Their method adjusts the penalty automatically and beat the standard GRPO approach on two Qwen models, including one with eight billion parameters. It also lets a model train in one precision format and deploy in a cheaper one.
arxiv-2606-08879:
Fukuyama argues that a detector's own resolution is part of what physicists should mean by infrared memory in quantum electrodynamics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. QED calculations are plagued by infrared divergences from photons of arbitrarily low energy. Classic mechanisms cancel the fake divergences in observable quantities. Fukuyama points out that one scale survives the cancellation: omega max, the highest energy of soft photons the detector cannot resolve.

Those unobserved photons are traced over, averaged out of the quantum description of the hard particles. The overlap between soft-photon states therefore depends on the resolution scale. Fukuyama's proposal is to define observable infrared memory through that scale. Memory is not a property of the soft sector alone, but of the split between observed and unobserved degrees of freedom. The reading bridges the traditional cross-section view with the modern picture of soft photons as carriers of quantum information.
arxiv-2606-09079:
Wang and colleagues slash the memory cost of long conversations by predicting which past parts it will need, in this 2026 arXiv paper. During generation, models keep a key-value cache of all past tokens, and for ultra-long contexts it overwhelms GPU memory. Lookahead Sparse Attention trains a Neural Memory Indexer to forecast demands, keeping only query-critical chunks in GPU memory. The indexer is a dual-encoder trained with retrieval methods, separately from the backbone.

On long-context suites including LongBench-v2, LongMemEval, and RULER, the cache footprint fell to 13.5 percent of the full-context baseline. Accuracy was preserved or improved, by 0.6 percentage points on average, because dropping context also denoises attention. At an extreme context length of 500,000 tokens, the cache overhead fell by over 90 percent without destabilizing reasoning. The report, built on the DeepSeek-V4 architecture, argues that for long context, less memory can be more performance.
arxiv-2606-09479:
Jiří Mayer and a large team of co-authors ask how optical music recognition can cope with real handwritten scores in this 2026 arXiv paper. Optical music recognition reads printed or written notation automatically, but today's systems are trained mostly on born-digital material. Library collections, by contrast, are mostly handwritten, and their varied handwriting makes existing systems fail, while heritage institutions cannot fund large labelled datasets.

The team provides a first baseline on real handwritten scores with complex piano music, annotated with fine-grained music graphs. They then test domain adaptation using fake handwritten images produced by the Smashcima synthesis tool. Some real in-domain data remained essential, but adding fake images brought significant improvement. Key point: the symbols inside the fake images did not need to come from the target collection, so the costly fine-grained annotation could be skipped.
arxiv-2606-09679:
Parthsarthi Rawat reports a contest system that spots who does what with the ball in broadcast soccer in this 2026 arXiv paper. The SoccerNet challenge asks for eight action classes. The base system, FOOTPASS, reads video in stages: one net scores each player, a graph net adds team context, and a decoder cleans the list.

Rawat adds four upgrades. Gradient checkpointing lets the full backbone train on a single graphics card. Graph scores feed into the decoder, which mixes tactical and visual cues. Class weights blunt a steep skew: passes outnumber tackles by two hundred thirteen to one in the training data. A cleanup chain then refines timing, fixes jersey mix-ups, and blends two models. The system scored a macro F1 of zero point five four eight on the test set. On the harder challenge set it reached zero point four four six.
arxiv-2606-09879:
Qingbo Wu and his co-authors fuse a transformer's steps so data stays on the chip longer in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is Tenstorrent's Tensix line, an edge inference chip. Transformer work swaps between memory-bound steps, like norms, and compute-bound matrix work. Each swap hauls mid-step data to off-chip memory and back, a slow and costly trip.

Their plan welds RMSNorm onto the matrix step in both the attention block and the feed-forward block. The pair then runs back-to-back inside on-chip SRAM, the fast local store. A network-on-chip multicast spreads inputs and weights across the core mesh from master nodes, which eases the fight for memory bandwidth. On the Wormhole board, three Qwen models were tested. Attention delay fell by up to thirty-seven percent, and the feed-forward part by near sixteen.
arxiv-2606-09979:
Parker and Alves de Oliveira ask how a puzzling class of small cosmic objects formed, in a 2026 arXiv paper on star and planet formation. The objects sit in IC 348, a star-forming region, and were found by the James Webb Space Telescope. They show an absorption feature at a wavelength tied to an unidentified hydrocarbon, a carbon-hydrogen compound, never before seen in such atmospheres outside the Solar System. Astronomers call them H-type objects.

One idea is that they formed like planets in discs around stars and were later ejected by passing stars. The authors compared their spatial distribution with stars and brown dwarfs in the cluster, finding them indistinguishable. Simulations of ejected planets, starting near five astronomical units from their hosts, produced a far more dispersed pattern. Because the simulated spread clashes with the observed layout, the team concludes these objects are unlikely to have a planetary origin.
arxiv-2606-10079:
Adrianov and Kreines prove that certain abstract branching patterns for maps between spheres can actually be realized, in a 2026 arXiv paper on algebraic geometry and topology. A covering of the sphere branches over points where sheets of the map join, and branch data record the local pattern at each such point. Their data involve patterns built from powers of two and three with extra parts not divisible by two or three.

The proof uses dessins d'enfants, children's drawings that encode coverings branched over three points as combinatorial graphs. With that explicit description, they establish realizability for the tetrahedral case families stated in the paper. As a corollary, realizability follows for a broader class of branch data with more critical values. The work belongs to the Hurwitz existence problem tradition, deciding which branching data occur, and this installment handles the first in a planned series of cases.
arxiv-2606-10279:
Su and his team deliver a warning for training medical language models with AI-written explanations, in a 2026 arXiv paper on medical machine learning. Supervised fine-tuning with machine-written rationale data is widely taken to help by teaching models not just what to predict but why. They test that belief on five-year Alzheimer's disease and related dementias prediction from long-term health histories. Across a large controlled experiment of five hundred four setups, rationale-based fine-tuning steadily and sharply hurts prediction scores compared with label-only fine-tuning.

Crucially, poor rationale quality is not the reason. Human experts confirmed the generated rationales are accurate and grounded in patient evidence. The same rationales improve scores when used as inference-time prompts instead of training targets. The authors name a built-in conflict between story plausibility and sharp classification.
arxiv-2606-10379:
Li and his team engineer light emission that flows in only one direction, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum optics. Nonreciprocal devices pass signals one way but not the other, and multiquanta emission, releasing photons in bundles, has remained little studied in that setting. Directional quantum squeezing, a trick that reshapes quantum noise unevenly, induces lopsided frequency detuning and photon hopping between the resonators, leading to directional driving of two-photon super-Rabi oscillation.

By harnessing the system's built-in dissipation, two types of two-photon bundle emission can be switched on by choice for a probe entering from one direction while being blocked from the other. Potential uses include chiral quantum emitters, which radiate preferentially in one direction, and photonic links immune to backscattering. The work shows this loss, usually a nuisance in quantum devices, acting as the control knob that enforces one-way bundle emission.
arxiv-2606-10679:
Ottavia Truttero and colleagues stress-test the analysis plan for a sky survey in this 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time will probe deep into the regime where galaxy bias, how galaxies trace dark matter, and baryonic feedback, gas physics reshaping matter, dominate systematics. Their three-by-two-point analysis combines three signals for the survey's first and tenth years, modelled with the BACCO emulator, through a new open-source pipeline.

First, a linear bias gives unbiased, percent-level constraints on the matter density and clustering strength only to a modest scale cut; beyond it a perturbative treatment is needed. A minimal variant with higher-order terms fixed stays unbiased at the deepest cut tested. And total neutrino mass detection looks possible once mid-range scales enter, yet the inferred value shifts with the bias model, a warning that detection is easier than measurement.
arxiv-2606-10779:
Hong-Minh and colleagues uncover the physical life of a stem-cell protein in this 2026 arXiv paper on biophysics. NANOG is a transcription factor that keeps embryonic stem cells pluripotent, and its intrinsically disordered region was suspected of driving assembly. Combining simulations, mass photometry, cryo-electron microscopy, and microrheology, the team finds NANOG above a concentration forms self-limiting micelles, 22 to 25 monomers with jumbled cores and DNA-binding domains exposed. Other disordered proteins form unbounded droplets instead.

The micelles overlap into a percolating network, a sol-gel transition: viscosity rises ten-thousand-fold as the fluid ages into a gel, an effect abolished by mutating that region. With DNA, gels form at natural concentrations of 1 to 10 micromolar. The micelles bridge DNA tangles and restrict genome motion. The authors propose such gel-like pockets, keeping a memory of their aging, help NANOG control gene expression in the nucleus.
arxiv-2606-10979:
Chen and colleagues give reinforcement learning a cleaner grip on operations problems in this 2026 arXiv paper. In inventory, queueing, and routing tasks, the feasible actions change with the state and obey capacity and integrality constraints, so standard algorithms, which expect a fixed action menu, need heavy custom engineering. Their Bellman-Taylor score decoding splits the job: a standard continuous-action learner outputs scores, and an optimization decoder converts them into feasible actions.

Because feasibility lives in the decoder, one solver serves many problems. The optimality gap splits into a structural part and a learning part. In a queueing network case study, a stock PPO implementation with the decoder learns a max-weight-style dispatching rule and beats classical routing heuristics and approximate dynamic programming benchmarks by a wide margin.
arxiv-2606-11079:
Lu and three co-authors introduce VISTA in a 2026 arXiv paper, a toolkit for evaluating interactive AI agents by simulating their users. Static benchmarks test isolated tasks and miss failure modes that emerge over multi-step conversations. Simulated users can probe agents at length, but older simulators offered few ways to judge the simulations themselves, and most handled only screen actions or only API calls, not both.

VISTA pairs a hybrid user simulator, mixing interface actions with API calls, with six metrics scoring realism, capability coverage, and interaction effectiveness. The authors test the toolkit in two settings, e-commerce shopping and education customer service. There VISTA produced more realistic and more comprehensive evaluations than existing methods, exposing more of what agents can and cannot do. The design goal is evaluation that tracks how agents behave with real users over full interactions, rather than how they score on frozen task lists.
arxiv-2606-11279:
Leonor Barreiros and three co-authors from Priberam Labs and Lisbon institutions present a keyword spotting system for speech recognition in a 2026 arXiv paper. Speech recognizers underperform on rare words, namely specialized terminology. Open-vocabulary keyword spotting with contextual biasing, steering output toward a supplied glossary, mitigates this. Existing systems, though, handle only glossaries of a few hundred terms before becoming an infeasible bottleneck.

The proposed system stores features with a memory footprint up to 128 times smaller than a comparable baseline. That lets users process massive term databases while remaining open, with no fine-tuning of the underlying speech model. The authors report entity recall similar to full-size solutions. Strikingly, this held even in languages not seen during training. They frame the result as making biasing practical for domains like healthcare and air traffic control, where correctly transcribing rare keywords is essential downstream.
arxiv-2606-11579:
Anurag Dwivedi leads a nine-author team using tensor networks to split quantum simulations across separate machines in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tensor network breaks a large mathematical object into linked smaller pieces. Applied to the operator that evolves a quantum system over time, it exposes a larger space where the evolution separates into independent lower-dimensional pieces. Those pieces can run in parallel, even on different kinds of hardware.

The team demonstrates the method on a trapped-ion quantum computer at Sandia National Laboratories. Their circuits use partial-entangling gates, which cut expected two-qubit gate error by more than thirty percent compared with standard fully entangling versions. They compute the vibrational spectrum, the pattern of shaking energies, of a small protonated water cluster, a system hard for classical methods. The quantum results match classical ones to within four wavenumber units, close to spectroscopic accuracy.
arxiv-2606-11779:
Nermeen Abou Baker, David Rohrschneider and Uwe Handmann detect batteries in X-ray images in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sorting waste batteries matters for recycling and safety, since damaged lithium-ion batteries can leak or catch fire, and manual inspection is risky. X-ray screening sees inside objects regardless of surface dirt or damage, making it attractive for automated sorting.

The authors use transfer learning in two steps. First they train a pre-trained YOLOv5 detector on a large dataset of electronic devices. The resulting weights are transferred to detect batteries and classify them into three lithium-ion types: prismatic, pouch and cylindrical. Battery detection reaches ninety-four percent precision, beating the original weights by five points, at about twenty-two milliseconds per image. Detecting whether a device is present at all reaches ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2606-11979:
Vicent Ribas Ripoll translates chemical reaction planning into algebra in this 2026 arXiv paper, published in the Journal of Computational Algebra. Click reactions are modular couplings prized in chemistry; the design question is which reaction families can run together without interfering. He encodes each family's allowed handle pairings as algebraic constraints.

From the compatibility data he builds an assembly ideal in a polynomial ring, whose solution set is exactly the feasible reaction triples. The ideal proves zero-dimensional and radical, so counting solutions is clean. Elimination ideals test whether a handle identifies its family uniquely, and a toric ideal measures redundancy in the compatibility relation. A multi-step version encodes plans running simultaneously, and an orthogonality graph caps how many plans can coexist. Instantiated on the real bioorthogonal click landscape, the machinery finds thirty feasible triples and a coexistence ceiling of four, all verified symbolically in SymPy.
arxiv-2606-12079:
Raffaele D'Avino and co-authors make a basic quantum randomness question computable in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a known quantum state is measured, the outcome holds intrinsic randomness, unpredictability built into the physics. The guessing probability measures the best chance an adversary, called Eve, has to predict that outcome using side information. Until now, no general method could compute this value for setups where state and device are known but not trusted.

The team rewrites the guessing probability as a semidefinite program, an optimization form that computers solve reliably. Applied to setups, the method pins down the exact certifiable randomness where only upper bounds existed. In one noisy qubit case, it confirms that an earlier analytic bound is exactly tight. The authors also show that entanglement between the preparing device and the measurement strictly raises Eve's guessing power, even for a simple two-outcome measurement on a single qubit.
arxiv-2606-12479:
Yu and co-authors fix the report cards used to train AI routers, so good routing decisions stop looking bad, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Routing sends each query to the best-suited language model or reasoning strategy. Reinforcement learning can train routers from feedback, but the reward is usually one blended number mixing correctness, format, and more. Credit assignment turns ambiguous: a good choice can score badly for the wrong reason. Rewards also vary wildly across tasks, so easy, high-variance cases dominate training.

Their framework, ReCal, first decomposes the reward hierarchically, estimating advantages component by component for clear, objective-level signals. A distribution-aware strategy then recalibrates learning itself: variance-aware reweighting and per-dataset normalization stop loud datasets from swamping quiet ones. Across seven datasets, ReCal improves routing performance and training stability over baselines. Informative hard cases get their fair share of optimization pressure.
arxiv-2606-12679:
Chen and McMillan present Fed-FBD, a redesign of federated learning for medical data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Federated learning trains one model across hospitals without pooling raw patient records. The standard method averages everyone's updates into a single model, so one malicious participant can corrupt the whole system, and departing participants cannot be removed.

Fed-FBD splits a ResNet image network into 6 functional blocks and keeps a warehouse of model variants, called colours, assembled from those blocks. Every block is stamped with the clients that trained it, so influence stays traceable and contained. Across 6 adversarial attacks, damage stays inside the attacker's own colours, with clean variants drifting by at most 0.01 in AUC, a ranking quality score. Removing a departed client takes under a second without retraining, and accuracy trails the standard method by only 0.3 to 3.1 percent on adequately sized datasets.
arxiv-2606-12879:
Wang and Ying study diffusion-network alignment, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It is a variant of the network alignment problem in which a rooted diffusion tree must be matched to the vertices of a network. The tree might come from a communication trace or contact tracing, and the network from a social graph. Unlike classic alignment, where both graphs are fully observed, this model captures an information asymmetry: the tree reveals only the diffusion structure, not the underlying network.

The authors present an algorithm based on tree correlation tests, which extract alignment information from local neighbourhoods by comparing how subtrees correlate with network neighbourhoods. Analysing the algorithm in the sparse graph regime, they show that with high probability all matched pairs it returns are correct. For each vertex of the diffusion tree they establish a lower bound on the probability that the vertex is correctly matched.
arxiv-2606-12979:
Pandya compares 2 ways of feeding experience into a JEPA world model under distribution shift, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Joint-embedding predictive architectures predict future states in latent space, but their predictor is static: when test-time dynamics diverge from training, nothing adapts. Operand-side injection adds an experience representation to the predictor's hidden state; operator-side modulation lets it generate weight changes through LoRA.

On a pre-registered comparison using Moving MNIST with a shift, the operator-side method, EPM-JEPA, scored 0.7848 against 0.8238 for operand-side EI-JEPA, a difference the author classifies as a null result. A non-pre-registered observation cuts the other way: EPM-JEPA improves 1.90 percent over the no-memory baseline score of 0.8000 across seeds, suggesting any benefit is specific to modulation. An analysis shows the measured trajectory reflects 3 processes, buffer cycling, target drift, and a LoRA settling transient, rather than convergence to equilibrium.
arxiv-2606-13279:
Choi, Son, and Lim tackle two-armed robot control in this 2026 arXiv paper. In bimanual work, what the robot needs to see changes as a task unfolds, and the two arms switch between working independently and moving in coordination. Standard vision-language-action policies, which map camera input and instructions to movements, push everything through one shared pathway. That design cannot separately track visual relevance and arm interaction. The authors split the problem at two levels, calling their approach dual-level decomposition.

A view-selective router adjusts how much each wrist camera contributes, emphasising the cues that matter for the stage. A mixture-of-experts action module, which routes decisions among sub-networks, separates coordinated motion from single-arm motion. The team evaluates on 6 simulated tasks in the RoboTwin benchmark and 3 long real-world tasks. Their model improves the average success rate over the baselines.
arxiv-2606-13979:
Ma extends an old link between curvature and topology beyond surfaces, to spaces with a special flatness property. The Cohn-Vossen inequality bounds a complete surface's total curvature by its Euler characteristic, a topological count. Yau conjectured a higher-dimensional analogue for manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, but counterexamples killed the broad version. His 2026 arXiv paper works on locally conformally flat manifolds, spaces locally like rescaled flat space, and verifies the conjecture there.

The tools include a refined singularity estimate for nonnegative superharmonic functions, which lie above their own averages in a precise sense. With it, Ma pins down volume growth for these spaces. He also proves a sharp gap theorem: spaces near the borderline case must be exactly that model. The gap result removes all extra assumptions earlier works needed. The results pin down how these integrals behave far out on this class.
arxiv-2606-14079:
Tanaka and Kawahara fuse deep learning with classic spectral methods to predict noisy, partly observed systems. Spectral learning builds predictive state coordinates from past and future data by canonical correlation analysis, with closed-form estimators, but depends on fixed feature maps. Their 2026 arXiv paper makes the features learnable: a neural encoder maps observations into a deep learned space, where a functional form of that correlation yields state coordinates. Transfer and observation operators follow as closed-form, ridge-regularized solutions.

The model, the Deep Spectral Encoder, supports Kalman-style filtering and Koopman mode decomposition in feature space. Tests on nonlinear oscillators and image sequences showed stable, superior performance against standard baselines. Spectrum recovery held up under noise and partial views. The approach keeps the statistical cleanliness of spectral estimates while letting learned features adapt to each system.
arxiv-2606-14179:
Islam and colleagues train a small tool-calling agent to near-frontier accuracy, practicing against a cache, not live tools. Big models orchestrate tool use well but cost too much. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents CacheRL, on three ideas. Trajectories are enriched with reasoning traces. A three-tier fuzzy cache replaces live calls, with token-level masking for fidelity, plus a cache-aware reward sparing the model punishment for mismatches.

It reached ninety-two percent process accuracy on tool-calling tasks, nearing GPT-5's ninety-four percent at 100x less compute. Fine-tuning plus GRPO lifted Qwen3-4B-Thinking's validation reward from zero point four three to zero point seven eight. Ablations show knowledge transfer matters most: removing it cut performance forty-one percent; cache-aware rewards added seventeen. Reinforcement learning mainly stabilized training, plateauing within zero point zero one of the fine-tuned baseline: data quality and reward design dominate.
arxiv-2606-14379:
Mentasti and co-authors write a 2026 arXiv paper in cosmology about gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime from violent events. A faint background hum of such waves may fill the universe from its earliest moments. The Sachs-Wolfe effect, caused by large-scale cosmic structure, slightly shifts the frequencies of waves passing through it.

The team shows that for backgrounds above a stated strength threshold, this effect stamps direction patterns and spectrum distortions onto the hum. A network of space detectors such as LISA and Taiji could detect those marks, and ignoring them could bias estimates of the background's origin. Because the same effect also marks the cosmic microwave background, matching patterns between the two would confirm the background is truly primordial.
arxiv-2606-14479:
Valero and co-authors show that impurity physics can amplify faint hints of quantum gravity in a 2026 arXiv paper. Some theories tweak the uncertainty principle at very high energies. They also tweak how particle energy relates to momentum. Such effects are normally far beyond reach. The authors build a deformed polaron-molecule model. It keeps low-energy behavior intact while adding these high-energy tweaks.

Near the crossover between polaron and molecule behavior, tiny tweaks grow large. They produce shifts in spectral and Ramsey signals that tests can resolve. The team ran the dynamics on a quantum computer. They checked the results on the QRed processor in Barcelona. Their work maps where the effective model stays valid. It also offers a concrete low-energy route to test quantum-gravity ideas.
arxiv-2606-14579:
Xinyu Qiu and co-authors improve training for GUI grounding in a 2026 arXiv paper. GUI grounding means locating the exact screen element a user instruction refers to. A popular reinforcement method, group relative policy optimization, samples attempts from one screenshot view, but groups often end up all failures or all successes, giving no useful comparison signal.

Their framework, VISTA, builds each comparison group from several views of the same screen, cropped so the target stays visible with its box remapped exactly. Rollouts are then compared across views that mean the same thing but look geometrically different. A self-verified cross-view anchor stabilizes the short coordinate outputs. Across five benchmarks and several Qwen vision backbones, VISTA consistently raised grounding accuracy, lifting one model's professional-screen score from about fifty-five to about sixty-three percent, with fewer prediction flips across views.
arxiv-2606-14679:
Pineci and Xu prove a simple inventory principle optimal in a 2026 arXiv paper. Online inventory optimization is online decision-making with physical memory: unsold stock carries over, so today's feasible orders depend on yesterday's choices. A natural principle keeps a hidden target inventory chosen by an online learner and orders up to its projection onto the currently feasible set.

The authors prove this principle is optimal for arbitrary bounded convex capacity sets, not just a single linear constraint as before. With gradient descent as the base learner, regret improves from inverse to inverse-square-root dependence on the common-demand probability, and a matching lower bound confirms optimality. The same idea yields the first polylogarithmic regret for strongly convex losses. Their norm alignment analysis reduces the inventory state to a one-dimensional queue, and experiments on synthetic and real data corroborate the theory.
arxiv-2606-14779:
Minchul Kang and co-authors pool memory and storage to serve long-context language models faster in a 2026 arXiv paper. Serving long prompts requires offloading key-value caches, the stored attention data, to host memory and solid-state drives, but current mechanisms were not designed for such lengths. They measured time-to-first-token near thirty-one seconds, over three times the typical ten-second requirement.

Their analysis blames serialized retrieval through one memory path and filesystem overhead consuming most of the drive retrieval time. Unified KV pooling merges several memory modules and drives into one logical pool, distributing caches by device bandwidth, while KV-passthrough bypasses the kernel filesystem using direct drive access from user space. Across three open models the design cut long-context time-to-first-token roughly fourfold against state-of-the-art systems, bringing every case under ten seconds.
arxiv-2606-14879:
Devarakonda and co-authors help camera-only robots explore unknown places in a 2026 arXiv paper. Mapping new terrain usually needs depth sensors or occupancy maps. A robot with a single camera cannot easily build them. Their system, VANDERER, explores with no map at all. It steers a pre-trained diffusion policy, a model that generates action sequences.

A Visual Curiosity Module guides the policy. It predicts what proposed actions would show the robot. A navigation world model makes those predictions. Actions whose views look novel get a curiosity reward. The policy is then nudged toward high-curiosity moves. Across varied simulated settings, VANDERER beat established baselines. It explored about thirteen point four percent more area than the NoMaD system. Visual curiosity and geometric curiosity tracked each other closely outdoors. That link lets cheap cameras stand in for richer sensors.
arxiv-2606-14979:
Rose and coauthors build a robust guidance method for aerocapture in a 2026 study. Aerocapture slows a spacecraft by diving through a planet's atmosphere, saving fuel and shortening cruise time. Entry state and air density are uncertain, and the dynamics are strongly nonlinear. The team steers the spread of possible outcomes, not just a single path.

Their algorithm samples starting states, flies nonlinear trajectories to atmospheric exit, and tunes guidance against the worst cases. The target is the fuel cost, measured as delta-V, at high percentiles across the sampled set. Monte Carlo tests cover two Mars scenarios and one Uranus scenario with dispersed conditions. Against a leading covariance steering method, the new approach cuts the ninety-ninth percentile and worst-case delta-V by five to fifteen percent. Mean delta-V does not rise, so the safety gain comes without an average fuel penalty.
arxiv-2606-15179:
Hu and coauthors present CONCORD, a 2026 framework for retrieval-augmented generation split between a device and the cloud. In this setup, private documents stay on the user's device while public knowledge sits in the cloud. Rules forbid sending documents across, so the two sides cannot merge their evidence. Older methods synchronize often and ship dense evidence back and forth. CONCORD instead treats the cloud as an asynchronous evidence source.

A waiting-debt controller decides at each decoding step whether waiting for the cloud is worthwhile. A certificate mechanism then requests only the remote evidence needed to fix the current token choice. Steps that consult the cloud keep the same greedy token as dense aggregation. Steps that time out commit with local evidence alone. On question answering and language modeling tests, CONCORD doubled throughput on one benchmark. It also cut per-token communication by about ninety-nine percent at similar quality.
arxiv-2606-15479:
Keripale and coauthors make symmetry-aware neural networks Bayesian in a 2026 machine learning paper.
