Steerable convolutional networks build rotation symmetry into their filters, so a rotated input yields a predictably rotated output, a strong advantage for shapes and molecules. But they are deterministic, offering no confidence. The authors place probability distributions over the filter coefficients instead, keeping symmetry exact while letting kernels vary.

Trained by a variational fit, the model matches its deterministic rival's accuracy and reports well-calibrated outputs. Under heavy added noise it keeps an accuracy edge of up to about six points. Its uncertainty is also useful, not decorative. Letting the model defer on its most uncertain cases raises accuracy by about four points across most of the test set. Higher stated uncertainty tracks higher error. For safety-sensitive three-dimensional vision, calibrated doubt beside built-in symmetry is what deployment demands.
arxiv-2606-15579:
Deng treats the behaviour of language-model agents like a genome in 2026, encoding each run as a sequence in a four-letter alphabet. The letters mark whether the agent explores, executes, plans, or verifies at each step. He applies sequence analysis, from n-gram mining to Markov transition matrices, to several hundred traces from a production agent system.

One trigram, plan-explore-plan, is the only significant high-risk pattern, cutting the success rate by ten points. Planning share is the strongest negative predictor of success, and agents almost never verify after executing: barely two percent of transitions. Deng builds Governor, a runtime system that injects corrective prompts when risky patterns appear, with data-learned rules and self-adapting thresholds. In deployment it raised task success by six points while cutting token use by forty-four percent. Two of the three findings replicate on two thousand software-agent trajectories.
arxiv-2606-15779:
Huynh and colleagues tackle a faithfulness problem in emotion AI in 2026: models explaining predictions by naming facial action units may cite units that did not drive them. Their system, FACR, grounds reasoning in a causal graph linking action units to emotions. A training objective enforces counterfactual faithfulness against that graph.

The rule: intervening on a unit the graph marks causal must move the prediction; intervening on an irrelevant one must not. On pain data, agreement between invoked units and the known composition jumps from eight percent to fifty-seven percent, at small detection cost. On a cross-dataset transfer, fidelity rises from fifty to eighty-four percent. A stricter test, agreement with truly active units, stays at control level for a learned graph, rising to fifty-nine percent only with a verified graph. Explanations can be made faithful to a structure; whether it is right is the harder question.
arxiv-2606-15879:
Cardona, Delgado, and Muñoz-Tello determine where the Sobolev norm of W^{k,1} on a Riemannian manifold is differentiable, in 2026. For exponents between one and infinity, the question reduces to the Fréchet differentiability of the L^p norm. The case p equals one is pathological: the norm is built from absolute values, with corners wherever derivatives vanish.

The authors find the set of Gâteaux differentiability points of the norm and compute the derivative there. Differentiability holds precisely where the function's derivatives, up to order k, vanish only on null sets. The derivative is then a sum of sign-weighted integrals pairing the two functions' derivatives. Where derivatives vanish on a set of positive measure, the corner survives and no derivative exists. The results hold for open sets in Euclidean space. Such characterisations underpin variational methods, where differentiating an energy is the first step toward minimisers.
arxiv-2606-16079:
Tasso and colleagues trace the motions of the oldest stars near galaxy centers in 2026, using cosmological simulations. Old inner stars formed during the earliest assembly stages, so their orbits keep imprints of formative events. The team studies stars older than 10 billion years within 5 kiloparsecs of the center, in thirteen Milky Way-mass FIRE-2 galaxies.

Most old inner stars formed inside their host galaxy, though accreted stars arrive prominently during the earliest stages. Accreted stars tend to sit on kinematically hot orbits, with more random motion than stars born in place. Using orbital circularity as the diagnostic, the authors find most old inner stars are dynamically hot and dispersion-supported. A subset of galaxies, including m12w, m12m, and Romeo, instead shows disk-like dynamics with residual rotation. Real surveys of the Milky Way bulge can test these simulated patterns.
arxiv-2606-16279:
Tokoro and co-authors map solar wind speeds in 2026 against the Sun's coronal magnetic field, aiming at better space-weather forecasts. Most past studies used near-ecliptic data dominated by slow wind, leaving fast wind poorly covered. Interplanetary scintillation observations give global speed coverage instead. Earlier work paired them only with the potential field source surface model, which misses key features of the field between the Sun and Earth.

The team adds the Schatten current sheet model on top, then runs a broad statistical study of wind speed. One combined parameter, the flux expansion factor over the surface field strength, splits the wind into two distinct groups. One group shows a strong negative correlation with that parameter, and the other shows none at all. Splitting by weak versus strong footpoint field strength reproduces the same split, and the exact threshold choice does not drive it.
arxiv-2606-16379:
Soares and co-authors measure how similar two learned representations are in 2026, using only the ordering of distances rather than the distances themselves. Comparing representations matters for model selection and science, but standard metrics shift their baselines between datasets, break under outliers, and grow too costly on large data. The authors build an ordinal-similarity framework around two indices, TSI for triplets and QSI for quadruplets. Each index scores how consistently two representations order the same neighborhoods.

The formulation is proved interpretable, robust to outliers, and computationally efficient, avoiding the heuristic approximations older metrics need. A formal result equates the triplet index with local neighborhood alignment as measured by mutual nearest neighbors, tying the new scores to a trusted notion. Experiments confirm the theory and show the indices scale to large datasets. Practitioners gain a similarity measure whose numbers mean the same thing across studies.
arxiv-2606-16479:
Langendörfer and co-authors audit in 2026 how much to trust the confidence scores of VGGT, the feed-forward network reshaping 3D reconstruction. VGGT, a best-paper winner at CVPR 2025, predicts camera poses, depth maps, and dense point maps straight from multiple images in seconds, in one pass with no iterative optimization. Photogrammetry gains speed and scale, but only if the model's uncertainty estimates deserve trust, since they gate quality assurance.

The analysis runs on the DTU benchmark dataset, examining the depth maps and point maps VGGT predicts. A confidence threshold of 2.0 proves a good choice for filtering the raw output, backed by both a causal justification and the empirical results. The authors recommend it as a starting point for dataset-specific tuning, while noting the trade-off: higher thresholds buy accuracy at the price of completeness, and some scenes will prefer a different balance.
arxiv-2606-16779:
Solodov leads the CMD-3 collaboration in a 2026 measurement of the neutral kaon mass at the VEPP-2000 collider in Russia. The kaon is a short-lived particle containing a strange quark, and its mass is a basic constant of particle physics. Precise values test detector methods and anchor other measurements.

The team uses more than six hundred thousand decays of short-lived neutral kaons into two pions, produced when electron and positron beams form a phi meson. Beam energy is monitored by laser back-scattering and calibrated against the known phi meson mass. The kaon momentum comes from the opening angle between the two pions, whose minimum fixes the mass cleanly. Their result agrees with earlier high-statistics experiments and carries a smaller total uncertainty. The largest error source is the energy calibration itself, a useful pointer for future collider mass measurements.
arxiv-2606-16879:
Fajman and Marshall test the stability of the matter-dominated universe in a 2026 relativity paper. The Einstein-de Sitter model describes a flat universe filled with matter, expanding at a steady power-law rate. With dust as the matter source, that model is famously unstable: tiny ripples grow into the seeds of cosmic structure.

Real matter has pressure, though, and the authors switch the source to a polytropic fluid, where pressure depends on density by a power law. Under Gowdy symmetry, which reduces the geometry's freedom, they evolve the Einstein-Euler equations numerically for small but generic disturbances. The perturbed universes stay close to the unperturbed one, pointing to stability. The contrast with dust is stark and marks a previously unknown stable regime of the coupled equations. The authors note that extra fluid components could still form structures while the main component smooths the large-scale geometry.
arxiv-2606-16979:
Karmitsa, Pahikkala and Airola scale pairwise kernel learning in a 2026 machine learning paper. Pairwise tasks predict outcomes for pairs of objects, like how strongly a drug binds a protein target. Kernel methods are expressive here, but the pair count explodes, making the core matrix computations unaffordable at real dataset sizes.

The key tool is a stochastic version of the generalized vec trick, a fast way to multiply the huge Kronecker-product kernel matrices that pairwise learning creates. Sampling batches keeps each multiplication cheap while preserving the kernel method's power. The full algorithm, SPaiK, pairs that trick with a new stochastic optimizer based on limited-memory bundle methods. Seven real drug-target affinity datasets provide the test bed. The authors report that kernel-based pairwise learning becomes feasible at scales previously out of reach, opening the approach to the large pair datasets common in drug discovery and recommendation.
arxiv-2606-17179:
Maruoka presents a 2026 arXiv paper asking why dimensional analysis works. The method extracts answers from the units of quantities alone, without solving the full equations. It sits behind much of physics and engineering practice. Maruoka grounds it in self-similarity, seen as the invariance of a form under scale changes.

Physical parameters combine numbers with units, and the paper applies the scale view to both. Dimensional analysis succeeds, Maruoka argues, because units and parameters partly share that scale invariance. When the two scale functions agree or differ, two kinds of similarity arise. The second kind splits further by whether its exponents involve dimensionless numbers. The result is three kinds of self-similar solutions in one unified classification.
arxiv-2606-17279:
Shen, Zhang, and Unberath present a 2026 arXiv paper on answering questions about surgical video, a task that needs reasoning over meaning, space, and time at once. Standard methods compress video into discrete tokens and fuse seeing with reasoning in one step. That split breaks smooth spatial and temporal links and, the authors argue, limits multi-step reasoning about what happens in an operation and why it matters.

Their framework trains a language model with reinforcement learning to reason over digital twin representations built by surgical foundation models. The twins are layered at frame, time-window, and whole-procedure level, each with uncertainty estimates attached. A new reward mixes format checks with accuracy judged through clinical plausibility and uncertainty-aware calibration. The team also built a colonoscopy benchmark with thousands of questions at three difficulty levels, reaching top scores there and on two existing benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-17379:
Meisenzahl and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on aligning pre-operative scans with a liver that deforms during surgery, a registration problem starved of live measurements. Biomechanical models keep estimates physically plausible but carry a steady bias from their simplifying assumptions. Pure learning methods, in turn, need lots of data and can produce implausible warps on new shapes, so the authors build a hybrid that corrects the physics model instead of replacing it.

The system learns only the residual deformation, the gap between the biomechanical prediction and the truth, as a graph neural diffusion over the liver mesh. Sparse live correspondences are treated as worked examples of that residual function, and a meta-learner infers the full correction from them in one feedforward pass. On a deformable liver phantom, accuracy and generalisation beat rigid, biomechanical, and data-driven baselines, especially on unseen shapes.
arxiv-2606-17579:
Wang and Vemuri present a 2026 arXiv paper reporting that bolting language model features onto graph neural networks can backfire, at least when done by plain concatenation. The usual story says such features help on standard citation benchmarks, and end-to-end pipelines built around them do succeed. But simply gluing the features to the input, with no joint training, cut accuracy sharply on two classic benchmarks in the authors' controlled tests. A third stayed within noise of its baseline.

The damage fades as backbones, splits, or encoders change, and flips to a gain on two other data sets tested. A simple measure of how well the language features alone separate classes predicts the sign of the effect better than homophily does. A dimension-matched ablation rules out size and weight-decay artefacts as the cause of the drop. The practical moral is to measure before concatenating, not after.
arxiv-2606-17979:
Shen and colleagues refine how image-generating models learn from rewards, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Reinforcement post-training for text-to-image models usually squeezes the final image's score into one number and applies it evenly to the whole generation. But generation has structure: early denoising steps set the layout, later ones add detail, and only part of the picture decides whether the text was honored.

Their method, STAR, reads text-image attention inside the model to find the regions the prompt truly cares about. It builds allocation maps that shift across steps and rollouts, then steers stronger policy updates into those key regions at almost no extra cost. Built on Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium, STAR steadily improved existing post-training methods, with the biggest gains where prompts demand precise content in specific places.
arxiv-2606-18079:
Fréour and colleagues build environmental cost into the blueprint of a future giant telescope, in a 2026 paper. The proposed Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope would carry a twelve-metre mirror and roughly two hundred fifty spectrographs, and could open in the 2040s. Rather than auditing impact after construction, the team treats sustainability as a design parameter from the earliest trade studies.

A life-cycle assessment prices the carbon of the spectrographs and detector cooling across the three instruments, and those numbers feed real design choices. One comparison stands out: designs using CMOS detectors with carbon dioxide cooling cut the annual operational footprint by about three fifths against CCD detectors with mechanical cryocoolers. The facility will also produce petabytes of data yearly, so the team weighs storage and processing strategies for their carbon cost as well.
arxiv-2606-18179:
Somasundaram and colleagues package the feature engineering behind ranking DNA regulatory elements into one reproducible tool, in a 2026 paper. ATAC-seq experiments flag thousands of candidate enhancers and promoters as open peaks. Labs must guess which few deserve costly functional testing. The signals used for that ranking, from coverage summaries to conservation scores, had no standard assembly pipeline.

Their open-source Python package, PyPeakRankR, pulls signal summaries, GC content, conservation scores, shape moments, and cell-type ranks into one peak-by-feature table. Extraction stays fixed and separate from ranking, so rival ranking plans can be compared fairly on identical inputs. It runs from a command line or Python API, handles cross-assembly scoring, and finishes thousands of peaks in minutes. A predecessor ranked in the top three of sixteen methods in a brain cell census challenge.
arxiv-2606-18379:
Wu and colleagues at Meta present RankGraph-2, a system for graph-based retrieval in recommendation at the scale of billions of nodes, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Building the graph, learning from it, and serving its results in real time are usually engineered separately, yet each stage constrains the others, and a bottleneck anywhere limits the whole pipeline.

RankGraph-2 designs all three stages together. Construction trims hundreds of trillions of possible edges down to hundreds of billions, correcting for popularity bias, and precomputes multi-hop neighborhoods so training needs no live graph service. A cluster index learned jointly with the model then cuts serving computation sharply, by more than four fifths in their accounting. The system beat strong graph baselines on recall by wide margins, lifted click and conversion rates in production, and has powered more than twenty retrieval launches across Meta's major surfaces.
arxiv-2606-18779:
Abanov and Cappelli derive the hydrodynamics of perfect fluids with quantum anomalies, from the fermionic path integral, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. Anomalies, quantum breaks of classical conservation laws, must be built into any hydrodynamic account of chiral fluids. Actions for such fluids had been offered using anomaly inflow claims.

Starting from the Dirac fermion in vector and axial gauge backgrounds, with a residual current-current interaction, the authors integrate out the fermions near the infrared limit. They obtain a semiclassical effective action. The result matches the hydrodynamic action offered for barotropic fluids with them at zero temperature. The same method yields two actions: for the Weyl fermion, and for a Dirac theory with independent vector and axial currents. The bulk-boundary terms they require appear as transgression forms. The derivation clears up the limited changes behind the fluid equations of motion.
arxiv-2606-18879:
Ghiba, Wollner, and Neff prove that two of the stability conditions of nonlinear elasticity imply a third, in the incompressible setting, in a 2026 continuum mechanics paper. Polyconvexity, rank-one convexity, and Hill's inequality are treated as independent requirements that an elastic energy should satisfy. Hill's inequality demands monotonicity of the Kirchhoff stress in the logarithmic strain. Examples show it alone does not guarantee that for stress.

Working on the special linear group of two-by-two matrices, the authors give proofs that both Legendre-Hadamard ellipticity and polyconvexity imply the weak form of Hill's inequality, for incompressible response. That shows how the rules fit. The 3D situation is different. There, ellipticity does not imply it, and a polyconvex energy of that kind violates it too, a counterexample the authors discuss. A midway open question they flag is whether an energy can be elliptic without being polyconvex in 3D.
arxiv-2606-19079:
Cassano and colleagues introduce ARIADNE in 2026, a routing method that picks the right adapter for a language model at inference time. One base model is now often paired with many task-specific adapters. Queries arrive with no task label, so the system must choose an adapter on its own. Past routers need access to adapter internals or extra router training, which limits scale and portability as pools grow and change over time.

ARIADNE needs no training and no adapter internals. Each adapter is summed up by centroids from embeddings of its own training data. A new input is routed to the adapter whose centroids sit closest in embedding space. Tests mainly use a small Llama instruct model across many diverse language tasks. The method recovers nearly all of the upper-bound performance there. At a larger task count, adapter choice stays strong.
arxiv-2606-19179:
Morwani and colleagues study compute and runtime tradeoffs for stochastic momentum methods in 2026. Heavy ball, Nesterov momentum, and accelerated stochastic gradient methods are training workhorses. Their benefit depends on two distinct quantities. Serial runtime counts iterations to a target accuracy, while compute efficiency measures total gradient cost. Larger batches cut runtime without hurting efficiency only when the contraction gap grows linearly with batch size, a condition this work makes precise.

For consistent linear regression with Gaussian covariates, the authors prove finite-dimensional lower bounds on batch-size tradeoffs. Heavy ball does not improve the efficiency frontier over plain stochastic gradient descent for arbitrary spectra. It instead preserves that efficiency over a wider batch window, letting larger batches cut runtime further. The accelerated variant is more spectrum-dependent. It improves small-batch efficiency for fast-decaying spectra, then trades that edge for runtime as batches grow. Synthetic experiments confirm these regimes.
arxiv-2606-19279:
Romero and colleagues present NeSyCat Torch in 2026, a differentiable tensor implementation of NeSyCat semantics for neurosymbolic learning. Such semantics is fragmented, since classical, fuzzy, probabilistic, and neural systems each define truth by their own rules. The NeSyCat framework unifies them under one inductive definition of truth, parametric in a monad and a truth-value aggregation structure. It lacked, however, an account of predicates and functions learned by neural networks.

The new implementation interprets computational symbols through neural networks, on tensor backends. A distribution monad gives reference semantics, while a lazy log-tensor monad supports stable training. A batch monad enables efficient batched learning, and monadic bind prunes unneeded branches. On the MNIST addition task, implementations in three frameworks beat rival systems in speed and accuracy. They nearly match the best specialized system in one uniform framework.
arxiv-2606-19479:
Ranveer Kumar Singh constructs a generating function for single-centred black hole counts in CHL models in 2026. CHL models are string theory compactifications with orbifold symmetry, used to count black hole microstates. The index for quarter-BPS dyons, charged black hole states, comes from a Siegel modular form.

That dyon index mixes single-centred and two-centred black holes. Singh subtracts the two-centred part to isolate the single-centred generating function. Black hole bound state metamorphosis, a CHL tool for how bound states rearrange, builds the two-centred piece. Convergence of the resulting generating function is proven for the cases N equals 2 and N equals 3. Here N labels the orbifold order of the model. Clean single-centred counts sharpen entropy matching tests for quantum gravity. The construction extends the method to general cyclic CHL models.
arxiv-2606-19679:
Masih Eskandar, Miquel Sirera Perelló, Stratis Ioannidis, and Jennifer Dy edit language model knowledge over a lifetime in 2026. Lifelong editing updates a model as facts change, while older knowledge must survive. Fixed-layer editing and heavy preprocessing limit current methods.

Their method, LOKI, chooses layers dynamically for each new sample. A Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion guides that choice. Gradient updates then project onto the null space of the model weights. No access to past knowledge is required, and no costly statistics gathering precedes edits. Across wide-ranging experiments, LOKI beats existing approaches. Average accuracy improves by up to 14 percent. Catastrophic forgetting shrinks as edits spread across layers by need, not by habit. Code is released openly, inviting labs to stress the method on new edit streams.
arxiv-2606-19879:
Eduardo Bittencourt, Mariam Campbell, Peter Dunsby, and Sergio Jorás write the stellar structure equations of a modified gravity theory in covariant form in 2026. Energy-Momentum Squared Gravity adds matter-squared terms to Einstein's theory. Static spherical stars are the test bed, described with the covariant one-plus-one-plus-two formalism.

For perfect fluids, the nonlinear matter corrections fold into an effective perfect fluid. Equilibrium equations then keep the classic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff shape in effective variables. Metric and scaled versions of the structure equations both follow. With an effective closure relation, the system reduces to a planar dynamical system. Critical points, finite and asymptotic, describe the stellar phase space globally. Linear equations of state recover the general relativity benchmark. Some sectors match relativity exactly or asymptotically, while dust breaks the planar reduction. The surface matching rule also shifts to vanishing effective pressure.
arxiv-2606-19979:
The IXPE Collaboration reviews supernova remnants in the era of X-ray polarimetry in 2026. The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer gives the first spatially resolved polarization maps of these exploded-star remains, probing magnetic field shape and turbulence where particles accelerate. Six young remnants have been observed, with published results for five, including Cas A, Tycho, and SN 1006. Polarization runs from about five percent to over thirty percent across the sample.

Cas A, Tycho, and SN 1006 show mostly radial fields, while two others show tangential patterns. The split does not track age simply, pointing instead to shock speed and surrounding density as the deciding factors. Radio-based expectations of a clean two-way split are challenged. Cosmic-ray acceleration models now face direct geometric tests.
arxiv-2606-20479:
Nastaran Darabi and four colleagues predict navigation failures in vision-language agents before they happen. Their 2026 paper notes that these agents post good average benchmark scores, yet fail through predictable trajectory-level breakdowns: oscillation, stagnation, and wasteful detours. Single-step action entropy does not catch such unfolding failures.

GroundControl measures the deviation from the expected distance-to-goal path, aggregated over an episode. A constant-velocity Kalman filter models how the distance should evolve, and normalized deviations accumulate into an uncertainty score. Because the signal watches the whole trajectory, it can flag a run going wrong while recovery is still possible. Catching failure early, rather than scoring single actions, is what deployment of navigation agents needs.
arxiv-2606-20679:
Yuxin Jiang and six colleagues present MemoryVAM in 2026, a memory system for robot manipulation policies based on video world models. Such policies predict future views to choose actions. Yet they see only a short window of past views. A long task can depend on an early event no longer visible. MemoryVAM adds episodic memory to restore that context.

A Recap-Cue module compresses each frame into compact memory tokens. A cue gate also judges task progress from memory and language. Tokens enter both the video backbone and the action decoder. Training uses video prediction, an extra reconstruction loss, and episode-boundary signals. No per-frame progress labels are needed. The same design fits UNet and diffusion transformer backbones by changing one injection point. On LIBERO-Mem, results improve.
arxiv-2606-20879:
Nicholas Arsenault and Mihai Tohaneanu prove local energy decay estimates in 2026 for the damped wave equation on certain non-stationary spacetimes. A spacetime is non-stationary when its geometry changes over time. Damping removes energy from waves. Local energy decay asks how fast wave energy leaves any bounded region. Such estimates are used to model many physical systems and to prove longer results about wave behavior.

The main technical result is a high-frequency estimate that holds in broad generality. One condition is required: light paths trapped in a compact region must be damped enough. When trapped rays are controlled, local decay follows. Thin spots in damping would let energy linger. Their condition names exactly what must be checked. Decay estimates of this kind support work on black hole spacetimes and other settings where waves interact with changing geometry over long times.
arxiv-2606-21179:
Jonas Schmidinger and five colleagues introduce a reject-to-remeasure framework in 2026 for routine soil spectroscopy that stays reliable. Lab tests of soil are accurate but costly and slow. Spectroscopy with machine learning is fast and cheap. Its accuracy, however, varies by property and by sample, so routine use is often distrusted. Their framework balances cost against reliability in an explicit way.

Samples are first read by spectroscopy. A model gives a value with an uncertainty attached. Values whose uncertainty exceeds set quality limits are rejected. Rejected samples go to standard lab tests instead. A regional spectral library from Québec shows the approach in action. Most samples keep the cheap path. Only doubtful ones pay the lab cost. Rejecting on uncertainty is a general pattern for using fast models where some errors are tolerable and others are not.
arxiv-2606-21479:
Chaya Halperin and Hillel Aharoni build a topological framework in 2026 for colloidal smectics, layered materials self-assembled from dense suspensions of rod-like particles. Unlike molecular smectics, these colloidal versions are full of grain boundaries where the layer direction turns by ninety degrees. Instead of treating those boundaries as flaws, the authors make them part of the ground state and reduce the structure to layers, half-layers, and domain walls.

From that reduced picture they classify defects and their combination rules. In two dimensions, point defects correspond to semi-directed cycle graphs, and the usual disclination charge does not uniquely identify a defect, since different graphs can share one charge. In three dimensions the surprise sharpens: the hedgehog charge of a point defect is not a topological invariant at all, changing smoothly as layers deform.
arxiv-2606-21779:
Víctor Duarte Melo presents FrogBard-512 in 2026, an experimental hash function offered with unusual candor about what it is not. The design runs a 2048-bit state as four 512-bit voices of eight 64-bit words each. Every round mixes public constants, reproducible byte substitutions, ARX quarter-rounds inside each voice, a parity-dependent braid across voices, and a lane shuffle. A sponge-like mode with a 1024-bit rate absorbs messages; a tree mode hashes 1 MiB leaves in parallel.

The evaluation is extensive: a million randomized API cases, fuzzing with libFuzzer and AFL++, sanitizer runs, and two 8 GiB randomness streams passing PractRand and Dieharder batteries. Avalanche behavior sits near ideal. Yet the author states plainly: no collision or preimage security is established, no independent cryptanalysis exists, and production systems should keep SHA-512, SHA-3, or BLAKE3. A research prototype, thoroughly tested and honestly labeled.
arxiv-2606-22079:
Huang and colleagues ask, in 2026, where the useful signal lives when pretraining medical language encoders. Such encoders are usually trained on small, hand-curated corpora, which limits scale and diversity. They test whether web-scale curation recipes, proven for large decoder models, also work for encoders in a terminology-dense field like medicine.

Two levers drive their recipe. A medical-term density filter keeps web documents rich in medical vocabulary. It beat the widely used educational quality filter on downstream tasks, and the two filters complemented each other. Signal-amplifying rephrasing, where a large model rewrites documents into denser versions, improved on raw web data by itself, and mixing rephrased with filtered data gave the largest gain. Instantiated on French, the recipe produced the FineMed corpus and DoctoBERT, a French medical encoder family that set a new state of the art on public benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-22179:
Sun and colleagues study, in 2026, a practical weakness of confidence scores from black-box language model classifiers. Pipelines use such scores to automate the confident calls and send the uncertain ones to human review. That selective prediction only works if an operator can threshold the score at a chosen risk level, which needs fine score resolution.

The authors name the shortfall the score granularity gap. They compare seven confidence constructions, from a single verbalized number to multi-query aggregation, across twenty-five model-dataset pairs. Correctly converted, single-shot verbalized confidence ranks cases surprisingly well. But it takes only a handful of distinct values, so only a few coarse thresholds exist however well it ranks. Multi-query aggregation widens the gap and helps weak models, yet can degrade already-strong ones. The paper turns these trade-offs into deployment guidance.
arxiv-2606-22579:
Yue Wang makes games with huge crowds robust to model error in this 2026 paper. Mean-field games describe settings with so many players that each reacts to the crowd's overall behavior, not to any single rival. Trained policies often fail when deployed: the real world differs from the simulator, and rival reactions widen the gap.

Wang builds an infinite-horizon, steady-state mean-field game with model error built into its dynamics. He proves a robust dynamic programming principle whose Bellman operator contracts. A fixed-point argument shows a steady robust equilibrium exists. He also gives the first concrete algorithm with a convergence proof. The result links to finite-player games whose worst-case model sets depend on the observed crowd. As the crowd grows, the mean-field policy yields near-equilibrium play there, with explicit error bounds. Tests confirm the robust design helps under several error models.
arxiv-2606-22679:
Matthew Dodelson, Om Gupta, Márk Mezei, and Diandian Wang track how a chaotic quantum system relaxes in this 2026 paper. The SYK model is a solvable model of strongly interacting fermions, widely used as a laboratory for quantum chaos and holography. Its quasinormal modes, decaying vibrations that set relaxation times, form at infinite temperature a Christmas tree pattern reminiscent of AdS black holes.

The authors generalize that computation to finite temperature. This lets them follow the modes from infinite temperature down to the cold regime of JT gravity, the theory of near-extremal black holes. They contrast the modes' movement with AdS black holes, dynamical phase transitions, and the large-p SYK chain. One pattern emerges: the relaxation rate grows steadily with temperature only at strong coupling, the gravitational regime. As byproducts come new results on operator growth, flagged as independently interesting.
arxiv-2606-22979:
Francesco Dimiccoli and colleagues report an accelerator experiment tied to the LISA space mission in a 2026 physics paper. LISA will listen for gravitational waves using free-falling metal test masses as reference points. Passing cosmic particles slowly charge those masses, and electric forces from the charge add noise. Earlier flight data from LISA Pathfinder showed more charging noise than pre-launch models predicted. One suspect is a spray of low-energy electrons knocked off nearby surfaces.

Dimiccoli and colleagues built the BART experiment to test that suspicion directly. They fire protons at a flight-like test mass inside a sensor shaped like the real one. They measure how charging changes as the test mass voltage varies. The setup gives the first direct laboratory check of the low-energy electron explanation. Results like these feed better noise models for the LISA gravitational reference sensor.
arxiv-2606-23179:
Joe Germany, Elie Abdo, and Joseph Bakarji prove that EML trees can approximate any well-behaved function in a 2026 paper. The EML function, built from exponential, minus, and logarithm, acts like a continuous version of the NAND gate from digital logic. Stacking it into trees gives a compositional building block for formulas. The authors study how expressive those trees are. They show the trees enjoy a universal approximation property across a broad class of smooth function spaces.

Germany and colleagues adapt classical neural network approximation arguments to this setting. A key step builds EML trees that mimic polynomial representations explicitly. They also propose a learning algorithm that fits the trees' parameters. Tests on practical optimization problems show the algorithm works. The results give EML trees a firm theoretical footing as a function approximation framework.
arxiv-2606-23279:
Mesfin Asfaw Taye proposes an internal-time model of aging in a 2026 theoretical paper. Calendar age is an incomplete measure of aging, the author argues. Bodies sharing the same chronological age can differ widely in reserve, damage, death risk, and remaining lifespan. The framework, built on a Principle of Biological Time Equivalence, counts physiological cycles instead of years. Internal time accumulates ticks like heartbeats or breaths. An entropy-normalized version weighs each tick by its entropy cost, expressing age as the fraction of a reference entropy and cycle budget already consumed.

Taye develops this nonequilibrium model as a coordinate for aging research. The entropy-normalized proper time aims to put individuals and species on one comparable scale. Repair processes enter the model through bifurcations, points where the balance between damage and repair can tip between regimes. The paper presents the definitions and works out their consequences.
arxiv-2606-23479:
Haowei Ye and colleagues demonstrate a magnetic-free Josephson diode effect in a 2026 condensed matter paper. The Josephson effect lets supercurrent flow between two superconductors without voltage. Interference devices built on it have always needed magnetic fields to control the phase. The diode effect, where supercurrent flows more easily one way than the other, was treated as an exotic signature of broken symmetries. Working with planar junctions of bismuth oxyselenide and bilayer graphene, the team shows the diode effect is instead a universal property of the Josephson effect itself.

Ye and colleagues replace the magnetic field with a supercurrent gauge field, built from high-kinetic-inductance superconductors. They establish that this gauge field acts like a magnetic field for interference purposes. The all-electric control scheme removes the reliance on external fields. It also offers a new tool for detecting broken-symmetry states.
arxiv-2606-23579:
Bogart, Fiori, Raigorodsky, and Velasco characterize the best possible small set expander graphs, in a 2026 paper on combinatorics and coding theory. A bipartite graph links two groups of vertices. It is a small set expander when every small set of left vertices touches many neighbors on the right. Optimal expanders push that neighbor count as high as the degree allows. Such graphs matter because codes built from them decode fast, and they interest post quantum cryptography.

The authors give a combinatorial characterization of optimal expanders based on girth, the length of the shortest cycle in the graph. They prove that optimal expanders exist for every set size threshold. Optimality at one size also yields new lower bounds, called transfer bounds, on neighbor counts for larger sets. As an application, they discuss codes for key exchange protocols that should resist quantum attacks.
arxiv-2606-23779:
Caminiti, Capeccia, and Sorce settle when one quantum field state can be physically excited out of another. Their 2026 paper covers a broad class of well behaved states with nonzero averages. Particles are excitations of a background state, and whether one state can be produced from another by local operations is a basic question. The team previously answered it for Gaussian states when their averages vanish. Real cases often have nonzero expectation values, called VEVs.

Excitability holds precisely when the correlation functions pass the earlier tests and the difference between the two states' VEVs stays bounded relative to those correlations. As a demonstration, the authors compute an example in anti de Sitter spacetime. Such a shift can be excited starting from the Klein Gordon vacuum exactly when its boundary shadow can be excited from the dual theory's vacuum.
arxiv-2606-23979:
Bianchini and Trifone compute the cheapest possible control effort needed to hold back an invasion front moving at any prescribed speed, in a 2026 paper on partial differential equations and control. An invasive species spreads by reaction and diffusion. A control term removes a fraction of the population at each place and time, as in pest eradication. The authors study traveling wave fronts and define the effort as the smallest total removal that can sustain such a front.

In the phase plane, they prove a unique optimal profile exists, characterized by first order conditions that are necessary and sufficient. The optimal control acts on part of a specific curve and varies smoothly with speed and growth law on a dense open set. The effort function is only once differentiable in speed and grows linearly for fast fronts; it is generally neither convex nor subadditive.
arxiv-2606-24379:
Taşel and Çiftci release a software library that lets everyday coders compute on data they cannot see. Fully homomorphic encryption allows arithmetic directly on encrypted values. Its cost and complexity have kept it out of normal software, though. ComputeFHE, published in SoftwareX in 2026, wraps the TFHE cryptosystem in a C++ library. It offers encrypted integer and fixed-point types, with arithmetic, logical, comparison, and oblivious array-access operations.

Developers write in a familiar imperative style, while the library handles the crypto underneath. Two engines are offered: standard gate-by-gate TFHE arithmetic, and an optimised arithmetic-logic-unit design built from encryption-friendly logic blocks. It slashes the number of expensive bootstrapping operations, with speedups near fourfold. A test mode supports testing and debugging without real crypto computation. Built on OpenFHE, ComputeFHE aims to make private apps a normal engineering project.
arxiv-2606-24479:
Li and colleagues rebuild lost camera raw files from the JPEG previews every camera saves. Metadata-based reconstruction exploits that free sRGB reference to recover the raw image. Context models grow expensive at 4K resolution, though, because attention costs explode with size. Their 2026 framework, MambaRaw, swaps attention for selective state space models. These scan sequences with far better scaling, estimating the entropy parameters driving the reconstruction.

Two lightweight modules form the spatial energy coupled context model. A tile block applies Mamba style selective scanning only to information dense tiles, spending computation where the image varies. An energy aware refinement module reshapes features to match the long tailed energy spread of raw signals. It begins as the identity, harmless by construction. Across Sony, Olympus, and Samsung camera datasets, MambaRaw improves on strong metadata-based rivals across the board. The design targets deployment, where 4K reconstruction must be fast.
arxiv-2606-25179:
A controller that walks one quadruped robot often fails on another body shape. David Rytz, Kim Tien Ly, and Ioannis Havoutis study where perception should enter morphology aware reinforcement learning so that locomotion controllers stay deployable across related quadrupeds.

Building on an existing body shape aware design, they train controllers on several reference quadrupeds with adaptive terrain curricula. They then compare three designs: a blind controller, one where only the critic sees perception, and a fully perceptive actor critic. Tests run in simulation on flat and rough ground and on real ANYmal hardware. Critic only perception beats the blind baseline on robustness and tracking steadiness, and stays steadier than the fully perceptive design when its sensors get noisy. Where sensing sits, and how the curriculum is built, prove decisive.
arxiv-2606-25379:
What changes when a novel becomes its sequel? W Frederick Zimmerman treats each book as one point in a sentence embedding space in 2026 and measures the arrow from original to sequel. That arrow is then split along axes drawn from the two books' own paragraphs, so each component names a real textual shift with passages at its poles. Thirteen verified author pairs from Project Gutenberg supply the test cases.

Three sequel types emerged: tiny formulaic shifts, one dominant axis, and many small moves combined. For Tom Sawyer becoming Huckleberry Finn, the largest axis was structural, the collapse of sheltered home life into a roaming adventure, while famous themes like vernacular voice rode smaller later axes. Twain's letters to Howells from the eighteen seventies name that same move in advance, and Zimmerman measures how much of the realised change the stated plan covers.
arxiv-2606-25779:
Stars can leak hypothetical dark photons, particles that mix faintly with ordinary light. The leak cools the star from inside. Stefan Vogl and Xun-Jie Xu turn in 2026 to red dwarfs, the smallest hydrogen burning stars, as a fresh testing ground. Earlier bounds came from the Sun, horizontal branch stars, and red giants. Red dwarfs evolve slowly, so extra cooling should mark their mass radius relation. The pair simulate dwarf evolution with dark photon losses switched on and compare against fresh, precise mass and radius measurements from eclipsing binary systems.

The cooling shrank and reshaped the model dwarfs in ways the binary data can rule out. The resulting limits on dark photon mixing are competitive with the classic stellar bounds. Across much of the parameter space they beat the solar limits outright. The smallest stars, it turns out, are sharp tools for particle physics.
arxiv-2606-25979:
Filip Cano, Thomas Henzinger, Konstantin Kueffner, and N. Ege Saraç study how to monitor discounted sums in running systems. Runtime monitors watch signals as events unfold. Raw readings are noisy, yet plain averages wash out local detail. Discounted sums sit between the two. Recent events weigh more than old ones. The team asks what a monitor can guarantee with finite memory.

Exact, sound monitoring turns out impossible with finite memory. The paper proves that limit for deterministic settings. An approximate notion of soundness rescues practice. It comes with explicit bounds on memory and observations needed. Stochastic processes get their own treatment through expected discounted sums. Pointwise and uniform soundness notions are defined there, with statistical optimality shown. A specification language for arithmetic over several discounted sums rounds out the work. Fairness monitoring for algorithms serves as a test case.
arxiv-2606-26379:
Xi Xiao and a large team of collaborators ask a basic question about visual prompt tuning. The method cheaply adapts image transformers with a few learned tokens. Does it matter how those tokens fuse with image tokens? Most work simply concatenates or adds them and never checks.

The authors search for the best fusion scheme per layer using differentiable architecture search, adding affine transformation and cross-attention to the usual options. Across 34 datasets the hybrid schemes beat standard prompt-tuning baselines with the backbone frozen, and give a better accuracy trade-off against speed and size. The lesson: fusion choice is a real design lever, and mixing schemes by layer works best.
arxiv-2606-26479:
Praneeth Narisetty and Shiva Nagendra Babu Kore examine defences that guard language model agents from outside the model. Tool-using agents face prompt injection, where hostile text in their inputs orders them to misbehave. Recent defences enforce security with fixed rules around the agent instead of retraining it. Several report near-total success on the standard AgentDojo benchmark. The authors distrust that evidence.

First, they organise the defences using classic security ideas. These include integrity levels, reference monitors that check every action, and least privilege. Second, they warn that all were tested only on fixed attack sets. Adaptive attackers, who study the defence first, broke similar earlier systems at high rates. The authors specify how an adaptive test should run, then ran one against the Progent defence. Progent cut average attack success about sixfold. A hand-crafted adaptive attack did no better than the standard one.
arxiv-2606-26679:
Counting regular expressions get a faster matching method from Martin Berglund, Brink van der Merwe, and Sicheol Sung, who make counting regular expressions faster to match. A counting expression states that a pattern repeats at least and at most a set number of times. Matching such expressions naively is slow. A recent data structure, the counting-set, updates many counter values at once. Branching paths, though, force counting-sets to be copied, and the copying dominates the cost.

The authors propose sparse counting-sets. Only essential counter values are stored and carried along. Replication overhead falls sharply as a result. Their matching algorithm keeps the simultaneous-update benefit while shedding the copying bottleneck. The work targets implementations where bounded repetition is common, such as validation of structured text. Efficiency gains come without changing which strings the expressions accept.
arxiv-2606-26879:
William Poulett and six colleagues present a pipeline that fabricates realistic hospital notes for patients who do not exist. Clinical AI tools need medical text to develop and test. Real notes are locked away for privacy. Synthetic notes, written by language models, offer a substitute. The challenge is keeping a long hospital story consistent from admission to discharge.

The pipeline works in three layers. Structured patient generation creates the person. A journey simulation plans their hospital course. Language models then write the notes themselves, varying style and detail like real clinicians. Built-in validation and augmentation steps check faithfulness and boost realism. The released data set holds seventy synthetic patients with twenty to fifty notes each. It is offered at several validation levels for different uses.
arxiv-2606-27179:
Gruica, Jany, and Kruglik study how storage codes can change shape cheaply when failure patterns shift. Large storage systems protect data with erasure codes, which rebuild lost pieces from survivors. Re-encoding everything under a new code wastes heavy resources. Code conversion instead edits the stored code directly, in the merge regime studied here. In their 2026 analysis, universal lower bounds on read and write costs are derived for arbitrary scalar linear codes.

Generalised Hamming weights, which track how subcodes grow, sharpen those bounds beyond distance-only estimates. The framework recovers known special-case bounds and can beat them when weight jumps appear. Reed-Muller codes then get explicit convertible constructions using the Plotkin decomposition, a way to build codes from smaller blocks. One natural parameter regime meets the write-cost bound exactly. Read cost is sharp for one starting block, with a gap left for the other.
arxiv-2606-27279:
Li and colleagues couple travelling spin waves to microwave photons inside a superconducting resonator. Spin waves are ripples of magnetic orientation moving through a material; photons here are microwave excitations in the resonator circuit. Hybrid magnonic systems promise quantum information tools, but most past work used uniform Kittel modes. The team fabricates the resonator directly on yttrium iron garnet films grown on a rare-earth-free substrate. In 2026, two propagating mode families are addressed.

Both Damon-Eshbach and backward-volume modes couple strongly to the resonator. Coupling strengths exceed both magnon and photon damping rates, the threshold for genuine strong coupling. The Damon-Eshbach setup also shows one-way, nonreciprocal radiation of the hybrid mode. That built-in directionality is prized for on-chip isolators. Spin-wave magnonics and cavity magnonics, long separate fields, move closer together. Quantum information applications gain a propagating, directional hybrid platform.
arxiv-2606-27379:
Yoon, Jun, and No argue that the term machine unlearning is being stretched past its meaning in language model research. This position paper reserves the term for dataset-defined deletion: removing a named forget set's influence so the model matches one retrained without that data. Many tasks now labelled unlearning, such as refusing harmful requests, removing an entity, or suppressing a behaviour, chase different, policy-driven goals. Those deserve their own names, like alignment, suppression, editing, or obfuscation, the authors contend, in a paper published in 2026.

Loose labelling is not harmless, because guarantees smuggled under one label get tested under another. Benchmarks built for deletion get reused to score suppression, rewarding surface silence while retraining equivalence goes untested. The authors call for terms tied to explicit guarantees and named reference models. Tests should match the objective actually claimed.
arxiv-2606-27779:
Animating a face for a two-person conversation is a balancing act. The face must reflect what is meant and felt. It must also move with the fine timing of speech. Hejia Chen and six colleagues propose MindFlow in 2026. MindFlow is a dual-pathway framework inspired by the ventral–dorsal model in neuroscience. One stream handles deep semantic reasoning. The other handles fine-grained motion control.

The ventral module replaces sentence-level modelling with a Chunk-State approach. Raw audio becomes an evolving chain of emotional states. Subtle tone cues and mid-sentence emotion shifts are captured that way. The dorsal module generates facial motion with a conditional flow matching network. High-frequency audio cues drive it, emotion states modulate it. A selective acoustic injector gates audio adaptively. That keeps talking and listening phases from interfering. Experiments show better semantic appropriateness and motion naturalness than state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2606-27979:
Applications often spread data across several storage media. Each medium, called a stash, has different speed and durability. Yiming Gao and three colleagues present DiStash in 2026, a transactional key-value store spanning pools of stash types. Memory, solid-state disks, hard disks, and non-volatile memory are the examples. One transaction can read and write copies across different pools. Applications no longer juggle consistency themselves.

DiStash prevents race conditions that would desynchronise copies across pools. It also guards against failures that lose key-value pairs. A pool can be set as ephemeral or durable storage. Contents can be replicated across pools or tiered exclusively. The implementation extends FoundationDB. Microbenchmarks and eBay's production workload quantify the design trade-offs. The system tolerated failures of stashes in either storage class. The implementation is open source. Cache-augmented databases and hierarchical storage structures are named applications.
arxiv-2606-28179:
Zuoou Li and colleagues, seven co-authors in all, want better links between heart imaging and disease. Studies usually test one imaging measurement at a time, which misses combined measures, such as ratios or products of features, that may track illness more closely.

Li's team built CPAgents, a system of three cooperating software agents. One spots statistical problems and suggests changes, one proposes new combined measures under medical and safety rules, and one checks candidates through staged tests, leaving a clear evidence trail. On a large population heart-imaging cohort, the discovered measures improved disease detection across nine disease categories. In most of the seventy-two test combinations, their measures ranked first, ahead of standard single measures.
arxiv-2606-28379:
Mike Hang Wang, Utkarsh Garg, Reza Davari, Huitian Jiao, Baolin Peng, Si-Qing Chen, and Tao Ge tackle agentic editing of long, structured documents. A small local edit can break cross-references pages away, and feeding the whole document to the model for every change is slow and error-prone.

Wang's team built LEDGER, which first maps a document into a lightweight dependency graph covering hierarchy, explicit references, hidden dependencies, and semantic links. For each edit, graph-guided retrieval fetches only the context that could be affected. On a curated benchmark of about nineteen hundred cases across document types and lengths, and across six leading models, consistency jumped from just over half to about three quarters. Token use fell at the same time. Low-effort reasoning with LEDGER matched high-effort baselines, suggesting explicit structure can substitute for expensive internal reasoning.
arxiv-2606-28479:
Cristhian Kapelinski and Diego Kreutz fine-tune small language models for computer security incident teams, whose training data, vulnerability scans, reveal internal network layouts and create privacy duties under European and Brazilian law. Two defenses are popular: differential privacy during training, and pseudonymizing identifiers with keyed hashes. Nobody had measured how the two compose.

Across ninety-six adapters on four small models, the team audited memorization with extraction attacks. Surprisingly, matched controls showed that simply making fewer optimizer updates reproduced the entire memorization reduction credited to private training. Differential privacy added its formal guarantee but no further drop. Pseudonymization removed identifiers from the exposure surface without creating a new target. Task quality stayed low throughout, a budget-conditional warning that such small models are not yet operational.
arxiv-2606-28579:
Miyahara and Yattselev study solutions of a nonlinear equation known as the sinh-Gordon Painleve III equation, used in physics models of surfaces and fields. They look at solutions that stay real along the positive line. A monodromy parameter, capturing how a solution changes when carried around a loop, describes them. Earlier work with Alexander Its covered behaviour far out; this paper fills in the changeover zone.

As the variables grow together, the authors map where each kind of behaviour holds. Smooth exponential behaviour extends over one region, its leading term switching at a stated threshold. Below that, behaviour turns elliptic, meaning repeating curved patterns. It fades into plain trigonometric behaviour as a key parameter shrinks toward zero. The analysis uses the Riemann-Hilbert method, which recasts such equations as problems about jumps in complex functions.
arxiv-2606-28679:
David Mellafe Zuvic, writing alone, audits a confusion at the heart of agent frameworks. Tool-using agents read untrusted content while holding tools that move money, send email, and touch infrastructure. Yet popular frameworks treat merely exposing a tool as if it were authorizing each call the model emits, arguments and all.

Auditing pinned public versions of LangChain and LangGraph, LlamaIndex, and the Stripe Agent Toolkit, Zuvic finds capability gating everywhere and deterministic per-call value authorization nowhere by default. His proposed ScopeGate runs every call through scope, authorization, money ceiling, and idempotency checks, denying by default. The same unauthorized payout that executed under a framework's default dispatch was denied under ScopeGate. His tested control reported no static bypasses and no successful unauthorized attempts across the reported runs, with no benign calls falsely denied.
arxiv-2606-28779:
Dhagat, Dabhi, Prajapati and Barad describe a banking service that customers use entirely by speaking on the phone. Built on Google's Dialogflow CX, a platform for conversation agents, the system handles balance questions, recent transaction lists and card activation. Sensitive steps need a PIN code for authentication, meaning proof of identity, before the agent will proceed.

When a request is complex or outside what the system covers, the call passes smoothly to a human agent instead of trapping the caller. The team stress tested the service with long calls, many callers at once and noisy sound, and report that it stayed fast and stable under those conditions. Customer data sits in cloud storage, which the authors say keeps real-time voice exchanges both quick and protected.
arxiv-2606-29079:
Wharton, Sutherland, Amza and Saslow argue that quantum circuits, for all their entanglement, can be described by quantities sitting at definite places in spacetime. Entangled state vectors cannot be fully broken into local variables, yet any experiment is built from circuit parts with well-defined locations. The authors analyse such circuits and present evidence about local weak values, gentle measurement outcomes tied to each qubit.

These weak values, they find, form a covariant tensor for each qubit, meaning the description transforms consistently between frames. The tensors do not evolve or collapse when distant qubits are measured. Their evolution through any circuit obeys covariant rules. Because weak values answer to past and future constraints, the quantities can only be fixed by viewing the whole circuit at once, including the final measurement choice. Since results hold for a universal gate set, the authors claim any quantum circuit admits such a realistic description.
arxiv-2606-29279:
Kwon shows how AI agents' memory systems can manufacture false confidence. Agent products compress conversations into stored facts later steps trust. In his constructed settings, a casual, hedged remark gets rewritten during memory consolidation into a confident, dated assertion, flat and trusted. The agent then treats that assertion like a verified fact, using it to grant every above-clearance request it faces. None of this needs an attacker: a once-true, never-corrected role is stored flat and acted on.

Isolating the cause, Kwon finds the agent keys not on the source, since attributed, unattributed and even forged claims grant alike, but on confident phrasing. Hedges are discounted, though reportedly is obeyed almost like a flat claim. Warning tags fail as fixes, and a blunt do-not-trust instruction backfires. Keeping the original tentative phrasing in the store works better, and one redundant source restores correct decisions.
arxiv-2606-29979:
Keitarou Matsumoto and seven colleagues study a powerful solar flare from October 2024. The X7.1 event occurred in the active region numbered 13842. They combine hard X-ray images with microwave observations from California. They also run a three dimensional simulation of magnetic gas above the Sun. Two spacecraft viewed the flare from different angles. That geometry lets the team locate emission sources in height.

The height of the main looptop source matches between both methods. Fast electrons glow there, above the flare loops. A second microwave source sits along a southward plasma ejection. It lines up with a stretched current sheet, where magnetic energy releases. That source shines only from the southern segment. Magnetic reconnection therefore seems to differ between strong and weak field regions. Spectral fits suggest a higher low energy cutoff for its electrons.
arxiv-2606-30079:
Hartmut Führ, in a solo paper, carries Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to a broad class of groups. The principle says no function and its Fourier transform can both be sharply localized. Earlier generalizations mostly stayed within Lie groups. Führ's 2026 paper works with locally compact abelian groups, a far wider setting. Distances there are measured with suitable invariant metrics.

His version integrates squared distances against the function and its transform. The group and its dual each carry their own metric. He compares his lower bound with the optimal Euclidean one. That comparison shows how much sharpness the general argument loses. He also formulates the principle for local fields explicitly. Such fields appear in number theory and harmonic analysis alike. The result unifies uncertainty inequalities across many concrete settings. It covers cases well beyond the familiar real line.
arxiv-2606-30279:
Kévin Le Balc'h and Philippe Souplet revisit what happens when solutions of heat equations grow without bound in finite time. Their nonlinearities grow slightly faster than linear, by a logarithmic factor. Such weakly superlinear equations sit at the edge of blow-up theory. The authors first pin down exactly where blow-up occurs. Then they turn blow-up into a control tool.

For growth powers between one and two, blow-up is global when time runs out. At the borderline power, blow-up is at least regional in extent. Precise upper and lower blow-up rate estimates accompany both cases. The results are new even without spatial localization of the nonlinearity. Existence time depends continuously on parameters and initial data too. Applying this, the linear heat equation becomes blow-up controllable. A localized feedback control forces global blow-up at any chosen time.
arxiv-2606-30479:
Chen Frydman and eight colleagues speed the slow expert work of guarding a company network against a specific attacker. Responding to an observed attacker usually takes weeks of analyst effort. A mitigation must be tailored and verified against the attack. It also must not break the production network. COHORT performs the whole procedure end to end. Testing happens on an emulator, never on live systems.

A multi-agent language model workflow proposes mitigation candidates. Agents implement them as device commands. A critique loop refines them through iterations. The emulator runs real vendor firmware for firewalls, switches, and routers. Each candidate faces offensive replay of the original attack. Connectivity checks reject fixes that break legitimate traffic. Approved fixes stack to expose combined effects. Results impress across three topologies and four attack scenarios. About forty-seven percent disrupted attacks while preserving connectivity. That rate is over four times a single-agent baseline's.
arxiv-2606-30579:
Shibing Chen, Yuanyuan Li, Dongmeng Xi and Zhe-Feng Xu prove a sharp geometric inequality about volumes of sets. The classical Blaschke-Santaló inequality bounds the volume product of a symmetric convex body and its polar. A many-body version, proposed by Kalantzopoulos and Saroglou, asks about several origin-symmetric sets at once, under a bound on pairwise inner products between their points.

The four authors prove that many-body version in full. The product of the volumes stays below the corresponding power of the unit ball's volume, and they characterise every case where equality holds. Their proof joins multi-marginal optimal transport, which matches several distributions at least cost, with a pseudo-Euclidean volume estimate. Through an equivalence shown by Kalantzopoulos and Saroglou, the same argument also establishes the functional version of the inequality proposed by Kolesnikov and Werner.
arxiv-2606-30979:
Melissa Rosowsky and 23 colleagues report a nearby Type II supernova whose late spectra break a pattern every comparable event follows. SN 2023rve exploded in the galaxy NGC 1097, about 15.4 megaparsecs away. It peaked at absolute magnitude minus 17.1, declined slowly through its plateau, and its light curve implies only 0.0064 solar masses of radioactive nickel. Hydrodynamic modelling points to a progenitor of about 14 to 18 solar masses and a weak explosion. A dense shell of circumstellar material reaches out to 2900 solar radii, evidence of heavy mass loss before the blast.

In the nebular phase, the ejecta thin out and the core shows through. There the spectra show narrow helium lines but no oxygen lines at all. That absence is unprecedented among Type II supernovae. Fewer than 10% of comparison events lack oxygen at similar epochs. The team discuss partial fallback onto the remnant, dust formation, mixing and continuing circumstellar interaction as explanations.
arxiv-2606-31179:
Liu and eighteen colleagues introduce HealthAgentBench, a benchmark suite for AI agents in health care. The suite holds 54 tasks in seven groups, each with its own environment. Tasks follow the patient journey and use many data types, from large clinical databases to huge pathology images that need close inspection.

Agents get short instructions, explore raw data, and carry out multi-step work scored as success or failure against expert labels. Frontier agents still score low overall. The strongest and most cost effective system, Codex with GPT-5.5, reaches only about 42 percent success. Results also split by task group, showing where agents handle records, images, or long workflows well and where they fail.
arxiv-2606-31679:
Overdulve, Jorissen and Michiels build a practical pipeline for digitizing pinned butterflies in 3D, a notorious gap in natural history collections. Macro lenses needed for the fine scales and hairs have a depth of field of only millimeters. No camera can slip beneath a fragile mounted specimen to photograph its underside. Wing patterns there often differ completely from the top.

Three ingredients combine. The first is handheld focus stacking, which merges many focal planes into one sharp image without a tripod. The second is a non-contact first-surface mirror system that reveals the ventral surface without touching the specimen. The third is a mirror-aware extension of 3D Gaussian Splatting that needs no segmentation masks. Reconstructions of four diverse specimens validate the workflow, producing photo-realistic models viewable from every direction.
arxiv-2606-31879:
De Groot, Marcos and Stefanes prove a van Benthem style characterization for the intuitionistic modal logic IK. Van Benthem's classical theorem identifies modal logic as exactly the bisimulation-invariant fragment of first-order logic. IK is an intuitionistic counterpart of the basic modal logic K, defined through translations provable in intuitionistic first-order logic.

The authors define IK-bisimulations between birelational models and prove a Hennessy-Milner style theorem for them. Supporting model theory is built along the way: intuitionistic analogues of Łoś's theorem, elementary embeddings and countable saturation. With those tools, IK is shown to be precisely the fragment of intuitionistic first-order logic invariant under IK-bisimulations. The result mirrors the classical theorem inside a fully intuitionistic setting.
arxiv-2606-31979:
Pragier and three others turn planar surfaces from a weakness of structure-from-motion into a source of constraints. Standard pose estimation rests on epipolar geometry, which degenerates when a scene is dominated by flat surfaces like indoor sports courts. Each plane seen across views, though, yields its own estimate of relative camera pose through homography decomposition.

Planar-SfM builds a pose graph from those homography estimates. Spectral embedding scores the edges by geometric and visual consistency, filtering unreliable ones before a maximally consistent spanning tree is extracted for pose recovery. On basketball court imagery, where current methods struggle, the approach performs better. On the unconstrained IMC Phototourism benchmark it matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2608-00079:
Zhang and Liu present LeapTalk for real-time talking-head video. Long-form and live generation face a latency-quality trade-off. Multi-step diffusion is too slow for streaming. Autoregressive methods drift in identity and accumulate errors. LeapTalk aims for stable video in a single forward step.

A single-step bridge distillation scheme drives the method. A Brownian bridge moves data to data, not noise to data. A persistent reference anchors identity across long videos. Heterogeneous distillation transfers skill from a diffusion teacher to the student bridge. Audio-driven guidance keeps lip sync fine-grained at one step. Tests show high-fidelity video at up to 200 frames per second. The method beat prior approaches on efficiency and stability, they report.
arxiv-2608-00379:
Wang and co-authors find explicit core loss equations by symbolic sparse search. Simple, readable equations guide high-frequency power magnetics design. Classic fits like the Steinmetz equation often lack accuracy. Machine learning lifts precision but drifts from physics. Their LSSI frame aims for both traits.

LSSI casts core loss for sine drives as symbolic regression on test data. A widened set of candidate functions extends the Steinmetz base. Sparse picks keep the top terms, with exponents and coefficients learnable. The result is a compact equation with four live terms. It scores R squared of 0.9999 and MAPE of 1.04 percent. Parameter count drops from 4,417 in neural methods to 15. Clear physics pairs with top accuracy here.
bailly-lettres-atlantide-1779:
Jean-Sylvain Bailly, a French astronomer of high rank, wrote on Plato's Atlantis as a grave question of history. Lettres sur l'Atlantide de Platon, printed in French in 1779, is the first modern scholarly treatise on the lost land. Bailly lost his head in the Revolution, but his letters lived on.

He argues that Atlantis was real and that its lore ties into the deep past of Asia. Plato, old myths, and star lore all enter his case. Donnelly took Bailly as his chief forerunner of the century before. The letters set the terms in which Atlantis would be argued for two hundred years.
baker-cyprus-as-i-saw-it-1879:
Samuel White Baker, the explorer of the Nile sources, surveyed Cyprus in 1879, the first year of British rule there. His Cyprus as I Saw It reports a tour of the whole island. Britain had taken Cyprus from the Ottoman Empire the year before.

Baker rides through the plains and mountains, noting farms, forests, ruins, and the island's many peoples. He judges roads, water, and fever with a practical eye and urges planting and reform. His wife Florence, who shared his African travels, was with him on the tour. The book is the first full English picture of Cyprus under its new rulers.
bebel-woman-and-socialism-1879:
August Bebel's Woman and Socialism appears here in the jubilee edition of 1910, issued by the Socialist Literature Company of New York in Meta L. Stern's authorised translation. Bebel, leader of German social democracy, opens on an age of great social transformations: restlessness in every stratum of society, and questions discussed in ever widening circles. The woman question stands among the most important of them.

Chapters trace women's work, marriage, and the professions across nations. Female physicians, he notes, practise in India, Abyssinia, Persia, Morocco, and China, gaining ground in Oriental countries where custom and religion make them a special boon. Germany, after long struggles, has at last taken a new step. Bebel argues that women's emancipation and socialism stand or fall together, in the book that taught two generations of European socialists their feminism.
bifolium-metallicum-seu-medicina-duplex-:
Pantaleon, styling himself a master of hermetic wisdom, published this Latin treatise at Nuremberg in the sixteen-seventies. Its title means a metallic two-leaf: a double medicine for metals and for sick men, invented by the princes of the hermetic art under the title of the philosopher's stone. The book promises the method set out without deceit, with all its circumstances, requirements, and manipulations, for lovers of the divine science.

A motto warns off critics: the work is praised by some, blamed by others, and known by few. Pantaleon complains that the doctrine was perverted by false opinions for one end — that man might lack neither health nor wealth, and know his Creator better. The sampled argument wrestles with a liquor that must dissolve and attack the sun, gold itself, in proper order. Few books state the stone's double promise, medicine for body and metal alike, so nakedly.
biruni-chronology-ancient-nations-sachau:
Al-Biruni compared the calendars of nations in The Chronology of Ancient Nations, written about 1000 and Englished by Sachau in 1879. The Arabic title, Athar-ul-Bakiya, names the signs of past centuries that survive in feasts and eras. Persians, Jews, Christians, and pre-Islamic Arabs all keep time differently, and al-Biruni lays their systems side by side.

Festivals, fasts, and New Year days get careful treatment, since a calendar is a people's memory in numbers. The book shows comparative science at a very early, very high level. Historians of astronomy and religion both draw on Sachau's version of this founding work.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol2-1879:
The second volume of Twiss's Rolls Series edition of Bracton appeared in 1879. Bracton's thirteenth-century treatise set English law in order for the first time, and Twiss printed it with a facing English translation. Each volume of the edition carried the vast work one stage further.

Volume 2 treats the law of persons, property, and inheritance as Bracton's England knew it. It explains who could hold land, how estates passed at death, and what rights wives, heirs, and lords held. The rules are drawn from decided cases, so the reader sees the common law reasoning its way forward. For students of medieval society, the volume is also a record of how land and family bound people's lives together.
brugsch-history-egypt-pharaohs-vol-1-187:
Heinrich Brugsch let the stones tell the tale in Vol. 1 of A History of Egypt under the Pharaohs, in English from 1879. Brugsch was a German sage who could read the script as few could. Henry Danby Seymour turned his work to English. Past tales leaned on Greek scribes. His rests on the walls and rolls of Egypt its own self.

Kings rise and fall by what their own stones claim. That shift was new and bold in its day. The tome takes the tale through its first great span. A mate tome ends the work.
brugsch-history-egypt-pharaohs-vol-2-187:
Heinrich Brugsch ends his stone writ tale in Vol. 2 of A History of Egypt under the Pharaohs, in English from 1879. The first tome set the rule: trust the walls and rolls, not late Greek tales. Here the tale runs on through wars, new realms, and the slow fall of the pharaohs to the rule of far kings.

Brugsch reads the stones in their own tongue, which gives his tale its force. Seymour's English prose is clear and grave. The pair was the first full past of Egypt in English from its own proofs. That feat still stands.
bustan-clarke-1879:
Captain H. Wilberforce Clarke published the first complete English Bustan in 1879, in prose, for Wm. H. Allen of London. Saadi wrote the Bustan, the Orchard, in verse in 1257, a year before the Gulistan.
