The budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae was the first eukaryote to have its genome fully sequenced, released in 1996 by a worldwide effort of hundreds of researchers. Since then it has been studied intensely, and the database team has curated its gene annotations as a model for other organism databases.

The article also presents the reference sequence's first major update. The new version, nicknamed S288C 2010 for the lab strain it describes, was re-read from a single yeast colony with modern sequencing technology, correcting errors and gaps left from the 1990s effort. The authors explain what changed, why a trusted reference matters, and how the updated sequence anchors future yeast genomics.
europmc-pmc3965079:
Jeffrey R. MacDonald, Robert Ziman, Ryan K. C. Yuen, Lars Feuk, and Stephen W. Scherer update the Database of Genomic Variants in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. The database catalogues structural variation, the large insertions, deletions, and rearrangements in human DNA, found in healthy control individuals around the world. Such a reference tells researchers and clinics which big variants are common background and which might matter in a patient.

The current version draws on 55 published studies with over 2.5 million entries from more than 22,300 genomes, pulled from the archival databases and re-curated for accuracy. Its genome browser gained comparison functions, and a new query tool gives flexible, interactive access. The catalogue feeds directly into clinical copy-number testing and other reference databases.
europmc-pmc3975579:
Dorothy K. Sojka and a large team settle the family relations of natural killer cells in eLife in 2014. Natural killer cells are innate immune killers of virus-infected and tumor cells. Most mouse research studied the conventional kind in the spleen, but the liver holds a second population that stays put in the tissue. Whether those liver residents were immature conventional cells, kin of the thymus type, or their own line was unknown.

Gene profiles, surface markers, function tests, and mice lacking specific developmental switches all pointed the same way: the tissue-resident cells are a separate lineage. Counting types across tissues, the authors identify at least four natural killer lineages: conventional, thymic, liver-and-skin resident, and uterine resident. The map matters because each lineage likely answers infection and pregnancy differently.
europmc-pmc4054779:
Roz Laing and eleven colleagues publish the genome and full transcript set of the barber's pole worm, in Genome Biology in 2013. Haemonchus contortus, a blood-feeding parasite of sheep and goats, is the standard test worm for drug and vaccine work. Its talent for evolving drug resistance threatens sheep farming worldwide.

The draft is the first genome for its worm family and the deepest transcript record for any parasitic worm. Overall structure and gene content echo the free-living model worm, but key parasite families have ballooned. The team maps genes for blood feeding, nerve function, and drug breakdown. Full repertoires for the known drug target families explain how several wormers act. Genes switched on in the gut and in parasitic life stages form a rich shortlist for vaccines and new drugs.
europmc-pmc4076979:
Mehdi Sargolzaei, Jacques P. Chesnais, and Flavio S. Schenkel presented a faster way to fill in missing genetic markers by borrowing information from relatives. Their methods paper appeared in BMC Genomics in 2014. Imputation cuts genotyping costs for genomic selection, but popular methods strain computing power in large populations.

Their approach starts with family data when a pedigree exists. It then searches for long shared chromosome stretches between a target animal and densely genotyped reference animals, shrinking the search window step by step to catch more distant kin. In cattle data sets, accuracy matched or beat two leading programs, with the best gains when close relatives were in the reference group. Because the method is deterministic, it stays fast on very large data.
europmc-pmc4122179:
Eva Miedes, Ruben Vanholme, Wout Boerjan, and Antonio Molina reviewed the plant secondary cell wall as a defence against pathogens. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014. The wall is no longer seen as a passive fence; it actively regulates defence and releases signal molecules that trigger immunity.

The review centres on lignin, the tough polymer that strengthens secondary walls. Pathogens must breach the wall to colonise tissue, and wall changes can raise or lower resistance. The same walls are a carbon-neutral feedstock for biofuels and materials, so engineers want to remodel them for easier processing. The authors warn that weakening wall-building or remodelling proteins for industry may cost the plant its pathogen resistance, a trade-off breeders must weigh.
europmc-pmc4125079:
Jeremy J. Berg and Graham Coop developed statistical tests for a population genetic signal of adaptation acting on traits controlled by many genes. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Such adaptation shifts variant frequencies only slightly at each of many sites, so standard genome scans miss it.

Genome-wide association studies now supply the effect size of many variants for a trait. The authors combine those weights with allele frequencies to estimate each population's mean genetic value for the trait. A neutral drift model, allowing any population relatedness, then flags values that scatter too widely or track an environmental variable too closely. Follow-up steps identify which populations drive the signal. The tests are far more powerful than single-site scans.
europmc-pmc4166679:
Francesc Coll, Taane G. Clark, and eight co-authors set out in Nature Communications in 2014 to build a stable typing code for the bacteria that cause tuberculosis. Strain type can shape how sick a patient gets, how fast the germ spreads, and whether drugs still work. Older typing schemes sorted strains in ways that did not always agree.

Scanning 1,601 genomes from around the world, the group found about 92,000 single-letter DNA changes. From the strain-specific ones they picked 62 markers that form a barcode. The barcode sorts isolates into all the main lineages and more sub-lineages than older tools, and it matches the standard classification well. Health labs can use it to type clinical samples fast.
europmc-pmc4304279:
Robert Vassar reviews drugs that block BACE1, an enzyme the brain needs to make the amyloid beta peptide tied to Alzheimer's disease. The review appeared in Alzheimer's Research and Therapy in 2014, and Vassar writes as sole author. Cutting amyloid production early is a leading strategy against the disease, and BACE1 sits at the first step of that production.

Making a blocker that reaches the brain through the blood brain barrier took years, but several candidates had entered human trials by the time of writing. Some were tolerated well; others dropped out over toxicity. The review weighs what the early trial results can and cannot yet say about whether the approach will slow the disease.
europmc-pmc4325379:
Richard L Mort, Ian J Jackson, and E Elizabeth Patton review melanocytes, the pigment cells that color skin and hair. Their review appeared in Development in 2015. Melanocytes start in the embryo's neural crest and migrate to the skin, hair roots, and a few inner sites, a simple story that makes them a model for harder development questions.

Pigment mutations in mice first revealed the genes involved, while chicken embryos showed the cell movements and zebrafish allowed live watching and gene editing. The review pulls these threads together, covering melanocyte stem cells as well. It closes with the lineage's role in melanoma, the dangerous cancer of these same cells, and what development teaches about it.
europmc-pmc4326479:
Paul Ganguly and Sreyoshi Fatima Alam review homocysteine, an amino acid in blood whose excess is tied to cardiovascular disease. Their review appeared in Nutrition Journal in 2015. Raised homocysteine, called hyperhomocysteinemia, has long been linked to heart disease and stroke, and the review asks how the damage is done.

One route runs through the brain and nerves. After stroke or head injury the blood brain barrier leaks, homocysteine reaches brain tissue, and it may stir the release of excitatory amino acids and stress hormones that deepen the lesion. Because the hypothalamus also steers heart function through sympathetic nerves, the authors argue this brain route can compromise the heart as well.
europmc-pmc4377079:
Stephen Burgess, Adam Butterworth, and Simon Thompson showed how summary data can serve a causal inference method, in Genetic Epidemiology in 2013. Mendelian randomization uses gene variants as natural stand-ins for a risk factor, to judge whether that factor truly causes a disease. Genome-wide studies publish only summary coefficients for each variant, not person-level data. The team asked whether combining those summaries across variants loses accuracy, and tested the idea in simulations.

Two summary methods matched the standard person-level approach in both accuracy and precision, even when genes interacted. Precision was overstated, though, when variants were correlated with each other. Weak variant tools caused little bias under a stated test. As a real example, the methods estimated that a 30 percent cut in LDL cholesterol would cut coronary disease risk by about two-thirds.
europmc-pmc4383879:
Fiona Cunningham and the Ensembl team reported the 2015 state of the Ensembl genome system in Nucleic Acids Research. Ensembl annotates genomes of chordates and key model organisms, adding gene models, comparisons, regulatory regions, and variation data. The year's headline was updated annotation on the new human genome assembly, GRCh38, while support for the older assembly continued on a dedicated site for researchers mid-project.

The regulatory build was reworked to flag regions of interest and show their activity across many data sets at once. New interfaces let users compare their own large data sets against Ensembl annotation directly. The programmatic REST service became a full offering, and the variant effect predictor handled more variants with summary statistics. The code base moved to GitHub under an open license, inviting outside contributions.
europmc-pmc4404679:
Qing Niu and co-authors tracked pig gut microbes across growth stages. Their study ran in Scientific Reports in 2015. Gut microbes help farm animals digest their feed. Pigs are livestock and also a research model. The team read bacterial gene markers in pig feces. They sampled at 28, 60, 90, and 150 days of age. They also measured how well the pigs digested feed parts. The parts included crude fiber and protein.

The team found 22 phyla and 249 genera of bacteria. Two phyla dominated at every age. Both microbe counts and microbe diversity rose with age. Crude fiber digestion rose with age as well. Thirty-six genera changed a lot over growth. Three phyla tracked with fiber digestion. Eleven genera tracked with it too. They included Campylobacter and Clostridium. The map helps explain why older pigs handle rough feed better.
europmc-pmc4443879:
Stéphane Pesant and co-authors, with the Tara Oceans Consortium coordinators, described open data resources from the Tara Oceans expedition in Scientific Data in 2015. The voyage, running from 2009 to 2013, sampled ocean ecosystems around the world. It gathered water measures and plankton, from viruses to small animals, at hundreds of sites across twenty ocean provinces, building a very large sample collection.

Making sense of that collection needs tools to find, check, and reach the data. The consortium placed sequence data in a public nucleotide archive. Environmental, chemical, and species data went into another open archive. The consortium also built online tools for searching the sets and for joint labeling of sequences and images. Detailed registries list every leg of the voyage, station, and sampling event. The article serves as a guide and index for anyone who wants to reuse the expedition's data.
europmc-pmc4466679:
Kei Mitsuhashi and a large team of co-authors tested pancreatic cancer tissue for oral bacteria in Oncotarget in 2015. Bacteria behind gum disease had been flagged as a possible risk factor for pancreatic cancer. Fusobacterium species, an oral group, are known to promote colon cancer, but no study had checked for them in pancreatic tumors.

Using records and tumor samples from hundreds of patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the team tested for Fusobacterium DNA and also profiled cancer gene mutations, two small RNAs, and methylation patterns. The bacteria were found in a small minority of tumors and did not track with any clinical or molecular feature tested. Survival analysis, however, linked tumor Fusobacterium status with outcome after accounting for other factors. The study opens, rather than settles, the question of whether oral bacteria play a part in this cancer.
europmc-pmc4491179:
Christopher Eames, Jarvist Frost, Piers Barnes, Brian O'Regan, Aron Walsh, and M Saiful Islam traced moving ions inside perovskite solar cells in Nature Communications in 2015. These cells, made from a hybrid lead iodide crystal, had risen fast in efficiency but behaved oddly: their current lagged behind voltage changes, and their electrical response at low frequency was huge. Ion movement inside the crystal was the suspect, but which ions move, and how easily, was unknown.

Combining first-principles calculations with measurements on a working cell, the team found that iodide ions migrate readily through empty lattice sites, with an energy barrier matching the device's response times. Other ions faced much higher barriers. The crystal is thus a mixed conductor, carrying both electrons and ions. That finding, the authors argue, has major implications for how perovskite solar cells should be designed and stabilized.
europmc-pmc4510779:
Fumiaki Imamura and six co-authors weigh sweet drinks and diabetes risk in a 2015 BMJ review. They pooled long-term studies of adults who began without type 2 diabetes, checking sugar-sweetened drinks, artificially sweetened drinks, and fruit juice. The team also asked how much of the diabetes burden in the United States and United Kingdom might trace to sugary drinks.

Seventeen cohorts gave 38,253 cases over about ten million person-years. Each daily serving of sugar-sweetened drink went with an 18% higher rate of new diabetes, or 13% after accounting for body weight. Survey data covered 4,729 US adults and 1,932 UK adults for the burden estimates. Fruit juice and diet drinks showed weaker, less certain links once weight was considered.
europmc-pmc4527079:
Tünde Pusztahelyi, Imre J. Holb, and István Pócsi review the chemical warfare between fungi and plants in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2015. Both sides make secondary metabolites, small molecules outside basic growth needs, in vast variety. The mix a fungus can produce, and when, shapes whether it lives off a plant, sickens it, or is fought off.

Plants answer with antifungal compounds and alarm signals that switch defenses on across the whole plant. Some fungi strike back by copying plant hormones, which bend plant growth or shut down the cell-death defenses meant to starve them. The review also covers toxins aimed at single host species, plant counter-compounds, and new gene-level findings in major pathogen pairs.
europmc-pmc4617279:
A 2015 study by Sebastian Memczak and colleagues deals with circular RNAs in human blood and their promise as biomarkers. Circular RNAs are ring-shaped molecules that resist breakdown and vary by tissue. The team sequenced RNA from whole blood to see what circles appear there. The work appeared in PLOS ONE.

They found thousands of circular RNAs that could be detected reliably in standard blood samples. Hundreds were present at higher levels than the straight RNA copies of the same genes. That means blood circles reveal activity from hundreds of genes that normal RNA tests miss. Because blood is easy to draw, these stable rings could become practical markers for disease studies and clinical tests.
europmc-pmc4619779:
Wan Y. Lam and Paula Fresco published a 2015 overview of ways to check if patients take their drugs as told. The World Health Organization says that, in rich countries, patients with long-term illness take on average only half of their doses. Missed doses worsen health and raise costs.

The authors weigh direct checks, drug store records, smart pill packs, pill counts, doctor judgement, and patient self-report. The tools that ask patients tend to show why doses get skipped. The tools that track behaviour give a sharper record of what was taken. No one method is perfect, so the review urges care in picking a tool, with cost kept in mind. Mixing several methods is, for now, the best path.
europmc-pmc4627579:
A 2015 study by Asier Marzo and colleagues deals with holographic acoustic elements for moving objects held in mid-air by sound. Focused ultrasound can levitate small items without contact. Earlier setups surrounded the target or allowed little movement. The team optimised the timing signals driving an ultrasonic array. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

With one emitter on a single side, they could shift, spin, and steer levitated particles. Their framework borrows hologram ideas from optics to design sound traps shaped as tweezers, twisters, or bottles. These shapes act as tractor beams or contact-free carriers. The authors point to uses inside the body, such as guiding drug carriers or micro-machines, where sound has the advantage of working alongside magnetic resonance imaging.
europmc-pmc4668279:
Peter Canning, Fiona J. Sorrell, and Alex N. Bullock published a 2015 review of the structural basis of Keap1 interactions with Nrf2. Keap1 normally targets the stress-response switch Nrf2 for destruction. When oxidative stress disables Keap1, Nrf2 accumulates and switches on protective genes. Drug developers chase this system for diseases from nerve degeneration to cancer. The review appeared in Free Radical Biology and Medicine.

Crystal structures now cover Keap1 alone and bound to its partners: the Cul3 scaffold, the Nrf2 substrate, and small-molecule blockers. Together they explain how Nrf2 binds at two sites and is marked efficiently for disposal. That three-dimensional model gives medicinal chemists a rational base for designing blockers that free Nrf2 on demand.
europmc-pmc4672879:
Lori Newman and colleagues published the World Health Organization global counts for four curable sexually spread infections in 2012. The four are chlamydia, gonorrhoea, trichomoniasis, and syphilis. Counts of how common each is, and of new cases, guide the planning of care and the case for funds.

Data came from reviews of studies from 2005 to 2012 and from syphilis tests in pregnancy care. Among women aged fifteen to forty-nine, chlamydia sat at 4.2 percent, trichomoniasis at 5.0, gonorrhoea at 0.8, and syphilis at 0.5. New cases in 2012 ran to about 131 million for chlamydia, 143 million for trichomoniasis, seventy-eight million for gonorrhoea, and six million for syphilis. Rates swung widely by region and by sex.
europmc-pmc4673179:
How the long non-coding RNA H19 drives epithelial to mesenchymal transition in colorectal cancer is the subject of a 2015 study by Wei-Cheng Liang and colleagues. That transition makes cancer cells more mobile and invasive. H19 is raised in many cancers, but its role in this process was unmapped. The work appeared in Oncotarget.

H19 ran high in mesenchymal-like cancer cells and in primary tumours. Forcing its expression sped the transition and tumour growth in dishes and in animals. H19 acts as a sponge for two small RNAs, miR-138 and miR-200a, freeing their target genes Vimentin, ZEB1, and ZEB2, all markers of the mesenchymal state. The study fills a missing link between microRNA networks and transition control in colorectal cancer.
europmc-pmc4678779:
Anthony Rhoads and Kin Fai Au reviewed PacBio sequencing in Genomics, Proteomics and Bioinformatics in 2015. PacBio is a method that reads single DNA molecules in real time, producing much longer stretches of sequence than the short-read machines that came before it. The review explains how the method works and where its long reads help most.

Long reads can close gaps in genome assemblies, span repeated regions, and reveal large structural changes in a person's DNA. They also let researchers read full gene transcripts, find new gene forms, and spot chemical marks on DNA bases directly. The authors describe hybrid plans that pair PacBio reads with accurate short reads to cut cost. Their survey shows why long-read sequencing opened problems that short reads alone could not solve.
europmc-pmc4728679:
K. L. Eales, K. E. R. Hollinshead, and D. A. Tennant reviewed how cancer cells adapt their metabolism to low oxygen, in Oncogenesis in 2016. Tumors often outgrow their blood supply, leaving inner regions starved of oxygen. Those low-oxygen zones hold some of the most malignant cells, so understanding their survival tricks matters. Oxygen shortage hits metabolism directly, cutting efficient energy production, and indirectly, through transcription factors that swap which enzyme versions a cell builds.

The review maps those metabolic rewiring steps and shows how common cancer gene defects amplify or soften them. Adaptations reach beyond energy: fat handling and other pathways bend to keep the cell alive. The result is not just survival but a more aggressive state. By charting which changes matter only under low oxygen, the authors highlight drug targets that might strike the tumor's hardiest cells while sparing normal tissue.
europmc-pmc4757479:
Zhuang Guo leads a twelve-author study in Scientific Reports in 2016 that reads gut microbes to tell gout patients from healthy people. Gout is a painful joint disease tied to uric acid build-up, and blood tests for it can miss cases or lag behind. The team asked whether stool microbes carry a clearer signal.

From 33 healthy people and 35 patients, they found the gut mix split sharply. Two Bacteroides species ran high in gout, while two helpful species ran low. Gene reads showed faults in uric acid breakdown and in making a gut-soothing acid. A test built on 17 microbe markers sorted a fresh group with close to nine in ten right. The team proposes a stool-based index as a gentle, non-invasive check.
europmc-pmc4846379:
Hod Dana and co-authors built sharper red calcium indicators for filming brain activity, reported in 2016. These protein sensors glow when calcium rises inside neurons, a sign of firing. Green sensors lead the field, but red light scatters less in tissue and allows two-color imaging. Older red sensors were too dim and slow to match the best green ones.

The new sensors, built on two red proteins and named jRCaMP1a, jRCaMP1b, and jRGECO1a, matched the top green sensor in tests. They worked in cultured neurons and in living mice, flies, fish, and worms. Deep imaging, paired colors, and light-based control can now run together in one experiment.
europmc-pmc4947579:
Polyxeni Nicolopoulou-Stamati and four co-authors argue that chemical pesticides put human health at risk and that farming needs a new concept. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Public Health in 2016. Pesticides protect crops, public health programs, and city green areas from pests, weeds, and disease carrying insects. Industrial farming has raised the chemical load on ecosystems sharply. The authors gather evidence on the harms that follow, for people and for the environment.

They describe pesticides as a real environmental health risk factor, not a side note. In reply they point to reform movements toward sustainable practice and food sovereignty, including the Nyéléni declaration. Such steps aim at food production that is safer for people and nature. The authors call the need urgent and structural. They argue small fixes to current practice will not cut the burden enough, so the concept of agriculture itself must change.
europmc-pmc5004279:
Eilis Hannon leads a 27-author study in Genome Biology in 2016 that joins gene and DNA methylation data on schizophrenia. Methylation is a chemical mark that can tune how genes act without changing the DNA code. The team measured these marks across the genome in 1,714 people drawn from three separate groups, and compared people with schizophrenia to those without it.

Several marked spots and regions differed in schizophrenia and held up across all three groups, even after allowing for smoking. The marks also tracked the combined weight of many small genetic risks. By linking marks to gene variants that control them, the team could point to likely causal control changes near known risk regions. The study offers a method other disease studies can reuse, and fresh leads on how schizophrenia risk may act.
europmc-pmc5016979:
Heidi R. Hofer and Rocky S. Tuan review the secreted helpers of mesenchymal stem cells in Stem Cell Research & Therapy in 2016. Interest in these cells for healing has shifted from the cells themselves to the rich mix they release. That mix can ease pain, support bone and cartilage repair, and help nerves and blood vessels, whether the cells come from the patient or a donor.

The review lists the main signals: classic growth factors and immune messengers, plus tiny RNAs shipped inside shed parcels called exosomes. Pathways involving nitric oxide and two named control switches help govern the release. The receiving tissue's own matrix also shapes the effect, and stem cells can remodel that matrix with cutting enzymes. Tuning the implant material may sharpen these effects. Trials now target tendon, ligament, and meniscus as well as joint surfaces.
europmc-pmc5112579:
Aaron T. L. Lun, Davis J. McCarthy, and John C. Marioni published a step-by-step workflow in F1000Research in 2016 for analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing data. Such data profile gene activity cell by cell, giving finer detail than bulk samples, but they are noisier and cannot be handled with bulk pipelines.

Built mostly on free Bioconductor software, the workflow runs from first checks to finished results. It covers quality control, cleaning and scaling the data, and judging each cell's cycle stage. It ends with finding the genes that vary most between cells. It then groups cells into clusters and picks marker genes for each group. Worked examples use public data from blood stem cells, brain cells, helper T cells, and mouse embryo stem cells, so readers can adapt the steps to their own studies.
europmc-pmc5163979:
R. Havelock Charles described his operation for elephantiasis in The Indian Medical Gazette, in a paper the record dates to 1901. Charles, professor of surgery at the Medical College Hospital in Calcutta, writes for surgeons in Europe and India who are beginning this work, and he stresses attention to detail throughout.

His series covers 140 consecutive operations on elephantiasis of the generative organs without a death, building on 60 cases he reported in 1897 with a further 80 since. Patients ranged from 16 to 62 years old, some wasted by malaria with enlarged livers and spleens, some carrying hernias or disease in the limbs as well. Because the operation is one of choice, not emergency, he argues that a fatal result would be especially deplorable, so technique and aftercare must be scrupulous.
europmc-pmc5164879:
Michael Gitlin reviewed lithium's side effects in the International Journal of Bipolar Disorders in 2016, writing solo. Lithium remains the gold standard for bipolar disorder, yet prescriptions have been falling, partly from worry about its harms, which also push patients to stop taking it.

Common effects such as thirst, excess urination, nausea, diarrhea, and tremor are usually no more than annoying. They yield to simple steps. These include timing the dose and keeping blood levels at the low end of the safe range. Specific problems can get their own antidotes. Weight gain and dulled thinking trouble patients more and are harder to fix. Lithium can also injure kidneys and disturb the thyroid and parathyroid glands. So regular blood monitoring is part of care. Most kidney effects stay mild, though a small share of patients worsen over time.
europmc-pmc5287579:
David M. Greig, conservator of the Royal College of Surgeons' Museum in Edinburgh, measured skulls of people with the condition then called Mongolian imbecility. The work appeared in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in June 1927. Continuing an earlier installment, the paper rests on measurements of three female skulls, aged sixteen, fourteen, and five, set against a published case by Dr. Fraser, a woman who died at forty.

Superimposed outline drawings show how closely the skulls match, from side and face, and Fraser's adult skull differs little from Greig's teenage ones, so their shape seems fixed early. All are broad and high-vaulted, with flat noses and large orbital openings. Greig cautions that the flattened face and back of head described in life owe much to soft tissue, since the bare bones do not show them. Survival to old age, he notes, was then exceptional.
europmc-pmc5306179:
Magdalena Jarosz, Magdalena Olbert, Gabriela Wyszogrodzka, Katarzyna Młyniec, and Tadeusz Librowski reviewed the health effects of zinc in Inflammopharmacology in 2017. Zinc is a trace mineral that the body needs for many enzymes and cell signals. It also helps control the immune response. The review centers on how zinc fights oxidation and swelling.

Zinc raises levels of metal-binding proteins that soak up harmful charged bits and guard cells. It boosts guard enzymes such as glutathione and catalase, and shields protein parts from rust-like harm. It can also push copper and iron out of risky binding sites. In lab studies, zinc lowered the action of NF-kB, a master switch for swelling genes, while lack of zinc raised that switch in severe infection.
europmc-pmc5431479:
Davis and co-authors build spatial statistics tools to characterize microglia activation from microscope images. Their methods study appeared in Scientific Reports. Microglia guard the central nervous system. They probe for distress and rush to injury sites. Their behavior can protect or harm neurons. Judging which role dominates is hard. Morphology labels lack any standard. Resting and activated are judged by eye. The team wanted unbiased numbers instead.

Their approach pairs image analysis with spatial statistics. It tracks cell shape and global density. Nearest neighbor distance adds spacing information. A regularity index captures pattern order. Cluster analysis uses soma size and roundness. That clustering split microglia into phenotype groups. The test case was a mouse optic nerve injury. New behavioral insights emerged from the phenotyping. The authors offer the tools as generic. Any brain region or disease state can use them. Fewer animals are needed per answer.
europmc-pmc5465179:
Deco and co-authors model the brain at rest and find it poised at peak readiness to switch states. Their modeling study appeared in Scientific Reports. At rest, brain activity flickers between network patterns. What drives those shifts was unknown. The team built whole-brain computer models. Brain scans of structure and activity set the limits for them. A clear rule emerged from the runs. The resting brain sits at the point of maximum switching readiness.

They also probed how brain areas differ. Each region's rhythm traits were tuned in turn. A core set of regions emerged from that search. This core drives activity across the rest of the brain. Its rhythms pull the wider network along. Split and joined activity balance at this poised point. The authors argue that models beat simple correlation studies. Models expose the causal machinery behind the scans.
europmc-pmc5493079:
This volume collects the meeting abstracts of the 36th International Symposium on Intensive Care and Emergency Medicine. The symposium met in Brussels in March 2016. Its proceedings appeared as a supplement to the journal Critical Care. Over 460 numbered poster abstracts fill the collection. No single author heads the volume; each abstract carries its own team.

Sepsis dominates the early sessions, with work on blood markers and immune failure. Other abstracts cover ventilation, trauma, infection control, and organ support. Most report small clinical studies or lab experiments from single centers. Read together, they snapshot the field's open questions at that time. The volume serves as a reference for intensive care researchers.
europmc-pmc5498979:
Wang and Xu present a review in Lipids in Health and Disease on aerobic exercise and blood lipids. Abnormal lipid levels raise the risk of heart disease. Drugs such as statins help, but some people cannot take them. Exercise offers a low-cost path with few side effects. The authors gather evidence on how training shifts lipid measures.

Standard markers include LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. Newer markers, such as non-HDL cholesterol and fats after meals, also feature. The review explains the pathways by which exercise may change these values. Fitness gains paired with statins cut death risk sharply in one cohort, they note. Regular aerobic training is urged for heart health.
europmc-pmc5514379:
Korolchuk and co-authors present a review in EBioMedicine on mitochondria in ageing cells. Senescent cells pile up in tissues as the body ages. Those cells hoard faulty mitochondria, their energy plants. The worn plants leak more harmful oxygen byproducts. Clearing old mitochondria, a process called mitophagy, falters in these cells.

The authors argue that this weak clearing drives much of the dysfunction. Faulty mitochondria help sustain the cells' inflammatory secretions. Those secretions spread harm to nearby healthy tissue. Metabolic trouble in ageing and obesity may trace back to this failure. Fixing mitophagy could thus extend healthy life, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5618779:
Qiu and co-authors test a cell-death pathway in diabetic heart injury for Oxidative Medicine and Cellular Longevity. Diabetic patients suffer larger heart attacks. Reopening the blocked artery adds its own damage. A fiery form of cell death, pyroptosis, may drive the extra harm.

The team made rats diabetic, then tied off a heart artery briefly. Diabetic hearts showed bigger infarcts after flow returned. Damage markers in blood ran higher too. The NLRP3 inflammasome was switched on harder in those hearts. More cells died by pyroptosis. A drug that blocks the inflammasome cut the injury sharply. Cell studies pointed at reactive oxygen species upstream. Scavenging them calmed the pathway as well. Readers get a targetable chain from high glucose to heart damage.
europmc-pmc5636879:
Baek and co-authors report an animal study in Nature Communications. It links cholesterol to the spread of breast cancer. A breakdown product called 27-hydroxycholesterol does much of the work. The team used mouse models of mammary cancer. A diet high in cholesterol alone raised metastasis. Blocking CYP27A1, the enzyme that makes 27-hydroxycholesterol, cut it sharply.

The effect ran through immune cells, the authors report. The compound raised neutrophil counts at distant spread sites. It also raised gamma delta T cells there. Cytotoxic CD8 T cells fell in number. Both neutrophils and gamma delta T cells were needed for the effect. The findings cast 27-hydroxycholesterol as a chemical messenger of high cholesterol.
europmc-pmc5640679:
Glentis and co-authors report a cell study in Nature Communications. It asks how tumors break through the basement membrane. That thin sheet holds early tumors apart from nearby tissue. Cancer cells can cut through it with enzymes. The team tested whether stromal cells also help. They focused on cancer-associated fibroblasts from colon tumors.

The fibroblasts promoted invasion without metalloprotease enzymes. Instead, they pulled and stretched the membrane. Their contractile force softened it and opened gaps. Cancer cells then migrated through those gaps. Tests used a mouse mesentery membrane as a model. The authors suggest blocking stromal force could slow aggressive tumors. That idea offers a fresh angle for therapy design.
europmc-pmc5711979:
Basso and co-authors present updated guidelines for autopsy study of sudden cardiac death. The guidelines appeared in Virchows Archiv. They come from a European pathology association. Sudden cardiac death is a major cause of death. Practice varies widely between pathologists. The document sets a minimum standard. It updates a version from ten years earlier.

New genetics knowledge drove the update. New diagnostic methods also played a role. The protocol details heart examination steps. It advises which tissue blocks to take. Sampling for toxicology is covered. Microbiology, biochemistry, and molecular tests are included. The authors address hospitals of all sizes. They hope adoption will lift standards across Europe.
europmc-pmc5722879:
Borrelli and co-authors assess how land use change this century has altered soil erosion worldwide. Soil loss harms farm output, carbon and nutrient cycles, and wider social conditions. Past global figures were old, rough, and based on coarse data.

The team built a global model at 250 by 250 metre detail. It joins remote sensing, map based modelling, and census data. They put soil loss in 2012 at 35.9 Pg per year. That is at least two times lower than the old reference value. Comparing 2001 with 2012, they find cropland growth drove a rise in loss. The sharpest rises fall in Sub-Saharan Africa, South America, and Southeast Asia. The poorest economies face the highest rates, while farm safeguards can offset some loss.
europmc-pmc5738879:
Gao and co-authors review materials used to repair bone and how stem cells react to them. Bone graft substitutes must support cell sticking, growth, and change into bone cells. Three classes get close review: active ceramics, degradable polymers, and degradable metals. Pore design also matters, from nano scale up to micro scale.

The review sums up stem cell types used as seeds for bone repair. It details how cells sense the material surface and turn toward bone making. Signal paths behind sticking and bone change get special focus. The authors close with open problems and next steps for the field.
europmc-pmc5739479:
Costa-Silva and co-authors review ways to find genes that change activity between conditions in RNA-Seq data. Such gene lists are key to explaining trait differences. Many mapping and testing methods exist, with no shared best choice. The team tested six mapping methods and nine testing methods on real data.

Mapping choice had little effect when a known genome was at hand, they find. Limma with voom, NOIseq, and DESeq2 gave the most steady results. Taking genes agreed on by five methods gave a highly accurate list. The authors built free software that runs the full set of tests.
europmc-pmc5753179:
Pándy-Szekeres and co-authors report the 2018 update of GPCRdb, a database for G protein-coupled receptors. These receptors mediate much human signaling and many drug effects. The update adds structure models across the full receptor set. It also adds about 150,000 ligands with activity data.

Each model uses a main template plus local ones for weak spots. Models come in inactive, middle, and active states for most classes. Ligand browsers sort by receptor, activity, traits, and shop availability. Users can download structures and data sheets for their own work. Three major studies are linked so readers can explore their findings in the database.
europmc-pmc5770679:
Liu and co-authors review the basics of advanced energy storage devices. The line between capacitors and batteries has blurred as designs mix both styles. One material can act either way, based on electrode design and the ions it hosts. Newcomers and veterans alike can find the mechanisms confusing.

The review sets out how the two device types match and differ. It covers tests that tell capacitive behavior from battery-like behavior. Rules for picking materials and shaping electrodes follow. The authors gather state of the art materials as examples. The aim is a clear guide for rational device design.
europmc-pmc5843579:
Mansouri and co-authors build OPERA, free software that predicts chemical properties from structure alone. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Regulators must judge thousands of chemicals that lack lab measurements. Models can fill the gap if their data are clean.

The team curated a public database down to high-grade records. Thirteen properties got models, from melting point to breakdown half-life. Each model uses a handful of plain, readable descriptors. The build follows the OECD rules for such tools. Predictions now cover over 750,000 chemicals on the EPA dashboard.
europmc-pmc5902779:
Hussain and co-authors review how chilling and drought together stress crop plants. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Plant Science. Cold and dry spells often strike crops at once. Combined stress harms growth and yield more than either alone. Plants answer with shape, body, and gene-level changes. Those joint answers differ from single-stress answers.

The review maps shared and unique responses to both stresses. It traces cross talk between the two response paths. Management options range from farm practice to gene engineering. Biotech routes for tougher crops get special attention. Gaps remain large despite recent gains, the authors note. Readers get a plan for building combined tolerance.
europmc-pmc5910679:
MacDonald analysed chronic valvular disease of the heart in hospital patients. The paper appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1914. He studied 58 aortic cases and 102 mitral cases. All were admitted to Glasgow Royal Infirmary wards. His focus was what patients said about prior illness. He also tracked what triggered symptoms and what they felt.

Valve defects rarely came in pure form, he notes. Narrowing and leaking usually appeared together. Causes he lists include endocarditis, syphilis, and strain. General vessel decay and birth defects also feature. Histories were often precise despite the long disease course. The paper shows early clinical reasoning from case records.
europmc-pmc5957579:
Rolleston gives an address on the medical aspects of Samuel Johnson. He spoke before the Royal Medico-Chirurgical Society of Glasgow in March 1924. The address appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Boswell's Life gives a minute account of Johnson's ailments. Few famous men invite more medical speculation, Rolleston notes. His own interest began in 1891 with a family manuscript.

The manuscript held the necropsy account of Johnson's body. It was written by James Wilson, who performed the dissection. Wilson had assisted Cruikshank, Johnson's doctor in his last illness. Rolleston traces that record and the volume that preserved it. The address weighs Johnson's health through such first-hand sources.
europmc-pmc6024779:
Oliveira and co-authors review toxins made by Staphylococcus aureus. Their article appeared in Toxins in 2018. This bacterium lives on skin and in noses. It can cause infections in homes and hospitals. Its toxins are a key part of its power.

Toxins can break down host cells and tissue links. They can also bend immune responses to help spread. Some toxins are tied to toxic shock syndrome. Others link to scalded skin syndrome or severe pneumonia. Drug resistance and biofilms make treatment harder. The review explains toxin types and their molecular actions. Readers get a guide to how toxins drive disease. That knowledge may help design ways to cut toxin output.
europmc-pmc6056679:
Hua and co-authors review why nanoparticle medicines struggle to reach clinics. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Drug-loaded nanoparticles can target diseased tissue precisely. They can also cut side effects on healthy tissue. Lab results have often looked highly promising.

Market progress has lagged far behind those results. The review maps the hurdles step by step. Biological behavior in the body is hard to predict. Making particles at scale, batch after batch, is tough. Safety, patents, and regulation add further barriers. Costs must also beat existing therapies clearly. The authors outline pathways for development and sale. Simpler designs stand a better chance, they argue. Readers get a reality check for nanomedicine translation.
europmc-pmc6060179:
Huang and co-authors design a stronger cathode for aqueous zinc-ion batteries. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. Manganese dioxide offers high capacity at low cost. Yet it changes phase and collapses during cycling. That decay ruins battery life at deep discharge.

The team slipped polyaniline layers between manganese dioxide sheets. The polymer held the layered structure together. The battery ran 200 cycles at 280 milliamp hours per gram. That is about 90 percent of the material's full capacity. It also lasted 5,000 cycles at lower use levels. Readers get a design route for safer, water-based storage batteries.
europmc-pmc6113679:
Primpke and co-authors present a methods article in Analytical and Bioanalytical Chemistry on a reference database for spotting microplastics. Microplastic particles are hard to identify as they get smaller and samples get more mixed. Infrared spectroscopy, called FTIR, is a flexible tool for the task. Automated analysis needs a well-built reference library.

The team designed a database from reference spectra grouped by cluster analysis. It covers the spectral range used to tell polymers apart. The database adapts to single-particle checks and to chemical imaging with FTIR microscopes. Those imaging methods produce large datasets that software must sort. The design aims to make automated identification more reliable across labs.
europmc-pmc6206279:
Shang and co-authors reviewed microbes in the chicken gut. A healthy gut helps chickens digest food and fight germs. It also supports growth and egg output. The review appeared in Frontiers in Veterinary Science. It covers gut roles and test methods.

The authors show how age, gut site, and diet shape the microbe mix. The microbes make vitamins and short fatty acids. They also block harmful germs and train the immune system. Old culture tests could find only a small share of species. New gene tests can census the whole mix at once. The authors compare old and new methods. They say better knowledge can improve bird health and output.
europmc-pmc6274679:
Plows and co-authors review the body processes behind diabetes in pregnancy. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The condition is called gestational diabetes. Blood sugar rises during pregnancy in women with no prior diabetes. It affects about one in six pregnancies worldwide. Rates are climbing with the obesity epidemic.

Weak insulin output meets long standing insulin resistance in most cases. Risk is higher with excess weight, older age, and family history of diabetes. Harms reach both mother and child. Mothers face more heart and diabetes risk later. Babies can grow too large and face birth problems. Children also carry higher later risk of obesity and diabetes. No cure or firm prevention exists yet. The authors map the known mechanisms and the gaps that still block one.
europmc-pmc6324079:
Huerta-Cepas and co-authors present eggNOG 5.0, a database of orthology relationships. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Orthologs are genes in different species from one ancestor gene. Knowing them helps trace gene history and function. The database adds functional notes to each group.

Version 5 covers 5,090 organisms and 2,502 viruses. Genome sets grew to 4,445 bacteria and 168 archaea. They add 477 eukaryotes picked for range and quality. In total, 4.4 million orthologous groups were computed. They span 379 levels of the tree of life. Each group carries alignments, family trees, and models. Tests show quality held up despite the doubling of genomes. Online tools now annotate new user data faster as well.
europmc-pmc6327179:
Zivanov and co-authors present a Bayesian method to fix motion blur in cryo-EM. Their paper appeared in IUCrJ. Cryo-EM images frozen molecules to rebuild their shapes. The electron beam itself makes samples shift during imaging. That movement blurs the finest details. New detectors record movies, so shifts can be tracked.

Each movie frame holds only a faint signal. The method estimates each particle's path through the frames. It uses probability rules to weigh weak evidence sensibly. Correcting the paths restores high-resolution detail. The approach sits inside a wider analysis workflow. It builds on earlier motion correction tools and refines them. Sharper maps help modelers build atomic structures from the data. The paper gives imaging labs a tested way to polish their particles.
europmc-pmc6340979:
Wu and co-authors review how food nutrients shape immune function. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Poor nutrition clearly weakens defense against infection. The review asks whether extra intake can help more. It focuses on several well-studied food parts. Omega-3 fats, zinc, and vitamins D and E lead the list.

Probiotics and tea compounds also feature. These agents can damp harmful inflammation. They can also boost useful anti-inflammatory signals. They steer immune cells and antigen presentation. The authors weigh lab findings against human trials. Evidence is strongest for correcting shortfalls. Extra doses beyond need show mixed results. The review gives a careful, evidence-graded guide for readers.
europmc-pmc6373179:
Fischinger and co-authors present a review in Seminars in Immunopathology on sex differences in vaccine immunity. Females usually build higher antibody responses than males after vaccination. They also report more side effects, and women face higher rates of autoimmune disease.

The review focuses on humoral immunity, the antibody arm that gives long-term protection. It weighs hormonal, genetic, and microbiome causes for the sex gap. Stronger female responses may resist infection better but carry an autoimmunity cost. The authors argue that vaccine trials and dosing should account for sex rather than treat all recipients alike. That shift could improve both safety and protection.
europmc-pmc6405479:
Ouanes and Popp review cortisol and dementia risk in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone. High levels may harm brain areas that support memory and thinking.

Studies link high cortisol to weaker memory, slower processing, and poorer social cognition. Animal work shows stress hormones can impair thinking and behavior directly. The hormone acts through two receptors with opposed effects, which complicates the story. The review asks how cortisol feeds Alzheimer's disease in particular. It calls for care in telling stress effects from early disease signs.
europmc-pmc6428879:
Perdomo and co-authors show that white blood cells called neutrophils help cause the harmful clots of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, an immune reaction to a common blood thinner. It was known that immune proteins bound to heparin switch on platelets, the small cells that plug wounds. That explained why platelet counts fall, but not why clots turn so severe. The missing piece sat in the neutrophils.

When the heparin complexes hit neutrophils, the cells threw out webs of their own DNA, a process called NETosis. Clots grown in flow systems and in mice held these webs, DNA, and platelets mixed together. Taking neutrophils away stopped clots from forming, and blocking the PAD4 enzyme did the same, though platelet counts stayed low. Signs of NETosis also showed up in patients, which points to new treatment angles.
europmc-pmc6477179:
Turco and co-authors work out how the cargo receptor p62 hands its loads to the autophagy machinery. Cells gather misfolded, ubiquitin-tagged proteins into condensates for disposal, and p62 organizes that gathering, but its signal to start building an autophagosome was obscure. A disordered stretch of p62, residues 326 to 380, proved to be the handshake.

It docks into a positively charged pocket on a dimeric domain of the scaffold protein FIP200, which the crystal structure revealed and the team named the Claw for its shape. Phosphorylation tightens the grip, and the same p62 segment cannot hold LC3B at once, forcing a sequence. Binding also throttled condensate growth in a rebuilt system, timing engulfment to cargo readiness.
europmc-pmc6526279:
Kourtis and co-authors review digital biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Their review appeared in NPJ Digital Medicine. Changes in thinking, behaviour, senses and movement can precede symptoms by years. Standard tests often miss those early shifts. Costly scans and genetic tests suit research more than routine use.

Phones and wearable devices offer a cheaper route. Their sensors can track daily function in a passive way. Data can be gathered often, with little burden on clinics. The authors map early disease signs to sensor types. Each domain of change gets matched device uses. The goal is objective, high-frequency digital phenotyping. That could sharpen early cohort finding for future trials.
europmc-pmc6537279:
Schoeman and Fielding review the envelope protein of coronaviruses, writing in Virology Journal. Coronaviruses mostly infect birds and mammals, but SARS and MERS showed how deadly they turn when they jump to humans. The envelope, or E, protein is the smallest of the virus's structural parts, yet it touches many stages of the viral life cycle.

E helps the virus assemble, bud and form its coat, and it acts as a tiny ion channel in cell membranes. Most hard data come from SARS-CoV work, covering the protein's shape, layout and links with viral and host proteins. Viruses stripped of E grow weakened, which makes them promising vaccine candidates. The authors map what is known and flag the gaps that still block antiviral drug design.
europmc-pmc6557979:
Weiss and Dahlke review how mesenchymal stem cells calm the immune system, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. MSC therapy is being tested for sepsis, transplants and autoimmune disease, with hopeful early results. Yet the cells vanish fast after infusion, which clashes with their lasting effects and leaves the mechanism murky.

Living MSCs act through secreted signals and direct contact, pushing monocytes toward calming forms and fostering regulatory T cells. The surprise the review centers on: dying, switched-off, and even fragmented MSCs can modulate immunity too, likely because immune cells respond to eating the remains. That matters for safety, since living MSCs carry unresolved tumor concerns. Dead preparations might keep the benefit while dropping that risk, though donor-versus-foreign cell questions remain open.
europmc-pmc6558879:
Twohig and Nielsen review the case that α-synuclein, the Parkinson's protein, also helps drive Alzheimer's disease, writing in Molecular Neurodegeneration. Alzheimer's is defined by amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Yet Lewy-type deposits built from α-synuclein appear in over half of autopsied Alzheimer's brains, and in nearly all cases of the inherited form.

The authors assemble the evidence strand by strand. Spinal fluid α-synuclein rises early, tracks with amyloid buildup and predicts faster decline. Lab work links the protein to tau's harmful phosphorylation, to amyloid's actions, and to the APOEε4 risk gene shared by both diseases. Sections on the protein's structure and normal job at synapses ground the argument: α-synuclein may be an active player in Alzheimer's, not a bystander.
europmc-pmc6571179:
Welsh and co-authors compare the two heart troponin tests head to head in the general population, writing in Circulation. Troponin T and troponin I both flag heart muscle damage, and sensitive versions detect faint traces in healthy people. Which trace means what has been guesswork, since studies usually measure only one.

The team measured both in 19,501 adults from the Generation Scotland study and followed their outcomes, adding a genome-wide scan for each marker. The two troponins told different stories. Troponin I tracked more specifically with cardiovascular disease and coronary events. Troponin T leaned toward death from non-cardiovascular causes. Both predicted heart failure and cardiovascular death, and the genetic drivers of each elevation looked distinct — a guide to choosing the right assay for each job.
europmc-pmc6602479:
Madeira and co-authors describe the EMBL-EBI search and analysis tool APIs. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. The institute gives free access to major bioinformatics applications. It also runs a full text search engine with strong cross-referencing. Both web pages and programmatic APIs expose these services.

Two frameworks carry the system: Job Dispatcher and EBI Search. Job Dispatcher runs tools such as BLAST, FASTA, and InterProScan. EBI Search indexes data resources in XML, JSON, and plain text. Recent upgrades improve links between public resources. The authors show integrations inside UniProt, Ensembl Genomes, and PDBe. The goal is data that is easier to find, reuse, and combine.
europmc-pmc6716579:
Ferretti and co-authors tracked how microbes pass from mother to baby in early life. A baby's gut microbes matter for lasting health, but their sources were unclear. The team followed 25 mother-infant pairs from birth to 4 months. Samples came from several body sites, and microbes were profiled at strain level.

A rush of microbes arrived at birth, then strong selection followed in the first days. Skin and vaginal strains stayed only briefly. Gut strains from the mother lasted longer and fit the infant gut better. Other maternal sources kept adding microbes after birth. The study maps the routes that seed a baby's microbiome.
europmc-pmc6723779:
Könönen and co-authors describe periodontitis, a disease of the tissues holding teeth in place. Plaque building up at the gum line starts inflammation. In susceptible people, that response shifts the mouth's microbes and damages the gum and bone beneath. Advanced disease is the main cause of tooth loss in adults.

Genes, habits such as smoking, and general health all shape the disease. The authors trace how plaque biofilms and immune cells interact in the gum crevice. Neutrophils patrol this border constantly, and their failure can speed destruction. Periodontitis also links to many chronic diseases. The review connects mouth health to whole-body health.
europmc-pmc6738079:
Munir and co-authors review lipid metabolism in cancer cells under metabolic stress. Tumors often outgrow their blood supply. Cancer cells then face low oxygen and scarce nutrients. They must balance making their own fatty acids against taking them up from outside. Fatty acids supply membranes, energy, and protein modification.

Shifts in lipid handling change how cancer cells survive and respond to therapy. Proteins that ferry fatty acids, such as FABP4, rise in stressed tumors and track with poor survival. An uptake channel called CD36 also increases when oxygen runs low. Blocking some of these proteins slowed tumors in mice. The review ties these adaptations to the harsh tumor environment.
europmc-pmc6857279:
Emms and Kelly present a major update of OrthoFinder, in Genome Biology. Comparing genomes across species starts with finding orthologs, genes descended from one ancestral gene. Grouping genes well underpins family trees, duplication histories, and most comparative work. Errors at this step poison everything downstream.

The updated tool now goes beyond grouping. From one run it infers orthologs, rooted gene trees, duplication events, and the rooted species tree, plus summary statistics. On the standard Quest for Orthologs benchmark it proved the most accurate method available. It matched or beat rivals on other tests too. Speed stays on par with the fastest heuristic tools, and the software is freely available.
europmc-pmc6880479:
Lambden and co-authors review the SOFA score in Critical Care. The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment grades how badly a critically ill patient's organs are failing. It was built to describe groups of patients, and it proved valid across many settings. Uses have since multiplied. A rise of 2 points or more now helps define sepsis itself.

Regulators even accept SOFA change as a stand-in measure of whether a new sepsis drug works in early trials. That raises the stakes on scoring each patient exactly the same way. Modern care, such as high-flow nasal oxygen, postdates the score and fits it awkwardly. The authors propose clarifications so serial scores stay accurate and comparable.
europmc-pmc6883579:
Wood and co-authors present Kraken 2, in Genome Biology. Metagenomics reads DNA from a whole environment at once. Each fragment must be labelled with the organism it came from. Kraken does that labelling by matching short substrings against a reference library. It is fast and accurate, but its memory demands are heavy.

Kraken 2 cuts memory use by 85 percent while running five times faster. The savings let researchers load far more reference genomes, which sharpens the labels. A new translated search mode compares protein translations instead of DNA letters. That mode raises sensitivity for viral samples, where DNA alone often misses distant relatives. Accuracy on standard tests stayed high.
europmc-pmc7069079:
Qiao and co-authors turn tumour exosomes into drug couriers in Theranostics. Cancer is the second leading cause of death worldwide, and patients need therapies that hit tumours with minimal collateral damage. Exosomes are nano-shuttles cells use to talk to each other. Tumour-derived exosomes carry a protein and lipid makeup much like their parent cells, which raised a question: do they also know the way home?

The team isolated exosomes from two cancer cell lines and tracked them in culture and in mice. Exosomes fused preferentially with their parent cancer cells, and injected ones homed to their original tumour tissue. Loaded with the chemotherapy drug Doxil, the engineered exosomes, called D-exo, targeted tumours and treated them better than the free drug. A proteome array pointed to the surface molecules guiding the homing. The authors cast the vesicles as Trojan horses built by the tumour itself.
europmc-pmc7093379:
Cardinale, Iacopo, and Cipolla review heart damage caused by anthracycline chemotherapy drugs, in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine. Anthracyclines have treated solid cancers and blood cancers since the 1960s. Their feared side effect, cardiotoxicity, can limit treatment and shorten life even when the cancer itself is controlled.

Damage appears to grow in stages, from cell injury to falling heart pump function and then heart failure if missed. Blood markers such as troponins can flag injury early, before symptoms. Treatment with ACE inhibitors like enalapril at that stage can prevent the decline. The authors call for a new classification of the condition and for early detection to become routine.
europmc-pmc7106979:
Rosenberg and co-authors report EV-101, a phase I trial of enfortumab vedotin in Nectin-4-positive solid tumors, in the Journal of Clinical Oncology. The drug joins an antibody to a cell-killing agent. It delivers that agent to tumor cells carrying Nectin-4. Most patients in the trial had metastatic urothelial carcinoma that had already progressed on other treatment.

The study enrolled 155 patients with this cancer, most after platinum chemotherapy. Rash, nerve damage, fatigue, hair loss, and nausea were the most common side effects, mostly mild. Among 112 patients treated at the chosen dose, 43 percent saw their tumors shrink. Responses lasted a median of 7.4 months, and median survival was 12.3 months. Readers get early proof that a targeted delivery drug can help where standard options run out.
europmc-pmc7164679:
Rockx and co-authors compare how COVID-19, MERS, and SARS develop in macaque monkeys, in Science. Animal models are essential for testing vaccines and drugs rigorously, even mid-emergency. They infected cynomolgus macaques with each of the three human coronaviruses and tracked disease and virus shedding.

SARS-CoV-2 favoured the nasal lining but also appeared in the gut. Older monkeys showed no severe symptoms, yet their lung damage resembled human disease. Shedding from the upper airways lasted long and peaked early, unlike the 2002 SARS virus and more like influenza. That early, hidden shedding explains why cases are hard to detect and isolation can fail, the authors note.
europmc-pmc7299279:
Wec and co-authors mine the immune memory of a SARS survivor to find antibodies that neutralize several related coronaviruses at once. Their study appeared in Science. The donor survived the 2003 outbreak of SARS, a cousin of SARS-CoV-2. From that person's memory B cells, the team isolated hundreds of antibodies against the viral spike protein.

The antibodies hit many sites on the spike. Of nine that strongly cross-neutralized, eight targeted the domain that binds ACE2, the human receptor both viruses use. Those eight also neutralized a bat SARS-related virus. Because new coronaviruses may emerge again, antibodies and vaccines aimed at these shared weak points could protect broadly rather than against one virus only. Mapping them gives vaccine designers concrete targets.
europmc-pmc7312579:
Lesser and Nienhuis survey how COVID-19 rules changed how active Canadians felt and how well they felt. Their study used an online survey taken while gyms, parks, and playgrounds were shut. It asked about exercise, time in nature, mood, and worry.

The split ran by past habits. Of people who had been inactive, 40.5% grew less active, yet a third grew more active. Of those who had been active, 22.4% fell off, while 40.3% did more. For the inactive group, doing more was tied tight to feeling better. Those who spent more time active outdoors also felt less worry. The team says health drives should aim first at people who move least.
europmc-pmc7441679:
Nataraj and co-authors review postbiotics and parabiotics, non-live products drawn from helpful microbes. Probiotics aid health through the gut, but keeping them alive limits food and drug uses. Interest is shifting toward their inactivated cells and the molecules they release.

Postbiotics are the mix of products that probiotics secrete, such as enzymes, vitamins, and short chain fatty acids. Parabiotics are inactivated probiotic cells or crude cell extracts. Both forms are pure, stable, and easy to store and scale up. They can act through known targets, which makes their effects more precise. The review covers how these compounds are extracted, purified, and identified. It also sums up their possible health gains and their promise for functional foods.
europmc-pmc7487779:
Choi and co-authors map how lung air sacs regrow after injury, cell step by cell step. They joined single-cell RNA sequencing with lineage tracing and organoid models. The target was the path from AT2 stem cells to mature AT1 cells.

A brief cell state, named damage-associated transient progenitors, arose during repair. The signal IL-1-beta from macrophages primed some AT2 cells to enter that state. The switch ran through a HIF1-alpha-driven shift in sugar use. That step was required to finish as mature AT1 cells. Lasting inflammation blocked the finish, so the brief cells piled up and repair failed. The work shows how an inflammatory niche steers stem cell fate. It also names where chronic lung injury may jam the process.
europmc-pmc7600579:
Castro-Barquero and co-authors review dietary strategies for metabolic syndrome. This syndrome groups belly obesity, blood fat faults and high blood pressure. Insulin resistance is also part of the cluster.

Lifestyle change is the main treatment strategy here. Diet quality and nutrient mix both showed benefits. Low-fat and restricted diets were compared in the review. Evidence favored Mediterranean and DASH diet patterns overall. These diets give advice that is easy to follow. They do not rely on strict restriction for patients. Cutting energy intake still matters for weight control. More physical activity is also crucial for gains. The review weighs plant-based and low-carbohydrate options too.
europmc-pmc7652679:
Zhu and co-authors review exosome isolation and characterization methods for cancer research. Exosomes are small vesicles released by many cell types. They carry proteins, nucleic acids, fats and metabolites.

Sizes run from about 40 to 160 nm across. Tumor cells release exosomes in strong amounts. They appear in blood, urine, saliva and other fluids. Their cargo can mirror the state of source cells. That makes them draws for liquid biopsy work. Uses include cancer diagnosis, outlook and disease watch. Their safety profile also suits therapy design ideas. The review covers isolation technology advances in detail. It also covers roles in spread, drug resistance and immunity. Hurdles for clinical use close the survey.
europmc-pmc7664279:
Liotta and co-authors chart nerve and brain symptoms in patients in hospital with COVID-19. They reviewed 509 patients admitted within a hospital network in Chicago, Illinois. They compared patients with and without such symptoms and tracked outcomes.

Symptoms were present at some point in 419 patients, or 82.3%. The most common were muscle pain, headache, and encephalopathy, a state of brain dysfunction. Strokes and seizures were rare. Brain dysfunction stood out: it linked to worse function at discharge and higher death rates within 30 days. Severe lung disease and younger age raised the odds of nerve symptoms.
europmc-pmc7732679:
Ramirez and co-authors review antibiotics as major disruptors of the gut microbiota. The gut community trains the immune system and supports body function. Antibiotics save lives, but they also strike this community hard. Effects can last and can spread between people.

Use of these drugs cuts species diversity and shifts metabolic work in the gut. It also selects microbes that resist drugs. Harms range from diarrhea to repeat C. difficile infection. Exposure in early childhood links to gut, immune, and brain-related conditions later. The authors call for more study of gut structure and for care in how often antibiotics are used.
europmc-pmc7873279:
Wacharapluesadee and co-authors report a research study on coronaviruses related to SARS-CoV-2 in Southeast Asia. The team searched for signs of these viruses in bats and pangolins. Their work bears on where the virus behind COVID-19 may have come from.

The authors report whole genome sequences from five bats in a Thai cave. The isolate they found, named RacCS203, was closest to a virus seen in Yunnan, China. Antibodies able to block SARS-CoV-2 also turned up in bats from the same colony. A pangolin at a wildlife checkpoint in southern Thailand carried such antibodies too. The team says the findings extend the known range of these viruses across a 4800-km span. They urge cross-border surveillance to find the direct ancestor of SARS-CoV-2.
europmc-pmc7911879:
Seleiman and co-authors present a review of drought stress in plants and ways to ease its damage. Drought is a key limit on crop growth across many regions. It arises from heat, strong light, and low rainfall together. Its effects on plants are broad, hitting form, function, and chemistry at once.

Plants cope through many built-in strategies. They close leaf pores, roll their leaves, and grow deeper roots. They store solutes that hold water and adjust their hormones. The review also covers outside help. Breeding and genomics offer long-term gains. Seed priming, plant hormones, and minerals such as silicon and potassium can support crops sooner. New omics tools help find the traits that matter. The authors gather these routes into one guide for farming under water scarcity.
europmc-pmc8022879:
Thompson and co-authors give early estimates of how well mRNA vaccines blocked infection in frontline workers. Their cohorts spanned eight U.S. locations from December 2020 to March 2021. The groups covered health care staff, first responders, and other key workers. All were tested each week for SARS-CoV-2, with or without symptoms. The study covered 3,950 people with no prior known infection.

Among those with no vaccine, 1.38 infections occurred per 1,000 person-days. Fully dosed people saw just 0.04 infections per 1,000 person-days. Those with one dose saw 0.19 infections per 1,000 person-days. The authors put vaccine effect at 90% for full dosing and 80% for partial dosing. The shots blocked infections with no symptoms too. The findings backed vaccination for all who could get it.
europmc-pmc8143179:
Ehuwa, Jaiswal, and Jaiswal survey Salmonella, food safety, and food handling practice. Salmonellosis ranks as the second most reported gut illness in the European Union. It spreads most often through tainted food.

The review traces sources such as poultry, cattle, feed, dried foods, and produce. It sets out the symptoms, from cramps and fever to bloody diarrhoea. The authors review control steps by governments, firms, and food handlers. They note that hospital cases fell, then rose again from 2016. Stronger controls at each step of food handling are their central call.
europmc-pmc8358979:
Puleston and co-authors find that polyamine metabolism decides helper T cell lineage fidelity. Making polyamines is one of the deepest shifts when T cells switch on. Its purpose was scarcely known.

Helper T cells must pick the right functional fate. Without the key enzyme ornithine decarboxylase, that choice failed badly. Cells voiced the wrong cytokines and lineage factors at once. Polyamines feed an enzyme that builds the amino acid hypusine. That step locks in correct subset identity. The study ties a basic metabolite to immune precision. Metabolism emerges as a guardian of T cell identity.
europmc-pmc8379179:
Mathios and co-authors test a blood-based way to spot lung cancer from cell-free DNA fragments. Their machine learning model reads genome-wide patterns in how the DNA is broken up. The study enrolled 365 people at risk for lung cancer.

The model was checked in a separate group of 385 people without cancer and 46 lung cancer patients. Combined with clinical risk factors, the CEA blood test, and CT imaging, it found 94 percent of cancers. It caught 91 percent of stage I and II cases. Fragment patterns also told small cell from non-small cell lung cancer with high accuracy. A higher score linked to worse survival.
europmc-pmc8402079:
Dobruch and Oszczudłowski review bladder cancer, the most common cancer of the urinary tract. Care for this disease stayed much the same for many years. New findings now open a fresh era in diagnosis and management.

The authors note that deaths have begun to fall where awareness and lower exposure to cancer-causing agents took hold. Surgery through the urethra is being refined toward stricter, higher-quality technique. New drugs serve patients whose tumors no longer respond to BCG therapy. The worth of wide lymph node removal is under test in trials. Work on tumor biology points toward care matched to each patient.
europmc-pmc8445379:
Lange and co-authors track body mass index trends in United States youth before and during COVID-19. More than one in six children face obesity, a threat to long-term health. During the pandemic, school routines broke down and daily life shifted in ways that could speed weight gain.

The report uses medical records for 432,302 people aged 2 to 19 years. It compares January 2018 to February 2020 with the months that followed. The rate of BMI increase roughly doubled during the pandemic period. Stress, irregular meals, more screen time, and less activity may all have played a part. The data come from the CDC.
europmc-pmc8593179:
Li and Wang set out the main forms of RNA sequencing and what each one does best. Bulk sequencing reads the average signal from many cells at once. Single-cell sequencing profiles one cell at a time, up to 20,000 cells in a run. Spatial sequencing adds place, so gene activity can be read in tissue context.

The authors compare cost, detail, and fit for each method. Bulk work gives a broad view but hides cell differences. Single-cell work finds rare cell types and splice forms. Spatial work shows where transcripts sit in a tissue sample. The review frames these tools as steps toward exact cancer care, where cell-level detail guides treatment choice.
europmc-pmc8685279:
Guo, Wang, and Li review the signal pathways that drive melanoma and the targeted therapies built on them. Melanoma is the most lethal skin cancer. It starts when pigment cells turn malignant. New drugs against driver genes and immune checkpoints have improved outlooks a lot.

Response rates stay low for many patients, though. Resistance to targeted drugs also arises in time. The review first covers subtypes, risk factors, and current care. It then maps the pathways behind growth, spread, and blood vessel support. Gene changes, gene regulators, and metabolic shifts all get a look. The authors close with progress on drugs for driver genes.
europmc-pmc9008579:
Pearce and co-authors pool prospective studies to chart how exercise dose maps to depression risk. Depression burdens about 280 million people worldwide. Exercise is a known guard, but its dose curve was fuzzy. Simple high-versus-low splits hid the shape. The team harmonized activity reports across studies. Risk could then be read at many dose levels. Adults in prospective cohorts formed the data. New depression cases were the outcome. The method borrows from drug dose studies.

Risk fell steeply at low doses, then leveled. At the full public health target dose, risk ran 25% lower. Half that dose still gave an 18% lower risk. No activity was the comparison point. Small amounts of movement thus buy large gains. The authors stress the early part of the curve. Getting inactive people moving a little matters most. Their curve can guide public health targets.
europmc-pmc9013379:
Yang and co-authors review how macrophages interact with ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death marked by lipid damage. Macrophages guard tissues, clear dead cells, and handle iron, lipids, and amino acids, so the two systems meet at many points. The review traces links through all three kinds of metabolism. It asks how macrophage states can push other cells toward or away from ferroptosis.

The authors then examine cancer care, where shifting macrophage behavior can trigger ferroptosis in tumor cells. They also flag open questions, such as how to aim this link at diseases beyond cancer by targeting macrophages in specific tissues.
europmc-pmc9264579:
Grindell and co-authors systematically review co-production, co-design, and co-creation to mobilise knowledge in health care. These co approaches aim to close the gap between research and practice. Partners work as equals and all forms of knowledge count. The team searched four databases for studies up to April 2021.

They included 24 international studies, mostly qualitative work, case studies, and protocols. Shared traits were equal partnership, creative problem solving, and repeated prototyping.
