Yameng Zheng and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a new mother with a misleading hormone. She was thirty-three and had lately given birth. A lump on her back brought her to care. Scans found masses in her liver, and blood tests showed high levels of a pregnancy hormone. That hormone can also leak from rare tumors. Tissue checks proved a poorly formed bile duct cancer of the liver. It had spread widely, including to the skin of her back.

The tumor itself made the pregnancy hormone, lab stains confirmed. No pregnancy-type tissue was found in it. Such secretion can fool teams into hunting a pregnancy or a germ cell tumor. The authors warn that a raised hormone after birth, with no pregnancy to explain it, needs a tumor hunt. A second blood marker, tied to gut cancers, was also high here. Together they pointed to the source.
pmc-13282179:
Chumin Ye and co-authors report a 2026 study on the wild population of a prized rosewood tree on Hainan Island, China. The tree, Dalbergia odorifera, is valued for fragrant heartwood and faces pressure from illegal logging and habitat disturbance. The team surveyed fifteen sample plots and used tree trunk width to sort trees into age classes. Interviews and standard population tables completed the picture.

Young trees made up more than three quarters of the population, so it looks growing at first glance. Yet old trees were largely missing, and deaths peaked in two age classes. High deaths among young trees and logging losses of mid-aged and old trees form a double bottleneck. Survival followed a steady-loss curve. The authors propose a phased plan: improve habitat for young trees, patrol against logging of older ones, and monitor the population over time to guide protection.
pmc-13282279:
Sajjad Abedini Chamgordani and co-authors present a 2026 study of Campylobacter contamination in broiler chickens in Isfahan Province, Iran. Campylobacter bacteria are a leading cause of food-linked diarrhoea, often passed through undercooked poultry. The team collected two hundred droppings samples from twenty flocks between October 2023 and March 2024. They grew the bacteria in special low-oxygen conditions and confirmed species with gene tests.

Four samples, two percent, carried Campylobacter, split evenly between two species. Every isolate resisted nine common antibiotics, including several first-line drugs, so all counted as multidrug resistant. One species stayed sensitive to one injected antibiotic. The low contamination rate is reassuring, but the total resistance pattern is not. The authors urge stricter rules on antibiotic use in poultry farming. They warn that resistant strains in chicken can reach people through food, narrowing treatment options for human gut illness.
pmc-13282379:
Christina Bronowski and co-authors report a 2026 summary of an international expert meeting on rotavirus immunity, held in Liverpool in March 2024. Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea in young children. Oral vaccines have cut disease worldwide, yet they work less well in low- and middle-income countries, where burden stays high. Experts gathered to review gut immunity, disease model systems, and lessons from other gut pathogens.

A central gap is the lack of proven correlates of protection, measurable signs that show a vaccine has worked. Without them, improving vaccines is partly guesswork. The report distils the meeting's talks into research priorities. It sets out a roadmap for advancing rotavirus immunology and for developing next-generation vaccines aimed at the settings where current ones underperform. The authors frame better gut-level understanding as the key to closing the effectiveness gap between rich and poor countries.
pmc-13282479:
Juan F Sandoval and co-authors present a 2026 study modelling how fermentation changes the smell of alternative protein foods. Smell decides whether consumers accept such foods. The team fermented surplus bread crusts, boosted with ryegrass protein, using three fungi at a warm temperature for up to seventy-two hours. This solid-state method grows fungi on moist solids rather than in liquid.

Chemical analysis found over one hundred fifty volatile compounds, the airborne molecules behind odour. A model based on a classic perception law predicted the smell profile from compound levels and thresholds. A trained tasting panel's scores checked the model. It tracked overall intensity and sweet, baked, and grassy notes well. Fungal notes such as fruity and earthy were predicted more weakly. The authors say the framework can guide developers to design fermentation that smells appealing, a key step for meat alternatives made from waste streams.
pmc-13282879:
Lemongrass oil, drawn from a strongly scented plant, is the test material in Asmaa M Arafa's 2026 antimicrobial work. New drugs are needed as more germs resist old drugs. The team took oils from distinct plant parts and asked what each oil held and how it acted.

Lab tests checked how well the oils stopped two types of bacteria and one yeast from growing. The team also tested effects on biofilms, which are slime layers that shield germs, and on cell stress. Gene tests in the two bacteria checked genes for biofilm growth and cell talk. Such oils may one day help weak drugs work better.
pmc-13282979:
Yuting Wu and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on lens power formulas for cataract surgery in keratoconus. The letter responds to a review and network analysis by Aljahdali and colleagues. Keratoconus warps the cornea, so lens choice before surgery is hard to get right.

The writers praise the review method but flag data points that look wrong. One formula name appears misspelled in a key table. Some table values show zero eyes in ranges where zero seems unlikely. Such values may reflect extraction or reporting errors in the source data. The letter asks for checks so surgeons can trust the ranked results.
pmc-13283579:
Livia Wunderlich and colleagues examined in 2026 whether sex changes how early activity after concussion relates to recovery in teenagers. Activity soon after concussion can aid recovery, yet studies often include both sexes without comparing them. The team assessed 188 adolescents within twenty-one days of concussion, while symptoms lasted, using symptom, mood, fatigue, pain, and dizziness scales.

About one third had started activity before their first visit, with similar shares among girls and boys. Girls reported worse symptoms, anxiety, and low mood than boys overall. Both sexes who had begun activity reported lower pain interference than inactive peers. A sex gap in dizziness appeared only among those yet to start activity. The study argues for sex-aware reading of early activity advice.
pmc-13283979:
Lijuan Wang and a large team studied in 2026 whether a simple blood index predicts severity in Guillain-Barré syndrome, an immune attack on peripheral nerves that weakens muscles. The triglyceride-glucose index combines two routine lab values and reflects insulin resistance. Records of 203 patients at Beijing Tiantan Hospital were analysed for severe disease and poor short-term outcome.

Higher index values independently raised the odds of severe disease and of a poor short-term result. Albumin levels and a standard muscle strength sum score acted in the protective direction. The index alone sorted cases only modestly, yet adding it to standard clinical markers lifted accuracy clearly for both outcomes. Internal checks held up well. The authors present the cheap index as a useful add-on for early risk calls.
pmc-13284079:
Luya Shi and colleagues mapped the research field of financial toxicity in cancer care in 2026 using bibliometric methods. Financial toxicity means the money strain that treatment places on patients, which can erode quality of life and adherence. The team mined two large databases for papers from 2003 to early 2026 and charted output growth, collaboration networks, and shifting themes with mapping software.

Publication volume climbed steeply over two decades, and the field grew more interdisciplinary. Early work mainly described economic burden, while newer work treats money strain as a changeable, system-level risk tied to social conditions. Social support and team-based management emerged as linked hotspots. Keyword trends pointed to measurement, behaviour effects, and health system responses as the next frontiers.
pmc-13284279:
Raphael Kabir Niloy and co-authors mined the human gut virus world in 2026 for wall-breaking enzymes that could fight drug-resistant bacteria. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria, and their endolysins chew through bacterial walls with high precision. The team analysed 9,141 gut metagenomic samples from 34 studies with standardised assembly and annotation pipelines.

They rebuilt 15,267 phage genomes and found 3,794 endolysins. Most phages targeted bacteria from two large gut phyla. The enzymes sorted into 296 families and mixed their parts freely: cutting domains often sat beside wall-binding motifs, and one enzyme carried fifteen distinct domains, the most reported in nature so far. The authors present the gut phageome as a rich store of enzyme variants for future drug design.
pmc-13284879:
Qindi Liu, Huanghuang Meng, and Hong Sun test three blood markers as outcome predictors in a 2026 study of severe pneumonia. Records covered 172 patients admitted from September 2023 to September 2025, split by outcome at 28 days into good and poor prognosis groups. Blood levels of NOX4, galectin-13, and cyclophilin A were measured by ELISA.

All three markers, plus standard severity and inflammation scores, were higher in the poor outcome group, the authors report. Each marker linked to worse outcome, and the three together sorted patients with high accuracy in curve tests. Decision analysis suggested useful benefit across a wide risk range. The authors propose joint testing at admission to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13285279:
Tao Lin and co-authors study fluid buildup in the inner ear and vitamin D levels in a 2026 clinical article. Endolymphatic hydrops is most common in Meniere disease, which brings repeat vertigo and shifting hearing loss. Delayed contrast MRI now lets doctors grade fluid buildup in the cochlea, balance organ, and canals.

The authors link vitamin D levels to hearing and balance measures on the healthy side, and link affected-side measures to the grade of fluid buildup in each ear part. Vitamin D may relate to early spells of vertigo and shifting hearing, they suggest. Early checks of vitamin D could matter for Meniere patients who show fluid buildup on scans.
pmc-13285679:
Five years of mud microbes from the far north Mediterranean form a 2026 dataset by Noemi Tomasi and co-authors. Surface seabed mud hosts busy single-cell crowds that drive chemical cycles, and seasonal reads from the Gulf of Trieste span June 2020 to May 2025. Sixteen mud samples from one long-watch station went through gene marker sequencing.

Reads were cleaned with a standard pipeline and named against a major reference bank. The set spotlights sun-eating cyanobacteria kin and ancient archaea groups. Crowds proved steady across seasons, with a high share of kinds found again and again at each rank. Raw files sit in a public archive for teams probing how seabed life rides climate and coast change.
pmc-13286079:
Juliana Sopko and a large team describe many-stream tracking of the 2024-2025 bird flu outbreak in the United States in a 2026 descriptive study. The H5 virus jumped from birds into dairy cattle and then into farm workers, while official data sat scattered across agencies. Their group fused human, animal, wastewater, gene, and policy streams into shared public tools during the event.

The team logged 70 confirmed human cases across 13 states, nearly all tied to farm work with animals. Their map joined those cases with hundreds of cattle and poultry outbreaks, and California stood out as the hub on every count. Wastewater checks in that state had caught the virus signal well before the first cattle case was confirmed there. The open timeline and map, built on a One Health frame, gave responders a single picture of a fast-moving event.
pmc-13286579:
Tamires de Sá Menezes and co-authors audit tooth decay claims on Instagram in a 2026 infodemiology study. Two raters coded 500 Brazilian Portuguese posts from 2018 to 2022 by author type, motive, truthfulness, and theme, then modeled what drives sharing and engagement. Cavities are Brazil's costliest oral disease, so bad advice there carries real weight.

Just over one post in five carried misinformation, mostly treatment claims posted by ordinary users. False posts actually drew a higher median interaction count than accurate ones, even though the link between falsehood and engagement did not reach formal significance. Business and health profiles, encouragingly, showed strong potential to spread sound content widely. False posts clustered on treatment, diet, microbes, and hygiene, while true posts leaned toward prevention, the authors report.
pmc-13286779:
Haiyan Huang and colleagues check which simple pre-surgery measures predict trouble after a stent repair inside the chest aorta. The 2026 study reviews 300 patients treated between 2015 and 2020 for type B aortic problems, including tears of the vessel wall. Delayed discharge past ten days and later major complications were the outcomes of interest.

Six percent of patients stayed long, and about thirteen percent suffered major events later. Slower walking distance, weaker grip, poorer nutrition scores, and higher inflammation markers each predicted problems on their own. Weak walking combined with poor nutrition or high inflammation multiplied the risk. A prediction chart built from these measures discriminated well. Cheap bedside tests, the authors argue, can sharpen risk judgment.
pmc-13286979:
Zhenhui Pan and co-authors describe a five-year-old boy whose heart failed suddenly during a common cold virus infection, revealing an inherited muscle disorder. The 2026 case report identifies a new variant in CAP2, a gene that maintains the cell skeleton of heart muscle. Both of the boy's copies carried the change, which truncates the protein and is predicted to abolish its function.

The authors frame the collapse as a double hit: a fragile heart meeting a viral trigger. Intensive therapy reversed much of the heart's enlargement and improved function. Early genetic screening is urged for children with unexplained heart problems or family patterns suggesting shared ancestry, and infection prevention matters greatly for known carriers.
pmc-13287479:
Faraaz Akhtar, Alistair Brownlee, and Cameron Crawford analysed wearable sleep records in 2026 covering 697 people and 185,143 nights across 49 countries. They asked how sleep length responds to season, daylight hours, latitude, and country, using layered statistical models that separate person and country effects.

Longer daylight meant slightly shorter sleep, by roughly 4.4 minutes for each extra hour of light. Once person and country differences were counted, simple season labels added almost nothing. Sensitivity to daylight did not grow clearly with latitude. Country habits mattered more than calendar season. The authors argue that global sleep patterns reflect local culture and individual routines most strongly.
pmc-13287679:
Ynara Maria Gomes de Sousa and co-authors compared two cattle-derived bone filler products in 2026 in rats with a standard 5 millimetre skull defect that cannot heal alone. Fifty-four rats received a plain blood clot, one named commercial filler, or a second filler, all under a dissolving membrane, with checks at three time points.

Both fillers supported new tissue better than clot alone. The second filler produced more mineralised tissue by days fourteen and twenty-eight, with denser structure. Early inflammation and vessel growth looked similar across fillers. The first filler built tissue more slowly, with later fibre organisation. The authors caution that animal results may not carry to dental patients.
pmc-13288679:
Hamideh Ebrahimi and co-authors pool how often Pakistani medical students report depressive symptoms in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched major databases plus Pakistani journals through September 2025, keeping observational studies that used validated tools such as the PHQ-9, BDI, or DASS-21, and graded study quality with a standard checklist.

Seventy-one studies giving 72 estimates and roughly 23,000 students produced rates anywhere from nine percent to ninety-four percent, with very high variation between studies. Estimates ran slightly higher in Sindh than elsewhere without firm statistical separation, varied by questionnaire, and crept upward in later publication years. Bias tests suggested some missing negative results, though adjusted pooling told a similar story.
pmc-13288879:
Joan Jimenez-Balado and colleagues introduce the SAGE study in 2026. Their protocol deals with fading memory in aging. The hippocampus often runs overactive early in Alzheimer's. Animal work blames weak inhibition. The transmitter GABA drives that brake. Estrogen also shapes the system.

SAGE will recruit 300 healthy adults. One hundred per decade will join. Ages run from fifty to seventy-nine. Two-thirds will be women. Brain and memory measures will be combined. The design asks if GABA breakdown drives overactivity. It also asks if that drives memory decline. Sex may change each link's strength. Precise treatment targets are the goal.
pmc-13288979:
Natasha E H Allott and colleagues test wearables for knee ligament tears. Their 2026 study ran in a London lab. Small motion sensors sat on thigh and shin. A trained physio did standard knee tests. Software learned to sort torn from sound knees.

The study held 50 people in all. Half had torn ligaments shown on scans. Half had sound knees with no past tears. Each injured leg paired with data from sound legs. Models were checked in ten split rounds. The work tests if cheap sensors can aid diagnosis. Full score details sit past the cut in this sample. So no firm accuracy claim is made here.
pmc-13289079:
Nuria Vazquez-Piqueras and colleagues detail a 2026 study plan in Spain. The study deals with strong antibiotics in surgery wards. Such drugs drive drug resistance. They are often used too long. One large hospital will host the work.

Past use will be read from 2022 to 2023. The new plan will run from 2024 to 2026. Teaching and fresh local guides lead the plan. An app and web tool will carry the guides. Each strong drug order will get a review. Allergy labels will be checked and fixed. Monthly drug use is the main measure. Safety checks will guard patient outcomes.
pmc-13289179:
Joanne E Mantell and colleagues study HIV services for migrant workers in 2026. Their study deals with Lesotho and South Africa. Workers cross the border for jobs. Many face blocks to HIV testing. Care links after testing are also weak.

The team spoke with 15 key informants. All worked with migrants in Lesotho. Roles spanned ministry staff and aid groups. Counselors, testers, and advocates also joined. Support fixes aimed at daily service gaps. Wider fixes aimed at rules and systems. Shared referral paths across the border led the list. Worksite HIV rules and flexible funds also featured. Care built for mobile lives is the core plea.
pmc-13290079:
Louise Dupraz and colleagues identify a 2026 gut bacterium, Sutterella, as a quiet troublemaker that worsens intestinal inflammation. Gut microbes normally train immunity and guard against infection, but some harmless residents turn harmful when the gut environment is disturbed. In bowel diseases such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, that disturbed balance drives severe inflammation through pathways still being mapped.

Lab and animal tests show the bacterium directly dampens lymphoid cell output of IL-22 and IL-17, weakening gut defense signals. In a chemical colitis mouse model, it raised inflammation while blocking IL-22 output as well. Secreted protein compounds block a sensing pathway called AhR in the cells. Human lymphoid cells reacted the same way.
pmc-13290779:
Support helps ALS caregivers directly, not by lightening their burden first, Nafiye Turkmenel and Ersin Uskun report in a cross-sectional study from 2026. They tested a stress-process model in 118 informal caregivers of people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Worse patient function meant heavier caregiver burden, while trouble communicating added little once caregiver traits were counted. Burden dragged both physical and mental quality of life down. Perceived social support, though, stayed positively tied to quality of life even after burden was in the model, and mediation tests found no sign that support worked through easing burden. Turkmenel and Uskun conclude services should attack burden and build support as two separate jobs, since each touches caregivers' lives on its own path.
pmc-13291179:
HIV testing at a cervix clinic in Sheffield is reviewed by Victoria L Parker and colleagues in a 2026 service check. National rules give no clear steer on such testing. Few clinics in England offer it. This clinic began standard testing in early 2023.

The check covered 367 patients with moderate or worse cell changes. Six already knew they had HIV. Rates in this group far topped the city average. Staff offered a test to most patients. Most of those asked said yes. All new test results came back negative. Nurses offered tests more often than consultants did. High uptake supports wider offers, the authors say.
pmc-13291779:
Yang Wang wrote a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on functional materials and device design for perovskite solar cells. Certified efficiency for these cells has now passed 26 percent, helped by tunable band gaps and strong light absorption. Wang argues that stability problems still block the road to market.

The collection gathers four invited articles. One models a dual-absorber cell pairing MAGeI3 with CsSnI3 in simulation, finding strong voltage, current, and fill factor even with moderate defect levels. A review article covers recent progress with self-assembled monolayers, among the other contributions. Wang frames the set as a snapshot of where materials design and device engineering now stand for next-generation solar power.
pmc-13292179:
Mahkameh Rafiee and co-authors pool a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on metabolic illness among older people living with HIV. Aging with HIV increasingly means managing blood pressure, weight, sugar, and cholesterol alongside the virus. The team searched five databases plus grey literature for English studies from 2013 to late December 2023.

Twenty-six studies qualified, most from North America and other developed settings. Pooled prevalence came to 40.7 percent for hypertension and 47.3 percent for high cholesterol among older patients. Diabetes affected 13.5 percent and obesity 26.1 percent of those studied in the combined estimates. Every condition ran higher in North America than elsewhere. The authors recommend routine screening, prevention programs, and diet and exercise support tailored to this group.
pmc-13292379:
Araceli Rodriguez-Muñoz and a large team test a fish parasite's danger to mammals in a 2026 study from Peru. The worm, Skrjabinisakis physeteris, rides in Pacific bonito eaten raw in ceviche. The group examined 787 bonito and found anisakid larvae in about half. Most larvae were Anisakis type II by shape, later matched to the species by DNA. Some were marinated in ceviche spices, then fed to Wistar rats.

About one larva in five caused lesions in the gut or beyond within two days. Spice exposure lowered both recovery and harm, especially after three hours of marinating. Damage included acute inflammation and dead tissue in the rat hosts. DNA from a mitochondrial gene grouped the worms with known reference sequences. The authors confirm the species on Peru's central coast and flag its food safety relevance. Marination helps but does not remove the risk of raw fish.
pmc-13293379:
Mirette I. Y. Eshak and colleagues mine public gene sequence archives for hidden viruses in fish, amphibians, reptiles, and birds, in a 2026 study. Their quarry is the bornavirus family, whose known members infect a wide range of animals and can occasionally reach humans. By screening read archives plus one new bird dataset, the team hunted for viral genomes that earlier surveys had missed.

The search turned up near-complete and partial genomes, including new orthobornaviruses in snakes and lizards and known bird viruses in new hosts. Fish-associated culterviruses appeared for the first time in reptiles and amphibians, widening their known range. A divergent genome in a gold-striped salamander may represent an entirely new genus. Some bird carboviruses lacked the usual surface protein genes, hinting they may rely on partner viruses to spread.
pmc-13293579:
Mengmeng Wang, Ping Zhang, and Min Shen report, in a 2026 case study, a Chinese patient with PAPA syndrome, a rare inherited inflammatory disorder named for joint inflammation, skin ulcers, and acne. The condition stems from changes in the PSTPIP1 gene.

Illness began at age 13, with skin ulcers and acne as the main signs in this patient. Gene testing found a new change in PSTPIP1 that neither parent carried. The report also reviews recent papers on signs, diagnosis, and care for the syndrome. Treatments aim at inflammatory pathways, with drugs blocking IL-1 or TNF signals among the options used. Wider awareness may speed diagnosis.
pmc-13293679:
Daniel Schallmayer and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a cracked plastic liner inside a thumb joint replacement that caused almost no symptoms. The patient, a 53-year-old cook, had a Touch prosthesis fitted in early 2024 for thumb base arthritis.

He felt only slight clicking when spreading his thumb, and standard X-rays and exam looked normal. A CT scan and stress X-rays hinted the ball sat off-center. Revision surgery found the fractured liner as the cause, and swapping the head restored smooth, silent motion. Regular checks are urged, since serious implant failure can hide behind mild signs.
pmc-13293979:
Alba Lillo Sierras, Sandro Bräunig, and coauthors give a 2026 protocol that shows RNA and protein together in routine bone marrow biopsies. Samples are formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded, the standard hospital format. Fluorescence methods mark two growth factor transcripts, TGFB1 and PDGFA1, alongside cell surface proteins that separate blood-forming cells from support cells.

The setting is acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where marrow fibrosis predicts worse outlook but its cause is unclear. Seeing exactly which cells make each factor, and where, can test whether support cells drive scarring. Because the method fits stored biopsy blocks, past cases can be studied without fresh tissue.
pmc-13294179:
Kyosuke Hoshikawa and coauthors use ultrasound stiffness tests to watch shoulder muscles make up for cuff tears in a 2026 study. Twenty-four patients with mean age near 66 years lifted the arm to the side. Stiffness, a proxy for muscle work, was read in three muscles at 30, 60, and 90 degrees. Tear size was measured at surgery.

Patients split into normal and odd deltoid work groups by stiffness shape. The odd group kept deltoid work high at each angle, clearly above normal at 30 degrees. Mate muscle shifts were more subtle. Mapping who leans too hard on the deltoid could guide rehab after repair.
pmc-13294879:
Al-Ali Hussein, Soon Huat Tan, and Vel Murugan Vadivelu design a three-part material for cleaning dye from water with visible light in a 2026 study. Single materials often waste light energy because separated charges recombine too fast. Their blend joins polypyrrole, titanium dioxide, and carbon nanotubes in one linked structure.

Polypyrrole harvests visible light, the oxide offers a stable reacting surface, and nanotubes carry electrons away quickly. Screening of acidity, dye level, and material dose found best settings that removed nearly all methylene blue in tests. The material kept most of its activity after five reuse cycles, and chemical analysis traced how the dye broke down.
pmc-13295079:
Dabin Huang and co-authors combine three bedside measures to warn of gut perforation in preterm babies in a 2026 study. Necrotizing enterocolitis can tear the bowel and kill quickly, yet early warning remains hard. Lactate, platelet size, and an organ failure score were tested together as a warning set.

Records covered 110 preterm infants with surgical bowel disease, half with perforation and half without. The perforated group showed higher values on all three measures and died more often before discharge. Lactate and platelet size independently flagged perforation risk, and the three measures together predicted both perforation and death better than any single measure alone.
pmc-13295779:
Marco Gemelli and colleagues link poverty to outcomes after major aorta surgery in a 2026 study. Twenty years of cases at one centre were split by a national deprivation index. Emergency repair of a torn aorta and planned major aortic operations were judged separately.

In the emergency group of 526 patients, the most deprived half died in hospital far more often and survived fewer years afterwards. Deprivation predicted death on its own in adjusted models for that group. In the planned group of 1,320 patients, no such gaps appeared for early or long-term outcomes, suggesting emergency pathways carry the inequality burden.
pmc-13295879:
Jiale Zhu and co-authors build a spatial map in 2026 of immune cells in breast cancer that has spread to the brain. Combining detailed tissue imaging with public single-cell and spatial data, they compare original breast tumours with brain deposits cell by cell.

Brain deposits had lost a welcoming tissue zone rich in memory T cells and other defenders. In its place grew a suppressive zone holding CD163-positive macrophages, invasive tumour cells and tired T cells. Signals that switch immunity off were also flagged. Tests in animals backed the idea that blocking those signals could help treat brain spread.
pmc-13296479:
Ijaz Ali and colleagues build a stretchy, transparent conductive hydrogel for soft electronics in a 2026 materials paper. Strong hydrogels often need fillers or complex multi-step designs that hurt clarity and scale. Their filler-free gel uses soap-like micelles to form reversible water-repelling domains inside a gelatine-reinforced network.

The finished gel stretched to many times its length while staying mostly transparent and springing back with little lasting strain. Salt gave it stable ionic conductivity, and it sensed strain across a very wide range with fast response. Repeated stretching cycles left its signal reliable. A one-pot recipe from low-cost parts makes the design attractive for wearable sensors and other flexible devices.
pmc-13296779:
Tony D. Baldini and colleagues ask how hydrogel stiffness changes stem cell behaviour under inflammatory signals, in a 2026 laboratory study. Fracture healing needs a controlled inflammatory phase, which severe trauma can throw into disorder. Human mesenchymal stem cells were grown in gels of three stiffness levels with two signalling proteins added.

On hard plastic, one signal suppressed a bone-formation marker by the third week. Combined signals on plastic pushed the cells to release a mixed, dysregulated set of inflammatory factors. Inside gels, that overreaction calmed, with stiff gels best at quieting inflammatory output and medium gels best for the bone marker. Tuning scaffold stiffness may help fracture scaffolds manage inflammation.
pmc-13297179:
Lin Xie and colleagues present a graph-learning network that predicts which drugs will bind which biological targets in a 2026 paper. Screening every drug-target pair in the laboratory is slow and costly, so computation narrows the field. Their model treats drug similarity, target similarity, and known interactions as separate relational views.

Each node in the network learns how much weight to give each view, based on its own structural situation. Cross-view comparison sharpens the representations further. On five benchmark datasets the model beat the strongest rival on both headline metrics. It also surfaced plausible new pairings from unlabelled candidates. Drug hunters get a prioritisation tool for screening and repurposing ideas.
pmc-13297579:
Qingfeng Zheng and colleagues build a spinning-disc chip that runs a full germ test for food poisoning bacteria, in a 2026 paper. Standard tests are slow, hands-on, and tied to costly lab gear, which blocks checks at the site. Their disc joins sample clean-up, DNA extraction, copying, and readout in one run, steered by spin valves and twin channels.

Magnetic beads first fish the target germs from the sample, then a fast copying method that needs no heat cycles multiplies their DNA. In spiked milk, the system found Salmonella at very low levels within one hour. Recovery rates stayed close to the true values with tight spread. A cheap, portable tester of this kind suits markets and farms with few resources.
pmc-13297779:
Chest scans clear more slowly in people with diabetes who are healing from viral lung disease, though diabetes may not be the root cause. Ana Maria Mihai and her team tracked 430 patients in a 2026 study, scoring lung harm on day 1 and day 6 of care.

The diabetes group came in worse off, with a mid score of 2.0 next to 1.0 for the rest. Both groups got better at the same pace, yet the gap was still there on day 6. Why patients left the study split sharply too: most exits in the non-diabetes group were people who left against advice, while deaths drove most exits in the diabetes group. Once the team weighed how sick people were at the start, the diabetes effect lost its force.
pmc-13297879:
Ying Wu and colleagues ask how soon the drug nusinersen starts to help patients with spinal muscular atrophy, in a 2026 study from a Beijing hospital. The drug was the first to change the course of this inherited muscle-wasting disease, yet the timing of benefit stayed vague. Sixty-two patients with types one to three received the drug for at least six months, with movement scored before each dose.

Nearly two thirds of those fully assessed reached a meaningful gain by six months, and about one in five gained or regained a movement milestone. The typical time to response sat near two months, inside the loading phase. Ultrasound guidance made spinal dosing succeed even in patients with bent or fused spines.
pmc-13298379:
Junjie Xu and others test fibre-reinforced, silicon-modified phenolic aerogel composites in a 2026 materials study. The goal was greater strength and heat endurance while keeping the material light and insulating. A uniform nanoporous resin matrix supplied thermal insulation, and fibre density was varied across samples.

Higher fibre density raised tensile strength at both room and elevated temperature, while thermal conductivity stayed low. During torch ablation, silicon compounds and quartz fibres formed ceramic surface layers that slowed material loss. The densest composite showed the lowest linear ablation rate. The authors present the balance of strength, insulation, and heat resistance as suited to demanding thermal protection uses.
pmc-13299279:
Two drug targets, hit at once, could push a harsh form of breast cancer to die. Sergio Assuncao Monteiro and his team reach that call in a 2026 study done by math and code. Their search paired logic nets of cell life with a strict math sieve to hunt pairs worth a drug.

The hunt lit on TK1 and VIM. A joint block on both drove the cell state 99.03% of the way to the death state. The pair beat all rivals and stayed on top at each tweak of the model's knobs. Drugs that hit each one are on hand now. A deep-learn check found plain breast tissue would shrug off the same block, which hints at a safe dose gap. Bench proof must come next.
pmc-13299379:
Professional soccer strains players' hormone balance for days, and responses may differ by ethnic background, synthesize Sandro La Vignera and Rosita A Condorelli in a 2026 review. They analyzed twenty-one studies of testosterone, cortisol, their ratio, growth hormone, and IGF-1 across training and competition.

Cortisol stayed elevated up to seventy-two hours after some matches, and the testosterone-to-cortisol ratio sagged during congested fixture runs. A gene variant affecting steroid excretion, UGT2B17, may partly explain group differences in testosterone measures, though the evidence is thin. About 7.4% of elite junior players developed non-functional overreaching with blunted hormone responses. The authors suggest individualized hormone monitoring and gentler post-match loads.
pmc-13299779:
L Donisi and others compare two operation approaches for fitting under-skin defibrillators, using a national French registry with five-year outcomes, published in 2026. Nearly five thousand patients got either the first three-incision technique or the simpler two-incision version, which became dominant by the end of the enrolment period. Endpoints were judged from one centre, with number-based adjustment for starting differences.

Overall complication rates proved comparable after adjustment. The three-incision approach carried independently higher local complications, especially infections and poor wound healing, plus more reinterventions. Lead problems did not differ. The authors support the two-incision method as standard practice for these implants.
pmc-13299979: Natalia Kurhaluk and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their review on antioxidants, the microbiota-gut-brain axis, and neurodegenerative disease. The notice is a correction only: all ten figures were replaced with newly prepared versions offering better resolution, labelling, and clarity, with no change to scientific content or conclusions. One cited reference was also swapped after the earlier source was retracted, replaced by a 2025 review from the same group on the vagus nerve, gut microbiota, and stress. The original article was updated.
pmc-13300179:
J Pontoppidan and colleagues describe a 2026 study of smartphone monitoring after catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation. Instead of standard electrocardiogram devices, patients used an app that reads tiny chest vibrations through phone motion sensors, a method called mechanocardiography. The retrospective study covered 640 patients offered free access to the app, and it tracked both app use and later repeat ablation in a Danish registry subgroup.

Of the patients offered the app, 81 percent activated it, and 68 percent were still using it six months later. Recurrence appeared in 40 percent during the first three months and 30 percent during months four to six. In the registry subgroup, early recurrence was strongly linked to repeat ablation. The authors argue that phone-based monitoring can support earlier, better informed decisions after ablation.
pmc-13300979:
M Elhadi and co-authors report a quality improvement project on risk factor care for atrial fibrillation at a district general hospital, published in 2026. A baseline audit of 150 patients admitted in July 2023 found patchy attention to alcohol, blood pressure, weight, diabetes, heart failure, and sleep apnea. The team answered with a clinician email, a teaching session for acute medicine staff, and a patient leaflet folded into nursing checklists, then re-audited through early 2025.

Documentation of alcohol intake jumped from fifteen to ninety-two percent, and the share receiving alcohol advice more than doubled, settling near sixty-two percent. Blood pressure care reached full guideline aligned intensification plans, as did heart failure and diabetes management by the final cycle. Weight advice and sleep apnea recognition improved more modestly, the latter still under a third. The authors credit staff awareness and plan structured checklists to hold the gains.
pmc-13301479:
Women with amyloid in their hearts are found later and fare worse than men, Ilenia Monaco and colleagues argue in a 2026 narrative review of sex disparities in cardiac amyloidosis. The survey covers how the infiltrative disease shows up, how it is caught, and how it is treated, with the male–female contrast running through each stage.

Women tend to be older at diagnosis, with disease that looks milder on standard measures yet carries a poorer outlook. Sex-neutral cut-offs, the authors contend, help explain the misses and delays. They press for sex-specific thresholds, wider use of multimodality imaging, and trials that enroll enough women to define the female pattern of the disease.
pmc-13301779:
A Estevez Paniagua and co-authors analyse, in a 2026 study, what shapes electrical measurements at the time of left bundle branch area pacing. This pacing method places the lead deep in the heart's dividing wall to activate the natural wiring system. Signal timings vary between patients, and the team wanted to know which clinical, anatomical, and procedural factors explain that spread.

The cohort held 149 people paced for slow heart rhythms whose main pumping function was preserved. A wider lower chamber predicted slower activation across several timing measures, and a longer natural QRS also meant a wider paced beat. True left bundle capture and related patterns mainly shortened one key timing interval rather than the overall beat width. The results help implanters interpret readings they see on the day.
pmc-13302079:
Sofia Bigardi and co-authors review, in a 2026 systematic review, ultrasound elastography for diseases of the womb. The technique measures tissue stiffness during an ordinary scan, which could help separate harmless growths from cancers. Two variants exist: one tracks deformation under probe pressure, the other measures travelling shear waves.

Twenty studies published between 2018 and early 2026 met the review criteria. Growths such as fibroids and adenomyosis usually felt stiffer than normal womb muscle, though telling those two apart was inconsistent. Cervical and womb-lining cancers also tended to measure stiffer than benign lesions, and stiffness may hint at how deeply a cancer invades. Methods varied so much between studies that firm thresholds cannot yet be set.
pmc-13302279:

Among 68 patients, sensory symptoms led aura features at 67%. Perfusion CT alterations appeared in 15 patients (22%), mainly as unilateral hypoperfusion outside a vascular territory. Automated RAPID software, available in nine of those fifteen, flagged alterations in five patients missed by qualitative reading, with all showing Tmax above four seconds. Male sex and aphasic aura were associated with perfusion alterations, and migraine with aura accounted for about 1% of stroke code activations. The authors conclude that automated analysis may sharpen acute diagnosis.
pmc-13327079:
Arbaaz Gill and team tracked United States public web interest in myopia-control glasses for kids around a key approval. Their 2026 study pulled weekly Google Trends search scores for 2025. It weighed parent-worded and brand terms before and after the Food and Drug Administration cleared Essilor Stellest on September 25, 2025. MiSight searches served as a same-time yardstick. A combined interest score averaged the chosen terms.

Mean combined interest rose from 9.39 before approval to 18.6 after approval, a rise of about 98%. The mean ratio to baseline rose from 0.353 at the start to 0.694 at the end over the same span. MiSight-linked searches stayed flat, which points to a Stellest-only response, not a broad trend. Scaling the scores points to growth past seasonal swings. The team warns web interest does not map straight to awareness, clinic use, or prescribing, but it may help doctors brace for more parent questions.
pmc-13328279:
Wenwen Liu and co-authors create new membrane-attacking antibacterials in a 2026 study. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus shrugs off many standard drugs, so the team built a family of phthalazine-based quaternary ammonium salts, compounds 2a through 2v, whose chain length could be tuned. Lab tests weighed killing power, safety, and how the best compound works.

Compound 2n led the family, stopping S. aureus, its resistant form, and two other species at 2 μg/mL in the minimum inhibitory tests reported, while sparing red blood cells up to far higher levels. It killed fast, resisted breakdown, and slowed biofilms, and probes showed torn membranes leaking cell contents, with DNA binding as a possible second hit.
pmc-13329979:
Alison Carroll and colleagues show light-driven storage of hydrogen in propane in a 2026 study. Storing hydrogen in chemical bonds avoids high pressure tanks. Propane is cheap and widely available, so the team tested turning propylene into propane at room temperature and pressure with a light-powered catalyst.

The catalyst pairs aluminium light catchers with titanium oxide and single platinum atoms. Light at 450 and 800 nm both drove strong propane output in the reported tests. Theory showed that light-made carriers at either colour hold enough energy for both reaction steps, splitting hydrogen and adding it across the carbon bond. Paired with earlier light-driven release, the cycle could store and free hydrogen under mild conditions.
pmc-13330479:
Pengyu Zhao and Shuai Geng pool studies on pharmacist care in China amid a shift from dispensing to patient care in a 2026 meta-analysis. Searches ran across eight databases to April 2026 for trials and comparison studies of pharmacist work such as prescription review and counselling. Bias was checked with standard tools.

In total, 32 studies entered the pool, with only 5 randomised trials among them. Pharmacist input linked to more single-drug antibiotic use and more sound prescriptions, and to fewer irrational prescriptions in the reported odds values. Spread between studies was wide, which limits exactness. The authors call the gains promising but early, and urge strong trials with patient-centred outcomes.
pmc-13330579:
Yi Zhang and colleagues trace the family history of STAYGREEN genes in tobacco plants in a 2026 study. Those genes steer chlorophyll breakdown, which drives leaf yellowing, maturity, and crop quality. The team compared gene copies across flowering plants, with focus on Nicotiana, whose doubled genome history may have expanded the family.

Family trees placed tobacco copies inside a conserved flowering plant lineage, with extra copies matching the doubled genome past in the reported analysis. Gene activity differed across tissues. Core catalytic parts stayed tightly conserved, while end regions varied by lineage. Most copies kept signals that send the protein to chloroplasts, though strength varied. The work frames how leaf ageing stays stable yet flexible.
pmc-13332579:
Danny R Vesevick and colleagues test 2026 whether the experimental drug RNS60 protects upper motor neurons in a mouse model of ALS with TDP-43 pathology. TDP-43 pathology appears widely in the cortex of people with ALS. RNS60 had previously improved mitochondrial growth and function in other preclinical models. The team treated TDP-43 mice and control mice, both with upper motor neurons marked by green fluorescent protein, with RNS60 or placebo every other day from day 30 to day 90.

Brain and spinal cord inflammation, mitochondrial structure, mitochondrial function, and neuromuscular junction health were measured. RNS60 cut the share of defective mitochondria in upper motor neurons sharply, from about half in untreated diseased mice to about one fifth in treated mice. Junctions in leg and diaphragm muscles were also assessed. The work supports RNS60 as a mitochondrial-protective candidate in TDP-43 ALS, while stressing that mouse results must still pass human trials.
pmc-13333179:
Christopher Tom and colleagues report a 2026 case linking diffuse large B-cell lymphoma to Agent Orange exposure in a Vietnam veteran. Agent Orange is a toxic herbicide mixture containing dioxin, used widely during Vietnam fighting in the 1960s and 1970s. The patient was an older veteran who came in with a right neck mass that kept growing after heavy combat exposure to Agent Orange. He was diagnosed with stage I diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with locally advanced, bulky disease.

He was judged at higher risk for systemic disease given skin breakthrough at presentation. Additional labs showed prior hepatitis B infection with immunity, a virus also linked to non-Hodgkin lymphoma risk and worse outcomes in large studies. He began six cycles of R-CHOP therapy: rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone. The case adds to the exposure history clinicians should take when lymphoma appears in Vietnam veterans.
pmc-13333279:
Jean Pierre Díaz-Paz and co-authors present a labeled dataset in 2026 for cleaning speckle noise from Sentinel-1 radar images. Radar pictures are grainy by nature, and training smart filters requires matched noisy and clean examples, which are hard to build honestly.

The dataset holds 512 by 512 pixel radar tiles in both VV and VH polarizations, gathered worldwide through an automated Python and Google Earth Engine workflow with random sampling and quality filtering. For each spot, cleaner reference images were made by averaging stacks of 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 passes, letting users study how averaging depth affects speckle removal. Land cover maps from ESA WorldCover v200 and a metadata file ride along, and benchmark scores including ENL, MSE, SSIM, and PSNR are supplied for sample tiles. The set is hosted on Mendeley Data as a reproducible training resource.
pmc-13333679:
Thomas Buttgereit and a large international team report on the first two years of the Chronic Angioedema Registry, known as CARE. Launched in October 2023, the registry gathers clinical and patient-reported data on recurrent angioedema of any type during routine care.

By December 2025, 550 patients had enrolled at 23 centers spread across 18 countries, meeting its early milestones on time. Hereditary angioedema and mast cell related forms were among the diagnoses tracked. A survey of physicians in the specialist center network explored why centers join or hold back, and how communication could improve. The report shows a global registry for a rare swelling condition can grow steadily, while naming practical barriers that slow wider participation.
pmc-13333779:
Jin Han and co-authors looked at ligustilide, a natural compound from Angelica sinensis and Ligusticum chuanxiong, for central nervous system disorders in a 2026 article. Ligustilide draws interest for calming inflammation, fighting oxidation, and protecting nerves.

Three sources were searched for studies through October 2025, and 55 original studies were left after screening. Evidence links the compound to help in ischemic stroke, vascular dementia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases, traumatic brain injury, and anxiety disorders. Its effects run through pathways including PI3K/Akt, MAPK, NF-kB, and Nrf2/ARE, lowering oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and mitochondrial failure. The review also covers how the body absorbs and clears ligustilide and what safety data exist, sketching what stands between the compound and clinical use.
pmc-13334079:
Jeong-Ah Yoon and co-authors tested a candidate probiotic strain, Pediococcus acidilactici MBEL10321, in a 2026 study pairing lab tests with genome sequencing. The strain came from Nuruk, a classic Korean fermentation starter.

In culture the strain survived acid and bile salts well and held back several pathogens, beating two control strains, among them Listeria monocytogenes, Bacillus cereus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Staphylococcus aureus. It showed no blood-cell-breaking activity. Its genome spans 2,044,106 base pairs with 1,980 protein-coding genes, and screens found no virulence factors, no drug resistance genes, and no transferable plasmid replicons. The paired safety and function evidence backs the strain as a probiotic candidate for food or supplement use.
pmc-13334979:
Chenhui He and co-authors built an ultrasound-driven sticky hydrogel for infected wounds in a 2026 materials study. Long-term infected wounds resist treatment because bacteria persist, tissue states vary, and antibiotics lose ground.

Their hydrogel, PA-ZA, embeds tiny composites of ZIF-8 studded with nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots in a polyacrylamide-alginate base. Set ultrasound, first at kilohertz then megahertz speeds, triggers tissue sticking, pushes nanoparticles through skin, and switches on sound-driven production of reactive oxygen species that kill bacteria. The gel proved body-safe and sped cell migration and blood vessel growth in vitro. In infected full-thickness wounds in animals, switching it on lowered bacterial burden, sped the end of inflammation, and hastened repair, with similar benefit in a deeper infection model.
pmc-13335479:
Patricia C Hernandez and co-authors showed how small molecules selectively block the DNA-chewing enzyme TREX1 in a 2026 structural biology study. TREX1 clears stray cytoplasmic DNA; losing it causes autoimmune disease, while blocking it in cancer cells can wake anti-tumor immunity.

X-ray crystallography revealed the inhibitors sitting in the active site, competing with the end of the DNA substrate and hydrogen-bonding to a conserved glutamate. Binding also locks a tyrosine, Tyr129, into an alternative pose that cannot grip DNA and opens a deep hydrophobic pocket that cradles part of the drug. That pocket explains why the compounds spare the close relative TREX2 and viral cousins. The structures give medicinal chemists a blueprint for selective TREX1 blockers.
pmc-13336379:
Jianya Luo and co-authors found a compound that resensitizes a dangerous hospital pathogen to an old antibiotic in a 2026 microbiology study. Acinetobacter baumannii shrugs off most drugs, and colistin, a last-resort option, is losing ground too.

A structure-based virtual screen against the bacterium's lipopolysaccharide transport system produced a somatostatin-like peptide, C4. Alone it barely kills, but with colistin the synergy is strong. Lipid and gene analyses showed C4 remodels the membrane, selectively building up phosphatidylglycerol and raising expression of mlaC, a phospholipid transport gene. Deleting mlaC erased both the lipid change and the synergy, while extra copies strengthened it. The work reveals membrane lipid management as a lever for rescuing colistin therapy.
pmc-13336779:
Zhaoqiang Jiang and a large team connect night shift work to higher blood pressure in a 2026 study of people and mice. Shift work scrambles the body clock, and the authors point to failing mitochondria, the cell's power units, as the main link. Mice on simulated night shifts developed higher pressure and disturbed clock genes such as PER1 and BMAL1.

The shifted mice also showed power-unit damage and oxidative stress. Human night workers showed the same pattern: longer shift exposure tracked with higher systolic and diastolic pressure and with disturbed clock and mitochondrial markers. The shared pathway helps explain the heart risks of night work and may guide ways to blunt them.
pmc-13336979:
Yiming Fu and colleagues study why windows for imaging the living mouse brain cloud over in a 2026 methods review and study. Thinned skull and clearing methods let multiphoton microscopes watch brain cells over time, yet image quality fades fast. Systematic tests with adaptive optics compared window types for lifespan, sharpness, and distortion.

Progressive skull regrowth emerged as the core limit across all types, steadily blurring signal and resolution. A local glucocorticoid delivery method stretched good performance to one month. Sealing the window with a drug-loaded hydrogel suppressed regrowth while keeping optics clear. The findings give labs a practical route to month-long, high-fidelity brain imaging and explain what ends it.
pmc-13339179:
Dawei Lin and colleagues studied mitral valve leakage in 2026 among patients receiving transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic regurgitation. Some patients also have functional mitral regurgitation, yet whether aortic valve replacement improves it and what predicts improvement was unknown. Patients treated at Zhongshan Hospital from June 2020 to June 2024 were enrolled.

Groups were split by whether mitral leakage improved one month after the procedure, and baseline, imaging, and follow up data were compared. Finding predictors helps heart teams counsel patients and plan extra mitral treatment when needed. The work refines expectations for combined valve disease treated by catheter.
pmc-13339779:
Chia-Heng Lin and colleagues compare victim choices among sexual offenders with and without severe mental illness in a 2026 forensic study. Court-referred evaluations in Taiwan from 2009 to 2022 supplied the records. Understanding pattern differences may sharpen risk assessment.

Among 86 men, 21 had psychotic or bipolar disorders and 65 did not as reported. Offenders with severe illness more often had adult and stranger victims in the reported comparisons, with odds near fourfold for each in adjusted models. Substance disorders were more common without severe illness. Small subgroup size urges caution, but distinct patterns suggest assessment should weigh diagnosis alongside victim history.
pmc-13341179:
How nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blockers protect the kidney from inside is reviewed by Eun Sil Koh and colleagues in 2026. Drugs such as finerenone cut albuminuria and improve outcomes in chronic kidney disease, but the exact vessel-level mechanics remain partly unclear.

The review gathers clinical and lab evidence on sodium handling and pressure inside the glomerulus. These drugs mildly increase sodium excretion, ease aldosterone-driven tightening of outgoing vessels, and restore feedback signals that guard against overfiltration. Whether they beat older steroidal blockers at fixing hyperfiltration is unproven. Their edge may instead be safety and tolerability that let patients stay on treatment.
pmc-13341479:
A gene that pushes colon cancer cells toward iron-driven death is studied by Haiying Sun and co-investigators in a 2026 analysis. RBMS3 had unclear significance, so the team mined pan-cancer and colon adenocarcinoma datasets, then validated findings in lab cultures.

Tumors expressed less RBMS3 than normal tissue, and low levels meant worse survival, supporting a tumor-suppressor role. Expression tracked with tumor stage, and adding it to staging improved a prognostic nomogram. Cell work showed M2 macrophages suppress RBMS3 through STAT3 signaling, weakening ferroptosis. The pathway names both a biomarker and a possible lever for treatment.
pmc-13343979:
Shumin Fan and colleagues screened tag stripping enzymes in 2026 for regulators of IRF7, the master switch for immune signal output, above all in myeloid cells. Virus infection swiftly triggers immune signal output that boosts antiviral responses in infected and nearby cells. Tagging of IRF7 with ubiquitin is key to its activation, yet molecular routes stayed poorly mapped.

A gene screen with an siRNA library of human tag stripping enzymes named USP2 as a positive switch and OTUD5 as a negative switch for IRF7 activity. OTUD5 bound IRF7 and blocked its K63 linked ubiquitin tagging. The switches offer new levers for tuning immune signal responses in viral infection and autoimmunity.
pmc-13344079:
Sojiro Amamoto and colleagues told of a retrograde recanalisation case in 2026 in a 90 year old woman on haemodialysis with a blocked dialysis graft. Chronic total occlusion at the venous join of an arteriovenous graft resists endovascular treatment, above all when antegrade approach through the graft fails. The patient grew progressive access failure from occlusion reaching to the downstream basilic vein.

Antegrade recanalisation had failed and surgical revision seemed less desirable given advanced age, frailty, and fragile skin. Preprocedural ultrasound found a downstream basilic segment fit for retrograde puncture, and ultrasound guided retrograde treatment restored access. The case offers a swap route when standard graft routes fail in frail patients.
pmc-13346079:
Joyce Jebet and co-authors systematically review tools for screening mothers' mental health across Africa in 2026. Pregnancy and new motherhood carry heavy mental burdens that clinics rarely test for. The team gathered African studies from 2014 to 2024 to see which questionnaires actually get used and how they perform.

The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale dominated the shelf, with the PHQ-9 common in Ethiopia and the SRQ-20 favored in West Africa. Studies clustered in South Africa, Ethiopia, and Nigeria, with samples from 37 to 3,311 women. Disorders stay common yet under-detected, and the authors push for screening folded into routine mother-and-child visits, better staff training, and tools fitted to local culture.
pmc-13346679:
Alita Mrema and co-authors studied in 2026 factors linked to low mood in Tanzanian women living with both HIV and cervical cancer. Cervical cancer is the top cause of cancer death in women in sub-Saharan Africa. It hits women with HIV hardest. Yet the mental health load of both diagnoses is poorly charted in Tanzania.

The team surveyed 160 women at least three months after cervical cancer treatment from January to June 2024. They measured low mood, social support, HIV stigma, and coping, plus clinical and life details. Pinpointing which factors track with low mood can guide screening and support in clinics that already manage two hard illnesses. Mental health care need not stay an afterthought.
pmc-13347079:
Juan Huang and colleagues test whether walking patterns can flag thinking decline in Parkinson disease, in a diagnostic study published in 2026. Patients classed as normal, subjectively declining, or mildly impaired did timed up-and-go walks, both plain and with a second task. While a wearable system recorded 209 motion measures for each trial.

Extra measures captured how much the added mental task cost each walker. Several learning models were trained to sort the three groups, checked with cross-validation and a held-out set. Importance tools were used to show which gait features drove each call. The aim is a low-burden clinic test that spots early decline without long paper testing.
pmc-13347379:
Aarti Gupta and colleagues characterise a doped bismuth ferrite powder for cleaning toxic chromium from water with sunlight, in a study published in 2026. Praseodymium and cobalt were added into the crystal without forming second phases, shrinking grain size. A combined heat-based instrument read thermal flow, energy gap, and charge lifetime in one pass.

Moderate doping improved heat flow and charge separation, while heavy doping added trap sites that sped charge loss and slowed heat spread in the reported measures. Under plain sunlight the best powder cut the harmful chromium form by about 96 percent within 120 minutes, turning it toward a safer form. Linked structure and heat data guide tuning of such cleaners.
pmc-13349779:
Chao Gong and colleagues reported a cohort study in 2026 on whether HDL cholesterol levels predict outcomes in non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy. They followed 297 patients who had cardiac magnetic resonance scans between 2017 and 2024.

Over a median 35 months of follow-up, 41 patients reached the main endpoint of death or heart transplant, and 97 reached a wider endpoint adding heart failure readmission. Lower HDL cholesterol was linked to higher risk in adjusted models, and patients with higher levels stayed event-free longer. Adjusting for estimated pulmonary artery pressure weakened the link somewhat. The authors propose HDL cholesterol as a cheap, routine marker for sorting risk in these patients.
pmc-13349979:
Jiahuan Tang and colleagues fine-tuned a multimodal GPT-4o model in 2026 to write diagnostic impressions for a tricky breast MRI finding. The finding is called non-mass enhancement. Earlier work showed public language models handled breast lesion grading poorly. This lesion type had never been singled out.

Records from 229 patients supplied scan images, reports, and clinical histories. Six model versions were built. Some were untuned. Others trained on text alone, or on images plus text. Their impressions were compared with three radiologists of differing experience. Other experts then graded the outputs. The study tests whether targeted training lifts AI reporting to a clinically useful level.
pmc-13350179:
Jiale Huang and colleagues used combined gene and chemistry profiling in 2026 to explain why blueberries fail after years in the same soil in Dalian, China. Soil was sampled around roots and away from them after zero, two, four, and six years of continuous cropping.

Microbial diversity fell steadily with cropping years, especially near roots, and communities separated clearly by period. Helpful microbe groups thinned while stress-tolerant ones grew, and soil chemistry showed accumulating compounds harmful to the plants themselves. The picture blames a sickened soil community plus self-poisoning as twin drivers of the decline, pointing growers toward soil restoration rather than more fertiliser.
pmc-13350379:
Chun-Ka Wong and a multicentre team reported Asia-Pacific experience in 2026 with cutting heart valve leaflets during catheter valve replacement to stop the new valve blocking a coronary artery. The registry covered consecutive patients at seven centres from 2019 to 2026 treated with two techniques, one slicing the leaflet and one burning through it with a radiofrequency needle.

Success meant completing the cut and implant with no coronary blockage, emergency surgery, stroke, or death. Most published proof comes from North America and Europe. Real-world results from this region tell local teams whether the demanding trick works in their own patients and systems.
pmc-13350479:
Ningbo Yin and colleagues pooled ultrasound strain measurements of the heart's right side in a 2026 meta-analysis, aiming to set normal values. Speckle tracking follows tiny heart muscle patterns to measure how the right atrium and ventricle deform, but healthy ranges were never standardised.

Studies of healthy adults published up to July 2025 were gathered from three databases. Pooled values covered ventricle strain and strain rates plus three phases of atrial strain, and subgroup checks probed race, sex, age, and the software and machine used. Reference numbers that account for equipment differences let clinicians tell true right-heart weakness from measurement noise.
pmc-13350679:
Yuhan Fan and co-authors used deep learning in 2026 to regenerate radiotherapy positioning images that clinics normally throw away. Cone-beam projections for head and neck cancer patients are bulky, so they are discarded after building the three-dimensional scan, yet later checks may need them.

Working from 50 patients, they first computed synthetic X-ray views from the stored scans, then trained networks to convert those into realistic projections. Three network designs were compared, with tests on scatter correction, scan sharpness, and training size. Regenerating discarded images from kept data could rescue old treatment records for review and research.
pmc-13351679:
Chenjia Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 case report on emergency non-heart surgery in a child with Eisenmenger syndrome. The condition marks late, untreated congenital heart disease with fixed high lung pressure, reversed blood flow, and low oxygen. An 11-year-old girl needed urgent surgery under general anaesthesia for a twisted right ovary.

Her lung artery pressure was 105/49 mmHg, and anaesthesia used etomidate, midazolam, vecuronium, and sufentanil, then propofol, remifentanil, and sevoflurane. Readings stayed stable during surgery, but a lung pressure crisis followed with fast heart rhythm, low blood pressure, and low oxygen. Amiodarone, treprostinil, bicarbonate, and oxygen restored normal rhythm, and she went home on day 11.
pmc-13351879:
Sen Lin and colleagues report a 2026 surgical technique for easing pressure on nerves at two neighbouring lower back levels through a single small cut. Endoscopic decompression is a key low-impact option for narrowed spinal canals. Reaching two levels often needs several cuts, so the team set out to do both through one opening.

Working over the top to the far side, they trimmed bone and removed thickened ligament at the L3-4 and L4-5 levels. Surgery took 115 minutes through a 0.7-cm cut with six brief X-ray checks. Pain scores fell from 8 to 0 by follow-up at 2 and 6 months, and the patient walked within 24 hours. The case shows the one-cut route is workable.
pmc-13352479:
Feiyang Liu leads a 2026 project building a scale for the healthy mental effects of exercise in Chinese college students. Existing tools capture only general or narrow mental outcomes after exercise. Scale items were drafted from theory, prior work, interviews, and open surveys, then tested in staged samples.

An early sample of 612 students shaped the item set, and a formal sample of 945 students checked reliability and validity. The final scale holds 55 items in five parts: emotional feelings, self-cognition, frustration coping, control and social efficacy, and social interaction. Variance explained per part ranged from 62.546 to 73.711 percent. A retest group of 597 students after 1 month supported stability over time.
pmc-13353379:
Xiaoyu Ma leads a 2026 review of oxidative enzymes that break down plant biomass. Plant walls are mostly lignocellulose, a tough mix that resists biological dismantling. The review maps how microbes, mainly filamentous fungi, attack with redox enzymes, including newly found AA families.

Laccases and lignin-active peroxidases lead lignin attack, while lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases and their redox partners cut sugar chains. Hydrogen peroxide acts as a shared middleman whose supply and use are tightly timed and placed. Non-enzyme radical systems join the synergy. Structural computing sharpens the picture, and the authors argue the knowledge can speed next-generation biorefineries for a circular bioeconomy.
pmc-13354279:
Sascha Gerd Decker and others matched virtual reality training with standard teaching for scoring psoriasis severity, in 2026. Care decisions depend on the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index, yet accurate and reproducible scoring needs practice. A virtual reality program might train doctors more effectively than a lecture alone.

In a random forward trial, one group received a classical lecture and the other trained with the VR-PASI program, and scoring was checked afterward. The study tests whether immersive practice helps grading skill in a seen way. Educators gain evidence for choosing training ways that produce dependable severity scores in clinic.
pmc-13354579:
Lee A Armstrong and others marked the EF-hand domain of MINDY3, a deubiquitinating enzyme, in 2026. MINDY enzymes prefer to cut K48-linked ubiquitin chains, which mark proteins for disposal. MINDY3 stands out because its speeding region spans nearly the whole protein, interrupted by an unusual EF-hand insertion whose function was unclear.

The team found that this EF-hand binds ubiquitin at three distinct sites, letting MINDY3 grip and fast cut long ubiquitin chains. It also binds the ubiquitin-like domains of RAD23A and RAD23B, proteins that shuttle cargo to the proteasome and assist DNA repair. The work explains how an architectural oddity gives MINDY3 its distinctive grip on ubiquitin chains.
pmc-13355279:
Mohamad Abou Chakra and co-authors studied in 2026 whether age changes how well two bladder treatments work for high-risk bladder cancer that has not reached the muscle. One treatment uses a weakened germ, BCG, placed in the bladder, and the other uses two chemotherapy drugs in sequence. Records covered 401 patients treated from 2011 to 2024.

Age, split into bands from under 60 to 80 and over, did not clearly predict cancer return in either group. Older patients on BCG showed a mild trend toward more returns, while older patients on the drug pair held steady over time. The authors say the trend in the BCG group deserves more study.
pmc-13355779:
Romana Erblich and co-authors studied in 2026 when traumatic cardiac arrest happens outside hospital and how timing shapes survival. Using records from thirteen helicopter rescue services from 2010 to 2019, they split cases by when the heart stopped: before crews arrived, after arrival at the scene, or during transport.

Nine of ten arrests had already occurred at the scene before the first unit arrived. Survival was highest when arrest came after crews arrived or during helicopter transport. Still, lasting return of circulation was possible even in early arrests, above all when the first heart rhythm was not flat. The authors say resuscitation in such cases is worthwhile.
pmc-13355879:
Abdul Nadim Asil and co-authors review in 2026 how studies define and use two key terms for personal response to ionizing radiation. Radiosensitivity and radiosusceptibility are often mixed up, though they point to distinct ideas: cell-level damage response versus risk of tissue harm and cancer. The team searched two databases and screened studies under standard review rules.

Radiosensitivity was mostly measured by DNA damage and repair tests, while susceptibility tied to normal tissue harm and cancer risk, and was named far less often. Personal response varied widely in all studies. The authors call for clearer definitions and shared methods to support personal radiotherapy and fair risk judgments.
pmc-13357079:
Wei Shi and co-authors mapped in 2026 how mitophagy, the cleanup of worn-out mitochondria, shapes the tumor surroundings in osteosarcoma, an aggressive bone cancer of teens. Single-cell gene data let them group the many cell types by their cleanup activity. They then traced cell-to-cell signals, gene networks, and links to patient survival.

Cleanup-active support cells sent strong blood-vessel growth signals, and cleanup-linked killer T cells looked worn out and less able to fight. Tumors rich in these cell types meant poorer survival, and the patterns also hinted at response to immune therapy. The authors suggest blocking, not boosting, this cleanup could aid treatment.
pmc-13358579:
Qinling Jiang and co-authors test a clever scan trick in a 2026 study on lung adenocarcinoma. Doctors now grade this cancer under a newer system that sorts patients by outlook more sharply. The team asked whether computer analysis of CT scans could predict the grade before surgery, using artificial images sharpened by a generative network.

They compared models built on these enhanced images with models built on normal scans, using patients from two Chinese hospitals. The sharper images were meant to reveal fine tumor texture that plain scans blur. If scan-based grading proves reliable, it could help surgeons plan the size of the operation before the first cut.
pmc-13359879:
Xukai Yang and co-authors measure three key elements across mountain forests in a 2026 study. On the southern slopes of China's Qilian Mountains, forests anchor regional ecology and nutrient cycling. The team compared carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in leaves, branches, and forest floor material for six common tree species.

Broad-leaved species generally held richer nutrient levels, while conifers stored more carbon per unit of nitrogen or phosphorus. As plant material became forest floor litter, nitrogen and phosphorus fell and the carbon ratios rose, signs that trees pull nutrients back before shedding leaves and that litter quality differs by species. The patterns guide how managers read nutrient health in these forests.
pmc-13361979:
Yoshihito Saijo and co-authors report a 2026 case of heart infection with a puzzling twist. A 24-year-old man with eczema came in with fever and painful skin spots on his hands and feet. Blood tests grew Staphylococcus aureus, and scans found a large, mobile growth on his tricuspid valve, which had torn and leaked badly. Right-sided heart infections usually send infected clots to the lungs, not the body.

His body-wide spots suggested infected material was reaching the left side of the heart. A bubble test showed blood crossing from right to left only after a straining maneuver, and none at rest. No fixed hole between the heart chambers explained it. The team traced the route to a temporary shunt within the lungs, a rare path that let the infection spread system-wide.
pmc-13362079:
Blanca T M Spee and co-authors tested whether Parkinson's disease changes how people judge art in a 2026 study. Parkinson's is now seen as a whole-body disorder touching perception, emotion, and reward. Art programs for patients usually focus on making art, not on viewing it. The team asked whether looking at art, and rating it, works differently in these patients.

Eighty-seven people with Parkinson's and 49 matched healthy controls rated 36 artworks online. They scored liking and beauty and reported emotional and color-linked responses. The study's verdict, reflected in its title, is that aesthetic judgment is largely preserved in Parkinson's. That finding suggests art-viewing programs need little content adaptation for these audiences, a hopeful note for museums and therapists planning inclusive sessions.
pmc-13362179:
Qiang Gao and co-authors used machine learning to predict long breathing support after heart surgery in preterm babies in a 2026 study. The surgery closes a ductus, a blood vessel that should shut after birth but stays open in many early babies. Some babies then need a breathing machine for a long time. The team reviewed 271 infants born at 32 weeks or less, treated from 2021 to 2025.

Babies were split at six days of support: 150 came off sooner and 121 needed longer. Birth weight, age at birth, weight at surgery, duct size, and breathing severity all differed between the groups. A method called SHAP showed which factors pushed each prediction. Flagging high-risk babies early can help teams plan care and counsel parents.
pmc-13362479:

pmc-13408479:

pmc-13413679:

pmc-13414579:

pmc-13414679:

pmc-13415679:

pmc-13415979:

pmc-13417479:

pmc-13418479:

pmc-13418879:

pmc-13419179:

pmc-13421079:

pmc-13421379:

pmc-13421479:

pmc-13422879:

pmc-13436079:

pmc-13436279:

pmc-13436679:

pmc-13437979:

pmc-13438179:

pmc-13438579:

pmc-13439479:

pmc-13440979:

The authors conclude the short protocol keeps validity with a shorter testing time.
pmc-13441879:

pmc-13444279:
Yngve Forslin and colleagues report a routine drain swap that turned life-threatening in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case paper. During a planned swap to a larger drain tube, the tube nicked the stump of his renal artery and massive bleeding followed.

Coil plugs added through the graft path sealed the stump at last, while the graft kept coils from drifting. pmc-13444479:
Rishav Kumar and colleagues compare two broiler stunning methods by the chemistry they leave in breast meat in a 2026 research note. Gas stunning and electric stunning both precede slaughter, yet their early meat chemistry had scant head-to-head data. Breast fillets came from Ross 708 birds under pilot plant terms, six per method.
