Gas-stunned meat ran more sour than electric-stunned meat, at p below 0.001 in their tests, while color marks matched. Wide chemical scans found 508 compounds, with five split by method at raw p below 0.05 in the screen. The authors share the split as a lead for meat quality work.
pmc-13445379:
Pharis B. Sasa and colleagues report a small case series on a weight-loss artery procedure done in an office lab, with patients going home the same day, published in 2026. The procedure blocks select stomach arteries to curb hunger signals, and past reports kept patients in hospital overnight. The team asked whether that stay is truly needed for safety.

Flow to the target stomach arteries stopped in every case, and all six went home the same day with no unplanned hospital stay. No side effects of any grade appeared over a median follow-up of nine months. The authors urge a larger planned trial.
pmc-13445879:
Md Tahidur Rahman and coauthors map a 2026 analysis of poor feeding drivers among children under five in Bangladesh, using the 2022 population and Health Survey. The team applied multi-factor variance and math models to height, weight, and wasting scores across ages and home factors.

Children aged 12 to 23 months scored lower by a wide margin than infants on all three growth scores. Mothers who were too thin dragged scores down, while mother's schooling and home wealth lifted them. The authors urge states and NGOs to put first mother's schooling and feeding, income earning for poor homes, and birth spacing.
pmc-13446179:
James Williamson and colleagues weigh a new computing workflow that aims to make base editing, a precise gene tweaking method, easier for labs to plan, in a 2026 commentary. Base editors swap single DNA letters without cutting both strands, which trims stray damage. Yet many labs still default to older CRISPR cutting, in part for want of friendly design tools.

It walks users through editor choice, guide design, delivery, and proof checks, with immune targets as the worked case. The commentary sets the tool in context and asks how far such pipelines can widen careful use of base editing.
pmc-13447079:
Xiaoying Li and colleagues review how the tumor's neighborhood rebuilds itself under treatment and breeds drug resistance, in a 2026 paper. Resistance was once blamed on tumor cells alone, yet the stroma, immune cells, vessels, and matrix around them shift under fire and carve safe niches. Those niches block drug entry, hide tumors from immunity, and shelter stem-like cells.

The review sorts the machinery: stiffening matrix signals, low-oxygen switches, gene mark changes, fuel rewiring, and bubble messages between cells. Counter-plans follow the same map, from softening stroma and retraining macrophages to fixing vessels and loading drugs in nanoparticles. The authors tie hope to place-aware gene reads and organ-like lab models that sort patients for paired attacks.
pmc-13447179:
Farah Yasmin and co-authors compare rural and city hospital care in a 2026 United States study of patients who had both heart failure and liver cirrhosis. Together the two conditions raise the risk of kidney injury, infection and long stays. Whether place of care widens those risks on a national scale was the question.

Hospital records from 2016 to 2022 yielded close to half a million stays meeting the study rules. About fifteen percent occurred in non-city hospitals. Death during the stay was slightly higher in rural settings, while city stays ran a little longer and cost more after price adjustment. Matched comparisons gave the same picture. The authors call for better regional access and support for complex care outside large cities.
pmc-13447279:
Mao and colleagues studied in 2026 why subtropical broadleaf trees release very different scent chemicals.  The team measured seven tree species from distinct lineages using cut branches in controlled settings. They combined gas analysis with measures of photosynthesis, meaning how leaves turn light into food, and with leaf traits.

Trees rich in isoprene showed higher photosynthesis rates and stronger electron transport, the flow that powers food making. Trees rich in monoterpenes had heavier leaves and relied more on stored chemicals released for defence. Emission profiles tracked leaf weight and photosynthetic capacity closely across species. The authors suggest future emission models should include leaf weight and electron transport as inputs. That change would sharpen forecasts of forest emissions under climate change.
pmc-13447379:
Yun-Hee Kim, Seyoung Shin and Jinuk Kim review brain rewiring after stroke and what it means for rehabilitation in 2026. Stroke often leaves lasting movement loss, while recovery leans on neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to remodel connections and reroute signals. Two forms anchor the account, one strengthening active links through use and one keeping overall network balance.

Intensive, task-focused practice taps the use-driven form, and repeated goal-directed training improves movement in animal and human studies. Robots, sensor feedback, brain stimulation, drugs and stem cells aim to boost the same processes with high, personalised doses. Results across those add-ons stay uneven, the authors note. They urge matching treatment to lesion features, brain markers and recovery stage, with combined approaches and precise tools as the way forward.
pmc-13447479:
Seyedeh Ala Mokhtabad Amrei and colleagues test a behaviour scale for executive problems in a fragile X related tremor disorder in 2026 work. The disorder stems from a moderate repeat expansion in a gene and erodes planning, control and thinking with age. A scale based on observed behaviour is widely used for executive function, yet its tie to brain scan markers in this condition was unexamined.

Fifty-six carriers with and without the disorder completed the scale, a brief mental test and computerised executive tasks, alongside brain scans. Worse scan scores tracked with worse scale scores in a strong pattern that survived adjustment for age, sex and repeat length. Computerised executive tasks rose with scan burden in a smaller complete sample, while the brief mental test moved the other way. The scale earns a supporting role beside other measures.
pmc-13448079:
Filip Milisav and co-authors test how nested modular structure shapes computation in brain-like networks in a 2026 modelling study. Brains organise into specialised subnetworks nested inside larger ones, yet what that layered layout buys computationally was unclear. A simple generator for multi-level modular networks let the team build artificial reservoirs, networks whose internal dynamics do the computing, with controlled structure.

Recurring loop motifs enriched in the layered design explained much of the advantage. Hierarchy itself, not just modularity, emerges as a functional asset.
pmc-13448279:
Battalapalli and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract DSAI-09, a head-to-head test of an interpretable imaging signature against two black-box artificial intelligence models. On the held-out Wisconsin test set it reached an accuracy in the high seventies. It clearly beat a standard deep network and a fine-tuned medical imaging foundation model, which managed only the low-to-mid sixties. The authors argue such transparency could cut unnecessary surgery for what is only treatment damage.
pmc-13448579:

Age, education and wealth shifted the chances only slightly, while media exposure and residence showed no clear link. pmc-13448679:
Anmol Mathur and co-authors present in 2026 an electrochemical system that pulls carbon dioxide straight from the air. With a tuned porous layer and pulsed current, the system ran steadily for over 50 hours at current densities about ten times higher than earlier devices of this kind. Modeling and cost analysis in the paper sketch how the design might scale.
pmc-13448879:
Sean Wharton and colleagues pool in 2026 the liver safety data from seven phase 3 trials of orforglipron, a once-daily GLP-1 pill for obesity and type 2 diabetes. Marked enzyme elevations occurred at equal low rates in both arms, six participants each, and every orforglipron case had another explanation, so none met the injury criteria. pmc-13449479:

pmc-13449679:

pmc-13449779:

pmc-13450479:

Clinicians gain a map for interventions that target confidence and adherence rather than traits themselves.
pmc-13452279:

pmc-13452379:
Ahmed and colleagues measured fat hormones and trace elements in 2026 in the blood of patients with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, before and after treatment. pmc-13452479:

pmc-13453479:

The film then grew as a two-layer structure with a compact mineral-rich inner layer. Graphite cells treated this way kept about four fifths of their capacity after 500 charge cycles at a fast rate. pmc-13453579:

pmc-13454079:

pmc-13454279:

pmc-13454579:

pmc-13455379:

pmc-13456379:

pmc-13457079:

pmc-13457279:

On the day, four families of psychological strategy have evidence behind them: pre-performance routines, attentional strategies that run implicitly, psychological skills training, and mindfulness-based approaches. pmc-13457379:

pmc-13458579:

pmc-13458779:

pmc-13460179:

Every nodule was removed without converting to open surgery, through wedge cuts or segment removal. pmc-13461179:

pmc-13461579:

pmc-13462679:

pmc-13463079:
Cong Wang and colleagues built a rock model in 2026 for deep tunnels and mines, where high ground stress bends the rules that shallow models assume. Older particle models fix contact stiffness, which flattens the early squeezing stage and misses how stiffness grows with pressure. The team tied stiffness to stress in real time, using triaxial tests on granite, slate, and sandstone.

An exponential link between early-stage stiffness and mean stress anchors the model, with a three-state rule that updates stiffness as contacts change and a calibration scheme across several pressures. Tests on carbon-rich slate matched full stress-strain curves well, catching shorter squeezing stages, stronger peaks, and a brittle-to-ductile shift. The tool should help engineers forecast rock failure before digging deep.
pmc-13463379:
Yagmur Unsal leads a 2026 case report of, the authors say, the first known patient whose CD70 deficiency appeared as severe type 1 diabetes. CD70 is an immune signaling protein; lacking it brings immune dysregulation, runaway inflammatory episodes, abnormal lymph cell growth, and cancer risk. The child arrived with severe diabetic ketoacidosis, failure of several organs, and later puzzles: repeated ketoacidosis, skin lesions, and celiac disease.

Gene testing confirmed a double-copy missense variant in CD70, and family studies backed the finding. A stem cell transplant from a donor treated the immune defect. After transplant, sugar control improved, with the median long-term sugar marker falling and daily insulin needs dropping. The authors argue the case shows an intact CD27 and CD70 signaling pair guards against immune attack on the pancreas's insulin-making cells. They point to that pathway as a candidate target for immune therapies against type 1 diabetes.

Fu and co-authors described in 2026 a faster way to multiply a rare medicinal orchid, Anoectochilus roxburghii. The plant is highly valued, endangered in the wild, and slow to reproduce on its own. Starting from stem segments with nodes, they built a lab culture system. The system grows protocorm-like bodies directly from buds. These are small cell clusters that behave like orchid seeds, and no messy callus stage intervenes.

On the best hormone mixture, each starting piece produced more than 30 new bodies. The authors call that multiplication rate rare for this species. The full cycle ran about 110 days to prepare sterile material and 160 days of body induction. Rooting took 90 days, and hardening off took 60 more. Every plantlet rooted on the strongest rooting medium. More than 95 in 100 survived the move to normal conditions. Chromosome checks showed no genetic drift at any stage.
pmc-13463579:
Alba Díaz González and four co-authors study death risk in dogs with acute pancreatitis, a sudden swelling of the pancreas. Some dogs heal in days, while others grow gravely ill. The team followed 134 owned dogs seen at a hospital and compared them with healthy dogs.

Two scores built from routine blood tests, both tied to creatinine, stood out at intake. One score pairs creatinine with albumin, and the other pairs white cell counts with creatinine. Dogs with higher scores died in hospital more often, and the scores beat single blood values at sorting risk. Since the tests are already routine, vets can flag fragile dogs early at no extra cost.
pmc-13463979:
Karel Huard and six co-authors review how to judge venous congestion, backed-up blood in the veins, in critically ill patients. Congestion can injure many organs and can shift within hours. No single test captures it well, so the authors join three ultrasound methods at the bedside.

Heart ultrasound grades how stiffly the heart fills, vein ultrasound scores excess flow in organs, and lung ultrasound spots fluid in the lungs. Worked examples and flow charts show how the three views correct each other's blind spots. A stiff heart with quiet veins tells a different story than swollen veins with dry lungs. Intensive care teams gain a fuller, faster read on fluid overload and organ risk.
pmc-13464079:
Luping Wang leads a team that targets SIRT6, a gene-tuning enzyme, to calm blood cancers with runaway neutrophil growth. A screen of gene-tuning compounds flagged a SIRT6 activator, MDL-800, as a strong brake on the excess growth. Zebrafish bred with a faulty sirt6 gene developed a like disease on their own.

The activator boosted the standard drug imatinib in fish and mouse leukemia models. It even restored drug response in resistant mouse tumors, which marks a fresh pairing for hard cases.
pmc-13464179:
Veronica Jimenez and colleagues tested a gene therapy in 2026 that raises the hormone FGF21 in aged mice, aiming to stretch healthy life rather than just lifespan. No approved drug yet sustains healthspan, though lifestyle steps help only while kept up. Old and very old mice of both sexes received a muscle-targeted viral vector carrying the FGF21 gene.

Treated mice normalised weight and fat, handled sugar better, kept liver detox power, resisted kidney ageing, and showed stronger hearts, muscles, and memory. Tissue studies pointed to better energy handling, cleaner protein control, and less inflammation, scarring, and amyloid build-up, with AMPK signalling switched on. The results mark FGF21 gene therapy as a candidate geroprotector, though human dosing and safety remain far off.
pmc-13464279:
Aguiar and Mioto wrote this 2026 editorial about a heart tumor that was misdiagnosed as benign. They discuss the case of a woman 31 weeks pregnant. She developed acute heart failure from two large left atrial masses. Three years earlier, surgery had removed a tumor labeled a myxoma. Re-examination of both the original and the new tissue showed cardiac myxofibrosarcoma, a rare cancer that mimics myxoma.

Fewer than five percent of primary cardiac sarcomas are this type, yet it tends to grow invasively and recur, so the label matters greatly for outcome. The authors explain that scans, however advanced, cannot reliably separate the two tumors, which both appear gelatinous and mobile in the left atrium. Only microscopic and immunostaining examination settles the diagnosis, and they argue the case was most likely a misclassification from the start, not a cancerous transformation.
pmc-13464879:
Xu and co-authors examined tumor tissue from 25 patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma in 2026. They tracked how immune cells inside the tumor change after chemotherapy combined with immunotherapy given before surgery. Samples taken before treatment and from the removed tumor were stained for three lymphocyte types. Lymphocytes are the white blood cells that attack cancer. Patients whose tumors vanished completely were compared against those whose did not.

Seven patients, 28 percent, achieved a complete pathological response. No living cancer remained at surgery for them. Only in that group did the shares of helper CD4 and killer CD8 lymphocytes climb after treatment. Their post-treatment levels also stood significantly above the non-responders' levels. B cells, marked CD20, barely moved in either group. Patients destined to respond started with relatively more CD4 cells. That starting share may help predict who benefits, independent of the commonly used PD-L1 test.
pmc-13464979:
Wenbin Xiao and six co-authors screen nine essential oils from Chinese medicinal herbs against food poisoning germs. Foodborne bacteria and their slimy biofilms resist many cleaners, so plant oils draw interest as natural guards. Four target germs, including Staphylococcus aureus and Listeria, faced each oil in growth and biofilm tests.

Honeysuckle oil led the pack, halting the widest germ range at low doses. It stripped mature biofilms of three germs by roughly half or more, though staph biofilms resisted. Scent analysis found 156 compounds across the oils, with honeysuckle rich in linalool and borneol. Growth curves and microscope views showed the oil stalling growth and wrecking cell surfaces, which backs its use as a food guard candidate.
pmc-13465079:
Mihai Adrian Păsărică and four co-authors review how uveal melanoma, a cancer inside the eye, rewires its chemistry to survive. Local treatment often clears the eye tumor, yet half of patients later face spread, chiefly to the liver, years down the line. Flexible fuel switching sits at the center of that staying power.

Tumor cells flip between sugar burning and oxygen-based burning as conditions demand. Fat handling and redox balance, the cell's rust defense, shift in step with the fuel choice. Each switch helps cells outlast drugs and outgrow rival clones. Set beside other cancers, the eye tumor's tricks look partly shared and partly its own. The authors map the switches as targets for stopping late spread.
pmc-13465679:
Huang and co-authors re-engineer a traditional Kyrgyz pastry to carry less fat. Their 2026 paper optimises Katima, a spiral-rolled layered pastry from Xinjiang normally made with abundant clarified butter. The tools were single-factor trials and response surface methodology. That is a statistical technique for tuning several ingredients at once. Butter, yeast, and salt emerged as the variables that mattered, judged by sensory score.

The validated optimum used about 12.7 grams of butter, with under a gram each of yeast and salt, per hundred grams of flour. It scored about 95 on sensory testing while cutting fat by about 37 percent against the traditional full-fat version. The reduced-fat pastry came out moister, harder, and chewier, with markedly lower peroxide and acid values, indicating better fat stability in storage. The authors offer the parameters as a standardised route to industrial production of a healthier ethnic pastry.
pmc-13466179:
Xueyan Liu and a large team built patient-specific lab models of hereditary angioedema, a swelling disorder caused by faults in the SERPING1 gene, reporting in 2026. The faults cut production of a blood protein that normally keeps swelling pathways in check. Human models that mirror each patient's own mutation have been missing.

Blood cells from four patients, each carrying a different kind of gene change, were reprogrammed into flexible stem cells and then grown into liver-like cells. Those cells matured properly and released the protective protein at near-normal baseline in form, yet each patient's cells faltered in mutation-specific ways. Gene-editing checks validated the platform, which the authors offer for testing tailored treatments.
pmc-13467679:
Özokan compared two ways in 2026 of building a family of ring-shaped molecules called decahydroacridine-1,8-diones, used as dyes and drug starting frames. One route mixed all parts at once in a single pot. The other prepared a key middle piece first, then finished in a second step. Six molecules were made by both routes.

The two-step route won on yield: after counting the first step, it returned roughly three fifths to two thirds of product, against about two fifths for the one-pot route. The one-pot mix also spun off side products. Özokan reads the gap as sequence control: forming the middle piece first steers parts into the desired ring, while lighting all reactions at once opens rival paths.
pmc-13467779:
Prieto Palomo and colleagues combined lab spectra, quantum calculations, and statistics in 2026 to read the vibrational fingerprints of four phenolic acids, plant compounds valued as antioxidants. Raman spectroscopy reads how molecules vibrate, giving a fingerprint of structure. How each chemical group shapes that fingerprint was the open question.

The four acids were measured as solids and in an alcohol-water mix, and their spectra were matched against computed ones. Solid samples gave the sharpest fingerprints and the clearest split between compounds. The three acids built on a longer chain shared strong bands from their linked double bonds, while gallic acid, built differently, sang a distinct tune led by its oxygen groups. Computer maps showed oxygen sites as the most reactive spots, which explains why solvent shifts those bands most.
pmc-13468479:
Zhen Li, Jinhui Hu, and Jian Xing design in 2026 the signal shaping for a wireless system that senses and communicates at once, aided by an active intelligent reflecting surface. Such surfaces, studded with tunable elements, can amplify and redirect radio waves, creating virtual line-of-sight paths for radar targets and phone users alike. The wrinkle is hardware imperfection at the base station transmitter, which injects distortion noise that couples with the surface own amplification noise.

The goal is to maximize radar signal quality while guaranteeing communication users their service levels and respecting two power budgets. Because the optimization problem is non-convex with coupled variables, the authors solve it by alternating: fixing some parts, optimizing others, and iterating. Future 6G base stations are expected to double as radar sensors, and designs that survive real hardware flaws, rather than assuming perfect radios, are the ones that will ship.
pmc-13468679:
Jie Gao, Liheng Li, Qi Liu, Ning Zhang and Yan Li published this 2026 review on plant polysaccharides as a treatment route for Alzheimer's disease. These sugar molecules from traditional Chinese medicine protect nerve cells in lab studies and seem safe. Yet they are barely absorbed from the gut and hardly cross into the brain, which clashes with their reported benefits. The authors argue the gut microbiome resolves that paradox.

In their account, the sugars act like prebiotics: gut bacteria ferment them into short-chain fatty acids and other small products. Those products enter the blood, cross into the brain, and calm inflammation through metabolic and immune pathways. Reviewed studies report less amyloid buildup, less tau protein change, restored synapse function and better cognition in disease models. The authors frame the sugars as gut-oriented agents rather than brain-targeting drugs, and lay out what this means for future therapies.
pmc-13469579:
Jiandong Zhao, Honghua Zhao, Benwang Li, and Xuyin Gong review in 2026 how deep reinforcement learning helps indoor robots dodge moving obstacles. Fixed rules cope poorly with cluttered, changing rooms where people and carts move at random. Learning agents that earn rewards through trial and error have become a popular alternative.

The review sorts the main algorithms into three families based on how they value actions, choose actions, or combine both roles. It then works through five technical problem areas, comparing the fixes each family has produced and what those fixes cost or gain. A shared reference frame for choosing algorithms is one stated aim. The authors close by naming the directions they judge most promising for indoor navigation research.
pmc-13469679:
Su and colleagues in China built in 2026 a rig and method to line up circuit board shots, so a robot can find each solder joint. Big boards fight back: parts crowd in one zone and thin in the next, light glints, and shapes warp. Stock match tools use one fixed rule for the whole board, which cracks on such mixed ground. Their rig holds the board still under a ring light, while the code bends its search by local crowd load.

The method tags board marks with a set code, then finds each tag's mate with a search that widens or trims by how dense the zone is. In cut tests, near nine in ten mates were true inliers, the sound core of a match. Line ups held firm through shifts in height, zone, and view. The team pitches the rig for plant checks and robot soldering.
pmc-13469779:
Guo-Ping Yang and colleagues graded short videos in 2026 about brain aneurysms on Douyin, China's TikTok, where medical advice spreads fast. Aneurysm rupture carries grim prognosis, so early detection messaging matters, yet video reliability was unmapped. One hundred videos were scored for content, quality, and reliability with global quality and DISCERN tools, plus engagement data.

Videos ran a median 77 seconds with high engagement, mostly from cerebrovascular specialists. Educational videos outscored case-sharing videos on quality, though reliability scores did not differ, and case videos drew more favourites. Engagement metrics correlated with each other but not with quality or tone, leaving viewers popular but only slightly reliable guidance.
pmc-13469879:
Ha-Neul Jo and colleagues report in 2026 that a calcium pump helps control blood vessel growth and barrier function in the brain and retina. The receptor Frizzled4 receives signals from Norrin and WNT proteins and is required for these vessels to form and seal properly. How the receptor itself is regulated had stayed unclear despite its importance as a drug target.

Using a proximity labeling method that tags nearby proteins, the team found the pump ATP2B1, also called PMCA1, sitting next to Frizzled4 in vessel lining cells. Removing the pump raised cell calcium, switched on a calcium driven program, and weakened Norrin signaling. Mice lacking the pump in vessel lining showed brain vessel defects matching weak Frizzled4 signaling. The authors suggest high calcium states may quiet this pathway in disease.
pmc-13470279:
Alam Ahmad Hidayat and colleagues publish in 2026 the full genome of a heat tolerant bacterium pulled from an acidic hot spring in Indonesia. The strain, named Pseudobacillus badius WCB-1, came from sediment at Kawah Putih in West Java. It was grown in culture, checked with a marker gene, and then confirmed by whole genome comparison methods.

Two sequencing technologies, a short read Illumina run and a long read nanopore run, were combined for the assembly. The genome spans just over four million DNA letters with a moderate share of the letters G and C. Annotation found 4,106 protein-coding sequences plus transfer and ribosomal RNA genes. Mining the sequence flagged several clusters that may produce useful natural compounds. The dataset is offered for comparative genomics work.
pmc-13470379:
Akhtar Hussain found exact soliton answers in 2026 for the (2+1)-D Kadomtsev-Petviashvili-Benjamin-Bona-Mahony formula. Curved change formulas govern events from neural motion to stuff edges, yet exact answers remain scarce. The new mapping method gave trig and growth-type answers, with contour, 2-D, and 3-D plots.

Answers held M-shaped, kink, bell, anti-bell, sharp, peakon, and sharp bell waves, both lone and sharp forms. A Galileo-style shift recast the formula as a moving system, whose chaos and response were studied. The new answer groups expand tools for mapping wave events ruled by this formula.
pmc-13471179:
Ataoğlu and co-authors interviewed internists in Türkiye in 2026 about deprescribing, deliberately stopping the acid-blocking stomach drugs called PPIs that patients often take for years needlessly. Twelve doctors, ten residents and two specialists, gave in-depth interviews in spring 2023, anchored by two patient vignettes. Answers were mapped onto a standard behavior framework.

Influences spanned twelve domains, with barriers piled on the system side: a fragmented health system, heavy workloads, and poor provider coordination. Patients also resisted, treating the pills as rescue drugs they expect to keep. Knowledge gaps and doubts about consequences added friction. Yet enablers existed too: doctors intended to deprescribe and held clear goals. Beliefs about consequences cut both ways, motivating and restraining. The authors conclude that good intentions are not enough. System fixes, shared records, clear guidelines, and patient education must carry the behavior change.
pmc-13471379:
El Ayat and colleagues tested whether eye-tracking patterns, measured while people view images, can help detect autism spectrum disorder with artificial intelligence. Their 2026 multi-site study combined two European datasets, 57 participants from France and 27 from Italy, giving 84 people in total, 40 of them autistic.

Four model types were compared, and a memory-based LSTM network scored highest, with an AUC of 0.859 on the ranking scale where 1.0 is perfect. A graph neural network with attention nearly matched it at 0.855 and reached the best specificity, correctly clearing 93.2% of non-autistic participants. Attention mechanisms, often assumed helpful, did not significantly lift the graph model's results. The authors argue either design could support objective screening where specialists are scarce.
pmc-13471679:
Negar Mottaghi-Dastjerdi and three colleagues described in 2026 a vaccine candidate designed entirely on a computer to attack stomach cancer. The design targets WISP1, a protein made in larger amounts by stomach tumours and linked to a poorer outlook, for which no effective vaccine yet exists. Using computer tools, the team picked pieces of the protein that the immune system can recognise, then joined them with linkers and an adjuvant that strengthens immune response.

Checks predicted the assembled protein would be stable, soluble, and able to trigger an immune response without allergy or toxicity, and modelling showed firm binding to an immune sensor called TLR4. Simulated responses included lasting antibody production and activation of memory immune cells. Every result so far is computational, so the candidate still needs bench and animal testing before anyone can judge whether it works in living bodies.
pmc-13472979:
Mamode and colleagues present a 2026 commentary on the collapse of kidney care in Gaza during the war that began in October 2023, arguing that not to act is itself an act. Before the war, Gaza had performed over one hundred living-donor kidney transplants and hoped to grow the program. Transplantation has now stopped entirely.

The main hospital in Khan Younis had thirty-one working dialysis machines for 238 patients in December, with no peritoneal dialysis supplies at all: no catheters, no fluid, no sterile space. Kidney failure patients who miss dialysis die within days to weeks, so rationing by scarcity is a death sentence delivered slowly. The authors, transplant professionals, write as witnesses and colleagues. Their plea is that medical neutrality cannot mean silence when a whole treatment system is dismantled.
pmc-13473079:
Lauren McAuley and eleven colleagues ran a 2026 pilot that sequenced the whole genome of one rectal cancer patient before and after treatment. Copy-number patterns were closely similar, while structural changes barely matched at all, and tumour purity, repetitive DNA, and strand bias helped explain the mismatches. pmc-13474679:
Runè van der Merwe and two colleagues tested in 2026 whether body size limits how much individual herbivores differ in diet within a population. They analysed carbon and nitrogen isotopes in droppings from 16 herbivore species, spanning about 10 to about 1,420 kilograms, across different reserves.

Body mass showed no effect on niche structure, and dispersion did not track ecological opportunity, though larger areas may widen niche widths. The authors conclude that factors other than size and intake needs shape individual diet differences in herbivores.
pmc-13474879:
Shuhei Nomura and a broad team ask in 2026 why healthy life expectancy figures disagree across Japan. Survey metrics matched the global model well for men but weakly for women. The records-based metric matched well for both sexes across the span. Mental disorders and body weight helped explain survey-model gaps in men. Knowing what each metric misses helps leaders pick the right gauge.
pmc-13475379:
Simone Rota and co-authors pool trial evidence on HER2-targeted treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer with HER2 amplification, a subgroup with poorer prognosis and resistance to standard EGFR therapy. Across them, about a third of patients responded and just over two thirds achieved disease control, with weighted median survival of 13.4 months and time without progression of five and a half months. Two regimens stood out: trastuzumab deruxtecan and trastuzumab with tucatinib showed higher response and control rates than the older dual blockade of trastuzumab plus pertuzumab. The authors conclude anti-HER2 therapy works in pretreated patients, while noting further studies are needed to confirm the ranking.
pmc-13476479:
Ronald S. Samia and four colleagues published this 2026 brewing study tracking thiols, the sulfur compounds that give hop-forward beers their fruit aroma, through pilot fermentations. Thiols occur at trace levels but smell potent, and steering release from hop precursors is hard. The team followed thiol levels daily in a lager yeast and an ale yeast, with and without dry-hopping, alongside yeast gene expression.

Without dry-hopping, thiol production peaked on days one to three, matching peak fermentation activity. The lager strain released more of one thiol, 3SH, than the ale strain, while another thiol showed no strain effect. Dry-hopping raised thiols, but 3SH did not rise in proportion to hop dose. pmc-13477279:

Adults were grouped as inactive, active at moderate intensity only, active at vigorous intensity only, or active at both.

Nearly 587,000 adults were followed for a median of ten years. Every active group had lower death rates than inactive adults, and the combined group fared best. Among people who mixed intensities, those who got more than a quarter of their activity from vigorous exercise had the lowest risk. The authors say intensity mix matters alongside total activity time.
pmc-13477379:
Xianglin Long and coauthors published a 2026 multiomics study identifying spondin-1, a protein tied to tissue scaffolding, as a candidate driver of atrial fibrillation. In a UK Biobank group of about 39,000 people, higher blood levels of the protein were linked to more new atrial fibrillation cases and larger left atria. pmc-13478179:
Eduard Petrosyan and coauthors published a 2026 study of PHGDH, an enzyme that starts serine production in cells, and its unexpected role in low-oxygen lung tumors. Sensitivity appeared only under complete removal of those nutrients. The authors warn that blocking this enzyme could backfire unless nutrient conditions are controlled.
pmc-13478379:

Bacteria thus sense sulfide through a three-cysteine cluster with a labile sulfur ligand.
pmc-13478479:

Their neurites were shorter, wider, and less branched, with fewer endpoints. Energy organelles looked abnormal, synaptic markers ran low, and cell spheres stayed smaller. The same shape problems appeared in fetal and postnatal human brain tissue, supporting the models as faithful tools for studying the condition.
pmc-13478879:
Liu and colleagues in China reviewed in 2026 nickel based anode stocks for potassium ion batteries, a cheap stand in for lithium cells. They swell a lot as potassium ions move in and out, and they pass electrons poorly, which slows charge.

The review sorts the field by kind: nickel oxides, sulfides, selenides, and more, down to mixed metal forms. For each, it weighs test scores from the newest lab work. Three fix paths stand out across the set: wrap grains in carbon, shrink parts to nano scale, and shape the inner build with care. Blends that mix all three scored best. The authors close with the gaps that stay, chiefly swell control over long cycle lives.
pmc-13479579:
Dongling Lian and coauthors published a 2026 cross-cultural audit of allergic rhinitis videos on YouTube and Bilibili, the Chinese platform. The team pulled the top 200 videos per platform from January 2022 to January 2025, then applied exclusion rules.

The final set held 240 videos, 91 from YouTube and 149 from Bilibili. Trained scales scored understandability, information quality, and overall quality. Engagement counts and posting seasons were compared with real-world allergy seasons to see whether uploads chase symptom peaks. The comparison exposes how two platform cultures handle the same disease, and where misleading or low-quality content concentrates.
pmc-13479979:
Shraddha Khanke and co-authors report a 2026 study of a learner-led teaching method called SNAPPS in pathology training. Thirty-five residents at three levels of training took part. pmc-13480079:

At the middle dose two of six patients hit such harm, and the team set that level as the dose to carry forward. Diarrhoea was the most common severe side effect. pmc-13483379:

Wall movement peaked at just 6.36 millimeters, far less than conventional unsupported designs allow in comparable ground. pmc-13483479:
Yan Wang and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how white spot syndrome virus, the scourge of farmed shrimp and crayfish, bends the cell's power plants to its will. Few animal viruses show such precise two-handed control of cell upkeep, and the lead protein offers a target for future defences.
pmc-13483579:

Retinopathy, meaning damage to blood vessels at the back of the eye, appeared in 58.7 percent of participants. Its presence correlated significantly with maternal seizures, early delivery, and low birthweight. No clear link appeared for delivery method, overall newborn outcome, or Apgar score. Because an eye exam is quick and noninvasive, the authors suggest retinal findings can flag pregnancies needing closer watch, alongside stronger maternal and child health education.
pmc-13483679:
Yuletta Adny Ambarsari and co-authors report surgical results for a four-part congenital heart defect in a developing country setting. Published in 2026, the retrospective cohort reviews 43 patients who had complete repair between April 2024 and April 2025. Records capture age, nutrition, oxygen levels, bypass times, hospital stay, complications, and deaths.

Most children arrived late, at a mean age above nine years, with two thirds underweight and most showing low blood oxygen. Deaths reached 11.6 percent overall and occurred only in children under two years old. Narrowing below the pulmonary valve lengthened bypass times. Limited intensive care capacity and late referral likely worsened results. The authors argue that late repair should still proceed, since careful preparation and aftercare can bring outcomes closer to global norms.
pmc-13484879:
Jake Grange and co-workers review if forms filled in by patients steer care choices in joint diseases marked by swelling. Their 2026 review searches four databases to February 2025. It covers three diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and axial spondyloarthritis. From near seventeen thousand records, 29 studies made the cut, most on the first disease.

The forms helped care in three ways. Most often, they guided drug changes in treat-to-target plans. They also aided talk in clinic visits and checks done at home. Staff followed form-based plans less well for complex patients. Home checks matched standard care results, though thin services cut their worth. Scores also built trust between patients and staff. Wide gaps in how forms are used waste much of what patients report.
pmc-13486679:
Simegn and a large team charted how blood sugar control evolves in Ethiopian patients who carry both type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, a pairing that multiplies complication risk. Their 2026 study pulled records for 600 such patients followed at Debre Markos hospital between 2014 and 2023. A flexible statistical model traced each patient's glycated hemoglobin, the three-month average sugar marker, over years of visits.

Average glycated hemoglobin ran high compared with the target range of the American Diabetes Association cited by the authors. Seven factors predicted worse trajectories, including injected medication use, obesity, kidney damage, heavier weight, and family history of diabetes. Uncontrolled blood pressure and more than six years of treatment also tracked poorer control over time. Simegn recommends tighter combined management of sugar and pressure rather than treating the two conditions in separate silos.
pmc-13487679:
Tiffany Tu and Alejandro Ochoa warn that pooling genome studies can quietly break when the studies share relatives. Published in 2026, the theory and simulation work starts from a live proposal to fix participation bias with sex-stratified pooling, which ignores that men and women from one population are heavily related. Between-study relatedness correlates test statistics and inflates false positives.

Simulations across family and population structures show ordinary pooling inflating badly whenever family links cross study borders, with inflation growing as samples grow. Genomic control patches the symptom yet costs real power in high-signal settings. The authors' correlated meta-analysis method, shipped as the metalcor package, models the correlation directly and restores calibration. Real data confirm severe inflation inside family studies and negligible effects in population studies up to ten thousand people.
pmc-13488279:
Shuyuan Zhang and co-authors build an artificial intelligence tool to spot cardiac amyloidosis in a 2026 multicenter study from China. The disease thickens the heart wall as abnormal protein deposits build up, and it is often mistaken for other causes of thickening. Heart tracings and ultrasound measures came from a Beijing hospital cohort, with patients from ten other hospitals held back for outside testing, and a learning system combined eleven model types.

Seven features carried the diagnosis, mixing tracing measures, wall thickness, blood pressure, and pumping indices. The combined model separated amyloidosis from its mimics with very high accuracy, and performance held up in the outside hospitals in the reported tests. A simplified score built from the same features also performed well for bedside use.
pmc-13488579:
Shala Cunningham and colleagues evaluate stroke rehabilitation training for physiotherapists in Myanmar in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Conflict and disruption have cut access to rehabilitation, although stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Seventeen professionals took blended training mixing online coursework, live mentoring, and hands-on clinical sessions, with surveys before training, after each stage, and at six months, judged against a four-level training evaluation model.

Self-rated knowledge and skill rose significantly, strongest for methods needing little equipment in the reported comparisons. Follow-up surveys showed evidence-based assessment and treatment entering routine practice for many participants. Seven therapists joined focus groups at six months to explain how changes held under local constraints. The authors present the tailored design as a model for fragile settings.
pmc-13490379:
Sun and co-authors sped up the scheduling mathematics for neighborhoods that share electricity and heat with each other. Community energy systems juggle power, heating, and cooling, and sharing between communities raises efficiency, but central scheduling is slow and exposes private data. Their 2026 study built a day-ahead stochastic model, which plans under green-power uncertainty, with dynamic prices set by an operator. They solved it with a new distributed algorithm that splits the problem apart.

Case simulations showed the sharing model and pricing scheme cut operating costs and carbon emissions for individual communities and the whole system. The new algorithm converged faster than the standard distributed approach it improves on, according to the comparisons reported. Privacy survives because each community solves its own sub-problem and exchanges only limited signals. Sun presents the scheme as ready for multi-community energy markets.
pmc-13491579:
Hai Wang and four co-authors examine a 2026 multicenter records study on blood pressure medicines during acute kidney injury. Drugs called ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers protect the heart and kidneys long term, yet doctors disagree about stopping them when kidneys fail suddenly. The authors sorted patients by whether these medicines were stopped, continued, or newly started.

The records covered 1,285 patients across several hospitals. People who stayed on the medicines had lower odds of kidney injury worsening within fourteen days than people who stopped them. A survival advantage seen before adjustment faded once other factors were counted, and starting the drugs looked no different from stopping them. The authors call for prospective trials because deaths were few and estimates were unstable.
pmc-13491679:
Eglė Šidlauskaitė and four colleagues set out in 2026 to derive bonding radii, the standard sizes chemists assign to atoms when deciding which atoms in a crystal are bonded. X-ray crystallography gives atom positions but rarely shows bonds directly, so distance rules do the everyday work. Existing radius sets lean on a commercial database or on hand-adjusted values, which limits open checking.

Their unsupervised workflow learns radii from crystal structures in the free Crystallography Open Database instead. Two atoms count as bonded when their distance is no more than the sum of their radii plus a small tolerance. Published sets can disagree by more than an angstrom for some elements, so an openly derived set matters. The paper lays out the method and the resulting radii for reuse by other researchers.
pmc-13492279:
Leonardo Bernal and eight colleagues combine chemistry software with machine learning in 2026 to hunt for old drugs that might fight aggressive prostate cancer. Advanced, treatment-resistant disease still kills many men, and repurposed medicines arrive with known safety records. Their workflow filtered candidates by chemical similarity and used applicability checks to weed out false leads before laboratory testing.

Screening the DrugBank library produced five candidates that slowed cancer cell growth in both flat cultures and three-dimensional models. An antifungal medicine, chlormidazole, performed best, acting mainly by pausing cell division rather than killing cells outright, and sparing non-cancer cells comparatively. It raised a cell-cycle brake protein and pushed cells into arrest. Chlormidazole also boosted the chemotherapy drug docetaxel, matching its effect at much lower docetaxel doses.
pmc-13493779:
Lavecchia and colleagues map how stress is arranged inside the rocks of peninsular Italy, work that feeds directly into earthquake hazard estimates. Their 2026 study rests on roughly 8,200 measurements of fault slip, the scratches and offsets left where rock masses slid past each other, gathered at outcrops across the country. From these they rebuilt the directions and relative sizes of underground stresses over roughly the last three and a half million years.

The team outline a belt of stretching crust about 1,000 kilometres long running through the Apennines, where the ground is being pulled apart. Stress directions form nested arcs at several scales, from single faults up to the whole crust, and they bend in line with the deep boundary beneath the crust. Modern earthquake records and satellite measures of ground movement point the same way, suggesting the old pattern still drives today's deformation.
pmc-13493879:
Joerg F Hipp leads a nine-author team probing in 2026 a brainwave signature of Dup15q syndrome, a rare genetic condition causing developmental delay, autism features, and epilepsy. Extra copies of a chromosome segment overload certain calming receptors, and children's brain recordings show unusually strong beta rhythms as a result. The team isolated that rhythm cleanly from background noise in fifty-two affected children and fourteen typically developing peers.

The beta excess was large, nearly two standard effect sizes above typical children. Among children without epilepsy, stronger excess meant lower cognitive scores and weaker everyday adaptive skills, both correlations solidly significant. That dose relationship supports the idea that overactive calming receptors drive real functional loss, not just a pretty signal. A measurable brainwave that tracks severity could help future trials judge whether treatments actually help.
pmc-13494079:
Shunming Zhang and co-authors ask, in a 2026 cohort study, whether people whose lab results clash with their body mass index face a different risk of heart failure. Body mass index, or BMI, gauges weight for height but says little about inner health. The team used UK Biobank data on 394,198 adults. They grouped people by how far markers such as blood sugar, blood fats, and C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, sat from what their BMI would predict.

Over a median follow-up past twelve years, groups whose inflammation or blood sugar ran worse than BMI suggested developed heart failure more often, in both men and women. Some other groups, such as women with higher than expected blood pressure, showed lower risk. Liver enzyme groups showed no clear link. The authors argue that sorting people by these marker patterns could sharpen efforts to prevent heart failure.
pmc-13495279:
Sufen Wang and colleagues run, in a 2026 randomized study, a teaching trial that blends problem-based learning with medical humanities in a pathology lab course. The course went to anesthesiology undergraduates at a Chinese medical university. Four classes were assigned by lot: two got the blended model and two got standard lecture-based teaching, with 115 students in all.

Both groups improved on theory exams, and final theory scores did not split clearly between them. A microscope image test leaned toward the blended group without quite reaching the bar for proof. Blended students did score higher on drive to learn, self-directed study skill, and communication, and they rated the teaching better overall. Ethics awareness and social responsibility scores did not differ. The authors offer the blend as a reference for reforming lab teaching, with gains in engagement rather than raw exam points.
pmc-13499879:
Zwirner and colleagues explore whether squeezing the spleen can tell forensic doctors how long someone has been dead. Temperature-based methods fail once a body equilibrates with its surroundings, leaving a gap at longer intervals. Their 2026 study collected spleen samples from 53 adult cadavers, spanning roughly two days to three weeks after death. The team measured the tissue's squishiness with an instrument that wiggles samples and records how they store and lose energy.

One measure, the loss modulus, which captures how much energy the tissue dissipates, fell significantly as time since death grew, while the storage measures showed no useful pattern. A threshold value on that measure gave strong evidence for death within about 200 hours, performing well on the authors' diagnostic accuracy analysis. The team presents spleen mechanics as a promising addition to the time-of-death toolkit, pending larger studies.
pmc-13500079:
Austin Erickson, Jennifer Griffith, and Trushar Patel chart in 2026 when and where urology conferences gather across the United States, using public listings from 2022 to 2025. Conferences anchor education, networking, and research sharing in the specialty, yet their calendars had never been mapped. Working from a Florida medical school, the team collected events from organiser sites and calendars, recording dates, frequency, and location for each meeting.

Eighty-five organisations held 293 events across the four years. Texas and California hosted the most, and the Western regional section led the sections, followed by the Southeast and South Central. Meetings lengthened slightly on average, and autumn dominated the calendar, with October the busiest month and July the quietest by a wide margin. The authors suggest spreading events more evenly across months and regions to ease scheduling clashes and improve access.
pmc-13500379:
Miku Goto and co-authors profile in 2026 the liver enzymes that break down drugs in squirrels, a group frequently treated with veterinary medicines despite almost no baseline data on their metabolism. The team combined gene sequencing, gene expression measurement, and functional tests on liver microsomes, tiny cell fragments carrying the enzymes, focusing on two enzyme families central to foreign chemical handling. Three squirrel species were compared with mouse and rat laboratory rodents, using the flea treatment fipronil as a test substance.

No clear squirrel-specific loss or major divergence appeared in the two focal enzyme families, and fipronil breakdown efficiency did not differ significantly among the species examined in the reported analysis. Wider expression profiling did show distinct patterns, with one enzyme family making up under one percent of major expression in the Eurasian red squirrel, below rodent levels. The work supplies baseline data for comparative wildlife drug metabolism studies.
pmc-13501779:
Mario Giuseppe Zotti leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 diagnostic study linking electrical nerve tests to muscle wasting seen on MRI in chronic lower back problems. The cohort took 100 consecutive eligible patients with chronic lumbar symptoms, drawn from 119 who underwent electrodiagnostic testing. Needle electromyography sorted them into confirmed chronic lumbar radiculopathy, a pinched or damaged nerve root condition, versus a symptomatic control group with normal electrical findings. Two independent observers graded multifidus muscle atrophy on MRI using a modified Goutallier scale and fat measurements.

Atrophy appeared in 98 percent of the confirmed radiculopathy group but also in 64 percent of the symptomatic controls, a significant gap with an odds ratio of 27.2 on that comparison. Grading showed most confirmed cases at mild to moderate levels, with 11 percent at the severe grade 3, which never appeared among controls. The authors propose the wasting pattern as a supporting biomarker, not proof on its own.
pmc-13504779:
Xiangyang Li and three colleagues ask how few muscle sensors a rehab glove system needs to read hand gestures, in a 2026 study. Wearable muscle-signal gear often uses eight or more channels, which adds bulk, power draw, and discomfort. Fewer channels would ease daily use if accuracy holds.

Their check plan rests on clean signal capture, a full search of all channel subsets from six sites, and stress tests with degraded signals. Data came from 24 healthy adults, judged by leaving one person out in turn. Three channels passed a 90 percent accuracy bar on average but failed badly for some users. Four channels scored higher and left no user stranded. The winning four sites sit on forearm muscles that drive the wrist.
pmc-13504979:
Timms and colleagues ran a feasibility study for a bigger question: can painting silver diamine fluoride on children's rotten baby teeth beat usual NHS dental care? The fluoride compound arrests decay without drilling, a prize for treating small children, but a trial inside British practices faces recruitment and retention hurdles. Their 2026 study randomised children aged one to eight with decay across eight practices, following them for a year and interviewing families and dentists.

Eight sites recruited 54 children, and nearly every eligible family approached agreed to join, an encouraging sign for willingness. The obstacles lay elsewhere: recruitment ran slower than the team planned, and keeping the randomised allocation intact inside busy practices proved tricky. The standard decay-scoring system also looked weak as the main outcome measure. Their verdict is a conditional yes: a definitive trial is feasible, with slower timelines, stronger randomisation support, and a better primary outcome.
pmc-13508279:
Zhengqing Bao, Jiaqi An, Guizhong Li, and Jianwei Wang pool studies on whether a simple blood ratio forecasts survival in urinary tract cancers, in 2026 work. The ratio compares fibrinogen, a clotting protein tied to inflammation, with albumin, a nutrition-linked protein. Earlier pooling had covered bladder and kidney cancers only thinly. The team searched three databases through March 2026 and found six studies with 1,603 patients in all. They combined risk figures for overall, cancer-specific, and disease-free survival.

Patients with a high ratio before surgery fared worse on every survival measure. The combined risk of death was more than double that of patients with lower ratios. The pattern held when kidney cancer and bladder cancer were judged apart. Disease-free survival also suffered in the high-ratio group. The authors argue this ratio offers a cheap warning sign for planning follow-up after surgery.
pmc-13510279:
Yuyang Wei, Weijie Fei, Jiarong Wang, and Luzheng Bi present Mechanics-AI, an open-source system that pairs physics simulation with machine learning for engineering design, in 2026 work. Direct simulation gives clear physical answers yet runs slowly and ignores real-world context, while machine learning runs fast yet needs much data and hides its reasoning. The design copies living bodies, where sensors read physical signals and the brain places them in context.

A first learning layer stands in for costly simulations, producing readable measures such as stress, strain, and heat or moisture fields. A second layer blends those measures with outside data to predict outcomes and suggest designs. The system tests eight methods, keeps the best for each task, and shows which physical factors drove each answer. Trials spanned brain injury prediction, a tissue-growth device, and low-carbon building design with recycled concrete.
pmc-13512979:
D'Amato and colleagues tested two things in hospitalized heart failure patients. First, whether a staging system called HLM, which grades heart, lung, and multiorgan involvement, predicts outcomes. Second, whether starting an SGLT2 inhibitor drug during the hospital stay helps at every stage. Their 2026 prospective multicenter study enrolled 711 consecutive patients admitted between late 2022 and mid 2025 and followed them for six months.

D'Amato found the combined endpoint of cardiovascular death or heart failure readmission in 82 patients, rising clearly with each HLM stage. Each stage step carried roughly forty percent higher risk regardless of drug status. Starting the SGLT2 inhibitor during the index admission was independently linked to about forty percent lower endpoint risk. The drug class also protects kidneys and metabolism, and benefit showed no weakening in advanced stages. The authors support combining whole-body staging with early drug initiation in routine heart failure care.
pmc-13515479:
Md Imran Hossain, Sitansu Sekhar Nanda, and Dong Kee Yi review, in a 2026 article, surface-engineered magnetic nanoparticles for rebuilding skeletal muscle. Lost or damaged muscle needs scaffolds that copy its aligned fibres, softness, and high energy use, and ordinary cell culture falls short. Tiny magnetic particles, tuned by their coatings, answer outside magnets without contact, which opens several tricks at once.

The review covers coating choices, both organic and inorganic, and the weaving of particles into scaffolds that respond to magnets. Aligned fields can line muscle cells up, guide stem cells and drugs to a target, and stiffen or move a construct on cue. Magnetic resonance imaging can then watch the implant without cutting. Hossain's team weighs the safety record and the body's handling of the particles. Regulation and long-term fate remain the gates between this platform and patients.
pmc-13516679:
Biondi and colleagues profiled oxidative stress and inflammation in horses naturally infected with Theileria equi, a tick-borne parasite that lives inside red blood cells and causes equine piroplasmosis. Their 2026 study enrolled thirty-five infected horses and twenty healthy controls, confirming infection by antibody testing and gene amplification. Measuring inflammatory signals plus markers of cell damage and antioxidant reserves in blood.

Biondi found infected horses had lower platelet counts and higher liver enzyme activity than controls. Two inflammatory messengers were clearly raised, showing persistent immune activation, while a damage marker from fat oxidation rose and the key antioxidant glutathione fell, consistent with worn-down defenses. The damage marker tracked with clinical severity scores and lower red cell counts, and antioxidant levels fell as white cell counts rose. The authors conclude chronic infection couples oxidative stress with sustained inflammation, and combined markers could help monitor disease and treatment.
pmc-13518479:
Xuan Xuan Song and four colleagues open the mail of a parasitic tapeworm larva in a 2026 study. Spirometra mansoni larvae burrow through human tissue, causing blindness or paralysis, and biopsy diagnosis is hard. Like many parasites, the larvae shed extracellular vesicles, tiny membrane parcels. The team cultured larvae, harvested the vesicles, and profiled their proteins and small RNAs.

The parcels measured eighty to one hundred fifty nanometres and carried the classic vesicle markers. Their protein cargo ran to twenty-seven hundred entries, rich in transport, secretion, and signalling roles. The RNA haul held thirty-seven known and one hundred eighteen new microRNAs, with targets touching cell death, cholesterol handling, and host interplay. Rabbit serum against the vesicles stirred a mixed but mainly Th1-style immune answer. Song's team offers the catalogue as a base for diagnostics and for decoding how the larva talks to its host.
pmc-13518879:
Chengming Ma and six colleagues build a mechanics-based method in 2026 for choosing how fast to flow back fracturing fluid from coalbed methane wells. Crews today pick rates by experience, which transfers poorly between wells. Flowing too fast drags out proppant sand and coal fines, damaging the fractures that carry gas.

Their model balances forces on particles before and after fracture closure, using measurable inputs such as particle size, fluid thickness, and pressure difference. Calculations for two wells gave critical proppant velocities spanning wide ranges depending on closure stage. Particle size, density, and pressure difference dominated the results. Ma and co-authors offer the workflow as a screening tool, openly noting no new lab validation.
pmc-13518979:
Barbara Szymanik, Sam Ang Keo, Franck Brachelet, and Didier Defer refine in 2026 a harmless way to find steel rebar hidden inside concrete. Crews must locate rebar and judge its state without harming buildings. Their method heats the concrete with microwaves and watches the surface with an infrared camera, since steel warms at another rate than concrete.

The study pairs fine computer models of a microwave source, broadband antenna, and steel-laced concrete block with matching bench tests. How the source fired and how the antenna sat against the sample both shaped the heat patterns on the surface. Matching mock and real heat maps, the team works toward settings that make rebar spotting precise and repeatable.
pmc-13520379:
Sylvester R Groen and colleagues compare in 2026 three questionnaires for adults living with faecal incontinence, asking whether a broader well-being measure adds anything beyond symptom and quality-of-life scales. Patients often value independence and stability, not only fewer accidents.

Data came from 72 trial participants, mostly women, with an average age near 67 years. The capability measure scored higher on its scale than the generic health measure and showed good agreement with related scores. Each tool separated known groups somewhat differently, with no single winner across all checks. Clinicians gain guidance on matching questionnaire choice to the question asked.
pmc-13522479:
Nawab John Dar, David Soriano-Castell, and Pamela Maher describe a long-lasting stress state in nerve cells exposed to excess iron in a 2026 laboratory study. Iron builds up in brain areas harmed by Alzheimer and Parkinson diseases, yet the effect of prolonged exposure was unclear. Cultured neuronal cells received either a brief exposure of hours or a chronic exposure lasting nine days.

Brief exposure caused little change and did not make cells more fragile. Chronic exposure raised iron-storage protein, damaged fat molecules, depleted a key protective chemical, and lowered a protective enzyme, while cells stayed alive. Those chronically stressed cells then died more easily when faced with further oxidative challenges. The authors name the state chronoferroptosis and present it as an early vulnerability stage.
pmc-13522879:
Juan Pablo Frias wrote a practical guide for doctors on spotting and treating hypercortisolism, a state of excess cortisol, the body's stress hormone. The guide aims at hard cases hiding inside stubborn type 2 diabetes, resistant high blood pressure, and adrenal growths.

A simple overnight drug test, where a steroid pill should switch cortisol off, forms the guide's main case-finding tool. Confirmed excess appears in under 4 percent of broad diabetes groups, but about one in four patients in selected high-risk groups fail the test. Mild cortisol excess without classic Cushing signs still raises blood pressure, diabetes, belly fat, and death risk. Surgery cures best when the source can be cut out, and Frias details drug options when it cannot.
pmc-13523279:
Chen Xu and colleagues describe a modified technique for placing an iliac branch device through the same-side leg artery in a 2026 two-center study. Branch devices preserve blood flow to the internal iliac artery during aneurysm repair, yet standard access routes can fail in patients with short or difficult anatomy. Twenty-three patients treated between 2023 and 2024, in whom the opposite leg route was judged unsuitable, received the balloon-anchored approach.

Deployment succeeded in every case, with the branch artery open and no major leaks on early imaging. At one year, the main device was open in all patients and the bridging stent in nearly all. No related reoperations were needed over a median sixteen months. Two minor complications occurred, supporting the technique as feasible for selected difficult anatomies.
pmc-13523379:
Jolanta Guz and colleagues follow chemical changes in DNA during chemotherapy for breast cancer in a 2026 study. Seventy-one patients received standard drug treatment before surgery, with blood and urine collected at four points and tumor tissue taken at operation. Levels of methylcytosine and its oxidized derivatives were measured by advanced chromatography, and activity of the genes that drive this demethylation pathway was assessed.

During treatment, several derivative levels in white blood cell DNA rose, while expression of the pathway genes fell. Patients whose pre-treatment levels of one derivative were lower in blood and urine, and whose tumors showed a particular post-treatment pattern, fared better over six years of follow-up. The authors link the pathway's behavior during therapy to disease-free and overall survival, suggesting prognostic value.
pmc-13523479:
Daryna Maruniak and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study, risk factors for massive bleeding after heart transplantation. The operation remains the standard for end-stage heart failure, yet heavy bleeding afterward raises illness and transfusion needs. Predictors, especially from bedside clot testing, were poorly described.

The single-center study included 75 adults transplanted between 2019 and 2025 who had preoperative ClotPro viscoelastic testing. Massive bleeding, defined by a standard bleeding scale, occurred in 31 patients, about four in ten. Transfusion use was high, and about one in six patients needed reoperation for bleeding. Many factors linked with bleeding in simple analyses, but only a clot firmness measure from the EX test stayed independent in adjusted analysis. The authors propose it for early risk flagging.
pmc-13524079:
Basu and colleagues showed in 2026 that two plant regulators best known for nitrate sensing also hold back sulfate uptake, linking two nutrient pathways in thale cress. Nitrogen and sulfur work together in crops, but the wiring between their control systems was largely unknown. The regulators, transcription factors TGA1 and TGA4, sit in the nitrate response cascade and also play roles in immunity.

Adding nitrate quickly raised sulfate uptake and use, then a delayed brake cut activity of the main sulfate transporter, and that brake required TGA1 and TGA4. Both factors bind the transporter's control region and dampen it directly. Plants missing both factors took up more sulfate, built more of the amino acid cysteine, and fared better under long sulfur shortage, while sulfur defense compounds also shifted. The authors say the pair keeps nutrient intake in balance and may help breed crops that use fertilizer better.
pmc-13526479:
Fernandez Placencia and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of eosinophilic cellulitis, or Wells syndrome, a rare skin inflammation that mimics bacterial infection. Their patient, a 72-year-old woman with lupus and other autoimmune conditions, first received antibiotics for red, swollen legs and seemed to improve. Three days after finishing the course she returned with itchy red plaques across arms and legs, swelling, and pain, and antihistamines did not help.

Blood tests showed a raised count of eosinophils, a white cell type tied to allergy and inflammation, and a high sedimentation rate, a general inflammation marker. A skin punch biopsy found eosinophil-rich inflammation around and between vessels, matching Wells syndrome, and steroid treatment brought improvement. The authors stress that recurrent cellulitis-like eruptions that answer antibiotics only briefly deserve an early biopsy, since clinic and lab correlation is what separates this mimic from true infection.
pmc-13526879:
Mumtaz Y Balkhi and colleagues showed that the SchistoShield vaccine triggers lasting immune memory in people on two continents. Published in 2026, the study examined blood cells from United States and African trial volunteers who had received the Sm-p80 plus GLA-SE vaccine. It targets schistosomiasis, a worm disease infecting about 250 million people. Recall tests re-exposed immune cells to the vaccine antigen in the lab.

Vaccinated volunteers produced strong effector and memory T-cell responses, releasing a broad mix of signaling proteins and killer molecules. Antibody-secreting cells specific to the antigen also appeared in volunteers followed over time. The authors read these hallmarks as signs of a potentially effective vaccine, building on earlier safety trials in the United States, Madagascar, and Burkina Faso. Readers get immunological backing for a vaccine aimed at a major neglected disease.
pmc-13527479:
Liyang Duan and Xianjie Wu describe, in a 2026 case report, treating a child's severe contact dermatitis from lacquer tree exposure with abrocitinib, a targeted immune drug. Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell reaction, and standard care relies on avoidance, topical steroids, calamine, and antihistamines, which can fall short in children with widespread disease.

An eight-year-old boy developed intensely itchy red papules and plaques over trunk and limbs for ten days after exposure to Toxicodendron vernicifluum. Three days of topical steroid, emollients, and an antihistamine failed as the rash spread to his face, with a severity score in the severe range. His parents declined systemic steroids over growth concerns, so after counseling the team started daily oral abrocitinib plus nightly cetirizine. Photographs chart facial clearing by day three and near resolution by day eleven.
pmc-13527979:
Emma J. Steel and seven colleagues report a 2026 qualitative evaluation of software that flags chest X-rays for priority reading in a Scottish NHS board. The qXR program from Qure.ai aims to speed lung cancer detection. Staff and patients were asked how acceptable they found it. Sixteen staff took part in interviews before and after rollout. Eight service users joined focus groups.

Staff saw the tool as a helpful adjunct that could shorten the path to scans and treatment. Patients also welcomed faster answers. They preferred brief anxiety with prompt action over long uncertainty. Radiology staff worried about accuracy, over-trust, and biased decisions. The authors say adoption will hold only if the tool fits existing systems and keeps proving itself.
pmc-13528079:
Nicholas C. Nicolaides, James Bradford Kline, and Luigi Grasso develop a blocker drug against a cancer shield protein in a 2026 study. Many tumors release CA125, a protein that coats treatment antibodies. Coated antibodies cannot trigger immune killing well. The team engineered fusion proteins to grab CA125 tightly. Their lead design, NAV-005, bound it with high strength.

In cell tests NAV-005 kept CA125 off treatment antibodies. Immune cells then killed targets at full strength again. A second killing route, driven by complement proteins, also recovered. Antibody-drug conjugates slipped past the shield too. They entered cancer cells and killed as intended. The authors say such blockers could rescue many existing antibody drugs. Clinical testing is the next step they propose.
pmc-13531079:
Jeffrey Yim and colleagues report in 2026 the catheter retrieval of a leg vein stent that migrated into the heart and straddled a valve. The 38-year-old patient felt palpitations and breathlessness one day after vein treatment. Imaging showed the stent crossing the tricuspid valve, causing severe leakage and brief dangerous rhythm bursts.

Two snares, one from each leg vein, gripped both stent ends under ultrasound guidance from within the food pipe, with surgeons standing by. Removal left only mild leakage and no fluid around the heart. The patient recovered smoothly, avoiding open surgery.
pmc-13532579:
Junlei Zhang and colleagues built a single-atom cobalt catalyst that cleans polluted water with unusual selectivity. Published in 2026, the study made a cobalt-on-carbon-nitride catalyst whose metal sites shift on activation by peroxymonosulfate, a common oxidant, from Co-N2O1 toward Co-N1O2. How metal coordination and spin states steer oxidation remains poorly mapped in such water-treatment systems.

The shifted site favored singlet oxygen while still producing sulfate radicals in parallel, speeding oxytetracycline breakdown more than fivefold over the bare support and beating over thirty rival catalysts. Activity held across diverse antibiotics and dyes, in complex water matrices, and under continuous flow. The authors link reaction-induced site change to spin-aware oxygen transfer, offering design rules for selective, durable treatment catalysts. Readers get a mechanism-led advance for water cleanup.
pmc-13534179:
Lei Luo and colleagues review in 2026 a long non-coding RNA called HIF1A-AS2 and its role across many human cancers. The RNA does not build proteins, yet raised levels appear in many tumour types and link to poor outlook. Lab studies tie it to cell growth, spread, drug resistance, and cell death control.

The RNA can sponge up smaller RNAs or bind proteins directly, lifting cancer traits through several paths. The review compares patterns across 12 cancer types and weighs barriers to clinical use. Readers see why this RNA draws interest as a diagnostic mark and drug target.
pmc-13534679:
Zhi-Ming Zeng and colleagues mapped how tau pathology spreads across Alzheimer stages in ordered layers. Published in 2026, the study integrated amyloid and tau PET scans, diffusion and resting-state MRI, and gene-expression maps across disease stages. Tau defines Alzheimer disease yet spreads unevenly, and the roles of amyloid, brain wiring, and intrinsic weakness were unclear.

Tau followed a hierarchical gradient that stratified by amyloid load and clinical stage. Amyloid patterns plus structural and functional links predicted tau patterns and explained much spatial variation. A leftover tau pattern tracked gene programs for signaling, synapses, energy, and RNA control, shifting by stage. Tau geometry also mediated links between network organization and symptoms. Readers get a joint marker tying amyloid, wiring, and weakness to decline.
pmc-13536579:
Yunho Jeong and colleagues describe in 2026 a rare skin B-cell lymphoma in a 12-year-old spayed female Shih Tzu dog. Skin B-cell lymphoma is extremely rare in dogs, so single cases still shape what vets know. The dog showed many nodules under the skin across the body.

Stains and flow tests confirmed B-cell type with clonal gene changes, while liver and spleen sampling found no spread. Standard four-drug chemotherapy brought only a brief partial response before fast progression. The case warns that this rare form can behave aggressively and resist usual treatment.
pmc-13536679:
Megha Anand leads a 2026 randomized trial comparing two hands-on approaches for tight hamstrings in desk-based computer workers. Thirty information technology professionals were split evenly between static stretching and myofascial release, a pressure-based soft tissue technique. Each group trained five times a week for three weeks. Knee extension range and a self-rated leg function scale were measured at the start and on three later days.

Both groups gained range and function over the three weeks, with no harmful events reported. Stretching produced slightly larger gains in knee extension by the second and third checks. The authors note those gaps were smaller than the smallest change the knee test can reliably detect, so the practical edge remains unclear. Function gains were also close between groups, and the short follow-up without a control group limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13538379:
Rajesh Kannan Megalingam and Naveen Prasaad Selvarajan present a hybrid network for predicting pedestrian crossing intent on Indian roads in a 2026 study. Crowded, unstructured streets with frequent blocking views and rule-bending walkers challenge models trained abroad. The design mixes image and graph networks with a gate that shifts weight between visual and motion clues by scene, plus a pose tool tuned for distant or partly hidden walkers. A new local road collection supports testing.

Accuracy reached moderate levels on both a standard foreign collection and the new Indian collection, with the fastest response times among compared methods.
